docs.title: Volume 9: Saṅgīta–Nāṭya
docs.text:
Music, Theatre and Dance · Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā

The Nāṭyaśāstra and its heirs: rāga and tāla, Hindustani and Karnatak music, classical and folk dance, and the theatres of India

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 9 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Saṅgīta–Nāṭya: Music, Theatre and Dance. Its subject is the performing arts of the Indian subcontinent — what the Sanskrit tradition called saṅgīta (song, instrumental music and dance taken together) and nāṭya (drama) — from the earliest theoretical text, the Nāṭyaśāstra, to the concert hall, the village square, the film studio and the diaspora stage of today.

The first three chapters introduce the field, the Nāṭyaśāstra and the theory of rasa and acting as it applies to performance. Chapters 4 to 11 deal with music: the theory of svara and rāga, the theory of tāla, the history of the treatises on music from the Dattilam to Bhatkhande, the Hindustani and Karnatak traditions (including the Persianate and Sufi music of north India), devotional music across regions and religions, the instruments, and the modern song of the regional languages, from Rabīndrasaṅgīt and Nazrulgīti to the Marathi stage song and the Assamese and Kannada lyric. Chapters 12 to 18 deal with dance: the later dance treatises, the grammar of pure and expressive dance, the language of gesture, and the forms now called “classical” — Bharatanāṭyam, Kathak, Odissi, Kuchipudi, Kathakaḷi, Mohiniyāṭṭam, Manipuri and Sattriya. The last five chapters turn to theatre (Sanskrit drama in performance, Kūṭiyāṭṭam and modern theatre; the regional popular theatres), to folk and tribal performance, to the music and dance of the North-East and the Himalaya, and to the institutions, media and debates of the modern period.

The book quotes primary texts only where the wording and the reference can be given with confidence, and it does not present claims that ancient texts anticipated modern science, or that particular rāgas, gestures or dances cure disease, as established facts. Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such; chapter numbers of the Nāṭyaśāstra follow Manomohan Ghosh’s edition and translation. Where the history of an art is contested — the fate of the devadāsīs and courtesans whose arts were “revived” in the twentieth century, the role of caste and hereditary communities, the origin myths of instruments and forms — the book tries to state the evidence and the main scholarly positions plainly. Rasa theory, which belongs equally to poetics, is treated more fully in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

The performing arts are learnt from teachers, not from books, and no description can substitute for listening and watching. The select bibliography is a guide to the standard studies, editions and translations, and the glossary explains the principal technical terms. Every quotation should, before scholarly use, be checked against a critical edition; the standard editions of the main treatises — the Baroda text of the Nāṭyaśāstra with Abhinavagupta’s commentary and Ghosh’s edition and translation, the Adyar text of the Saṅgītaratnākara and its translation by Shringy and Sharma, the editions of the Dattilam, the Bṛhaddeśī, the Abhinayadarpaṇa and the Nṛttaratnāvalī — are listed in the bibliography and named where they are first discussed.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Saṅgīta and Nāṭya
docs.text:
This volume is about the performing arts of the Indian subcontinent: music, dance and theatre as they were theorised in Sanskrit, Tamil, Persian and the regional languages, and as they have been practised in temples, courts, shrines, villages, salons, concert halls and film studios over more than two thousand years. It covers the classical traditions that have their own treatises and specialised teachers — Hindustani and Karnatak music, the dance forms now called “classical”, Sanskrit drama and Kūṭiyāṭṭam (the Kerala temple theatre that is the only living tradition of Sanskrit performance, though a regional art of the second millennium rather than a survival of Kālidāsa’s stage) — but also the devotional music of the Sufi shrine and the Sikh gurdwārā, the regional dance-dramas, and the folk and tribal performances that have always existed beside them and fed into them.

Two older words cover most of this ground. Saṅgīta is the medieval Sanskrit name for the combined art of song, instrumental music and dance. Nāṭya is the ancient name for drama, understood as a total art in which speech, song, instrumental music, gesture, dance, costume and make-up work together to produce an aesthetic experience in the spectator. What follows explains these terms, the kinds of evidence from which the history of the arts is reconstructed and the outline of that history, and then three themes that run through the whole volume: the people who made the arts and the communities to which they belonged; the ways in which knowledge of performance has been transmitted; and the relationship between performance and the sacred.

docs.title: 1.1.1 Saṅgīta
docs.text:
In modern Indian languages saṅgīt or saṅgītam simply means “music”. In the medieval treatises the word had a wider sense. Śārṅgadeva’s Saṅgītaratnākara (“Ocean of Saṅgīta”), composed in the first half of the thirteenth century at the Yādava court of Devagiri, opens its account of the subject with a definition that later writers repeated many times:

Saṅgītaratnākara 1.1.21

gītaṃ vādyaṃ tathā nṛttaṃ trayaṃ saṅgītam ucyate

“Song, instrumental music and dance — these three together are called saṅgīta.”

The Saṅgītaratnākara accordingly devotes its first five books to sound, scales, rāgas, ornaments, compositions and rhythm, its sixth to instruments and its seventh to dance (Shringy and Sharma 1978). Song is placed first and treated as primary: instruments follow song, and dance follows instrumental music. Śārṅgadeva also divides saṅgīta into two kinds, mārga (“the path”), the ancient, rule-bound art said to have been discovered by Brahmā and practised by Bharata and others before Śiva, and deśī (“regional”), the music and dance that please people in different regions and change with time. In practice the mārga music described in the old texts had largely gone out of use by Śārṅgadeva’s time, and nearly everything the later treatises describe is deśī (Rowell 1992; Widdess 1995). The distinction between a learned, codified art and a popular or regional one, and the constant movement of material from the second into the first, is one of the oldest ideas in Indian thinking about performance (Section 1.7).

docs.title: 1.1.2 Nāṭya
docs.text: The older and larger frame is nāṭya. The Nāṭyaśāstra (“Treatise on Nāṭya”), ascribed to the sage Bharata and compiled between about 200 BCE and 200 CE, is the earliest surviving text on the performing arts in India. It treats drama as the master art, and it discusses music and dance chiefly as components of a theatrical performance: the playhouse and its consecration, the preliminary rituals, the movements of the body, the hands and the eyes, the representation of emotion, the types of play and plot, costume and make-up, the scales and modes of music, the instruments, the songs (dhruvā) sung during the action, and the distribution of roles among actors. Its origin myth, in which the god Brahmā creates drama as a “fifth Veda” open to all classes of society, makes the claim that nāṭya contains all knowledge, all arts and all crafts (Ghosh 1950; Vatsyayan 1996). The text, its structure, its history and its theory of the body are the subject of Chapter 2; its theory of emotion and of the spectator’s experience, rasa, is treated from the performer’s point of view in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 1.1.3 Nṛtta, nṛtya and nāṭya
docs.text: Later writers distinguished three ways in which the body can perform. Nṛtta is “pure” dance, movement that follows rhythm and creates beauty of line and pattern but does not represent anything; nṛtya is expressive dance, in which gesture, facial expression and movement interpret the words and emotions of a song; and nāṭya is drama, the representation of a story by actors. The Nāṭyaśāstra itself knows nṛtta but not yet this threefold scheme, which is found in Dhanañjaya’s Daśarūpaka (late tenth century) and in the Abhinayadarpaṇa attributed to Nandikeśvara, and which has become the basic vocabulary of modern dance teaching. Every classical dance form combines the three in different proportions: a Bharatanāṭyam recital alternates passages of nṛtta with passages of nṛtya, while Kathakaḷi and Kūṭiyāṭṭam are primarily nāṭya. Chapter 13 discusses the distinction in detail (Bose 1991).

docs.title: 1.1.4 Lakṣaṇa and lakṣya
docs.text: A final pair of terms describes the relation between the texts and the arts. Lakṣaṇa is the definition or rule given in a treatise; lakṣya is the actual practice that the rule describes. The authors of the treatises were well aware that practice came first and that their rules were descriptions of what good performers did, not the other way round; some of them say explicitly that where practice and text disagree, the treatise must follow practice. The history of Indian music and dance is therefore not the history of the application of a fixed theory but of a long conversation between theorists and practitioners, in which the texts constantly lagged behind, systematised, and sometimes reshaped the living arts (Rowell 1992; Bose 1991). A reader of this volume should keep in mind that a description in a Sanskrit text — of a rāga, a hand gesture or a dance step — does not by itself show how it was performed in the text’s own time, let alone that it is performed the same way today.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Treatises
docs.text:
The history of the performing arts is reconstructed from several kinds of evidence, each with its own limitations. The most explicit are the treatises (śāstra) on music, dance and drama, a large literature in Sanskrit and, from the fourteenth century, also in Persian and in the regional languages. Table 1.1 lists the most important works discussed in this volume. Their dates are often uncertain, and many survive only in late manuscripts or in incomplete form.

The 72-mela scheme Rāg Darpan (Persian) Faqīrullāh 1666 Music at the Mughal court Hindustānī Saṅgīt Paddhati V. N. Bhatkhande 1910–1932 The ten-thāṭ system

The texts were written by learned men, usually Brahmins or courtiers, for patrons and connoisseurs. They tell us how the arts were classified and what educated people thought about them, but they rarely describe the social life of performers, and they are often conservative, repeating the categories of earlier texts long after practice had changed. Chapter 4 traces how the rāga concept emerged from Mataṅga to Śārṅgadeva and beyond, and Chapter 6 follows the literature of music theory as a whole from the Dattilam to Bhatkhande; Chapter 12 discusses the later dance treatises, including the regional texts on which the modern dance forms have drawn.

From the late fourteenth century music in north India was also written about in Persian, in a literature long ignored by historians who looked for the history of Indian music only in Sanskrit; its study has transformed the understanding of the period between Śārṅgadeva and the nineteenth century (Section 7.2) (Schofield 2010; Bor et al. 2010).

docs.title: 1.2.2 Literature, inscriptions and images
docs.text: Poetry, drama and narrative literature describe performances and performers vividly, though not always realistically. The Sanskrit plays of Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century) include scenes of dance and music lessons; the Tamil epic Cilappatikāram, usually dated to the middle centuries of the first millennium, describes the training and debut of the courtesan-dancer Mātavi in such detail that it has become a key source for early Tamil music and dance (Parthasarathy 1993). Inscriptions record gifts to temples for musicians and dancers, the names and duties of temple women, and the patronage of kings. Sculpture and painting provide images of instruments, dancers and ensembles over two thousand years, from the reliefs of Bharhut and Sanchi to the temple sculptures of the Cōḻa period and the rāgamālā paintings of the Rajput and Deccani courts (Chapter 4) (Vatsyayan 1968; Ebeling 1973). Images and literary descriptions must be read with care: sculptors and painters followed their own conventions, and a carved figure in a dance-like pose does not tell us how a dance moved in time.

docs.title: 1.2.3 Living practice and its limits
docs.text: The most important evidence for the arts of the last two or three centuries is living practice itself: the repertoires, techniques and oral knowledge of hereditary and institutional lineages, documented by ethnographers, historians and practitioners. Here the risk runs the other way. Performers often describe their art as ancient and unchanged, but most living traditions have been reshaped many times, and some of the most important changes took place in the twentieth century. Much of the historical writing reviewed in this volume — on Bharatanāṭyam, Kathak, Odissi, Hindustani music and the Karnatak concert — shows how claims of antiquity were made, for good and bad reasons, during the nationalist reconstruction of the arts (Bakhle 2005; Weidman 2006; Soneji 2012; Walker 2014). The reader will meet these debates repeatedly. Recognising that a form took its present shape in the 1930s does not make it less valuable or less Indian; it makes its history more interesting.

docs.title: 1.3.1 Before the texts
docs.text: The earliest evidence for performance in the subcontinent is visual. Rock paintings at Bhimbetka and other sites in central India, of widely varying and often uncertain date, show groups of figures in what appear to be dances. From the Indus (Harappan) civilisation of the third millennium BCE come a small bronze female figure from Mohenjo-daro, popularly called the “dancing girl”, and a few other figurines and seal images; whether the bronze represents a dancer is not known, and no Harappan text can be read. Claims that the classical dance forms descend directly from these objects are speculation.

docs.title: 1.3.2 The Vedic period
docs.text: The Vedic hymns (the Ṛgveda is usually dated c. 1500–1200 BCE, the later Vedic texts c. 1200–500 BCE) were recited with pitch accents that are still preserved in traditional recitation, and the melodies (sāman) of the Sāmaveda, sung by a special class of priests at the soma sacrifice, are the earliest Indian music of which something is known in detail (Rowell 1992; Howard 1977). The Vedic texts also mention harps or lutes (vīṇā, vāṇa), drums, flutes and cymbals, and describe rites at which women danced and played. The Nāṭyaśāstra and the Dattilam connect the sacred music of the theatre’s preliminaries (gāndharva) with the Sāmaveda, but the link between Vedic chant and the later art music is indirect and its details are not documented; the accents, the chant and the question of continuity are discussed in Chapter 4 (Rowell 1992; Nijenhuis 1970).

docs.title: 1.3.3 The early historic period
docs.text:
Buddhist and Jaina texts of the last centuries BCE mention professional musicians, dancers, actors and story-tellers, and the stone reliefs of the Buddhist monuments of Bharhut and Sanchi (2nd–1st century BCE) show celestial women dancing to the music of harps, flutes and drums. The Hāthīgumphā inscription of King Khāravela of Kaliṅga (1st century BCE) records that he entertained his capital with dance, song and instrumental music. Gold coins of the Gupta king Samudragupta (r. c. 335–375) show the king seated, playing a harp-like vīṇā. It is to this world of royal courts, cities and wealthy patrons that the Nāṭyaśāstra belongs, and to its later centuries that the great Sanskrit dramatists belong: Bhāsa (before Kālidāsa; the thirteen “Trivandrum plays” attributed to him are of debated authorship), Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century), Śūdraka (Mṛcchakaṭika, c. 3rd–5th century) and later Viśākhadatta, Harṣa (r. 606–647) and Bhavabhūti (early 8th century). Their plays and the theatre that performed them are the subject of Chapter 19 (Keith 1924; Richmond et al. 1990).

The Buddhist and Jaina canons add evidence of another kind, the more valuable because it comes from outside the courtly theory. The precepts taken by Buddhist novices, and by lay people on fast days, include abstention from watching dancing, singing, instrumental music and shows, a rule that presupposes how common such entertainments were. The Jātaka stories of the Buddha’s former lives are full of court musicians, dancers and festival performances. In the Guttila Jātaka the Bodhisatta is Guttila, the master vīṇā player of Banaras, whose ungrateful pupil Musila challenges him to a public contest before the king; at the contest Guttila breaks the strings of his vīṇā one by one and goes on playing on the bare instrument, while Musila’s vīṇā, its strings broken in the same way, falls silent (Cowell 1895–1907). The Jātakas cannot be dated closely — the prose in which most of them are preserved belongs to a commentary of the middle of the first millennium CE, although many of the stories are older — but they show the vīṇā as the instrument of the professional master, music as a competitive art judged by royal patrons, and the teacher–pupil bond as both a bond of obligation and a source of rivalry. Jaina canonical texts include dance, song and instrumental music among the arts (kalā) a cultivated person was expected to learn, and describe gods honouring the Jinas with spectacles of music and dance. Such sources tell us what the arts meant to monks, merchants and lay devotees, an audience that the Sanskrit treatises rarely consider.

In the Tamil south, the anthologies of Caṅkam poetry (early centuries CE) describe bards (pāṇar) who played the yāḻ, a harp, and women dancers (viṟali) who travelled from patron to patron, and distinguish melodic modes called paṇ associated with the landscapes of Tamil poetry. The Cilappatikāram gives the first extended Tamil description of a dancer’s training, of a stage and of an accompanying ensemble, and its medieval commentary by Aṭiyārkkunallār is a major source for early Tamil music (Parthasarathy 1993). Tamil literature thus provides a second ancient theoretical and literary tradition beside the Sanskrit one; the two interacted but neither can be reduced to the other.

docs.title: 1.3.4 Temples, courts and devotion (c. 600–1500)
docs.text:
In the second half of the first millennium the great temples became major centres of performance. Temple inscriptions in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra and Odisha record the endowment of musicians, drummers and dancing women; the Cōḻa temples of the tenth to thirteenth centuries carry sculptural sequences of the 108 karaṇas described in the Nāṭyaśāstra, most completely on the gateway towers of the Naṭarāja temple at Chidambaram, where the figures are accompanied by the relevant verses of the text (Vatsyayan 1968; Gaston 1982). In Kerala, Sanskrit drama was performed in temple theatres by hereditary actors in the form now called Kūṭiyāṭṭam, the only surviving tradition of Sanskrit theatre (Chapter 19).

Devotion (bhakti) shaped the music of this period profoundly. The Tamil Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava poet-saints, the Nāyaṉmārs and Āḻvārs (c. 6th–9th centuries), composed hymns to be sung in temples; the Śaiva hymns, collected as the Tēvāram, are still sung by temple singers (ōtuvār) in melodic modes descended from the old paṇs (Peterson 1989). In the twelfth century Jayadeva composed the Gītagovinda, a Sanskrit song-cycle on the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa that became the most widely performed devotional text of medieval India, sung and danced in Odisha, Kerala, Manipur and elsewhere. Later bhakti poets — Annamācārya (1408–1503) and Purandaradāsa (1484–1564) in the south, the Vārkarī poets of Maharashtra, Kabīr, Sūrdās and Mīrābāī in the north, Caitanya and his followers in Bengal, Śaṅkaradeva in Assam — composed songs that are the basis of much later devotional and art music, and in several regions devotional movements created their own forms of theatre and dance, such as the Vaiṣṇava dance-dramas of Assam and Manipur (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 1.3.5 Persianate courts and Sufi shrines (c. 1200–1800)
docs.text:
From the thirteenth century the courts of the Delhi Sultanate and later the regional sultanates brought Persian poetry and music, and Persian and Central Asian musicians, into contact with Indian music. The Sufi orders, especially the Chishtīs, made music a central part of their devotional assemblies (samāʿ), and the poet Amīr Khusrau (1253–1325), a disciple of the Chishtī saint Niẓāmuddīn Awliyāʾ, became the emblem of this synthesis. Later tradition credited Khusrau with inventing qawwālī, several rāgas and genres, and even the sitār and the tablā; the last two claims are certainly false, and the others are traditions rather than documented facts (Chapter 7) (Sharma 2005; Qureshi 1986).

Under the Mughals (1526–1857), and at the courts of the Rajputs, the Deccan sultanates and later the successor states such as Awadh, north Indian music developed the genres, instruments and institutions of what is now called Hindustani music: dhrupad, which flourished at the court of Mān Siṃh Tomar of Gwalior (r. 1486–1516) and at the court of Akbar, where Tānsen (d. 1589) sang; khayāl, which became the leading vocal genre in the eighteenth century; the hereditary lineages of court musicians; and new instruments such as the sitār and later the sarod and tablā. Music was performed in courts and in the households of nobles, in the salons of courtesans, at Sufi shrines and in Hindu temples, often by the same musicians. Katherine Schofield has shown that the Mughal elite themselves regarded this music as a learned, “classical” art with its own canon, long before the nationalist reformers of the twentieth century used the word (Schofield 2010; Bor et al. 2010). In the south, the Vijayanagara empire (1336–1565) and the Nāyaka and Maratha courts of Thanjavur, Madurai and Mysore patronised the music and dance from which the Karnatak tradition and Bharatanāṭyam developed (Chapters 8 and 15). The gradual divergence of north and south Indian art music into two distinct systems, visible in the treatises from the sixteenth century, is discussed in Chapter 4.

In the Punjab, the Sikh Gurus made sung devotion the centre of worship. Guru Nānak (1469–1539) is remembered as travelling with the Muslim rabāb player Bhāī Mardānā, and the scripture compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604 and later given its final form as the Guru Granth Sahib arranges its hymns by rāga. Sikh kīrtan, sung by rabābī and rāgī musicians, is one of the major living traditions of rāga-based devotional music (Chapter 7) (Singh 2000; Mann 2001).

docs.title: 1.3.6 The colonial period and the twentieth century
docs.text:
The decline of the Mughal court and the fall of the princely courts of Awadh and elsewhere in the nineteenth century dispersed many musicians and dancers to smaller courts, to the cities and to the salons of courtesans, while the British administration, missionaries and Indian social reformers came to regard the professional female performers of north and south India as immoral. The “anti-nautch” campaigns that began in the 1890s, and later legislation against the dedication of girls to temples, removed much of the traditional patronage of women performers (Section 1.4).

At the same time, Indian nationalists set out to recover and reform the arts as symbols of national culture. Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande (1860–1936) collected compositions from hereditary musicians, classified rāgas into ten thāṭs and published notated textbooks; Vishnu Digambar Paluskar (1872–1931) founded music schools from 1901 and set music in a devotional and respectable frame; the Madras Music Academy (1928) gave the Karnatak concert its institutional centre; the Kerala Kalamandalam (1930) and Kalakshetra in Madras (1936) became the model institutions for the training of dancers; and new dance forms were reconstructed from older practices and given Sanskritic names, beginning with the renaming of the court and temple dance of Tamil Nadu as Bharatanāṭyam in the 1930s (Bakhle 2005; Weidman 2006; Meduri 2005). After independence the Sangeet Natak Akademi (1952–53), All India Radio, the universities and later the Indian Council for Cultural Relations created the institutional structure of the “classical” performing arts that still exists. The film industry, recording, radio and television transformed popular music and dance, and the diaspora carried the arts across the world (Chapter 23).

docs.title: 1.4 Performers and Their Communities
docs.text:
Most histories of Indian music and dance until recently were histories of texts, theories and great masters. The people who actually performed — and the social worlds that sustained them — were often invisible, or described in ways that suited later ideologies. The research of the last forty years has changed this picture, and the chapters of this volume try to reflect it.

Before the twentieth century, music and dance in India were for the most part hereditary professions practised by particular communities. In the north these included the kalāwants, the court singers of dhrupad; the ḍhāḍhīs and mirāsīs, Muslim communities of genealogists, singers and accompanists, some of whom became the great khayāl and instrumental lineages; the kathaks, Hindu families of story-tellers and dancers; and the courtesans (ṭawāʾif, bāījī), women singers and dancers who were among the leading performers and patrons of ṭhumrī, ghazal and khayāl in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The professional world was hierarchical: soloists ranked above accompanists, and the players of the sāraṅgī and the tablā, who accompanied courtesans, were held in lower esteem than the singers and instrumentalists who performed alone (Neuman 1980; Perron 2007).

In the south, the court and temple dancers later called devadāsīs and their male relatives — the dance masters (naṭṭuvaṉārs) and the nāgasvaram and tavil players of temple music — formed communities with their own matrilineal inheritance, their own professional knowledge and their own patrons. Women were dedicated to a temple deity, served in its rituals, danced at its festivals and at the courts, and often lived in long-term relationships with patrons outside marriage. Their status was ambiguous: they were auspicious and skilled, sometimes wealthy and literate, but also outside the norms of conjugal respectability, and their position depended on patronage relations that were at once artistic, economic and sexual (Kersenboom-Story 1987; Orr 2000; Soneji 2012). Similar communities of women performers existed in Odisha (the mahārīs of the Jagannātha temple), Andhra and Karnataka, and in different forms in north India.

The reform movements of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries attacked these communities from several sides. Missionaries, colonial officials and Indian reformers — including members of the hereditary communities themselves, such as Muthulakshmi Reddy — campaigned against temple dedication and the “nautch”; the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act of 1947 outlawed dedication in the Madras Presidency. Many families left the profession and sought respectability under new caste names such as Iśai Vēḷāḷar (“cultivators of music”). Meanwhile the dance itself was taken up, renamed and reshaped by middle-class and often Brahmin performers, most famously Rukmini Devi Arundale (1904–1986), who presented it as an ancient, spiritual temple art purified of the hereditary dancers’ associations; others, such as the hereditary dancer T. Balasaraswati (1918–1984), insisted that the art could not be separated from its own tradition (Srinivasan 1985; Meduri 1988; Meduri 2005; Knight 2010). In the north, a parallel process marginalised courtesans and, increasingly, hereditary Muslim musicians, as music was moved into schools, recast in devotional Hindu terms and opened to the respectable middle classes (Bakhle 2005). In the south, the Karnatak concert came to be dominated by Brahmin performers and audiences, while the non-Brahmin hereditary musicians of the temple tradition were pushed to its margins (Subramanian 2006; Krishna 2013).

These histories are painful and still debated. The reforms ended practices that exposed girls and women to exploitation, opened the arts to many people previously excluded from them, and gave them new dignity and institutional support. They also dispossessed the communities that had created and preserved the arts, and erased much of their memory. The chapters on Bharatanāṭyam, Kathak, Odissi and Hindustani and Karnatak music try to tell both sides plainly, without romanticising the past (“the devadāsī was simply a revered consecrated artist”) or adopting the moral judgements of the reformers. A similar honesty is needed about caste in the folk and ritual arts, where many forms are the hereditary work of communities regarded as low or untouchable, and about gender, since women were excluded from many theatrical and ritual forms, from Kathakaḷi to Kūṭiyāṭṭam’s male roles, until the twentieth century (Chapters 18, 19 and 21) (Morcom 2013).

docs.title: 1.5 Transmission: Teachers, Lineages and Institutions
docs.text:
Music and dance in India have been learnt above all from a teacher, by imitation and repetition, over many years. The relationship between teacher (guru, ustād) and pupil (śiṣya, śāgird) was traditionally a personal and often lifelong bond, in which the pupil served the teacher, frequently lived in his household, and received the teacher’s knowledge gradually and at the teacher’s discretion. In the Hindustani tradition, the formal acceptance of a disciple was marked by the tying of a thread (gaṇḍā bandhan). Knowledge was regarded as the property of a family or a lineage, to be passed on in full only to sons, nephews or the most trusted disciples (Neuman 1980).

Lineages of this kind have different names in different traditions. In Hindustani music they are gharānās (“households”), named after a city or court — Gwalior, Agra, Jaipur–Atrauli, Kirana and others for khayāl — and defined by a family core and a distinctive style; Daniel Neuman has shown that the gharānā as a named institution became prominent only in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, as musicians moved from courts to cities and needed to establish their credentials (Neuman 1980). In Karnatak music the lineages of disciples descending from the great composers are called śiṣya paramparās, and in dance the styles associated with particular teachers or families are often called bāṇi (in Bharatanāṭyam) or gharānā (in Kathak). The lineages preserved not only repertoire but also performance practice: ways of ornamenting a note, phrasing a rāga, executing a step or interpreting a line of poetry, which no notation or text records.

Notation existed in India from an early date — in Sāmavedic chant, in inscriptions such as the music inscription of Kudumiyamalai in Tamil Nadu, usually dated to the seventh or eighth century, and in the treatises — but it was used as an aid to memory rather than as a score, and the main vehicle of transmission remained oral. In the twentieth century the founding of music and dance schools, colleges and university departments, the publication of notated textbooks and the arrival of recording created new forms of transmission alongside the old. These changes widened access but also standardised the arts, and the tension between institutional and lineage-based teaching runs through the modern history of every form treated here (Chapter 23).

docs.title: 1.6.1 Nāda
docs.text:
Indian thought about music has long given sound a religious and cosmological significance. The idea that the universe is pervaded by, or emerges from, a primal sound appears in the Vedic praise of speech (vāc), in the grammarian Bhartṛhari’s doctrine of śabdabrahman (the absolute as “word”), and in the yogic and tantric idea of an “unstruck” inner sound (anāhata nāda) heard in meditation (Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā; Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama). The music treatises took up this idea as nāda-brahman, “sound as the absolute”. Śārṅgadeva begins his account of sound by praising nāda as the source of song, of instrumental music and of dance, and describes the production of musical sound in the body in terms drawn from the physiology of his time (Shringy and Sharma 1978; Beck 1993).

These ideas are important for understanding how musicians have thought about their art, and they underlie the devotional framing of much Indian music. They are not, however, a physical or physiological theory in the modern sense. The correspondences that some popular books draw between the seven notes and the cakras of the yogic body, the planets or the animals said to produce each note are later and mostly modern elaborations of particular traditions, not general doctrines of the music treatises, and they are not treated in this volume as facts about sound or the body. The claim that particular rāgas cure particular diseases is likewise a modern belief without good evidence (Section 4.13).

docs.title: 1.6.2 Śiva Naṭarāja
docs.text:
The best-known image of the sacredness of dance is the bronze of Śiva Naṭarāja, “king of dancers”, in its classic form created in Tamil Nadu under the Cōḻas in the tenth to twelfth centuries (Figure 1.1). Śiva dances within a ring of flames, his right foot on a small figure (Apasmāra or Muyalakaṉ) who represents ignorance, his left leg raised across his body. One right hand holds a small drum (ḍamaru), one left hand a flame; the second right hand makes the gesture of reassurance (abhaya), and the second left hand stretches across the body in the “elephant-trunk” gesture, pointing to the raised foot. In Tamil Śaiva theology the dance enacts the god’s five activities (pañcakṛtya): creation, preservation, destruction, concealment and grace. Ananda Coomaraswamy’s essay “The Dance of Śiva” (1918) made this interpretation famous in the West (Coomaraswamy 1918); later scholars have shown that the icon and its theology grew together over several centuries, centred on the temple of Chidambaram, where Śiva is believed to dance eternally in the “hall of consciousness” (citsabhā) (Smith 1996; Gaston 1982).

Figure 1.1. Śiva Naṭarāja, bronze, Tamil Nadu, Cōḻa period, c. 1000 (Cleveland Museum of Art, 1930.331). The god dances within a ring of flames, his right foot on the small figure of ignorance and his left leg raised across his body. Photo: Cleveland Museum of Art (open access), CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Nāṭyaśāstra itself connects dance with Śiva: in its fourth chapter Śiva teaches the vigorous dance (tāṇḍava) to Bharata through his attendant Taṇḍu, and the goddess Pārvatī is credited with the delicate style later called lāsya. The pairing of a vigorous, “masculine” style with a delicate, “feminine” one has been used to classify movements and whole dance forms ever since, although in practice both styles are danced by men and women alike (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 1.6.3 Sacred and secular
docs.text: Much Indian music and dance has a religious context: the temple ritual and festival, the Sufi assembly, the Sikh gurdwārā, the Vaiṣṇava kīrtan, the village goddess festival, the possession dances of Teyyam and Bhūta Kōla. Much of it, however, was always performed at courts, in salons and in public entertainments, and the treatises discuss performance mainly as an art that gives pleasure and aesthetic experience to cultivated spectators. Kapila Vatsyayan has argued that Indian music, dance, sculpture and architecture share common principles of form and a common religious and philosophical background (Vatsyayan 1983, 1968). Historians of the modern period have added that the emphasis on the spiritual and devotional character of the classical arts was greatly strengthened in the twentieth century, when it helped to make them respectable and to distinguish them from the arts of courtesans and from Western entertainment (Bakhle 2005; Meduri 2005). The two observations do not cancel each other. The arts were never merely religious or merely secular, and their meaning has always depended on who performed them, for whom and where.

docs.title: 1.7 Unity and Diversity
docs.text:
The traditions described in this volume share much: a theory of melody based on rāga, a theory of rhythm based on tāla, a vocabulary of gesture and expression derived in large part from the Nāṭyaśāstra and its successors, a repertoire of stories from the epics, the Purāṇas and devotional poetry, and the aesthetic ideal of rasa. They are also extremely diverse. Two systems of art music, Hindustani and Karnatak, have distinct rāgas, tālas, genres, instruments and institutions (Chapters 7 and 8). The Persianate and Sufi music of north India and the Deccan, with its Persian and Urdu poetry and its genres such as qawwālī and ghazal, and the Sikh kīrtan of the Punjab, are distinct traditions with their own histories, not merely variants of a “Hindu” music. The theatre of the subcontinent includes Sanskrit drama, the regional dance-dramas such as Yakṣagāna and the Bhāgavata Mēḷa, popular theatres such as Nauṭaṅkī, Tamāśā, Jātrā and Bhavāī, puppet theatres and the modern stage (Chapters 19 and 20).

Above all, the classical arts have always existed beside a vast world of folk and tribal music, dance and ritual performance: work songs, life-cycle songs, the epic singers of Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu, the Bāuls of Bengal, the harvest and festival dances of every region, the masked dance-dramas of Chhau and the ritual possession performances of Teyyam, and the music and dance of the Adivasi communities of central and northeastern India (Chapter 21) (Vatsyayan 1976; Blackburn et al. 1989). The division between “classical” (śāstrīya) and “folk” (lok) is in part the old distinction between mārga and deśī, but in its modern form it is largely a creation of the twentieth century, institutionalised by cultural academies and broadcasting; many forms now called classical grew out of regional practices, and many “folk” forms are technically demanding arts with their own specialists and teachers. Tribal knowledge and performance are treated more fully in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

docs.title: 1.8 The Dance Forms Treated in This Volume
docs.text:
Table 1.2 lists the dance forms that the Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises as “classical” (their centres are mapped in Figure 20.1), together with Chhau, which the Ministry of Culture also includes in its list; hence one often reads that India has “eight” or “nine” classical dances. The category is an institutional one: it was created in the decades after independence, and the criteria used — a connection with Sanskrit treatises, a codified technique, a lineage of teachers and a history of temple or court patronage — were applied gradually and not without controversy. Sattriya was added only in 2000. Many other forms, such as Yakṣagāna, Kūṭiyāṭṭam, the Bhāgavata Mēḷa or the Gauḍīya Nṛtya of Bengal, have comparable claims and are treated elsewhere in the volume (Vatsyayan 1974; Singha and Massey 1967; Ragini Devi 1972).

docs.title: 1.9 How This Volume Is Organised
docs.text:
The chapters fall into four groups, though the book is not formally divided into parts. The first three introduce the foundations. After this introduction, Chapter 2 describes the Nāṭyaśāstra: its date and structure, its origin myth, its theatre and preliminaries, its analysis of the body in movement — the karaṇas, cārīs and maṇḍalas — and its account of styles, conventions and dramatic genres. Chapter 3 presents the theory of rasa and bhāva and the four modes of acting (abhinaya) as they matter to performers; the philosophical debate about rasa is treated more fully in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

Chapters 4 to 11 are devoted to music. Chapter 4 traces the theory of pitch and melody from the Sāmaveda and the Nāṭyaśāstra’s śrutis, grāmas and jātis to the rāga and its modern classifications, and the history of musical notation. Chapter 5 explains the theory of rhythm and metre in the ancient texts and in the two modern systems. Chapter 6 follows the literature of music theory from the Dattilam and Mataṅga through the Saṅgītaratnākara and the regional treatises to Bhatkhande. Chapter 7 describes Hindustani music, its genres, gharānās and regional centres, its Persian literature, and the Persianate, Sufi and Sikh traditions of north India. Chapter 8 describes Karnatak music, its composers, its 72-mela system and its modern concert culture. Chapter 9 surveys devotional music across regions and religions: the Tamil temple hymns, the southern bhajana, the abhaṅg and kīrtan of Maharashtra, the temple music of the Puṣṭimārga, Bengali kīrtan, the Sikh scripture, the Shia majlis, and Jain and Newar Buddhist song. Chapter 10 treats the instruments, from the ancient classification into strings, winds, drums and solid instruments to the sitār, vīṇā, tablā and mṛdaṅgam. Chapter 11 follows the authored song of the modern regional languages: Rabīndrasaṅgīt and the other song-makers of Bengal, the songs of Kazi Nazrul Islam, the Bengali modern and mass song, the Marathi stage song and bhāvgīt, the Assamese song of Jyotiprasad Agarwala, Bishnu Rabha and Bhupen Hazarika, the southern lyric and the Urdu ghazal-song.

Chapters 12 to 18 are devoted to dance. Chapter 12 introduces the Abhinayadarpaṇa and the later dance treatises and their account of the head, eyes, neck and stances. Chapter 13 explains the grammar of pure and expressive dance shared by the classical forms. Chapter 14 sets out the language of hand gestures. Chapters 15, 16, 17 and 18 describe the classical forms: Bharatanāṭyam; Kathak; Odissi and Kuchipudi; and Kathakaḷi, Mohiniyāṭṭam, Manipuri and Sattriya.

The last five chapters turn to theatre and to the living landscape of performance. Chapter 19 covers Sanskrit drama, its dramaturgy and its performance, Kūṭiyāṭṭam, puppet theatre, the Parsi and other company theatres, and modern Indian theatre. Chapter 20 describes the regional popular theatres — Yakṣagāna, Terukkūttu, Jātrā, Tamāśā, Nauṭaṅkī, Bhavāī, the Rāmlīlā and Rāslīlā and others — and their performers and patrons. Chapter 21 surveys folk and tribal music, dance and ritual performance. Chapter 22 turns to the North-East and the Himalaya: the songs and dances of Assam beyond the sattras, the hill peoples of Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills, the ritual music and masked dance of Tibetan Buddhism, the Sufi music of Kashmir, and the drummers and deity processions of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Chapter 23 considers the modern and contemporary period: institutions and patronage, recording, radio and cinema, the history of music and dance education, the diaspora, contemporary dance, the international recognition of Indian arts and the debates that surround them.

Related subjects are treated in other volumes of the series: poetics, the theory of rasa and Sanskrit and Tamil literature in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā; language, phonetics and prosody in Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā; temple architecture and sculpture, including the sculptural evidence for dance, in Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa; the yogic body in Volume 5, Yoga Taraṅgiṇī; and tribal and folk knowledge in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

Note: A note on names and spellings

Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words and pre-modern names are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST), and Tamil words in a standard transliteration (with ḻ and ṉ). Names of modern persons, institutions and places are given in their usual English spelling (Rukmini Devi Arundale, Kalakshetra, Thanjavur). For the dance forms the volume uses Bharatanāṭyam, Kathak, Odissi, Kuchipudi, Kathakaḷi, Mohiniyāṭṭam, Manipuri and Sattriya. Hindustani and Persian terms are given in a simplified transliteration (khayāl, gharānā, ṭawāʾif). Chapter numbers of the Nāṭyaśāstra follow the edition and translation of Manomohan Ghosh (Ghosh 1950); other editions number some chapters and verses differently.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Rowell (1992) is the best introduction to early Indian music and its thought, and Widdess (1995) to the early history of rāga. Vatsyayan (1968) and Vatsyayan (1974) remain the standard surveys of classical dance in literature, sculpture and practice, and Vatsyayan (1976) of folk dance; Bose (1991) examines the Sanskrit dance texts. Richmond et al. (1990) surveys the theatre traditions. For the social history of performers, begin with Neuman (1980) and Bakhle (2005) for north India and Soneji (2012), Srinivasan (1985) and Weidman (2006) for the south; Schofield (2010) rethinks the idea of the “classical” in Mughal music. Smith (1996) and Coomaraswamy (1918) discuss the dance of Śiva.

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Nāṭyaśāstra
docs.text:
Nāṭyaśāstra 1.116

na taj jñānaṃ na tac chilpaṃ na sā vidyā na sā kalā nāsau yogo na tat karma nāṭye ’smin yan na dṛśyate

“There is no knowledge, no craft, no learning, no art, no discipline and no action that is not seen in this drama.”

The Nāṭyaśāstra, “the treatise on drama” ascribed to the sage Bharata, is the oldest surviving Indian text on the performing arts and the work to which almost every later theorist of music, dance and theatre in South Asia refers. It treats as a single subject what modern institutions divide into separate disciplines: the building of the playhouse and its consecration, the preliminary rites, acting with body, voice, costume and inner feeling, dance, the structure of plays, the languages of the stage, prosody, the theory of aesthetic experience (rasa), the scales and melodic types of music, rhythm, instruments, songs, the types of character and the distribution of roles. A reader who opens it expecting a philosophy of art finds instead a working manual, full of measurements, lists and rules, and it is as a manual for performers that it is read here: its date and transmission first, and then the parts that bear most directly on performance, from the building of the theatre to the music. Its theory of rasa and of the four modes of acting is the subject of Chapter 3; its account of hand gestures is treated with the later gesture manuals in Chapter 14; and its classification of plays, which belongs as much to literature as to the stage, is discussed further in Chapter 19 and in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

docs.title: 2.1 The Text, Its Date and Its Transmission
2.1.1 Authorship and date
docs.text:
The text presents itself as the teaching of the sage Bharata to other sages, who ask him about the origin and nature of the “Veda of drama” (nāṭyaveda). “Bharata” is also, in the text and in later usage, a name for the actor; the sons of Bharata are the first troupe. Most scholars therefore treat the ascription as traditional and regard the work as the product of a school of performers and theorists rather than of one author (Vatsyayan 1996; Rangacharya 1996). A modern explanation of the name as an acronym of bhāva, rāga and tāla (“Bha-Ra-Ta”), often repeated in dance schools, is a folk etymology: it is not found in the text or its commentators and cannot explain a name that is far older than the use of rāga for melody.

The Nāṭyaśāstra is a composite work. Passages in verse (mostly in the anuṣṭubh metre, with some āryā verses that the text itself describes as traditional) alternate with prose; there are repetitions, inconsistencies and sections that look like later insertions; and the manuscripts fall into recensions that differ in the number and order of chapters. A date of compilation between about 200 BCE and 200 CE, with older material incorporated and some later additions, is the range most widely accepted (Vatsyayan 1996; Tarlekar 1975). Its language, its references to the dramatic genres and to regional styles, and the absence of any reference to the classical playwrights such as Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE) are consistent with this range. Earlier claims of a much greater antiquity rest on tradition, not on evidence.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Recensions, editions and translations
docs.text:
The text survives in two main recensions, one of thirty-six and one of thirty-seven chapters, and chapter numbers differ between printed editions. It was printed in the late nineteenth century in the Kāvyamālā series and in partial European editions; the first critical edition, with Abhinavagupta’s commentary, was edited by M. Ramakrishna Kavi for the Gaekwad’s Oriental Series (Baroda, 1926–1964) (Ramakrishna Kavi 1926–1964). Manomohan Ghosh produced both an edition of the text and the first complete English translation (Ghosh 1950); Adya Rangacharya’s translation (Rangacharya 1996) is a readable alternative.

Chapter numbering used in this volume

Chapter numbers of the Nāṭyaśāstra in this volume follow Manomohan Ghosh’s edition and translation, which has thirty-six chapters (Table 2.1). Other editions (for example the Kāvyamālā and Baroda texts) number some chapters differently, so that the chapter on the cārīs, chapter 11 in Ghosh, is chapter 10 in others. Verse numbers vary even more and should always be checked against a named edition.

Table 2.1. The contents of the Nāṭyaśāstra in Ghosh’s numbering Chapters Subject 1 The origin of drama; the “fifth Veda”; the first performance 2–3 The playhouse (nāṭyamaṇḍapa); worship of the gods of the stage 4 The tāṇḍava dance: 108 karaṇas and 32 aṅgahāras 5 The preliminaries of a performance (pūrvaraṅga) 6–7 Rasa and bhāva 8–10 Movements of the minor limbs (head, eyes, brows, etc.), of the hands, and of the other limbs (chest, sides, waist, thighs, shanks, feet) 11–13 Cārīs (movements of the legs and feet), maṇḍalas (combinations of cārīs), and gaits 14 Zones of the stage (kakṣyā), regional styles (pravṛtti) and the two modes of representation (dharmī) 15–19 Verbal acting: phonetics and grammar, metres, diction (lakṣaṇa, alaṅkāra, guṇa, doṣa), languages, modes of address and intonation 20–22 The ten types of play; the structure of the plot (sandhi); the dramatic styles (vṛtti) 23 Costume and make-up (āhārya) 24–27 General acting (sāmānyābhinaya); dealings with courtesans; varied representation (citrābhinaya); success in performance (siddhi) 28–33 Music: tones, scales and melodic types; stringed and wind instruments; time-measure (tāla); songs of the stage (dhruvā); drums 34–36 Types of character; distribution of roles; the descent of drama to earth

docs.title: 2.1.3 The origin myth: a “fifth Veda”
docs.text:
The first chapter tells how, at the end of the golden age, the gods asked Brahmā for a diversion that could be seen and heard, and which, unlike the Vedas, would be open to all classes, including the Śūdras who were barred from Vedic learning. Brahmā composed a fifth Veda, the nāṭyaveda, drawing on the four:

Nāṭyaśāstra 1.17

jagrāha pāṭhyam ṛgvedāt sāmabhyo gītam eva ca yajurvedād abhinayān rasān ātharvaṇād api

“He took recitation from the Ṛgveda, song from the Sāmaveda, acting from the Yajurveda and the sentiments from the Atharvaveda.”

Bharata and his hundred sons staged the first play, on the gods’ victory over the demons, at the festival of Indra’s banner. The demons, offended, disrupted it; Viśvakarman was then commanded to build a playhouse, and the gods each undertook to guard a part of it. The story does three things. It claims Vedic authority for an art whose practitioners were, in historical fact, often of low social status; it explains the ritual consecration of the stage; and it defines drama as an imitation (anukaraṇa) of the actions of the three worlds, offering instruction and pleasure to every kind of spectator. The text closes (chapter 36) with a second story, in which Bharata’s sons mock the sages in a satirical play and are cursed to lose their status, so that drama descends to earth through a human king. Scholars have read the two stories together as an acknowledgement of the ambivalent position of actors in early Indian society (Byrski 1974; Lidova 1994).

docs.title: 2.2.1 The playhouse
docs.text:
Chapter 2 describes the theatre building (nāṭyamaṇḍapa or prekṣāgṛha). It distinguishes three shapes — rectangular (vikṛṣṭa), square (caturaśra) and triangular (tryaśra) — and three sizes, measured in hastas (cubits): a large house of 108 hastas, a medium one of 64 and a small one of 32. The text assigns the largest to the gods and recommends the medium rectangular hall, 64 by 32 hastas, for human audiences, because in a larger house the words of the actors would not be heard clearly and the expressions of their faces would be lost. It asks that the hall be built like a mountain cave, in two levels, so that voices and instruments resonate.

The hall was divided between the auditorium and the stage (Figure 2.1). Its length was halved, the front half forming the auditorium, with seats built in rising tiers, and the rear half was halved again: its front part held the stage and its rear part the tiring-room (nepathyagṛha). The stage had a front acting area (raṅgapīṭha) and a raised rear area (raṅgaśīrṣa), flanked by side structures called mattavāraṇī; from the tiring-room the actors entered through two doors, with the musicians seated between them. How the front stage and the side structures fitted into the plan is not clear from the text, and modern reconstructions differ.

Figure 2.1. Schematic plan of the medium rectangular playhouse (vikṛṣṭa madhyama) of Nāṭyaśāstra ch. 2, drawn only with the proportions the text states: a hall of 64 by 32 hastas (cubits), its front half the auditorium and its rear half divided equally between the stage and the tiring-room, which are joined by two doors with the musicians placed between them. The front stage (raṅgapīṭha) and the side structures (mattavāraṇī) are not drawn, because their size and position are reconstructed differently by different scholars; no early theatre built to this plan is known to survive.

The text gives detailed instructions on the choice and testing of the ground, the measuring, the laying of the foundations, the raising of the pillars and the decoration of the walls, each accompanied by rites; chapter 3 describes the worship of the stage gods and the consecration of the new stage before the first performance (Tarlekar 1975).

Whether actual theatres followed these prescriptions is unknown. No early theatre building has been securely identified (the rock-cut chamber at Sītābeṅgā in Chhattisgarh is sometimes so described, but its function is uncertain), and the temple theatres (kūttampalam) of Kerala, which are the closest surviving structures, date from the second millennium (Chapter 19). Claims made in some modern writing that the text anticipated modern architectural acoustics go beyond what it says: its concern with audibility and visibility is practical and expressed in practical terms.

docs.title: 2.2.2 The preliminaries (pūrvaraṅga)
docs.text:
A performance did not begin with the play. Chapter 5 describes the pūrvaraṅga, a long sequence of musical items, songs, dances and rites that consecrated the stage, honoured the gods, warded off obstacles and prepared the audience. Ghosh’s text lists nineteen items. Nine are performed behind the curtain by the musicians, from the arrangement of the instruments (pratyāhāra) and the seating of the singers (avataraṇa) to the instrumental pieces called āsārita; ten follow in front of it, among them the benediction (nāndī) recited by the director (sūtradhāra), the raṅgadvāra, the dances called cārī and mahācārī, the comic dialogue of the director, his assistant and the jester (trigata), and finally the prarocanā, which introduces and praises the play. The text acknowledges that the full sequence was long and allows it to be shortened (Ghosh 1950; Tarlekar 1975).

Something of the pūrvaraṅga survives in the long preliminaries of Kūṭiyāṭṭam and Kathakaḷi (Chapters 18 and 19), and its spirit in the invocatory items with which classical dance recitals still begin, though the modern items are not direct descendants of the ancient ones.

docs.title: 2.3.1 Tāṇḍava and lāsya
docs.text:
Chapter 4 tells how, after the first performance, Brahmā took Bharata to Śiva, who added dance to drama. Śiva’s attendant Taṇḍu taught the vigorous dance (tāṇḍava) to Bharata, and Pārvatī is credited with the delicate style (sukumāra, later called lāsya). The text explains that pure dance (nṛtta) conveys no particular meaning but is added because it creates beauty and is auspicious. Its later chapters list ten “limbs of lāsya” (lāsyāṅga; some recensions add two more), short song-and-dance items performed mainly by women, such as geyapada (a seated singer with instruments), sthitapāṭhya, āsīna, puṣpagaṇḍikā, pracchedaka, trimūḍhaka, saindhava, dvimūḍhaka, uttamottamaka and uktapratyukta (a sung dialogue).

The pairing of tāṇḍava with Śiva and men and lāsya with Pārvatī and women became a commonplace of later writing on dance, often expanded into a metaphysical complementarity of Śiva and Śakti. The Nāṭyaśāstra itself is less schematic: it describes tāṇḍava movements performed in worship and lists lāsya as a set of items, not as a gendered essence. The familiar lists of seven tāṇḍavas of Śiva (ānanda, sandhyā, and so on) belong to later texts and iconography, not to Bharata.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Karaṇas and aṅgahāras
docs.text:
The heart of chapter 4 is the list of 108 karaṇas. A karaṇa is defined as a combined movement of the hands and feet (hastapādasamāyoga) in dance; each is described in terms of a particular position or movement of the feet (cārī), the legs and trunk, and the hands, often with a characteristic standing position. The list begins with talapuṣpapuṭa and ends with gaṅgāvataraṇa (“the descent of the Ganges”); among the best known are alāta (“firebrand”), ūrdhvajānu (“raised knee”), bhujaṅgatrāsita (“startled by a snake”, a leap with the leg drawn up, the pose of many images of Śiva Naṭarāja), lalāṭatilaka (the foot raised to touch the forehead) and gajakrīḍita (“elephant’s play”). Sequences of karaṇas form the thirty-two aṅgahāras; the chapter also describes four recakas (circling movements of the neck, hands, waist and feet) and the piṇḍībandhas, group formations made by dancers in the pūrvaraṅga in honour of particular deities (Vatsyayan 1968; Bose 1991).

The descriptions are terse and technical, and their interpretation has always depended on teachers and commentators. Abhinavagupta’s commentary on chapter 4 is one of the fullest parts of his work, but it too is partly corrupt.

docs.title: 2.3.3 The karaṇas in sculpture
docs.text:
From the eleventh century, karaṇas were carved on the walls of temples in the Tamil country. The great temple at Thanjavur, built by the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I and completed about 1010, has a series of karaṇa figures on the first storey of its central tower; the series was left incomplete (it is usually counted as 81 figures). At Chidambaram, the temple of Śiva Naṭarāja, the gateway towers (gopuras) built in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries carry panels of dancers for all 108 karaṇas, several of them inscribed with the corresponding verse of the Nāṭyaśāstra (Figure 2.2); similar series exist at other temples in the region (Vatsyayan 1968; Smith 1996). These sculptures show that the karaṇas were known and valued in a particular region and period. They are evidence for how sculptors and their patrons understood the text, not a record of a continuous dance practice from Bharata’s time.

Figure 2.2. Dance reliefs on the eastern gopura of the Naṭarāja temple at Chidambaram, thirteenth century: a composite of photographs of individual panels, with a view of the rows of framed panels on the inner wall of the gateway (lower right). Photo: Ms Sarah Welch, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Modern attempts to reconstruct the karaṇas as performable movements, most notably by the dancer and scholar Padma Subrahmanyam from the 1970s onwards, combine the text, the commentary and the sculptures. They are creative reconstructions, valuable in their own right, and the dancers who made them have usually said so; they should not be mistaken for the recovery of an unbroken tradition.

docs.title: 2.3.4 The body as instrument
docs.text: Chapters 8 to 10 analyse the body into major limbs (aṅga: head, hands, chest, sides, waist and feet), minor parts of the face (upāṅga: eyes, eyelids, eyeballs, brows, nose, cheeks, lower lip and chin) and, in later usage, subsidiary limbs (pratyaṅga: neck, arms, back, belly, thighs and shanks), and they describe and name the movements of each with their uses. Among them are thirteen movements of the head; thirty-six glances (dṛṣṭi), divided into eight that express the rasas (such as kāntā for the erotic and karuṇā for the pathetic), eight that express the corresponding stable emotions (such as snigdhā, “affectionate”, and dīnā, “dejected”) and twenty for the transitory states; nine movements of the neck; five each of the chest, sides, waist, thighs and shanks; and the movements of the eyebrows, nose, cheeks, lips and chin. Chapter 9 describes the hand gestures: twenty-four for a single hand, thirteen for combined hands and a further group of “dance hands” (nṛtta-hasta), together with the ways the hands move. These are treated, with the later lists of the Abhinayadarpaṇa, in Chapter 14; the later manuals’ simpler lists of head, eye and neck movements are described in Chapter 12.

docs.title: 2.3.5 Cārīs, maṇḍalas, standing positions and gaits
docs.text:
Chapter 11 defines the cārī as a movement of one foot, together with the shank and thigh, and gives thirty-two of them: sixteen “earthly” (bhaumī), performed on the ground, such as samapādā, śakaṭāsyā, eḍakākrīḍitā (“ram’s play”) and mattallī; and sixteen “aerial” (ākāśikī), in which the leg is raised or the dancer leaves the ground, such as ūrdhvajānu, alātā, bhujaṅgatrāsitā, hariṇaplutā (“deer’s leap”) and bhramarī (a turn). The text says that dance, movement on the stage and even fighting are all composed of cārīs. It also describes the standing positions (sthāna), six for men (among them vaiṣṇava, samapāda, vaiśākha, maṇḍala, ālīḍha and pratyālīḍha, several of them the postures of archery and combat) and others for women. Chapter 12 combines cārīs into twenty maṇḍalas, ten earthly and ten aerial, used especially in fights and battle scenes. Chapter 13 describes gaits (gati) appropriate to characters of different rank, sex, age and state of mind, and to animals and vehicles (Ghosh 1950; Bose 1991).

Comparisons that make the Nāṭyaśāstra the “earliest systematic codification of human movement in world literature” are hard to test and add little; it is enough to say that it is the oldest surviving Indian analysis of movement for performance, and an unusually detailed one.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Zones and regional styles
docs.text: Chapter 14 explains the zones of the stage (kakṣyā): by moving from one zone to another an actor indicates a change of place, and the stage can represent several places at once. The same chapter describes four regional styles of production (pravṛtti): the Āvantī (associated with western and central India), the Dākṣiṇātyā (the south), the Pāñcālī (the north) and the Oḍhra-Māgadhī (the east), each characterised by a preference for certain dramatic styles. The scheme is evidence that performance practice was already regionally diverse when the text was compiled.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Lokadharmī and nāṭyadharmī
docs.text:
The text distinguishes two modes of representation. Lokadharmī (“the practice of the world”) reproduces ordinary behaviour, speech and dress; nāṭyadharmī (“the practice of the stage”) uses the conventions of the theatre: stylised gait and gesture, verse and song, asides, the representation of things not physically present, and the use of dance. Bharata treats the theatrical mode as essential to serious drama, and much of the text is a codification of its conventions (Ghosh 1950; Byrski 1974).

The distinction remains useful. Kūṭiyāṭṭam and Kathakaḷi, with their codified gestures and make-up, are at the nāṭyadharmī extreme; much modern theatre and cinema works mainly in a lokadharmī mode; and the classical dance forms move between the abstraction of pure dance and passages of more naturalistic mime. Modern comparisons with Brecht’s “alienation effect” or with the Japanese Nō are interesting analogies, but they compare different theories made for different purposes.

docs.title: 2.4.3 The dramatic styles (vṛtti)
docs.text: Chapter 22 describes four styles (vṛtti) that colour a performance as a whole: the verbal style (bhāratī), dominated by speech and used by male actors; the grand or “sattvic” style (sāttvatī), marked by energy, courage and the expression of strong feeling; the graceful style (kaiśikī), marked by charm, music, dance and the presence of women, suited to love and comedy; and the violent or energetic style (ārabhaṭī), with fights, magic, deceit and tumult. The four pravṛttis of chapter 14 are defined by their preference for particular vṛttis.

docs.title: 2.4.4 Types of play and plot structure
docs.text: Chapter 20 classifies plays into ten types (daśarūpa), from the full-scale nāṭaka, with a well-known story and a royal or divine hero, and the prakaraṇa, with an invented story and a hero who may be a brahmin, minister or merchant, to one-act forms such as the monologue (bhāṇa) and the farce (prahasana). Chapter 21 describes the structure of the plot in terms of five stages of the hero’s action (avasthā), five elements of the plot (arthaprakṛti) and five junctures (sandhi) with their many sub-divisions. These categories were systematised in Dhanañjaya’s Daśarūpaka (late tenth century) and are discussed in Chapter 19 and, as literary theory, in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

docs.title: 2.4.5 Characters and their language
docs.text: The Nāṭyaśāstra grades characters as high, middling and low (uttama, madhyama, adhama) and describes types of hero, heroine and attendant (chapters 24 and 34). Its chapter on languages (18) prescribes Sanskrit for kings, brahmins, ascetics and other high-ranking men, and Prakrit for most women, for children and for men of low status, with particular dialects for particular groups. The convention, followed by the classical plays, built the social hierarchy of caste and gender into the sound of the stage; in the text it is presented simply as propriety (aucitya) (Keith 1924; Raghavan 1993).

docs.title: 2.4.6 Costume and make-up
docs.text: Chapter 23 treats āhārya, the “extraneous” means of representation, under four heads: models and stage properties (pusta), ornaments (alaṅkāra), the painting of the body and face (aṅgaracanā) and the representation of living creatures (sañjīva). It gives the primary colours and their mixtures, and prescribes complexions and dress for characters according to their region, rank, occupation and, in some passages, social class; it describes crowns, wigs, beards and garments for gods, kings, ascetics, women of different kinds and others. Later traditions developed their own conventions. The make-up of Kathakaḷi and Kūṭiyāṭṭam, for example, with its green faces for noble heroes and red beards for violent villains, is a regional system that owes something to the general principle of the Nāṭyaśāstra, that colour and costume classify character, but it is not a direct transcription of the text’s prescriptions (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 2.4.7 The director and the troupe
docs.text: The sūtradhāra (literally “holder of the string”, perhaps originally the measurer of the stage) directs the troupe, speaks the benediction and introduces the play. The text describes the qualities required of him and of the other members of a company: the actor, the actress, the jester, the musicians and the stage hands. The closing chapters on the types of character and the distribution of roles (34–35) give advice on casting according to physique, voice and temperament, and allow women to play men’s roles and men women’s in some circumstances (Tarlekar 1975).

docs.title: 2.5 Success, Spectators and Judges
docs.text:
Chapter 27 deals with the “success” (siddhi) of a performance, and is one of the earliest discussions anywhere of how a performance is to be received and evaluated. It distinguishes two kinds of success. “Human” success (mānuṣī siddhi) is shown by the audible and visible responses of the spectators: smiles and laughter, cries of approval, applause, the raising of hair in excitement, tears at pathetic scenes. “Divine” success (daivikī siddhi) is a deeper, quieter response, when the spectators are absorbed in the emotional states represented and the house is full and undisturbed. The text then lists the faults (ghāta) that mar a performance — those due to fate or accident, to the actors themselves, and to rivals in the audience who seek to disrupt it — and gives detailed lists of the errors an actor may commit: forgetting lines, inappropriate gestures, mistakes in rhythm, poor costume, a crown falling off (Ghosh 1950; Tarlekar 1975).

The same chapter describes the ideal spectator (prekṣaka): a person of good character and education, attentive, free from prejudice, who understands the arts involved and who responds to the joy and sorrow of the characters as if they were his own. Since few spectators possess all these qualities, the text recognises that different spectators will be pleased by different things — the young by love, the learned by philosophy, the pious by religious themes, the common people by comedy and spectacle. For competitions between troupes it provides a panel of judges (prāśnika), experts in different fields such as ritual, dance, music, prosody, grammar and costume, each of whom assesses the aspects of the performance that fall within his competence. The idea of the sensitive spectator was developed by later theorists into the concept of the sahṛdaya, “one whose heart is in tune”, which is central to the theory of rasa (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 2.6 Women in the Text
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra assumes a theatre in which women perform. In the origin story of chapter 1, when Bharata reports that the graceful style (kaiśikī) cannot be performed by men alone, Brahmā creates celestial women (apsaras) skilled in it, and the first performance is given with their participation. Actresses (nāṭakīyā), women singers and dancers are among the members of the troupe described in the text; the graceful style and the delicate dance (sukumāra, lāsya) are associated especially with women; and the text gives careful instructions for the representation of female characters of every rank. Its classifications of heroines — by social position, by relation to the hero and by emotional situation, including the eight situations of the heroine in love (aṣṭanāyikā) — became the basis of a long tradition of poetic and choreographic typology (Chapter 3).

The text’s view of women is nevertheless that of its society. Women speak Prakrit, not Sanskrit, on stage; heroines are classified largely by their relation to men; and chapter 25, on “external” representation, concerns the conduct of the courtesan and her relations with clients, a subject that the text treats as part of the knowledge an actor or playwright needs. Modern readers have drawn opposite conclusions from such passages, some emphasising the presence and skill of women performers in early Indian theatre, others the ways in which the text fixed them within a hierarchy of gender and status. The text supports both readings, because it describes a theatre that depended on women’s skill while keeping them in their place.

docs.title: 2.7 Theories of Origin
docs.text:
Where did Indian drama come from? The Nāṭyaśāstra’s own answer is mythical, and modern scholars have proposed several historical ones. In 1882 the German Indologist Ernst Windisch suggested that Sanskrit drama had been influenced by Greek New Comedy, which might have been known in the Hellenistic kingdoms of north-western India; he pointed to similarities of plot and character and to the word yavanikā for the stage curtain, which he connected with yavana, “Greek”. The theory was criticised from the start: the similarities are general, the curtain of the Indian stage differs from anything in Greek theatre, and the word may mean simply a cloth of foreign make. Most scholars now reject direct Greek influence. Other theories have sought the origin of drama in the recitation of epics, in ritual dialogues of the Ṛgveda, in the dramatic elements of Vedic ritual, in popular mimes and in puppet or shadow theatre; Richard Pischel’s argument that drama grew out of puppetry, for example, rested partly on the name sūtradhāra, “holder of the strings”. A. B. Keith reviewed these theories in detail and concluded that Sanskrit drama arose in India from a combination of epic recitation, religious ritual and popular entertainment, a view still broadly accepted (Keith 1924).

What is certain is that by the time of the Nāṭyaśāstra a mature theatrical tradition existed, with professional troupes, playhouses, a ritual of consecration and a body of theory; that fragments of Buddhist plays by Aśvaghoṣa (first to second century CE) found in Central Asia show the classical form already established; and that the theatre of the following centuries developed this tradition in India’s own terms. Byrski and Lidova have argued that the ritual elements of the text — the preliminaries, the consecration of the stage, the myth of the victory of the gods — are central rather than incidental, and that drama was understood from the beginning as a kind of sacrifice (Byrski 1974; Lidova 1994).

docs.title: 2.8 Music in the Nāṭyaśāstra
docs.text:
Chapters 28 to 33 form the oldest substantial treatise on Indian music. They classify instruments into four groups — stringed (tata), wind (suṣira), drums (avanaddha) and solid (ghana) — a classification still in use (Chapter 10). They describe the seven notes (svara) and the twenty-two microtonal intervals (śruti) by which the octave is measured; the two parent scales (grāma), the ṣaḍja-grāma and the madhyama-grāma (a third, the gāndhāra-grāma, said to exist only in heaven, belongs to later texts, not to Bharata); the modal series (mūrchanā) derived from them; and the eighteen melodic types (jāti), each defined by a set of characteristics such as its initial, predominant and final notes. The jātis are the ancestors of the later rāgas. Chapter 31 deals with time-measure (tāla), the five ancient mārga tālas and the silent and sounded gestures used to keep time; chapter 32 with the songs of the stage (dhruvā), sung at entrances, exits and changes of mood; and chapter 33 with the drums and their strokes. These subjects are taken up in Chapters 4 and 5 (Rowell 1992; Widdess 1995).

The music of the Nāṭyaśāstra was music for the theatre, and its religious form, the gāndharva, is distinguished from the music of the play. Little of it can be reconstructed as sound, and the relation of the jātis to any living music is a matter of historical inference, not of continuous practice.

docs.title: 2.9 Commentators and Later Reception
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra was studied and commented on for a thousand years. Most early commentaries are lost and are known only through quotations in the work of Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016 CE), the Kashmiri philosopher and critic, whose Abhinavabhāratī is the only commentary to survive in substantial form. Abhinavagupta cites and criticises his predecessors — among them Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa, Śrī Śaṅkuka and Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka on rasa, and his own teacher Bhaṭṭa Tauta — and his interpretation of the rasa-sūtra became authoritative for later Indian aesthetics (Chapter 3; Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā) (Gnoli 1968; Pollock 2016). The commentary survives in few and faulty manuscripts, and parts of it, including much of the commentary on the music chapters, are lost or very corrupt.

After Abhinavagupta, the Nāṭyaśāstra was read through later syntheses. Dhanañjaya’s Daśarūpaka became the standard handbook of dramaturgy. Śārṅgadeva’s Saṅgītaratnākara, composed in the first half of the thirteenth century at the Yādava court of Devagiri, absorbed the Nāṭyaśāstra’s music and dance into a larger system that also described the regional (deśī) music and dance of its own time; its seventh chapter, on dance, became the model for later dance treatises (Shringy and Sharma 1978). Regional manuals such as the Abhinayadarpaṇa and the Hastalakṣaṇadīpikā (Chapters 12 and 14) carried parts of the tradition, often in simplified or altered form. By the early modern period, as V. Raghavan and others have shown, most practitioners knew the Nāṭyaśāstra, if at all, through such intermediaries and through their teachers (Raghavan 1993).

The modern prestige of the text dates largely from the twentieth century, when editions, translations and studies made it available again and when the dance forms that were being reconstructed as “classical” sought authority in it. Its authority in the modern dance world is therefore partly a modern creation. The living forms have their own vocabularies, repertoires and regional histories, most of which are much later than Bharata; the Nāṭyaśāstra supplies a shared theoretical language, not a set of instructions that the modern forms simply carry out (Vatsyayan 1996; Soneji 2012).

docs.title: 2.9.1 Beyond India
docs.text: Indian epic stories, iconography and court arts travelled to Southeast Asia from the first millennium CE, and dance figures appear in the reliefs of Prambanan in Java (ninth century) and of Angkor in Cambodia (twelfth century). The dance-dramas of the region — the Khmer and Thai masked dramas based on the Rāmāyaṇa, Javanese and Balinese dance — share themes and some principles with Indian forms. How far the Nāṭyaśāstra itself was known there is uncertain; claims that particular Southeast Asian reliefs reproduce particular karaṇas are debated, and the living forms of the region have long and independent histories of their own (Brandon 1993).

docs.title: 2.10 The Legacy of the Text
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra remains the foundation of Indian thinking about performance in three ways. It provides a shared vocabulary — rasa and bhāva, abhinaya, nṛtta, karaṇa, cārī, hasta, tāla, lokadharmī and nāṭyadharmī — in which practitioners of very different forms can talk to each other. It offers a model of the performing arts as one integrated art, in which music, dance, speech and spectacle serve a common aesthetic end. And it is a historical document of extraordinary value for the theatre of its time, for the organisation of performing troupes, and for the social world they inhabited.

It should also be read critically. It is a normative text written from the perspective of the patrons and theorists of a courtly and priestly theatre; its hierarchies of character and language are those of its society; and it tells us more about how performance was to be classified and judged than about what any particular performance was like. Its greatest modern interpreters, from Manomohan Ghosh and V. Raghavan to Kapila Vatsyayan, have read it in this double light, as a work of theory to be understood on its own terms and as a historical source to be placed in its time (Vatsyayan 1996; Raghavan 1993).

docs.title: Further Reading
