docs.text: Ghosh (1950) is the standard complete English translation, and Rangacharya (1996) a more readable one. Vatsyayan (1996) is a concise introduction to the whole text, Tarlekar (1975) a study of its stagecraft, and Byrski (1974) and Lidova (1994) discuss its ritual and religious context. On dance in the text and its later reception see Vatsyayan (1968) and Bose (1991); on the music, Rowell (1992). Raghavan (1993) gathers a lifetime’s work on the Sanskrit theatre in performance.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Rasa, Bhāva and Abhinaya in Performance
docs.text:
The theory of rasa, “taste” or aesthetic relish, is the best-known contribution of the Nāṭyaśāstra to Indian thought. It was formulated for the theatre, and it was in the theatre that its terms — the determinants, consequents and transitory states of emotion, the stable emotions and their rasas — had their first practical meaning: they told the actor what to show and the spectator what to look for. From the ninth century onwards the theory was taken up by literary critics and philosophers and became the centre of a long debate about the nature of aesthetic experience; that debate, and the application of rasa to poetry, are treated in Volume 8 of this series, Kāvya Kalpalatā. This chapter is concerned with rasa in performance: the analysis of emotion that the actor and dancer use, the four means of acting (abhinaya) by which emotion is made visible and audible, the conventions of character and situation that give expressive dance much of its repertoire, and the spectator for whom all this is done.

Nāṭyaśāstra 6, prose after v. 31, before the rasa-sūtra

na hi rasād ṛte kaścid arthaḥ pravartate

“No meaning proceeds without rasa.”

docs.title: 3.1 The Rasa-sūtra and the Analysis of Emotion
docs.text:
The sixth chapter of the Nāṭyaśāstra defines rasa in a single prose sentence:

Nāṭyaśāstra 6, prose after v. 31 (placement varies between editions)

vibhāvānubhāvavyabhicārisaṃyogād rasaniṣpattiḥ

“Rasa arises from the union of the determinants, the consequents and the transitory states.”

Bharata explains the sentence with the analogy of cooking: as a dish acquires its taste from the combination of many ingredients and spices, so the stable emotions, combined with the other states, become rasa, which the spectator “tastes”. For the performer each term names something concrete (Ghosh 1950; Masson and Patwardhan 1970):

Vibhāva (determinant). The causes of an emotion: its object or support (ālambana), for example the beloved, and the circumstances that excite it (uddīpana), such as moonlight, a garden in spring or the sound of the flute. In performance the determinants are supplied by the story and the poetry, and are often themselves shown in mime: the dancer depicts the moon, the bees, the river. Anubhāva (consequent). The outward signs of emotion: glances, movements of the brows and lips, gestures, gait, changes of voice. These are what the actor actually does. Vyabhicāribhāva (transitory state). Also called sañcāribhāva: passing feelings that arise and subside within a dominant mood, such as anxiety, joy, shame, recollection or weariness. Bharata lists thirty-three (Table 3.2). Sthāyibhāva (stable emotion). The enduring emotion that the other elements serve and that becomes rasa for the spectator. There are eight, one for each rasa.

The Nāṭyaśāstra adds eight sāttvikabhāvas, involuntary signs of strong feeling: paralysis (stambha), perspiration (sveda), horripilation (romāñca), change of voice (svarabheda), trembling (vepathu), change of colour (vaivarṇya), tears (aśru) and fainting (pralaya). Because they cannot be produced at will, the text says that the actor must achieve them through concentration of mind (sattva); this is the origin of the idea, central to later teaching, that expressive acting requires inner absorption as well as technique. Altogether the text counts forty-nine bhāvas: eight stable, thirty-three transitory and eight involuntary.

docs.title: 3.2 The Rasas
docs.text:
Bharata names eight rasas and gives each a stable emotion, a colour and a presiding deity (Table 3.1).

Nāṭyaśāstra 6.15 (Ghosh’s numbering; 6.16 in some editions)

śṛṅgārahāsyakaruṇā raudravīrabhayānakāḥ bībhatsādbhutasaṃjñau cety aṣṭau nāṭye rasāḥ smṛtāḥ

“The erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible, and those called the odious and the marvellous: these eight are declared to be the rasas in drama.”

Table 3.1. The eight rasas of the Nāṭyaśāstra (ch. 6), with the later ninth Rasa Stable emotion English Colour Deity Śṛṅgāra rati (love) Erotic dark (śyāma) Viṣṇu Hāsya hāsa (mirth) Comic white the Pramathas Karuṇa śoka (grief) Pathetic dove-grey Yama Raudra krodha (anger) Furious red Rudra Vīra utsāha (energy) Heroic pale gold (gaura) Mahendra (Indra) Bhayānaka bhaya (fear) Terrible black Kāla Bībhatsa jugupsā (disgust) Odious blue Mahākāla Adbhuta vismaya (astonishment) Marvellous yellow Brahmā Śānta śama (calm) or nirveda Tranquil not in Bharata’s list; see below

Bharata’s descriptions are practical. Love has two forms, love in union (sambhoga) and love in separation (vipralambha); the comic is graded into six kinds of laughter, from the faint smile (smita) and the smile that shows a little of the teeth (hasita), proper to superior characters, through vihasita and upahasita, to the coarse apahasita and atihasita, proper to low characters; the heroic arises in giving, in righteous action and in war. For each rasa the text lists its determinants, the consequents by which the actor should show it, and the transitory states that accompany it. The four rasas of love, fury, heroism and disgust are called the sources of the others: the comic arises from love, the pathetic from fury, the marvellous from heroism and the terrible from disgust.

docs.title: 3.2.1 Śānta and later rasas
docs.text:
Whether there is a ninth rasa, the tranquil (śānta), was debated for centuries. It is not in the core list of the Nāṭyaśāstra, though some manuscripts contain a passage on it that is probably a later insertion. It is first clearly listed by the Kashmiri critic Udbhaṭa (late eighth century) and was defended at length by Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016 CE), who argued that its stable emotion is the knowledge of truth and that it is the rasa corresponding to the goal of liberation; after him “the nine rasas” (navarasa) became the usual phrase (Raghavan 1940; Masson and Patwardhan 1970). Later theorists proposed further rasas — of parental affection (vātsalya), of devotion (bhakti) and others. The most influential of these proposals was made in the sixteenth century by Rūpa Gosvāmin, a theologian of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava movement, who made devotion to Kṛṣṇa the one true rasa and recast the classical categories as kinds of devotional love; his theory shaped the devotional performing arts of Bengal, Odisha and Manipur (Pollock 2016).

In modern dance teaching the “nine rasas” are often taught as nine facial expressions, each with a fixed set of movements of the eyes, brows and mouth. This is a useful pedagogical device, but it simplifies the theory: for Bharata, rasa is not an expression on the actor’s face but an experience produced in the spectator by the whole performance.

docs.title: 3.3 The Transitory States
docs.text:
The thirty-three transitory states are the expressive actor’s most detailed resource. Each is defined in the Nāṭyaśāstra by its causes and by the consequents through which it should be shown. Several are not emotions in the modern sense but physical or mental conditions — sleep, sickness, intoxication, even death — that the actor must be able to represent.

Table 3.2. The thirty-three transitory states (vyabhicāribhāva) of the Nāṭyaśāstra (ch. 7), in Bharata’s order State Meaning State Meaning nirveda despondency, world-weariness viṣāda despair glāni weakness, languor autsukya impatience, longing śaṅkā apprehension nidrā sleepiness asūyā envy, jealousy apasmāra epilepsy, loss of control mada intoxication supta sleep, dreaming śrama weariness vibodha awakening ālasya indolence amarṣa indignation dainya wretchedness avahitthā dissimulation cintā anxiety ugratā ferocity moha confusion, distraction mati understanding, resolve smṛti recollection vyādhi sickness dhṛti contentment, steadiness unmāda madness vrīḍā shame, bashfulness maraṇa death capalatā inconstancy trāsa fright harṣa joy vitarka deliberation, doubt āvega agitation jaḍatā stupor garva arrogance

In performance the transitory states give a dominant mood its colour and movement. A dancer interpreting a song of love in separation may pass, within a single line, through longing (autsukya), recollection of a past meeting (smṛti), anxiety (cintā), a flash of joy as she imagines the lover’s return (harṣa) and despair (viṣāda) when she realises he has not come, all held within the stable emotion of love. The practice of elaborating a single line of text through a succession of such states, each shown with a different set of gestures and glances while the musicians repeat the line, is the core of expressive improvisation (manodharma) in Bharatanāṭyam and of the long elaborations of Kūṭiyāṭṭam and Kathakaḷi (Chapters 15, 18 and 19).

docs.title: 3.4 The Four Means of Acting
docs.text: The word abhinaya is derived from the root nī, “to lead”, with the prefix abhi, “towards”: it is what “leads” the meaning of the play to the spectators. The Nāṭyaśāstra distinguishes four kinds (Ghosh 1950; Vatsyayan 1996).

docs.title: 3.4.1 Āṅgika: acting with the body
docs.text: Bodily acting uses the major limbs, the face and the subsidiary limbs, each with its named movements (Chapter 2): the movements of the head, eyes, brows and lips; the hand gestures (Chapter 14); the positions and movements of the chest, waist and legs; the cārīs and gaits. The text distinguishes three applications: the representation of the body itself, of the face, and of movement through the whole body. Bodily acting is the domain that dance shares most fully with drama, and the later dance manuals (Chapter 12) are largely manuals of āṅgika.

docs.title: 3.4.2 Vācika: acting with the voice
docs.text: Verbal acting includes everything that is spoken or sung: the text itself, its metres and figures of speech, the languages of the stage (Sanskrit for some characters, Prakrit dialects for others), the modes of address, and the delivery of speech with appropriate pitch, tempo and intonation (kāku). In the dance forms the voice is usually the singer’s: the dancer interprets a song sung by the vocalist, and the words of the song — in Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Odia, Hindi, Braj or Manipuri — determine what the body shows. In the dance-dramas the actors may speak (as in Kūṭiyāṭṭam and Yakṣagāna) or remain silent while the singers sing their words (as in Kathakaḷi).

docs.title: 3.4.3 Āhārya: costume, make-up and properties
docs.text: The “extraneous” means of acting comprise costume, ornaments, make-up and stage properties (Chapter 2). In the modern forms they range from the restrained costume and jewellery of the solo dance forms, whose conventions were largely fixed in the twentieth century, to the elaborate make-up, head-dresses and skirts of Kathakaḷi, Yakṣagāna and Kūṭiyāṭṭam, which transform the actor into a type before a word is sung.

docs.title: 3.4.4 Sāttvika: acting with inner feeling
docs.text: The fourth means is the representation of the involuntary states listed above, and more generally the quality of inner concentration (sattva) that makes acting convincing. Bharata ranks performances in which sattva predominates as the best. The tradition has always debated how far the actor should actually feel what he represents; Abhinavagupta’s view, that the actor too experiences the generalised emotion without being overwhelmed by it as by a personal feeling, is one influential answer.

docs.title: 3.4.5 General and varied acting
docs.text: Two later chapters of the Nāṭyaśāstra deal with the combination of the four means. “General acting” (sāmānyābhinaya, ch. 24) discusses the harmonious use of all of them and describes the types of men and women, their temperaments and the stages of love; “varied acting” (citrābhinaya, ch. 26) shows how to represent things that cannot be brought on the stage: the seasons, the times of day, the sun and moon, birds and animals, distant and invisible objects. Much of the mimetic vocabulary of the modern dance forms — the gestures for the lotus, the bee, the peacock, the moon — is of this kind.

docs.title: 3.5 Characters and Situations
docs.text: Expressive dance in India has inherited from the theatre and from poetry a repertoire of typical characters and situations, above all those of love.

docs.title: 3.5.1 The heroine and the hero
docs.text: The Nāṭyaśāstra (ch. 24) describes eight heroines (nāyikā) according to their situation in love: the heroine who has dressed and prepared the house for her lover (vāsakasajjā); the heroine pining in separation (virahotkaṇṭhitā); the one whose lover is under her control (svādhīnabhartṛkā); the one separated by a quarrel she now regrets (kalahāntaritā); the one whose lover comes to her bearing the marks of another woman (khaṇḍitā); the one deceived by a lover who fails to keep a tryst (vipralabdhā); the one whose husband is away on a journey (proṣitabhartṛkā); and the one who goes out to meet her lover (abhisārikā). Later rhetoricians multiplied these classifications, and the eight became a favourite subject for poets, painters and musicians; the aṣṭanāyikā remain a staple of the dance repertoire. The hero (nāyaka) is classified as noble and exalted (dhīrodātta), light-hearted (dhīralalita), calm (dhīrapraśānta) or haughty (dhīroddhata), and in love poetry as faithful, impartial, deceitful or shameless; the confidante (sakhī), to whom the heroine speaks, is often the implied listener of the dancer’s song.

docs.title: 3.5.2 Love, devotion and the problem of the erotic
docs.text:
Much of the expressive repertoire of the classical dance forms consists of love songs. In the padams of Kṣetrayya (seventeenth century) and the jāvaḷis of the nineteenth century, the heroine addresses a god — Kṛṣṇa as Muvva Gopāla, or Murukaṉ — or a king or patron in the language of human love, often frankly sexual. Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda (twelfth century), the basis of much Odissi repertoire, is at once an erotic poem and a devotional one. For the devotional traditions this is no contradiction: from the Tamil Āḻvār and Nāyaṉār poets to the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas, human love was the most intense available language for the love of god, and the devotee could be cast as a woman longing for an absent lover.

In the twentieth century this repertoire became a battleground. Reformers who campaigned against the dedication of devadāsīs regarded the erotic songs of their repertoire as evidence of immorality; some of those who reconstructed the dance for the concert stage removed or “spiritualised” them, while others, notably Balasaraswati, insisted that the śṛṅgāra of the hereditary repertoire was itself devotional and should be performed as it had been taught. The history of this debate, and its consequences for the women whose art was being reshaped, is told in Chapter 15 (Soneji 2012; Knight 2010).

docs.title: 3.5.3 Improper rasa (rasābhāsa)
docs.text: Later theorists described as rasābhāsa, a “semblance of rasa”, the case in which an emotion is presented improperly, against the conventions of propriety (aucitya): love that is not reciprocated, or felt for an improper object, as Rāvaṇa’s for Sītā; heroism displayed against an unworthy opponent; emotions attributed to animals or to characters thought incapable of them. The concept thus concerned the content of what was represented and its fit with social and literary norms, not, as is sometimes said, the insincerity of a performer. Its social assumptions — about whose emotions counted — are themselves part of the history of the theory.

docs.title: 3.6 The Spectator
docs.text:
Rasa is experienced by the spectator, and the theory demands a particular kind of spectator: the sahṛdaya, “one whose heart is in tune”, whose sensibility has been formed by familiarity with poetry and performance and who can respond to a representation without either indifference or merely personal involvement. The Nāṭyaśāstra itself describes the qualities of the ideal spectator and the signs (laughter, tears, applause, horripilation) by which success (siddhi) in performance can be judged (ch. 27; see Chapter 2).

How exactly rasa arises in the spectator was the subject of the debate between the commentators Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa, Śrī Śaṅkuka, Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka and Abhinavagupta, known mainly through Abhinavagupta’s report. In the view that prevailed, Abhinavagupta’s, the play does not produce the emotion of a character in the spectator, nor does the spectator merely infer it; rather, the situation presented on the stage is “generalised” (sādhāraṇīkaraṇa), freed from the particular persons involved, and awakens latent impressions (vāsanā) of the corresponding emotion in the spectator’s own mind, which he then “tastes” in a state of absorbed wonder (camatkāra). Abhinavagupta also analysed the obstacles that prevent this experience — an implausible presentation, the spectator’s preoccupation with his own pleasure or pain, inadequate means of presentation, doubt — and explained the function of music, dance and the conventions of the stage as means of removing them. The theory is treated in detail in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā; for the present purpose it is enough to note that it gave the performer a demanding task, to present emotion in a form that is at once vivid and impersonal (Gnoli 1968; Pollock 2016; Ingalls et al. 1990).

The comparison of aesthetic experience with the bliss of the realisation of brahman is often attributed to Abhinavagupta. He does compare the two, while insisting on their differences; the famous phrase calling rasa “brother to the tasting of brahman” (brahmāsvāda-sahodara) is from a later and simpler work, Viśvanātha’s Sāhityadarpaṇa (fourteenth century).

Note: Modern comparisons

Writers on rasa have compared the sahṛdaya with the “implied reader” of modern literary theory, sādhāraṇīkaraṇa with “aesthetic distance”, and the communication of emotion in performance with research on empathy and “emotional contagion”. Such comparisons can illuminate both sides, but they are analogies between theories built for different purposes. The claim, sometimes made, that modern neuroscience has “confirmed” the rasa theory has no basis in published research.

docs.title: 3.7 The Tamil Tradition: Meyppāṭu
docs.text:
Sanskrit was not the only language in which Indian theorists analysed the expression of emotion. The Tamil grammar Tolkāppiyam, whose third book on subject-matter (Poruḷatikāram) is of uncertain date but probably belongs to the first half of the first millennium CE, contains a section on meyppāṭu, literally “that which appears in the body”: the outward manifestation of feeling. It lists eight meyppāṭu: laughter (nakai), weeping (aḻukai), contempt or humiliation (iḷivaral), wonder (maruṭkai), fear (accam), pride or valour (perumitam), anger (vekuḷi) and joy (uvakai), each with four causes. The eight correspond closely to the eight rasas of the Nāṭyaśāstra, and scholars have long debated whether the Tamil scheme was borrowed from the Sanskrit, the Sanskrit from a wider South Asian tradition that also produced the Tamil, or whether the two developed in contact. The Tamil scheme belongs to a theory of poetry rather than of the stage, and its own context — the classification of poetic situations into “interior” (akam, love) and “exterior” (puṟam, war, praise and public life) — is quite different from Bharata’s (Parthasarathy 1993).

The Cilappatikāram, with its description of the dancer Mātavi and of performances in which emotion is shown through gesture and song, and the medieval commentaries on it, show that a Tamil vocabulary for the performing arts existed alongside the Sanskrit one. The Tamil Isai movement of the twentieth century, and some modern Bharatanāṭyam dancers, have drawn on this heritage to emphasise the Tamil roots of the dance. Tamil poetics is treated more fully in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

docs.title: 3.8 Training the Face and the Eyes
docs.text:
The theory of bhāva and rasa becomes performance only through years of training. In the Kerala theatres, where facial expression is most highly developed, actors practise daily exercises for the eyes, brows, cheeks and lips. Kathakaḷi students perform eye exercises (kaṇṇusādhakam) in which the eyes are moved in set patterns — side to side, up and down, in circles and figures of eight — while the head is held still, often in the early morning, so that the eyes acquire strength, range and control; they then learn to show each of the nine rasas by a fixed configuration of eyes, brows, cheeks and mouth, and to move from one to another without a break. Kūṭiyāṭṭam actors cultivate a similar discipline of the eyes (netrābhinaya); the great Cākyār actor Māṇi Mādhava Cākyār (1899–1990), whose book Nāṭyakalpadrumam describes the techniques of his tradition, was famed for the expressive power of his eyes (Zarrilli 2000; Richmond et al. 1990).

In the solo dance forms, abhinaya is taught more through the learning of particular compositions than through separate exercises. A student of Bharatanāṭyam or Odissi first learns the gestures for the words of a song and the basic expressions for the feelings it names, then gradually learns from the teacher how to vary and deepen them in repetition, and only after years of study improvises freely. Teachers in all the forms insist that facial expression cannot be learnt as a set of masks: the dancer must imagine the situation, the person addressed, the time and place, so that the expression arises from the imagined situation rather than being placed on the face. This is a practical version of the old debate about whether the actor should feel what he represents (above): the trained performer creates the conditions for a feeling without being overwhelmed by it.

docs.title: 3.9 Rasa and Its Audiences
docs.text:
The classical theory assumed a particular audience: courtly, educated in Sanskrit poetry, familiar with the conventions of the stage and with the stories represented. The audiences of Indian performance have always been more varied. Temple festival audiences included people of every class, many of whom did not understand Sanskrit; the audiences of Kathakaḷi in Kerala villages watched through the night, following the story through its familiar episodes rather than the words of the songs; the audiences of the courtesans’ salons were connoisseurs of Urdu and Braj poetry and of music, but not necessarily of Sanskrit poetics. Other aesthetic vocabularies were in use alongside the Sanskrit: the Persian and Urdu language of connoisseurship (zauq, “taste”), the Sufi concept of the ecstatic state (ḥāl) produced by music in the assembly (Chapter 7), and the devotional vocabulary of the bhakti movements, for which the aim of performance was not aesthetic savouring but love of god (Qureshi 1986).

In the twentieth century the classical forms acquired new audiences: the urban middle class, the national and international festival, and, through the diaspora and touring, spectators who did not share the languages or the religious culture of the performers. Dancers responded in different ways — by explaining the stories and gestures before performance, by choosing themes of wider appeal, by reducing the proportion of expressive dance in favour of rhythmic virtuosity, or by creating new work in which abhinaya is applied to modern subjects (Chapter 23). Whether rasa in Bharata’s sense can be experienced by a spectator without the cultural preparation the theory assumes is a question that performers and critics continue to discuss. The theory itself suggests a nuanced answer: the sahṛdaya is made, not born, and familiarity with a tradition is acquired by attending to it.

docs.title: 3.10 Rasa in the Living Forms
docs.text:
The modern performing arts use the vocabulary of rasa in different ways. Kūṭiyāṭṭam and Kathakaḷi retain the most elaborate techniques for showing the stable and transitory states (above), and in Kūṭiyāṭṭam the actor may spend an evening developing a single verse through the emotions it implies (Chapter 19). In Bharatanāṭyam, Kuchipudi, Odissi and Mohiniyāṭṭam, abhinaya is concentrated in the song-based items — the varṇam, padam, jāvaḷi and aṣṭapadī — and in improvised elaboration of a line. Kathak has its own expressive genre in the interpretation of ṭhumrī and bhajan, much of it improvised while seated or standing in place (bhāv batānā). In music, the association of rāgas with particular rasas is a later and looser tradition, discussed in Chapter 4.

Across all these forms the theory of rasa gives performers and connoisseurs a common language for talking about what a performance does to its audience. It is a language with a history: formed in the theatre of the early centuries CE, refined by Kashmiri philosophers, transformed by devotional theologians and revived, in the twentieth century, as part of the reconstruction of a “classical” Indian heritage. Used with that history in mind, it remains one of the most subtle vocabularies for the analysis of performance available in any tradition.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Bharata’s chapters on rasa and bhāva are translated in Ghosh (1950), and the rasa chapter with Abhinavagupta’s commentary in Masson and Patwardhan (1970). Pollock (2016) is an anthology of the main texts of the debate, with an introduction; Gnoli (1968) translates and discusses Abhinavagupta’s account of aesthetic experience; Raghavan (1940) is the classic study of the number of rasas. De (1960) surveys the history of the theory in poetics. For rasa in dance practice see Vatsyayan (1968).

docs.title: Chapter 4: Svara and Rāga
docs.text: The rāga is the central concept of the art music of South Asia, in both its northern (Hindustani) and southern (Karnatak) forms. A rāga is not simply a scale. It is a melodic entity with a recognisable personality: a set of notes with particular relations of emphasis, characteristic phrases and turns of melody, ornaments proper to particular notes, typical ways of ascending and descending, and associations of mood, season or time of day. Musicians speak of “singing a rāga” as one might speak of portraying a person; a composition is “in” a rāga, and an improvisation unfolds it. How such an entity can be described at all — by its notes (svara), the microtonal intervals (śruti) between them and the ornaments (gamaka) that carry them, by the history through which the concept took shape, by the schemes that classify it and the times and feelings attached to it — is the question that runs through the sections below. The Hindustani and Karnatak traditions are described in Chapters 7 and 8, and rhythm in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 4.1 The Word and the Idea
docs.text:
The word rāga comes from the root rañj, “to colour, to tinge, to delight”, and in ordinary Sanskrit means colour, passion or affection. Its use for a melodic type is first clearly attested in Mataṅga’s Bṛhaddeśī, a treatise on the “regional” (deśī) music of its time, composed in the second half of the first millennium CE (dates proposed range from about the sixth to the ninth century). Mataṅga’s definition, much quoted by later writers, plays on the root:

Mataṅga, Bṛhaddeśī 281 (Trivandrum edition)

yo ’sau dhvaniviśeṣas tu svaravarṇavibhūṣitaḥ rañjako janacittānāṃ sa ca rāga udāhṛtaḥ

“That particular sound, adorned with notes and melodic movements, which colours the minds of people, is called rāga.” Later writers quote the verse with the ending sa rāgaḥ kathito budhaiḥ, “is called rāga by the wise”.

The definition stresses two things: a rāga is a specific configuration of notes and movements (varṇa, ascending, descending, stationary and mixed melodic motion), and its purpose is to please or move the listener. Both ideas remain central. A modern musician would add that a rāga is learnt from compositions and from teachers, not from a definition, and that two rāgas with the same notes may be quite different because they use those notes in different ways (Widdess 1995; Jairazbhoy 1971).

docs.title: 4.2.1 The seven svaras
docs.text:
Indian music names seven notes (saptasvara): ṣaḍja (Sa), ṛṣabha (Ri or Re), gāndhāra (Ga), madhyama (Ma), pañcama (Pa), dhaivata (Dha) and niṣāda (Ni). The syllables sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni are used for solmisation (sargam in the north, svara in the south), and in modern practice Sa is the tonic, fixed at whatever pitch suits the singer or instrument and sounded continuously by the drone. The names are old and partly obscure. Later texts give traditional explanations — ṣaḍja is “born of six”, because it is produced with the help of the nose, throat, chest, palate, tongue and teeth — and associate each note with the cry of an animal or bird, from the peacock for Sa to the elephant for Ni. These associations are part of the tradition’s own imagery; they are not acoustic descriptions.

Sa and Pa are fixed (acala): they have only one position. The other five notes are “movable” (cala) and have two or more positions. In modern Hindustani terminology Re, Ga, Dha and Ni each have a natural (śuddha) and a flat (komal) form and Ma a natural and a sharp (tīvra) form, giving twelve positions in the octave. Karnatak theory uses the same twelve positions but names them differently, with three names each for the positions of Ri, Ga, Dha and Ni; because some positions have two names (the second Ri and the first Ga are the same pitch, as are the third Ri and the second Ga), the twelve positions (svarasthāna) carry sixteen names. The dual naming is what allows the 72-mela scheme described in Chapter 8 (Figure 8.2).

docs.title: 4.2.2 Śruti
docs.text:
Ancient theory measured the octave not in twelve semitones but in twenty-two śrutis, the smallest intervals “that can be heard”. The Nāṭyaśāstra and the Dattilam distribute them among the notes of the ṣaḍja-grāma in the proportions 4, 3, 2, 4, 4, 3, 2: Sa stands on the fourth śruti, Ri three above it, Ga two above Ri, and so on (Figure 4.1) (Nijenhuis 1970; Rowell 1992).

Figure 4.1. The twenty-two śrutis and the seven notes of the two grāmas of the Nāṭyaśāstra and the Dattilam. Each note stands on the last śruti of its interval, and the numbers below each row give the size of the intervals in śrutis (4, 3, 2, 4, 4, 3, 2 in the ṣaḍja-grāma). In the madhyama-grāma Pa stands one śruti lower, so that the intervals below and above it become 3 and 4.

The śrutis are not equal steps. The ancient texts use them as a means of counting intervals of three sizes — large (four śrutis), middle (three) and small (two) — and the experiment described in the Nāṭyaśāstra, in which two vīṇās are tuned and one is lowered step by step, shows how the twenty-two steps are counted and is usually interpreted as describing intervals of the kind found in just intonation; it does not divide the octave into twenty-two equal parts. Dividing 1,200 cents by twenty-two gives an average of about 54.5 cents, but this is only an average; descriptions of śruti as “the twenty-second root of two” misrepresent the theory.

The values of the śrutis were much debated by twentieth-century theorists, who proposed reconstructions based on just intonation, on cycles of fifths and on other principles. Measurements of actual performance, made by ethnomusicologists since the 1960s, have shown that intonation in both traditions is flexible: the pitch of a note depends on the rāga, the phrase and the ornament, so that the flat Ga of one rāga may differ audibly from the flat Ga of another (Jairazbhoy 1971). The twenty-two śrutis are best understood as a theoretical framework from the past rather than as a fixed set of pitches used today.

docs.title: 4.2.3 Grāma and mūrchanā
docs.text: The Nāṭyaśāstra derives its melodies from two parent scales (grāma). The ṣaḍja-grāma has the intervals given above; the madhyama-grāma differs in that Pa is one śruti lower. Later writers mention a third, the gāndhāra-grāma, which they say was current only in heaven and not on earth; the Nāṭyaśāstra itself names only two. Each grāma yields seven modal series (mūrchanā) by starting on each of its notes in turn. From these the text derives its eighteen jātis, melodic types defined by a set of characteristics: the initial note (graha), the predominant note (aṃśa), the upper and lower limits (tāra, mandra), the final and penultimate cadential notes (nyāsa, apanyāsa), the notes used sparingly or frequently (alpatva, bahutva), and the forms with six or five notes (ṣāḍava, auḍuva). Seven jātis are “pure”, named after the seven notes, and eleven are “mixed” (Rowell 1992; Widdess 1995). Several of these characteristics, especially the predominant note and the cadential notes, reappear in the later concept of rāga.

docs.title: 4.3 From Vedic Chant to Rāga: A History
4.3.1 Vedic chant
docs.text: The oldest Indian music that survives in continuous practice is the chanting of the Vedas. The hymns of the Ṛgveda (c. 1500–1200 BCE for the core) are recited with three pitch accents: the raised (udātta), the unraised (anudātta) and the “sounded” (svarita), a falling or compound accent that follows a raised syllable. The svarita is not a “middle” note between the other two; it is a movement of pitch. The Sāmaveda sets Ṛgvedic verses to melodies (sāman) that use a wider range of notes, transmitted orally in several schools and recorded in manuscripts with numerical and syllabic notations. The relation between Sāmavedic chant and the later art music is a matter of debate. The later tradition insisted on the connection, and the Nāṭyaśāstra says that song was taken from the Sāmaveda; but the scales and genres of the theatre music it describes were already different from those of the chant. Vedic chanting was inscribed by UNESCO on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (proclaimed 2003).

docs.title: 4.3.2 The music of the Nāṭyaśāstra and Dattila
docs.text: The Nāṭyaśāstra (c. 200 BCE–200 CE) and the slightly later Dattilam describe a highly systematised art music, the gāndharva, used in ritual and in the preliminaries of the theatre, alongside the songs of the plays themselves (dhruvā). Its theory — śruti, grāma, mūrchanā, jāti — was transmitted in the texts for more than a thousand years after the music it described had ceased to be performed (Nijenhuis 1970; Lath 1978).

docs.title: 4.3.3 Mataṅga and the deśī rāgas
docs.text: Mataṅga’s Bṛhaddeśī is the first surviving text to give a systematic account of rāgas. It names and describes melodic types called grāma-rāgas, derived from the jātis, and also regional types (bhāṣā, vibhāṣā and others), and it treats deśī music, the music of the regions and of ordinary people, as worthy of systematic description (Widdess 1995). The distinction between mārga, the “path” of the ancient, canonical music, and deśī, the music of the regions, remained fundamental to Indian music theory, and the history of Indian music can be read as a series of “regional” musics that were in turn codified and made classical.

docs.title: 4.3.4 The Saṅgītaratnākara
docs.text: For the history of rāga, the decisive text after Mataṅga is Śārṅgadeva’s Saṅgītaratnākara (first half of the thirteenth century), whose author, contents and commentators are described in Section 6.5. It names 264 rāgas, sorting them into the categories inherited from Mataṅga and separating those “famous in former times” from those “famous now”, and it became the common authority of north and south. Yet by the time of its commentators the music it described had already changed, and much of its rāga theory could no longer be related precisely to practice. Its opening chapter, which describes the body as the seat of sound and relates the production of musical sound to the vital breath, the centres (cakra) and channels of yogic physiology and the doctrine of nāda, belongs to the religious and philosophical frame of the work, not to its musical analysis.

docs.title: 4.3.5 Divergence of north and south
docs.text:
From the fourteenth century the music of the north and the south developed in different directions, though they continued to share much theory and a common vocabulary. In the north, music at the courts of the Delhi sultans and their successors absorbed Persian and Central Asian musicians, instruments and genres; new rāga names appeared, some of them Persian or Arabic in origin (Hijāz, Zīlaf and probably Yaman), and theorists from the sixteenth century onwards wrote in both Sanskrit and Persian to reconcile older theory with new practice (Chapter 7). In the south, the theorists of Vijayanagara and its successor states classified rāgas under parent scales (mela), a line of thought that led from the treatises of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries (Section 6.6) to the scheme of seventy-two melakartas, whose history is told in Section 8.3. The north reorganised its rāgas in its own way in the early twentieth century, in V. N. Bhatkhande’s system of ten thāṭs (Bor et al. 2010; Widdess 1995). Table 4.1 lists the main landmarks.

Table 4.1. Landmarks in the history of melodic theory (dates approximate) Text or development (date) Significance Vedic chant (from c. 1500 BCE) Accented recitation; Sāmavedic melodies Nāṭyaśāstra (c. 200 BCE–200 CE), Dattilam (early centuries CE) Śruti, two grāmas, mūrchanā, eighteen jātis Mataṅga, Bṛhaddeśī (second half of 1st millennium CE) First systematic account of rāga; deśī music Śārṅgadeva, Saṅgītaratnākara (13th century) Comprehensive synthesis; 264 rāgas named Rāmāmātya, Svaramelakalānidhi (c. 1550) Classification of rāgas under melas Veṅkaṭamakhin, Caturdaṇḍīprakāśikā (mid-17th century) The 72 possible melas Govindācārya, Saṅgrahacūḍāmaṇi (18th century) Named scheme of 72 complete (sampūrṇa) melakartas V. N. Bhatkhande (1860–1936) Ten thāṭs; codification of Hindustani rāgas

docs.title: 4.4 The Anatomy of a Rāga
docs.text:
Although the two traditions describe rāgas in somewhat different terms, the elements they attend to are similar; Table 4.2 gives some of them for well-known Hindustani rāgas.

Notes and their forms. The selection of notes, which may differ in ascent and descent. A rāga may use all seven notes (sampūrṇa), six (ṣāḍava) or five (auḍava); some use more than one form of a note. Ascent and descent. Āroha and avaroha summarise the typical upward and downward movement. They are often not straight scales but zigzag (vakra) patterns: Rāga Bhīmpalāsī, for example, omits Re and Dha in ascent but uses them in descent. Important notes. Hindustani theory names a predominant note (vādī) and a second, consonant one (saṃvādī), usually a fourth or fifth apart; other notes are “assonant” (anuvādī) and notes foreign to the rāga “dissonant” (vivādī). The concepts derive from older theory, but their application to individual rāgas owes much to Bhatkhande, and musicians do not always agree with his assignments. Karnatak theory speaks of notes that give the rāga its life (jīva svara) and of notes on which phrases rest (nyāsa). Characteristic phrases. The pakaḍ (“grip”) or calan (“movement”) of a Hindustani rāga, and the prayogas or sañcāras of a Karnatak one, are the phrases by which a listener recognises it. Rāgas with the same notes are distinguished above all by their phrases: Bhūpālī and Deśkār use the same five notes, but Bhūpālī centres on the lower part of the octave and Deśkār on the upper. Ornamentation. The way particular notes are approached, sustained or oscillated (see below). Range and register. Some rāgas dwell in the lower register, others in the upper. Associations. Mood, time of day or season, and, for some rāgas, a deity or iconographic image.

docs.title: 4.4.1 Gamaka
docs.text:
Gamaka, ornamentation in the widest sense, is indispensable to rāga. The Saṅgītaratnākara lists fifteen kinds, among them tiripa, sphurita, kampita, līna, āndolita, vali, āhata, ullāsita, humphita, mudrita and miśrita (Shringy and Sharma 1978). Karnatak theory traditionally speaks of ten kinds (daśavidha gamaka), including āroha and avaroha (ascent and descent), ḍhālu (a sliding movement), sphurita and pratyāhata (stressed repetitions), kampita (oscillation) and āndola (swing), and modern teachers also speak of jāru (slides); in practice the heavy oscillations of notes such as Ga and Ni in Rāga Tōḍi or Śaṅkarābharaṇam are essential to their identity. Hindustani musicians use a different vocabulary: mīṇḍ (a slide between notes), kaṇ (a grace note), andolan (a slow oscillation, as on the flat Ga and Dha of Darbārī Kānaḍā), gamak (a forceful oscillation), murkī and khaṭkā (quick turns). The intonation of a note cannot be separated from the ornament that carries it.

docs.title: 4.5.1 Rāga and rāgiṇī
docs.text: From about the fourteenth century, northern writers organised rāgas into “families”: six principal male rāgas, each with five or six wives (rāgiṇī) and sometimes sons (putra) and daughters. Several different systems (mata) were current, named after legendary or earlier authorities — Śiva, Bharata, Hanumān, Kallinātha — and they disagree about which rāgas were principal and which rāgiṇīs belonged to whom; in the system associated with Hanumān the six were Bhairava, Kauśika (Mālkauns), Hindola, Dīpaka, Śrī and Megha. The scheme was not a musical classification in the strict sense, since a rāgiṇī need not share notes with her rāga; it was a poetic and mnemonic way of ordering a growing repertoire (Ebeling 1973).

docs.title: 4.5.2 Rāgamālā: rāgas in poetry and painting
docs.text:
The family system inspired a body of verse in Sanskrit, Hindi and Persian describing each rāga and rāgiṇī as a person in a scene — a hero, a lovelorn woman, an ascetic — often with a season and a time of day; texts such as Kṣemakarṇa’s Rāgamālā (late sixteenth century) became the basis for sets of paintings. Rāgamālā (“garland of rāgas”) painting flourished from the late sixteenth to the nineteenth century in the Rajput, Deccani, Mughal and Pahari courts. Each painting depicts the scene associated with its rāga, usually with an inscription naming it and sometimes the verse that describes it (Figure 4.2). The paintings are among the most beautiful products of Indian visual art; they illustrate the poetic and emotional associations of rāgas, not their notes (Ebeling 1973; Wade 1998).

Figure 4.2. Kāfī, from a rāgamālā series of the Bundi or Kota school, Rajasthan, c. 1725. The Devanāgarī inscription at the top calls Kāfī the daughter (putrī) of Megha rāga, the rāga of the rainy season: this set places her in the tier of the rāga’s children rather than among his wives (rāgiṇīs), one of the ways in which the family systems differ. Ragamala painting, Bundi/Kotah, c. 1725; Klaus Ebeling Ragamala collection, Cornell University Library; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 4.5.3 Mela and thāṭ
docs.text:
The southern mela system and the northern thāṭ system both group rāgas under parent scales. In the south, the seventy-two melakartas are complete seven-note scales generated systematically, and every rāga is assigned to one of them as a “derived” (janya) rāga; the scheme and its mathematics are described in Chapter 8. In the north, Bhatkhande grouped the rāgas current in his time under ten thāṭs, each named after a well-known rāga (Table 4.3) (Bhatkhande 1910). Both systems are classifications of scales and so cannot capture the phrases and ornaments that distinguish rāgas with the same notes; and the thāṭ system does not accommodate every rāga comfortably. They remain useful for teaching and for orientation.

Table 4.3. The ten thāṭs of Bhatkhande (komal notes in lower case; M\('\) = tīvra Ma) Thāṭ Notes Some rāgas Bilāval S R G M P D N Bilāval, Alhaiyā Bilāval, Deśkār Khamāj S R G M P D n Khamāj, Deś, Tilak Kāmod Kāfī S R g M P D n Kāfī, Bāgeśrī, Bhīmpalāsī Āsāvarī S R g M P d n Āsāvarī, Jaunpurī, Darbārī Kānaḍā Bhairavī S r g M P d n Bhairavī, Mālkauns, Bilāskhānī Toḍī Bhairav S r G M P d N Bhairav, Rāmkalī, Jogiyā Kalyāṇ S R G M\('\) P D N Yaman, Bhūpālī, Hindol Mārvā S r G M\('\) P D N Mārvā, Pūriyā, Sohinī Pūrvī S r G M\('\) P d N Pūrvī, Śrī, Pūriyā Dhanāśrī Toḍī S r g M\('\) P d N Toḍī, Multānī, Gujarī Toḍī

docs.title: 4.6 North and South Compared
docs.text:
Because the Hindustani and Karnatak traditions share a common ancestry and a common set of twelve note positions, many of their scales coincide, and some rāga names are used in both. The correspondences are a frequent source of confusion. Two rāgas with the same scale may be quite different in phrase, ornament and character; two rāgas with the same name may have different scales. Table 4.4 sets out the most important correspondences between Bhatkhande’s thāṭs and the Karnatak melakartas, and some rāgas that share a scale.

Table 4.4. Shared scales in the two systems (komal notes in lower case; M\('\) = tīvra Ma) Scale Hindustani thāṭ Karnatak melakarta Rāgas sharing the scale S R G M P D N Bilāval 29 Dhīraśaṅkarābharaṇam Bilāval; Śaṅkarābharaṇam S R G M P D n Khamāj 28 Harikāmbhōji Khamāj; Harikāmbhōji S R g M P D n Kāfī 22 Kharaharapriyā Kāfī; Kharaharapriyā S R g M P d n Āsāvarī 20 Naṭabhairavi Jaunpurī; Naṭabhairavi S r g M P d n Bhairavī 8 Hanumatoḍi Hindustani Bhairavī; Karnatak Tōḍi S r G M P d N Bhairav 15 Māyāmāḷavagauḷa Bhairav; Māyāmāḷavagauḷa S R G M\('\) P D N Kalyāṇ 65 Mecakalyāṇi Yaman; Kalyāṇi S r G M\('\) P d N Pūrvī 51 Kāmavardhini Pūrvī; Pantuvarāḷi S r G M\('\) P D N Mārvā 53 Gamanaśrama Mārvā; Gamanaśrama S r g M\('\) P d N Toḍī 45 Śubhapantuvarāḷi Hindustani Toḍī; Śubhapantuvarāḷi

Some examples show how misleading names can be. The Karnatak Tōḍi uses the scale of the Hindustani Bhairavī thāṭ, with every movable note in its lower form, while the Hindustani Toḍī has a sharp Ma and natural Ni and corresponds to a different mela. The Karnatak Bhairavi is not the Hindustani Bhairavī: it belongs to the twentieth mela, uses the higher Dha in ascent and the lower Dha in descent, and has a different character. The Karnatak Hindōḷam, a pentatonic rāga (S g M d n), corresponds in its notes to the Hindustani Mālkauns, whereas the Hindustani Hindol is quite another rāga with a sharp Ma. Pentatonic rāgas such as Mōhanam in the south and Bhūpālī in the north share the same five notes (S R G P D) and are often treated as equivalents, but each is sung with the phrasing and ornamentation of its own tradition.

Exchange between the two systems has continued into modern times. The Karnatak rāga Haṃsadhvani, traditionally credited to Rāmasvāmi Dīkṣitar, the father of Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar, was taken into Hindustani music in the twentieth century; Kīravāṇi and Cārukeśi, both melakartas, are now also played by northern musicians, often in a lighter style. In the other direction, Karnatak musicians have adopted a number of northern rāgas, usually with the suffix “Hindustani” or under names such as Behāg, Sindhubhairavi and Dēś, and sing them mainly in the lighter items at the end of a concert. Such borrowings are always adaptations: a rāga that passes from one system to the other acquires the ornamentation and phrasing of its new home (Viswanathan and Allen 2004; Jairazbhoy 1971).

docs.title: 4.7 Three Rāgas in Portrait
docs.text: General descriptions of rāga can be made concrete by looking at a few individual rāgas as musicians describe them. The following portraits are brief and simplified; every musician would add qualifications.

docs.title: 4.7.1 Yaman and Kalyāṇi
docs.text:
Yaman is perhaps the first serious rāga that a Hindustani student learns, and one of the most frequently performed. It uses all seven notes with sharp Ma, and its character comes from the way it moves: phrases often begin from Ni below the tonic and rise through Re to Ga (N R G), so that Sa is passed over in ascent; Ga and Ni are the resting points, and the sharp Ma is approached and left smoothly. It is sung in the first part of the night and is regarded as serene and expansive. Its name is usually taken to be Persian, and older sources distinguish it from the closely related Kalyāṇ, a name of Sanskrit origin; the compound name Yaman Kalyāṇ is now used for a variant that also touches natural Ma in descent (Jairazbhoy 1971).

The Karnatak Kalyāṇi uses the same scale but a quite different vocabulary of phrases and gamakas, and is regarded as a “major” rāga suitable for extended ālāpana and for the main item of a concert. All three composers of the Karnatak “Trinity” wrote in it, and Tyāgarāja’s song Nidhi cāla sukhamā (“Is wealth happiness?”) is among its best-known compositions. A listener who knows only one of the two will recognise the shared scale in the other, but not the rāga.

docs.title: 4.7.2 Bhairav and Māyāmāḷavagauḷa
docs.text: Bhairav, named after the fierce form of Śiva, is the principal morning rāga of the north and was the first of the six male rāgas in several of the medieval family systems. Its flat Re and flat Dha are sung with a slow oscillation (andolan), and the contrast between these heavily inflected notes and the natural Ga and Ni gives it its solemn, devotional character. The Karnatak Māyāmāḷavagauḷa has the same scale but is sung without the slow oscillations of Bhairav and with its own phrases. It has a special place in Karnatak teaching: by a tradition that goes back to Purandaradāsa in the sixteenth century, the elementary exercises (sarali varisai, janṭa varisai, alaṅkāra) have been taught in this rāga, so that it is the first rāga every southern student learns (Viswanathan and Allen 2004).

docs.title: 4.7.3 The two Toḍīs
docs.text: The Hindustani Toḍī, usually called Miyāṃ kī Toḍī and associated by tradition with Tānsen, is a late-morning rāga with flat Re, Ga and Dha and sharp Ma; it dwells on the flat Ga and Dha, and its Pa is used sparingly. The Karnatak Tōḍi, as noted above, has the scale of the Hindustani Bhairavī and is one of the most important rāgas of the southern repertoire, almost inseparable from its ornaments: the flat Ga, Dha and Ni are not sung as steady pitches but as oscillating, sliding movements, and a performance of Tōḍi by a senior musician can extend for an hour or more of ālāpana, tānam, composition and improvisation. The two rāgas share a name and a sombre beauty, but nothing else that a listener would notice. The example shows why both traditions insist that a rāga is defined by its movement and ornament, and not by its scale alone.

docs.title: 4.8 Rāga beyond the Art Music
docs.text:
The rāga is the organising principle not only of the concert music of the two classical traditions but of much of the devotional and popular music of South Asia. The Tamil Śaiva hymns of the Tēvāram are sung in melodic modes called paṇ, inherited from early Tamil music, which twentieth-century scholars have tried, with varying success, to identify with modern Karnatak rāgas. The hymns of the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, are arranged under thirty-one main rāgas, from Sirī Rāg at the beginning to Jaijāvantī at the end, and the tradition of Sikh kīrtan has preserved some rāga forms that differ from those of the modern Hindustani concert (Singh 2000). The devotional song traditions of the Vārkarīs of Maharashtra, the Vaiṣṇavas of Bengal and Assam and the Kṛṣṇa temples of Vraj (haveli saṅgīt) all use rāgas, sometimes in archaic forms.

The movement also runs the other way. Many rāgas of the art music have names that point to regional or folk origins — Māṇḍ from Rajasthan, Pahāṛī from the hills, Sindhurā, Sorath, Gujarī — and the “light” rāgas used in ṭhumrī and in the closing items of concerts, such as Pīlū, Khamāj, Kāfī and Bhairavī, are flexible, mixing notes of more than one form and borrowing phrases freely. Indian film music, for most of the twentieth century the most widely heard music in South Asia, has drawn constantly on rāgas, sometimes in faithful settings and more often by borrowing the mood and characteristic phrases of a rāga in songs that also use harmony and Western instruments (Chapter 23) (Morcom 2007). In this wider sense, the rāga is less a technical device of a learned art than a shared way of thinking about melody across the subcontinent.

docs.title: 4.9.1 The time theory
docs.text:
Hindustani musicians associate most rāgas with a time of day or night, divided into eight watches (prahar) of about three hours, and some with a season: the Malhār rāgas with the monsoon, Basant and Bahār with spring. Associations of rāgas with times and seasons are found in medieval texts, but the systematic “time theory” (samay) taught today was formulated largely by Bhatkhande and his contemporaries, who related it to the notes used. In outline: rāgas with flat Re and natural Ga and Ni (Bhairav, Pūrvī, Mārvā) belong to the twilight hours of dawn and dusk (sandhiprakāśa); rāgas with natural Re, Ga and Dha follow them in the morning and in the first part of the night (Bilāval, Yaman); and rāgas with flat Ga and Ni belong to the middle of the day and of the night (Āsāvarī, Kāfī, Darbārī). Rāgas with sharp Ma are mostly evening rāgas. Table 4.5 gives conventional assignments (Bhatkhande 1910; Jairazbhoy 1971).

Table 4.5. Conventional times of some Hindustani rāgas Time Rāgas Dawn Bhairav, Rāmkalī, Lalit (just before dawn) Morning Toḍī, Bilāval, Āsāvarī, Jaunpurī Midday Sāraṅg (Vṛndāvanī, Gauḍ) Afternoon Bhīmpalāsī, Multānī, Paṭdīp Dusk Pūriyā Dhanāśrī, Mārvā, Śrī First part of the night Yaman, Bhūpālī Second part of the night Bihāg, Deś, Kedār, Khamāj Late night Darbārī Kānaḍā, Mālkauns, Bāgeśrī Before dawn Sohinī, Paraj

The scheme is a convention, and an elastic one. Musicians differ over the times of many rāgas; Bhairavī is sung at the end of a concert whatever the hour; seasonal rāgas may be sung at any time in their season; and recordings, broadcasting and evening concerts have loosened the practice. Karnatak music has a few comparable associations (Bhūpāḷam at dawn, for example) but does not observe a systematic time theory. There is no evidence that the time theory reflects a physiological effect of particular scales at particular hours, though such claims are sometimes made.

docs.title: 4.9.2 Rāga and rasa
docs.text: Medieval texts assigned rasas to jātis and rāgas, and musicians continue to speak of the mood or feeling (bhāva) of a rāga: the serious gravity of Darbārī, the devotional tenderness of Bhairavī, the brightness of Kalyāṇi in the south. Such associations are real for listeners formed in the tradition, but they are learnt associations, they vary between musicians and periods, and the same rāga can carry different moods in different compositions. The rasa theory itself, formulated for drama, was applied to music only loosely (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 4.10 Improvisation
docs.text: A rāga is realised in performance through a combination of composition and improvisation (manodharma, literally “the mind’s own way”). Both traditions begin with an unmetred exploration of the rāga: the Hindustani ālāp and the Karnatak ālāpana. In Hindustani instrumental music the ālāp is followed by joḍ, with a steady pulse but no rhythmic cycle, and jhālā, in which rapid strokes on the drone strings create a climax. In metred music, improvisation takes many forms: rapid melodic runs (tān in the north; kalpana svara in the south, sung to the names of the notes), variations on a line of the text (bol-tān, bol-banāv in the north; niraval in the south), and rhythmic play with the words and the beat (Chapter 5). The balance between fixed composition and improvisation differs between genres and between the two traditions; the Karnatak repertoire places greater weight on the large body of fixed compositions, the Hindustani khayāl on the elaboration of brief compositions (Chapters 7 and 8).

docs.title: 4.11 Learning Rāga
docs.text: Rāgas are learnt orally, through the imitation of a teacher, in a relationship that in the hereditary communities of musicians was also a relationship of family, patronage and loyalty (Chapter 1). Teaching proceeds from exercises in pitch and rhythm (the Karnatak sarali varisai and alaṅkāras, the Hindustani palṭās), through simple songs, to compositions in which the phrases of a rāga are embedded, and finally to improvisation. A saying current among musicians, “śruti is the mother, laya the father”, expresses the priority given to secure intonation and rhythm. Notation, introduced on a large scale in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries by Bhatkhande, Paluskar and the southern publishers of compositions, made repertoire widely available but has never replaced oral teaching, because what distinguishes a rāga — its ornaments and intonation — is precisely what notation cannot record (Section 4.12).

docs.title: 4.12 Notation and the Written Record
docs.text: Indian music has been transmitted above all by ear, from teacher to pupil, but it has never been entirely without writing. Its notations have usually been aids to memory for people who already knew the music, not scores from which an unfamiliar piece could be performed, and their history shows what each period thought worth fixing in writing and what it left to the teacher.

docs.title: 4.12.1 Vedic chant and the treatises
docs.text: The oldest Indian musical notations belong to the Sāmaveda. The songbooks (gāna) of the Kauthuma school mark the melodic movement of each syllable with small numerals written above the text, and other schools use letters or syllables for the same purpose; Wayne Howard’s study shows that these signs record the pattern of the chant only in combination with an oral tradition that supplies its details (Howard 1977). From the Nāṭyaśāstra and the Dattilam onwards, theorists referred to the notes by the first syllables of their names — sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni — and this solfa became the basis of all later Indian notation. The medieval treatises, the Saṅgītaratnākara above all, illustrate their accounts of rāgas and compositions with short notated examples in these syllables, with additional signs for duration and ornament. The examples are often corrupt in the manuscripts, but Richard Widdess has shown that they can be read critically and used to recover the melodic outlines of early rāgas (Widdess 1995).

docs.title: 4.12.2 The Kudumiyamalai inscription
docs.text:
The most remarkable early musical document of India is a rock inscription at Kudumiyamalai in the Pudukkottai district of Tamil Nadu, carved in a southern script of the Pallava period and usually dated to the seventh or eighth century. It sets out melodic material in seven sections, each headed by the name of a grāma-rāga of the kind described by Mataṅga, written in solfa syllables whose vowels are varied (sa, si, su, se and so on), apparently to mark ornaments or variants of the notes. A closing line ascribes the composition to a king who was a disciple of a teacher named Rudrācārya; the identity of the king is uncertain, and an attribution to the Pallava king Mahendravarman I, once popular, is not proved. The inscription shows that a notation of this kind was in use in the south long before the great treatises, and that the grāma-rāgas of the theorists were practical melodic types, studied by students and taught by masters (Widdess 1979, 1995). Figure 4.3 shows part of the inscribed rock face.

Figure 4.3. Detail of the music inscription at Kudumiyamalai, Pudukkottai district, Tamil Nadu (seventh or eighth century), carved in a southern script of the Pallava period. A group of larger characters is set in a carved frame among the rows of smaller syllables. Photo: R.K.Lakshmi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 4.12.3 Printed notation in the north
docs.text: Printing brought notation into a new role. From the late eighteenth century European residents in India transcribed Indian songs into staff notation, usually adding harmonised accompaniments for the drawing room, and in the nineteenth century writers in Bengal debated whether staff notation or a notation in Indian script was better suited to Indian music; Indian notations prevailed (Farrell 1997). The two great reformers of the early twentieth century each devised their own system. Bhatkhande’s notation writes the solfa syllables in Devanāgarī, marks the lower and upper octaves with a dot below or above the syllable, flat (komal) notes with a short line beneath and the sharp Ma with a vertical stroke above, and shows the divisions of the tāla with the signs used for sam, tālī and khālī (Chapter 5). Through his six-volume collection of compositions, the Kramik Pustak Mālikā, and the music schools that used it, his system became the standard notation of north India. Paluskar’s rival system, with its own signs, was used in the schools of the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya (Bakhle 2005). In Bengal the songs of Rabindranath Tagore were published with their notation, a practice that helped to fix the melodies of Rabīndrasaṅgīt and to make them a canon.

docs.title: 4.12.4 Printed notation in the south
docs.text: In the south the decisive publication was Subbarāma Dīkṣitar’s Saṅgīta Sampradāya Pradarśini (1904), produced under the patronage of the court of Ettayapuram. Written in Telugu script, it gives the compositions of Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar and of other composers in notation, with a set of signs for the different kinds of gamaka, together with descriptions of the rāgas in the tradition of Veṅkaṭamakhin; it remains a primary source for the Dīkṣitar repertoire (Subbarāma Dīkṣitar 1904). A few years earlier A. M. Chinnaswami Mudaliar had published Karnatak compositions in European staff notation. In the following decades publishers in Madras printed the songs of Tyāgarāja and many other composers in Tamil and Telugu notation for the new middle-class students of music. Amanda Weidman has shown that notation, in the hands of the new teachers and institutions, both preserved the repertoire and changed ideas about it: a printed version came to be regarded as the “correct” one, against which the variants of different lineages could be judged (Weidman 2006).

docs.title: 4.12.5 What notation does not record
docs.text: Every Indian notation records the sequence of notes and their relation to the tāla more fully than it records ornament, intonation and dynamics, and none records the improvisation that is central to performance. Musicians therefore use notation to learn and remember compositions, but learn the rāga itself from a teacher. Dance has no traditional notation at all: the sequences of the dance forms are transmitted through the dancer’s body and through the recited syllables of the rhythmic passages, and the dance treatises describe positions and movements, not choreographies. Since the mid-twentieth century the sound recording, and since the late twentieth century the video recording, have done for performance what notation never could, and have become the principal written record, in the widest sense, of the performing arts (Chapter 23).

docs.title: 4.13 Rāga and Healing: Claims and Evidence
docs.text:
Medieval texts and later popular tradition attribute extraordinary powers to rāgas: Dīpak to kindle lamps, Megh Malhār to bring rain, others to heal particular diseases. In the modern period a “rāga therapy” movement has assigned specific rāgas to specific ailments — anxiety, insomnia, high blood pressure — and such lists circulate widely.

Health and Safety Note

Listening to music can be relaxing and pleasurable, and music therapy is a recognised discipline in which trained therapists use music to support the care of patients. But there is no good evidence that particular rāgas treat or cure particular diseases. Published studies of “rāga therapy” are mostly small and uncontrolled, and claims that a rāga lowers blood pressure, cures insomnia or aligns the body with circadian rhythms should be treated as claims, not as established facts. Music is not a substitute for medical diagnosis or treatment.

The legends of Tānsen’s Dīpak setting lamps alight or a singer’s Malhār bringing rain belong to the poetry of music, in which a rāga performed perfectly embodies the season or scene it evokes. They tell us how much music mattered to its listeners, not what it can do to the body.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Rowell (1992) is the best introduction to early Indian musical thought, and Widdess (1995) the authoritative study of early rāgas. Jairazbhoy (1971) analyses the structure and evolution of Hindustani rāgs, and Nijenhuis (1974) surveys the history of theory. Shringy and Sharma (1978) translates the Saṅgītaratnākara. On rāgamālā painting see Ebeling (1973), and on music and painting at the Mughal court Wade (1998). On early notation see Widdess (1979). Beck (1993) discusses the religious ideas of sound (nāda) that frame much of the theory.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Tāla: Rhythm and Metre
docs.text: If rāga organises pitch, tāla organises time. A tāla is a cycle of a fixed number of time units, divided into sections and marked by a pattern of claps, waves and finger-counts or by the strokes of a drum; it repeats throughout a composition or improvisation, and every phrase is measured against it. The first beat of the cycle (sam in Hindustani music, samam in Karnatak) is the point of arrival towards which rhythmic and melodic phrases are directed and on which performers and listeners meet. Indian rhythm is cyclical in this practical sense: a performance is a succession of cycles, often hundreds of them, within which the musicians create tension and release. The ancient theory, the two modern systems, tempo and rhythmic transformation (layakārī), the spoken languages of the drums and the cadences built on them are taken here in that order; the drums themselves are described in Chapter 10, and rhythm in dance in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 5.1 Basic Terms
docs.text: Tāla. The rhythmic cycle; also, in older usage, the hand gestures that keep time. A traditional etymology, found in medieval texts, derives tā from Śiva’s tāṇḍava and la from Pārvatī’s lāsya; it is a pious word-play, not a historical derivation. Mātrā (Hindustani), akṣara (Karnatak). The unit of time, the “beat” of the cycle. Āvartan (Hindustani), āvartana or āvarta (Karnatak). One complete cycle. Vibhāg (Hindustani), aṅga (Karnatak). A section of the cycle. Tālī and khālī. In Hindustani music the sections are marked by a clap (tālī) or, for the “empty” section, by a wave of the hand (khālī); on the drum the khālī section is usually played without the resonant bass strokes, so that a listener can tell where in the cycle the music is. Sam. The first beat of the cycle and the strongest point of arrival. Laya. Tempo; more broadly, the sense of a steady flow of time. Karnatak musicians also speak of kāla, the “speed” or level of subdivision. Ṭhekā. In Hindustani music, the standard pattern of drum syllables (bol) that identifies a tāla and is played as the accompaniment’s base.

docs.title: 5.2 Tāla in the Ancient Texts
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra (ch. 31 in Ghosh’s numbering) and the Dattilam describe a system of time-measure for the ritual and theatre music of their age. Time was measured in units of short (laghu), long (guru) and extra-long (pluta) duration, borrowed from the prosody of syllables, and organised into a small number of “path” (mārga) tālas, among them cañcatpuṭa, cācapuṭa, ṣaṭpitāputraka and udghaṭṭa. The units were made audible and visible by gestures (kriyā): sounded ones such as the clap with the right hand (śamyā), with the left (tāla) or with both (sannipāta), and silent ones (niḥśabda) such as counting on the fingers or moving the hand outwards and inwards. These tālas could be performed at different speeds and in more or less elaborate forms (Rowell 1992; Lath 1978; Nijenhuis 1970).

As with melody, the ancient mārga system was preserved in the texts long after it ceased to be practised. The Saṅgītaratnākara (thirteenth century) describes the mārga tālas and also lists 120 “regional” (deśī) tālas, many of them the ancestors of later southern tālas. Its chapter on tāla applies to rhythmic patterns the combinatorial procedures that Indian prosodists had developed for metres: the systematic listing of all possible patterns of a given length (prastāra), the calculation of their number (saṅkhyā), and the finding of a pattern from its position in the list (naṣṭa) and of its position from the pattern (uddiṣṭa) (Shringy and Sharma 1978). The method goes back to the prosodist Piṅgala’s Chandaḥsūtra, composed in the last centuries BCE, and the triangular array of numbers used to count combinations of long and short syllables — the array known in Europe as “Pascal’s triangle” — is explicitly described in Halāyudha’s tenth-century commentary on Piṅgala. These are genuine achievements of Indian combinatorics, discussed further in Volume 11, Gaṇita; they are historical, not evidence that musicians performed mathematics in the modern sense.

Later writers summarised the theory of tāla under ten “vital elements” (daśa prāṇa): time (kāla); the “path” (mārga), the scale of duration; the actions that mark the units (kriyā); the sections of the cycle (aṅga); the starting point (graha); the class of a tāla by its basic number (jāti); its subdivisions (kalā); tempo (laya); the pattern of change of tempo or of phrase length (yati); and the systematic permutation of patterns (prastāra). The scheme is still taught in Karnatak music and dance, and several of its terms — graha, jāti, yati — have kept their technical meanings in modern practice (below and Chapter 13). Medieval and early modern texts also list large numbers of deśī tālas, and lists of 108 tālas, each with its sequence of aṅgas, were preserved by the dance masters of the south, who used some of them in composing rhythmic passages for dance.

docs.title: 5.3.1 The sūḷādi sapta tālas
docs.text:
Modern Karnatak music organises its principal tālas in a scheme of seven “sūḷādi” tālas, so called after a genre of composition attributed to Purandaradāsa (1484–1564) and the Haridāsa composers. Each tāla is a fixed sequence of three kinds of section (aṅga):

Laghu (symbol I): a clap followed by finger-counts; its length is variable. Drutam (symbol O): a clap and a wave, two beats. Anudrutam (symbol U): a single clap, one beat.

The length of the laghu is fixed by the “class” (jāti) of the tāla: three beats in tiśra, four in catuśra, five in khaṇḍa, seven in miśra and nine in saṅkīrṇa. Each of the seven tālas can therefore take five forms, giving thirty-five tālas in all (Table 5.1). Each beat can in turn be subdivided in five ways (gati or naḍai, below), so that theorists speak of 175 tālas (Viswanathan and Allen 2004).

Table 5.1. The seven sūḷādi tālas and the number of beats in each of the five jātis (in bold, the standard jāti of each tāla, understood when the tāla is named alone; Ādi tāla is the catuśra form of Triputa) Tāla Aṅgas Tiśra (3) Catuśra (4) Khaṇḍa (5) Miśra (7) Saṅkīrṇa (9) Dhruva I O I I 11 14 17 23 29 Maṭhya I O I 8 10 12 16 20 Rūpaka O I 5 6 7 9 11 Jhampa I U O 6 7 8 10 12 Triputa I O O 7 8 9 11 13 Aṭa I I O O 10 12 14 18 22 Eka I 3 4 5 7 9

docs.title: 5.3.2 Tālas in practice
docs.text:
Only a few of these tālas are in common use. By far the most frequent is Ādi tāla (“first” tāla), which is catuśra-jāti Triputa: a laghu of four beats (a clap and three finger-counts) followed by two drutams (clap–wave, clap–wave), eight beats in all (Figures 5.2 and 5.1). Ādi tāla is used in two speeds, with one or two beats of the hand to each akṣara (the latter, “two-kaḷai” form, for slow varṇams and long kṛtis). Rūpaka (in practice often counted as three beats of double length), Miśra Jhampa, Khaṇḍa Aṭa and Tiśra Triputa are also used. Two tālas outside the sūḷādi scheme are very common in songs and dance music: Miśra Cāpu, of seven beats grouped 3+2+2, and Khaṇḍa Cāpu, of five beats grouped 2+3; their name, “cāpu”, is thought to reflect their origin in folk and devotional song.

The first exercise every Karnatak student learns shows how a melody is laid against the hand-count. The sarali varisai in Rāga Māyāmāḷavagauḷa (Chapter 4) runs up the scale and down again, one note to each beat of Ādi tāla, and is then repeated at twice and four times the density; Figure 5.1 notates the first of these exercises in its first two speeds.

Figure 5.1. The first sarali varisai exercise in Rāga Māyāmāḷavagauḷa, set to Ādi tāla: the eight beats are marked by a clap and three finger-counts (the laghu) and two claps each followed by a wave (the two drutams). At first speed one note falls on each beat, ascending in one cycle and descending in the next; at second speed two notes fall on each beat. R\(_1\), G\(_3\), M\(_1\), D\(_1\) and N\(_3\) are the forms of the notes in this rāga (Figure 8.2); a dot marks the upper Sa.

docs.title: 5.3.3 Gati and naḍai
docs.text:
Within any tāla each beat can be subdivided into three, four, five, seven or nine units, the five gatis (or naḍais, “gaits”), each recited with its own syllables (Table 5.2). A performer may change the gati while the tāla remains the same, moving for example from four to five subdivisions per beat; such changes are a basic resource of Karnatak improvisation and of the drum solo.

Table 5.2. The five gatis (subdivisions of the beat) and their recitation syllables Gati Units per beat Syllables Tiśra 3 ta ki ṭa Catuśra 4 ta ka dhi mi Khaṇḍa 5 ta ka ta ki ṭa Miśra 7 ta ki ṭa ta ka dhi mi Saṅkīrṇa 9 ta ka dhi mi ta ka ta ki ṭa

docs.title: 5.3.4 The starting point (eḍuppu)
docs.text: A Karnatak composition need not begin on the first beat of the cycle. Its starting point (eḍuppu, also called graha) may be on the beat (sama), before it (atīta) or after it (anāgata); in Ādi tāla many kṛtis begin half a beat or a beat and a half after the samam. The eḍuppu is the point to which improvised phrases (kalpana svara, niraval) must return, and its placement gives each composition a distinctive rhythmic profile.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Tāla and ṭhekā
docs.text:
Hindustani tālas are described by their number of mātrās, their division into vibhāgs, the pattern of tālī and khālī, and above all by their ṭhekā, the characteristic sequence of drum syllables played on the tablā or pakhāvaj. In notation, the sam is marked “x”, the khālī “0” and the other claps by numbers. Table 5.3 gives the commonest tālas (Clayton 2000; Kippen 1988), and Figure 5.2 sets the sixteen-beat Tīntāl beside the Karnatak Ādi tāla: both are cycles that return to their first beat, but one is counted on the hands and the other is recognised by the sound of the drum.

Left: Ādi tāla as it is counted on the hands, a laghu (I) of a clap and three finger-counts followed by two drutams (O) of a clap and a wave. Right: Tīntāl with its ṭhekā: four sections of four beats, marked x (sam), 2, 0 (khālī, the “empty” section, dashed, in which the resonant strokes of the left-hand drum are mostly withheld) and 3.
