Tīntāl, of sixteen beats, is the most widely used tāla in Hindustani music, for vocal and instrumental compositions at all tempos and for Kathak dance. Ektāl, the fourteen-beat Jhūmrā and the sixteen-beat Tilvāḍā serve the slow (vilambit) khayāl; Jhaptāl and Rūpak are used for medium-tempo compositions; Dādrā and Kaharvā, with their lilting groupings, for ṭhumrī, ghazal, bhajan and much light and folk music; Dīpcandī (fourteen beats) for ṭhumrī. Rūpak is unusual in beginning with a khālī: its first beat is “empty”. Cautāl and Dhamār, played on the pakhāvaj, are the tālas of dhrupad and dhamār (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 5.4.2 Metre and ṭhekā
docs.text: Martin Clayton has shown that a Hindustani tāla is best understood as a metre in the full sense, a hierarchy of beats and sections against which the listener hears the music, while the ṭhekā is a particular realisation of it on the drum. The same tāla can be realised differently at different tempos, and at very slow tempos, as in vilambit khayāl, where a cycle of Ektāl may last a minute or more, the individual mātrās are filled with subsidiary strokes and the singer’s sense of time depends on the drummer’s articulation of the ṭhekā (Clayton 2000).

docs.title: 5.5 Laya and Layakārī
docs.text:
Three basic tempos are recognised: slow (vilambit), medium (madhya) and fast (drut), with very slow (ati-vilambit) and very fast (ati-drut) extremes. In Hindustani music the tempo of a performance typically increases gradually from beginning to end. Karnatak music usually keeps a steadier basic tempo but moves between levels of subdivision, the first, second and third “speeds” (kāla).

Layakārī, “rhythm-making”, is the art of playing with the relation between the surface rhythm and the underlying pulse. Its simplest forms are the multiplication of the density of notes or syllables per beat — double (dugun), triple (tigun), fourfold (caugun) — relative to the base (ṭhāh); more complex forms use ratios such as 3:2 (āḍ), 5:4 (kuāḍ) and 7:4 (biāḍ), which produce cross-rhythms against the pulse (Table 5.4). In dhrupad and dhamār, the singer recites the text of the composition in successive layakārīs while the pakhāvaj player keeps or answers the cycle; in khayāl and instrumental music the same principle governs the rhythmic play of tāns and bol-tāns (Sanyal and Widdess 2004; Clayton 2000).

Table 5.4. Some ratios of layakārī (notes or syllables per beat of the basic pulse) Name Ratio Effect ṭhāh 1:1 one unit per beat dugun 2:1 double density tigun 3:1 triple density caugun 4:1 fourfold density āḍ 3:2 three units in the time of two; a “limping” cross-rhythm kuāḍ 5:4 five units in the time of four biāḍ 7:4 seven units in the time of four

docs.title: 5.6 The Languages of the Drums
docs.text:
Indian drummers learn and transmit their art through spoken syllables, each of which stands for a stroke or a combination of strokes. On the tablā, nā or tā is a ringing stroke on the rim of the right-hand drum, tin a stroke on its inner area, ge or ghe a resonant stroke on the left-hand drum, ke or ka a closed, damped stroke on it, and dhā and dhin combine a right-hand stroke with the resonant left-hand ge; compound syllables such as tirakiṭa and dhāge represent rapid groups of strokes (Kippen 1988). The pakhāvaj has its own, heavier syllables (dhumakiṭa, gadi gana). On the mṛdaṅgam the basic syllables (sollu) include ta or tha, dhi, thom, nam, ki and ṭa, and the strokes combine the right-hand head with the open or closed bass of the left. Because the syllables can be recited, a composition can be taught, memorised and performed vocally; the recitation itself is an art (paḍhant in the north, konnakkol in the south).

The syllables are not an arbitrary code. Dancers use related syllables for footwork (Chapter 13), singers and instrumentalists imitate drum phrases, and the compositions of the drum repertoire — recited by the drummer before he plays them, or by a dancer’s teacher (naṭṭuvaṉār) as the dancer performs — are among the most refined forms of Indian rhythmic art.

docs.title: 5.6.1 Tablā compositions and gharānās
docs.text: The tablā repertoire, transmitted in hereditary lineages (gharānās) associated with Delhi, Ajrāḍā, Lucknow, Farrukhābād, Banāras and the Punjab, distinguishes fixed compositions such as qāida (a theme with systematic variations ending in a cadence), relā (a rapid, rolling composition), gat, ṭukṛā, paran (originally a pakhāvaj form) and chakkardār compositions (a cadence repeated three times so that the final stroke of the third falls on sam). James Kippen’s study of the Lucknow tradition shows how the repertoire was tied to the social history of the hereditary families who taught it (Kippen 1988).

docs.title: 5.6.2 The Karnatak percussion solo
docs.text: In a Karnatak concert the percussionists — mṛdaṅgam, often with ghaṭam, kañjīrā or morsing — play a solo (tani āvartanam) after the main composition, exploring the tāla through changes of gati, alternating exchanges in which the phrases are progressively shortened (koraippu), and composed cadences (mōrā and korvai), before handing back to the melodist with a final cadence that lands on the eḍuppu of the composition (Viswanathan and Allen 2004).

docs.title: 5.7.1 Tihāī
docs.text:
The most characteristic cadential device of Hindustani music is the tihāī (“threefold”): a phrase played or sung three times so that the last note or stroke of the third statement falls on the sam. The arithmetic is simple but must be exact. If a phrase of \(n\) beats is separated from the next by a rest of \(g\) beats, the tihāī lasts \(3n + 2g\) beats, counting the final arrival; in a sixteen-beat cycle, a phrase of five beats with a rest of one beat (5 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 5 = 17) begun on the sam ends on the sam of the following cycle (Figure 5.3).

Figure 5.3. The arithmetic of a simple tihāī in Tīntāl: a phrase of five beats, stated three times with a rest of one beat between statements (\(3 \times 5 + 2 \times 1 = 17\) beats), begun on the sam of one cycle, ends on the sam of the next.

Composers build elaborate tihāīs in which each of the three statements is itself a smaller tihāī, or in which the three statements are spread across several cycles. The pleasure of the device lies in its predictability: the listener knows that an arrival is coming and waits for it.

docs.title: 5.7.2 Mōrā and korvai
docs.text: The Karnatak equivalents are the mōrā, a short phrase repeated three times to reach the samam or eḍuppu, and the korvai, a longer composed cadence that may combine several phrases in decreasing or increasing lengths, each section repeated three times, and that is often calculated to fit different speeds or gatis. Korvais are used both by percussionists and by dancers, for whom they form the climactic sequences (tīrmāṉam) that close passages of pure dance (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 5.7.3 Cross-rhythm and displacement
docs.text: Both traditions exploit the tension between groupings of beats and the cycle. A drummer may group the sixteen beats of Tīntāl as 5+5+6 or play phrases of seven against a pulse of four; a singer may begin a phrase off the beat so that its stresses fall against the claps. The skill lies in creating maximal tension while never losing the cycle, so that the return to sam is felt as a resolution.

docs.title: 5.8 Rhythmic Dialogue
docs.text: Rhythm in Indian music is a matter of interaction between performers. In Hindustani concerts the soloist and the tablā player engage in passages of question and answer (savāl-javāb), the drummer reproducing or answering the soloist’s rhythmic phrases, in progressively shorter exchanges, until both arrive together on the sam. In Kathak, the dancer and the drummer engage in similar exchanges, the dancer’s feet answering the drum. In Karnatak music the percussionists respond continuously to the melodic and textual rhythms of the singer, and in the tani āvartanam to each other. The audience participates too: listeners in both traditions keep the tāla with their hands, and the shared arrival on sam is often greeted with audible approval.

docs.title: 5.9 Konnakkol and Vocal Rhythm
docs.text: Konnakkol, the recitation of rhythmic syllables as a performance art, has developed in the Karnatak tradition from the teaching practice of drummers and dance teachers. Its practitioners recite complex compositions in changing gatis at high speed, keeping the tāla with the hands. In the late twentieth century the ghaṭam player T. H. Vinayakram, a member of the guitarist John McLaughlin’s group Shakti from the mid-1970s, and later his son V. Selvaganesh brought konnakkol to international audiences through such collaborations with jazz and fusion musicians, and it has since been taken up by percussionists and teachers of rhythm in many countries (Lavezzoli 2006).

docs.title: 5.10 Tāla and the Forms of Composition
docs.text:
Each genre of Indian music has its favoured tālas and its own way of relating melody to the cycle. In dhrupad and dhamār (Chapter 7) the climax of a performance is often rhythmic rather than melodic, as the singer recites the words of the composition in successive layakārīs against the pakhāvaj (Sanyal and Widdess 2004). In khayāl, by contrast, the slow cycle of the “great” (baṛā) khayāl is a frame within which the singer develops the rāga at leisure, returning periodically to the first line of the composition (the mukhṛā) to arrive on sam; the fast choṭā khayāl and the tarānā give more scope for rhythmic play. In the sitār and sarod gats, normally in Tīntāl, the stroke patterns of the right hand (bol) interact with the drum strokes much as the words of a song do (Clayton 2000; Miner 1993).

In Karnatak music most kṛtis are in Ādi, Rūpaka, Miśra Cāpu or Khaṇḍa Cāpu tāla. The varṇam, a composition used both as a study piece and as a concert opener, is often in Ādi tāla of two kaḷai or in Aṭa tāla. The most demanding rhythmic genre is the pallavi of the suite called rāgam–tānam–pallavi: a single line of text set to a melody that may be composed in a complex or unusual tāla, with a structural pause (arudi) that divides it, and then developed by the singer through melodic variation (niraval), performance at different speeds (trikālam), changes of gati and passages of improvised svaras. A singer’s command of layam is judged above all in the pallavi (Viswanathan and Allen 2004).

Devotional and light genres generally use simpler metres. Bhajan, ghazal and ṭhumrī are sung in Kaharvā, Dādrā, Dīpcandī or Rūpak; in qawwālī the chorus claps the beat while the ḍholak and tablā drive a gradually accelerating rhythm towards the moments of ecstasy that the genre seeks (Chapter 7) (Qureshi 1986). Sikh kīrtan uses both art-music tālas and the simpler metres of devotional song, played on the jōṛī, a pair of drums related to the tablā.

docs.title: 5.11 Tāla in Dance and Theatre
docs.text: In dance the relation between rhythm and movement is direct: the dancer’s feet are themselves a percussion instrument. The rhythmic units of the southern forms — the jatis danced to the naṭṭuvaṉār’s recited syllables and closed by triple cadences (tīrmāṉam) analogous to the drummer’s mōrā and korvai — and the Kathak dancer’s ṭukṛās, parans and tihāīs, danced mostly in Tīntāl against a repeated melodic phrase (lahrā), are described with the grammar of pure dance in Chapter 13 and with the individual forms in Chapters 15 and 16. The theatres of Kerala have their own drums and rhythmic systems, from the miḻāvu of Kūṭiyāṭṭam to the ceṇṭa, maddaḷam and iḍakka of Kathakaḷi, to which the actors’ movements and the cadences of their gesture-language are timed; the temple drum ensembles of Kerala, such as pañcavādyam and ceṇṭa mēḷam, have developed some of the most elaborate rhythmic structures of any Indian music (Chapters 10 and 18).

docs.title: 5.12 Keeping Time
docs.text:
The practice of marking the tāla with the hands is as old as the theory. The ancient kriyās described above survive in modified form in the Karnatak practice of counting the tāla with claps, waves and finger-counts, which singers, drummers and many listeners do throughout a performance; it is common to see a whole audience at a Karnatak concert keeping Ādi tāla together. In Hindustani music the tāla is usually kept by the drummer alone, and listeners who mark it do so more discreetly, though the tālī–khālī pattern of claps and waves is taught to every student.

Small cymbals also keep time in many traditions: the mañjīrā of north Indian devotional song, the jhāñjh and kartāl of kīrtan, the tāḷam of the Bharatanāṭyam conductor and of Kerala temple music, and the cymbals (kartāl) and clappers of folk and devotional music throughout the subcontinent. In ensembles that lack a drum, these idiophones are the timekeepers; in larger ensembles they double the drummer’s articulation of the cycle. The Sanskrit word tāla itself originally referred to the clap and to the cymbals that sounded it, and the classification of instruments in the Nāṭyaśāstra places cymbals among the “solid” (ghana) instruments (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 5.13 Rhythm Beyond the Classical
docs.text: The classical tāla systems are only part of India’s rhythmic culture. Folk and devotional music across the subcontinent uses its own drums, metres and rhythmic idioms — the ḍhol rhythms of Punjabi bhāṅgṛā, the dholak of north Indian women’s songs, the frame drums (ḍaph, tappaṭṭai) of processions and rituals, the khol of Bengali and Assamese devotional song and the pung of Manipur (Chapters 18 and 21). The lilting six- and eight-beat metres of Dādrā and Kaharvā, and the seven- and five-beat cāpu tālas of the south, are generally thought to have come into art music from such popular sources. The boundary between “classical” and “folk” rhythm has always been permeable.

docs.title: 5.14 Interpretations of Rhythm
docs.text: Writers on Indian music have often linked the cyclical structure of tāla with Indian conceptions of cyclical time — the cycles of the ages (yuga) and of creation and dissolution — and have related the three tempos to the three qualities (guṇa) of Sāṃkhya philosophy. These are modern interpretations, sometimes suggestive, but they are not found in the classical treatises on tāla, which are practical and technical. Cyclical metres are in any case found in many musical traditions. What is distinctive in India is the elaboration of the cycle into a medium for sustained improvisation and dialogue, and the creation of a spoken rhythmic language that allows rhythm to be composed, taught and performed with extraordinary precision (Clayton 2000; Rowell 1992).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Clayton (2000) is the fundamental study of rhythm and metre in Hindustani music; Kippen (1988) studies the tablā tradition of Lucknow; Sanyal and Widdess (2004) describes rhythm in dhrupad. For the Karnatak system see Viswanathan and Allen (2004), and for the ancient theory Rowell (1992) and Lath (1978).

docs.title: Chapter 6: The Treatises of Music: From the Dattilam to Bhatkhande
docs.text: For two thousand years Indian musicians and their patrons wrote about music. The result is one of the largest technical literatures on music in any pre-modern civilisation: several hundred works in Sanskrit, with others in Persian, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil, Hindi, Marathi and Bengali, ranging from short manuals to encyclopaedias of many thousand verses. Chapter 4 traced the central idea of this literature, the rāga, from the Nāṭyaśāstra to the modern classifications, and Chapter 5 its theory of rhythm. This chapter looks at the texts themselves: who wrote them, for whom, where and why; what each added to the tradition it inherited; and how they should be read. It follows the literature from the music chapters of the Nāṭyaśāstra and the Dattilam, through Mataṅga, the royal compendia of the eleventh and twelfth centuries and Śārṅgadeva’s Saṅgītaratnākara, to the regional treatises of the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries and the reformers of the colonial period. The Persian literature on Indian music is treated in Chapter 7 and the dance treatises in Chapter 12; here they appear only where they bear on the history of musical theory.

docs.title: 6.1 The Shape of a Tradition
docs.text:
The Sanskrit literature on music (saṅgītaśāstra) has some features that a modern reader needs to keep in mind. Its works are mostly in verse, usually the anuṣṭubh metre of the epics and the śāstras, with occasional prose; they were meant to be memorised and recited as well as read. Their authors worked by compilation as much as by original statement. A medieval treatise typically begins with the received doctrine, often quoting or paraphrasing earlier authorities at length, and then adds what its author regarded as new: the regional (deśī) rāgas, compositions, instruments or dances of his own time and place. Many works survive only because later compilers quoted them, and many of the authorities named in the texts — Kohala, Viśākhila, Tumburu, Kāśyapa, Yāṣṭika, Durgāśakti and others — are known only from such quotations (Nijenhuis 1977; Rowell 1992).

The literature is also, for most of its history, a literature of courts. Several of its authors were kings or claimed to be: Someśvara III of the Cāḷukyas, Nānyadeva of Mithilā, Kumbhakarṇa of Mewar, the Recharla king Siṃhabhūpāla, the Maratha king Tulajā of Thanjavur. Others were ministers, court poets or Brahmin scholars attached to a court, and the works name their patrons with care. To write on music was a mark of royal accomplishment, and a treatise was a gift to a dynasty’s reputation as well as a manual. This explains both the strengths of the literature — its learning, its system and its preservation in court libraries — and its limits: it records the music that was valued at courts, describes performers only as the patron saw them, and has almost nothing to say about the music of the village, the women’s quarters or the low-caste professional, except as the raw material of new deśī categories.

Three ideas organise the whole literature. The first is the distinction between mārga and deśī: the “path” of the ancient, canonical music believed to have been revealed by the gods and recorded by Bharata, and the “regional” music of particular places and people. The second is the distinction between lakṣaṇa, the theoretical definition of a thing, and lakṣya, the thing as found in practice, which theorists from Mataṅga to Bhatkhande invoked when they had to admit that the music of their time did not fit the books. The third is the authority of the Nāṭyaśāstra itself: almost every later author begins by placing his work in the line of Bharata, even when, as often happened, the music he describes would have been unrecognisable to the earlier text. The history of the literature is in large part the history of how successive writers reconciled the authority of the past with the music of their own day.

docs.title: 6.2 The Gāndharva Texts: The Nāṭyaśāstra and the Dattilam
docs.text:
The music chapters of the Nāṭyaśāstra (chapters 28–33 in Ghosh’s numbering) were described in Chapter 2. Their companion is the Dattilam, a compact treatise of some 240 verses ascribed to Dattila, whom later tradition made one of the sons or pupils of Bharata. It is probably somewhat later than the musical chapters of the Nāṭyaśāstra, which it closely resembles, and is usually placed in the early centuries CE. Mukund Lath’s study and translation, and Emmie te Nijenhuis’s edition, made it the best-understood of the early texts (Lath 1978; Nijenhuis 1970).

Both texts describe gāndharva, a music that they define as consisting of three components: notes (svara), time-measure (tāla) and words (pada). Gāndharva was not ordinary song. It was a sacred, fixed repertoire, performed in the preliminaries of the theatre and in ritual, whose correct performance was believed to please the gods and to produce unseen merit (adṛṣṭa); its rules were correspondingly strict. The songs of the play itself, the dhruvās, belonged to a different category, gāna, which was valued for its visible effect on the audience (Chapter 19). Lath has argued that this distinction explains much about the later tradition: the theory that the treatises preserved for centuries was the theory of a ritual music, not of the music people heard, and when later authors repeated the grāmas, mūrchanās and jātis, they were preserving the theory of a sacred art rather than describing the music around them (Lath 1978; Rowell 1992).

The content of the Dattilam is technical and systematic. It defines the twenty-two śrutis and their distribution among the notes; the two grāmas and their fourteen mūrchanās; the forms of a mūrchanā with six or five notes; the jātis with their characteristic notes; and the “path” (mārga) tālas with their gestures (Chapter 5). It also describes the gītakas, the large ritual song-forms of gāndharva, built from fixed sections and performed in strict order. What makes these early texts so valuable is their coherence: the jāti system is a carefully worked-out modal theory, in which each melodic type is defined by a set of functional notes — initial, predominant, final, penultimate, limits of range, notes to be emphasised or avoided — and this functional way of thinking about a mode survived the disappearance of the jātis themselves and passed into the theory of rāga (Widdess 1995).

docs.title: 6.3 Mataṅga and the Discovery of Deśī
docs.text:
Between the Dattilam and the next major surviving text lies a gap of several centuries, partly filled by the authorities quoted in later works. The text that ends the gap is Mataṅga’s Bṛhaddeśī (“The Great Treatise on Regional Music”), composed in the second half of the first millennium CE; its date cannot be fixed more closely, and proposals range from about the sixth to the ninth century. The text survives in a damaged state: its surviving portion breaks off in the middle of its account of composed songs. Prem Lata Sharma’s edition and translation is the standard one (Sharma 1992).

The title announces the novelty. Mataṅga defines deśī music, in contrast to the ancient mārga, as the music current in the different regions, sung for their own pleasure by women, children, herdsmen and kings. He does not reject the gāndharva theory; much of his work restates and discusses it, and he quotes earlier authorities, some of them otherwise lost, on disputed points. But he extends the theory to new material. His treatment of the notes includes a discussion of nāda, the sound from which music arises, and of the nature of śruti; his account of melodic types introduces the grāma-rāgas, derived from the jātis, and a wider class of regional melodies called bhāṣā and vibhāṣā, which he takes partly from the lost work of an authority named Yāṣṭika. These melodies are grouped under styles of singing called gīti. Above all, he gives the first known definition of rāga (Chapter 4), which treats it as a melody characterised by its notes and movements and defined by its effect on the listener, and he applies the term to melodic types of the deśī world (Sharma 1992; Widdess 1995).

The surviving part of the text also begins the systematic description of composed songs (prabandha), the vernacular and Sanskrit song-forms of the courts and temples, which later treatises were to describe at much greater length. With Mataṅga the centre of gravity of the theory moves from the ritual music of the past to the living music of the regions, and every later Sanskrit treatise follows his example in combining the two. The Kudumiyamalai inscription in Tamil Nadu (Chapter 4), which sets out melodies under the names of grāma-rāgas of the kind Mataṅga describes, shows that this theory was used by practising musicians in his period (Widdess 1979).

Abhinavagupta’s commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra (c. 1000), the Abhinavabhāratī, belongs to the same world. Its discussion of the music chapters, though damaged in the manuscripts, shows a scholar trying to explain an ancient system he no longer heard by reference to the rāgas and practices of his own time, and it preserves many quotations from lost writers on music. Its main influence lies in the theory of rasa (Chapter 3), but for the historian of music it is a reminder that the ancient theory was already being read, by the eleventh century, as a classical text in need of interpretation.

docs.title: 6.4 The Royal Compendia of the Eleventh to Thirteenth Centuries
docs.text:
The eleventh and twelfth centuries produced a cluster of works on music written at the courts of the Deccan, of eastern India and of the west. They share a pattern: a restatement of the mārga theory, followed by a long account of the deśī rāgas, compositions, instruments and dances of the court.

Nānyadeva’s Bharatabhāṣya. Nānyadeva (r. c. 1097–1147), the Karṇāṭa king of Mithilā in northern Bihar, wrote a long commentary on the music of the Nāṭyaśāstra, also known as the Sarasvatīhṛdayālaṅkāra. Besides discussing the ancient theory it describes the rāgas of its time and gives notated examples, and Richard Widdess has used its notations, with those of Mataṅga and Śārṅgadeva, to reconstruct the outlines of early rāgas (Widdess 1995). Someśvara’s Mānasollāsa. The encyclopaedia of royal life compiled at the court of the Cāḷukya king Someśvara III of Kalyāṇa (1131) treats music, instruments and dance among the “pleasures” (vinoda) of a king (Chapter 12). Its section on song describes rāgas and many kinds of prabandha, among them songs in Kannada and other regional languages, and it is valuable precisely because it records the courtly music of the Deccan without much concern for the mārga theory. Jagadekamalla’s Saṅgītacūḍāmaṇi. A treatise attributed to Someśvara’s successor, Jagadekamalla II (r. 1138–1151), continues the same Cāḷukya tradition. Pārśvadeva’s Saṅgītasamayasāra. The work of a Jain author of the twelfth or thirteenth century, it gives an unusually full account of deśī music: rāgas, phrases, compositions, regional tālas and dance. Its author’s Jainism is a reminder that the music treatises were not the preserve of any one religious community.

These works show music as one of the arts of a cultivated court, discussed in the same terms across a large part of the subcontinent. They also show that the repertoire of rāgas was growing and changing rapidly. Names that become prominent in later music — Bhairavī, Toḍī and Gurjarī among them — appear in this period among the bhāṣā and deśī rāgas, and the older grāma-rāgas retreat into the theory. The Gītagovinda of Jayadeva, composed in Bengal or Odisha in the twelfth century, belongs to the same moment: its songs, as transmitted in the manuscripts, carry the names of the rāgas and tālas in which they were sung, and the work became one of the most widely performed texts in Indian music and dance (Chapter 17).

docs.title: 6.5.1 The author and his court
docs.text: The Saṅgītaratnākara (“Ocean of Music”) of Śārṅgadeva summed up this literature and became its standard authority. Śārṅgadeva tells us that his family came from Kashmir: his grandfather Bhāskara had migrated to the Deccan, and his father Soḍhala served the Yādava kings of Devagiri. Śārṅgadeva himself was an official at the court of Siṃhaṇa (r. c. 1210–1247), and the work belongs to the first half of the thirteenth century. Its importance owes much to its timing. Within a century of its composition the Yādava kingdom fell to the Delhi Sultanate, and the music of the north was transformed by the courts of the sultans; the Saṅgītaratnākara thus became the last great statement of the theory before the northern and southern traditions diverged, and both looked back to it as their common source (Shringy and Sharma 1978; Rowell 1992).

docs.title: 6.5.2 The seven chapters
docs.text:
The work is divided into seven chapters, whose contents are summarised below; the chapters on tāla, instruments and dance are discussed in Chapters 5, 10 and 12.

  1. Svaragata (on the notes). The chapter opens with the origin of sound in the body, drawing on yogic physiology and the doctrine of nāda: the word itself is explained as a union of breath (na) and fire (da). It then treats śruti, svara, grāma, mūrchanā, the patterns of notes (tāna), the varṇas (types of melodic movement) and their ornaments (alaṅkāra), and the jātis.
  2. Rāgaviveka (the discrimination of rāgas). The chapter classifies 264 rāgas in the categories inherited from Mataṅga and his successors — grāma-rāgas, uparāgas, bhāṣās and others — and then turns to the rāgas “famous in former times” (pūrvaprasiddha) and “famous now” (adhunāprasiddha), the latter including categories called rāgāṅga, bhāṣāṅga, kriyāṅga and upāṅga. The distinction between ancient and current rāgas is Śārṅgadeva’s own acknowledgement that the music of his day had moved beyond the older theory.
  3. Prakīrṇaka (miscellany). Here are the qualities of the composer (vāggeyakāra) and the singer, the qualities and faults of voice, the fifteen gamakas (Chapter 4), the elaboration of rāga without text (ālapti) and the phrase-types (sthāya) from which a performance was built.
  4. Prabandha (composition). The theory of composed song (below).
  5. Tāla. The mārga tālas and 120 deśī tālas.
  6. Vādya (instruments). The four classes of instrument, with detailed accounts of the vīṇās, flutes and drums and their techniques.
  7. Nartana (dance). Dance and drama, mārga and deśī.

docs.title: 6.5.3 The composer and the composition
docs.text:
Two parts of the work have been particularly influential for the history of musical form. The first is Śārṅgadeva’s portrait of the ideal composer, the vāggeyakāra, “maker of words and song”. Such a person, he says in effect, should be master of grammar, lexicon and prosody, of the rāgas and tālas, of the regional languages and their idioms, of the rasas and the arts of poetry, and should have a fine voice and a sense of propriety. The ideal of the composer who writes both text and music and sings his own compositions is one that later traditions — the Haridāsas, the dhrupad singers of Gwalior, the Karnatak Trinity — were to embody.

The second is the theory of prabandha. Śārṅgadeva distinguishes “bound” (nibaddha) music, composed and set to tāla, from “unbound” (anibaddha) music, such as the ālapti that explores a rāga without text or metre — a distinction that corresponds to the alternation of improvised ālāp or ālāpana and composed song in modern concerts. He analyses a prabandha in two ways. Its “sections” (dhātu) are the udgrāha (opening), the melāpaka (link), the dhruva (the fixed, refrain-like section that must not be omitted) and the ābhoga (conclusion), sometimes with an additional antara. Its “limbs” (aṅga) are six kinds of material that may be combined: svara (sol-fa syllables), biruda (words of praise), pada (meaningful text), tena (auspicious syllables such as tena), pāṭa (drum syllables) and tāla. The number of limbs a song contained determined its class. The prabandhas themselves are grouped into large families, among them the sālagasūḍa, a group of seven song types (dhruva, maṇṭha, pratimaṇṭha, nissāru, aḍḍatāla, rāsaka and ekatālī) from which the names of several later southern sūḷādi tālas (Dhruva, Maṭhya, Aṭa, Eka), and the sūḷādi song itself, appear to derive (Shringy and Sharma 1978; Rowell 1992).

The vocabulary of this theory survived the songs it described. The names dhruva and ābhoga reappear in the dhrupad (dhruvapada) and its fourth section, the ābhog (Chapter 7); the combination of sol-fa, meaningful text and drum syllables reappears in the tarānā of Hindustani music, the tillāna of the south and the rhythmic compositions of the dancers. Continuity of names does not prove continuity of music, but the analytical habits of the prabandha theory — the composition as a set of sections and materials — persisted in the way Indian musicians thought about form.

docs.title: 6.5.4 The commentators
docs.text: Two great commentaries extended the authority of the Saṅgītaratnākara into the following centuries. The Sudhākara of Siṃhabhūpāla, a fourteenth-century king of the Recharla dynasty in Telangana who also wrote on drama, and the Kalānidhi of Kallinātha, written at Vijayanagara under Devarāya II (r. 1424–1446), explain the text line by line and discuss its difficulties. Kallinātha in particular was aware that the rāgas of his own day often differed from those described by Śārṅgadeva, and his comments are among the earliest explicit discussions of the gap between lakṣaṇa and lakṣya. Both commentaries are printed with the text in the Adyar edition, the standard Sanskrit text, and the edition and translation by R. K. Shringy and Prem Lata Sharma makes the work accessible in English (Subrahmanya Sastri 1943–1953; Shringy and Sharma 1978). The commentaries also show how quickly the text became a classic: within two centuries of its composition, a work that had recorded the music of the Yādava court was being read as a description of timeless principles.

docs.title: 6.6.1 North and south
docs.text:
After the thirteenth century the literature divided along the lines of the music itself (Chapter 4). In the north, Sanskrit treatises continued to be written at Rajput, regional sultanate and Mughal courts, but they increasingly shared the field with works in Persian and in Hindi; in the south, the courts of Vijayanagara and its successors produced the treatises that led to the mela system. Table 6.1 lists the main works of the period from the twelfth century to the early nineteenth; the dates of several are uncertain.
