docs.title: 6.6.2 The northern compendia
docs.text:
The fourteenth and fifteenth centuries produced several large compilations in the tradition of the Saṅgītaratnākara. The Jain author Sudhākalaśa wrote his Saṅgītopaniṣatsāroddhāra in 1350 as an abridgement of his own larger work, with accounts of rāgas, prabandhas and dances. The Saṅgītaśiromaṇi, compiled in 1428 by a group of scholars for a Muslim ruler in north India, arranges the received doctrine in a clear and systematic way — a Sanskrit compendium in the line of Śārṅgadeva made for a sultan’s court, and one more sign that Hindu, Jain and Muslim patrons shared a learned musical culture — and Emmie te Nijenhuis’s edition and translation of its musical portions has made it one of the most accessible of the medieval handbooks (Nijenhuis 1992). The Saṅgītarāja, ascribed to Rāṇā Kumbhakarṇa (Kumbha) of Mewar (r. 1433–1468), a king who also wrote a commentary on the Gītagovinda, is the most ambitious of them: a vast encyclopaedia of recitation, song, instruments, dance and rasa that draws heavily on Śārṅgadeva and on many other sources (Nijenhuis 1977).

These works were monuments of court learning, and they say less about the music actually played at the courts of their time than their size suggests. The music that was transforming north India — the songs of the Sufi assemblies, the new genres and instruments of the sultanate courts, and the dhrupad of Gwalior — appears in them only indirectly. For these one has to turn to works in other languages. The Hindi treatise associated with Mān Siṃh Tomar of Gwalior, the Mānakutūhala, is lost in its original form and known chiefly through Faqīrullāh’s Persian adaptation, the Rāg Darpan of 1666, which is discussed with the other Persian writings in Chapter 7.

A northern work of a different kind is Locana’s Rāgataraṅgiṇī, from Mithilā. It classifies the rāgas of its time under twelve parent scales (saṃsthāna), in a way that anticipates the later thāṭs, and quotes songs of the Maithili poet Vidyāpati (fourteenth–fifteenth century) as examples. Its date is disputed: earlier writers placed it in the twelfth century, but the quotations from Vidyāpati show that it cannot be earlier than the fifteenth, and some scholars place it in the seventeenth. Whatever its date, it shows that a classification of rāgas by scale was being attempted in the north as well as the south.

docs.title: 6.6.3 The mela in the south
docs.text:
In the south the decisive step was taken at Vijayanagara. Rāmāmātya, a minister at the court of Rāma Rāya, wrote his Svaramelakalānidhi in 1550. He complained that the theorists of his time described a music that no one played, and set out instead to describe the rāgas of current practice. His method was to group them by their parent scale (mela), which he explained in terms of the frets of the vīṇā: a set of rāgas that could be played on the same arrangement of frets belonged to the same mela. He recognised twenty melas. The classification grew out of the practice of the fretted vīṇā, then the principal art instrument of the south, and it subordinated the ancient categories of grāma and jāti to the organisation of real scales (Nijenhuis 1977; Widdess 1995). Later southern writers cite a lost Saṅgītasāra ascribed to Vidyāraṇya, the fourteenth-century scholar associated with the founding of Vijayanagara, as an earlier authority for the mela idea; the work does not survive and its contents cannot be checked.

The idea spread quickly. The Rāgavibodha (1609) of Somanātha, a scholar from Andhra, classified rāgas under a larger number of melas and gave its examples in a notation for the vīṇā with signs for ornaments. At Thanjavur, the Saṅgītasudhā, attributed to the Nāyaka king Raghunātha and probably written by his minister Govinda Dīkṣita, and then the Caturdaṇḍīprakāśikā of Govinda’s son Veṅkaṭamakhin carried the theory further. Veṅkaṭamakhin’s demonstration that seventy-two melas are mathematically possible, and the completion of the named scheme by Govindācārya in the eighteenth century, are described in Chapter 8. The title of Veṅkaṭamakhin’s work refers to the “four pillars” (caturdaṇḍī) of the music of his time — ālāpa, ṭhāya, gīta and prabandha — a reminder that even this most theoretical of works set out to describe the forms of a living practice.

The court of the Maratha kings of Thanjavur (1676–1855) continued the tradition. The Saṅgītasārāmṛta attributed to King Tulajā (r. c. 1729–1735) describes rāgas with their characteristic phrases and ornaments as well as their scales, and gives an account of the dance of the court (Chapter 12); it is one of the main sources for southern music in the generation before the Trinity (Subramanian 2006).

docs.title: 6.6.4 Bridges between north and south
docs.text:
Several authors of the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries carried southern ideas north. The most important was Puṇḍarīka Viṭṭhala, a scholar from Karnataka who worked first at the court of the Fārūqī rulers of Khandesh, for whom he wrote the Ṣaḍrāgacandrodaya, and then for the Kachhwaha rulers of Amber, for whom he wrote the Rāgamālā, the Rāgamañjarī and the dance treatise Nartananirṇaya. His works apply the southern method of classification by mela to the rāgas of the north, and record northern names and forms of the period of Akbar; the Muslim and Rajput courts for which he wrote show how freely learning moved between Muslim and Hindu patrons (Nijenhuis 1977).

Ahobala’s Saṅgītapārijāta, of the seventeenth century, is notable for defining the positions of the twelve notes by the length of the string of a vīṇā at which each is produced, the first attempt in the Sanskrit literature to fix the pitches of the notes by measurement. It was widely copied in the north, and its method was taken up by the Gond king Hṛdayanārāyaṇa of Garha-Mandla in his Hṛdayakautuka and Hṛdayaprakāśa. Dāmodara Miśra’s Saṅgītadarpaṇa (early seventeenth century), by contrast, is largely an abridgement of the Saṅgītaratnākara, but it became one of the most widely copied of all Sanskrit music texts, partly because of its verses describing the rāgas and rāgiṇīs as persons, which fed the tradition of rāgamālā painting (Chapter 4).

At Bikaner, Bhāvabhaṭṭa, the son of a musician from the Mughal court, wrote several works for Mahārāja Anūp Siṃh (r. 1669–1698), among them the Anūpasaṅgītaratnākara, the Anūpasaṅgītavilāsa and the Anūpāṅkuśa. They are compilations, but they show the Rajput courts of the Mughal period continuing the Sanskrit tradition alongside the Persian and Hindi music culture of the imperial court, and the library that Anūp Siṃh assembled at Bikaner preserved many manuscripts on music that would otherwise have been lost.

docs.title: 6.6.5 The fretted vīṇā and the theory of scales
docs.text:
Many of the theoretical innovations of this period were made by theorists who were also players of the fretted vīṇā, and their theory bears the marks of the instrument. Already the Nāṭyaśāstra had demonstrated the śrutis with a pair of vīṇās (Chapter 4), but the harp it used had open strings, one for each note. The stick zithers and lutes of the medieval period had frets, and on a fretted instrument a scale is a physical arrangement: a set of positions on the neck, fixed for as long as the frets are not moved. Rāmāmātya’s melas were, in the first place, arrangements of the frets of the vīṇā, and his classification grouped together the rāgas that could be played without moving them. Somanātha’s notation in the Rāgavibodha records the strokes and finger movements of the vīṇā player, defining ornaments in terms of what the hand does on the string, and Ahobala’s method of locating the notes by measuring the length of the string is a description of where to place the frets. In the south, the Thanjavur tradition credits the Nāyaka king Raghunātha (early seventeenth century), the patron of Govinda Dīkṣita, with a vīṇā whose frets were fixed for all twelve positions of the octave, so that any rāga could be played without re-fretting; the modern Sarasvatī vīṇā, with its twenty-four fixed frets over two octaves (Chapter 10), is the result of this development, and Veṅkaṭamakhin’s demonstration of the seventy-two possible melas presupposes exactly such a fretboard of twelve positions.

This connection helps to explain both the power and the limits of the scale-based classifications. A fretted instrument makes the selection of notes visible and countable, and so encourages a theory of rāga as a choice among scales. But the rāgas themselves, as singers and players knew, were defined as much by phrases, ornaments and intonations that no fret fixes: the oscillating Ga of Tōḍi or the slow āndolan of Darbārī are made by bending the string or the voice between the frets. The mela and thāṭ systems are thus, in part, theories of an instrument applied to a music that was, above all, vocal — a point that modern musicians, who use the classifications for orientation but learn rāgas from compositions and teachers, have always understood (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 6.6.6 Persian and vernacular theory
docs.text: From the fourteenth century the Sanskrit treatises are only part of the story. The Persian literature on Indian music (Chapter 7) began as translation and explanation of the Sanskrit theory for Persian-reading patrons, but it became a tradition in its own right, describing musicians, genres and repertoires that the Sanskrit texts ignored. In the vernaculars, works in Hindi, Bengali, Telugu, Marathi and other languages explained rāga and tāla to new readers, often in the form of song collections with theoretical introductions. One Persian work marks a turning point in the theory itself. In the Naghmāt-i Āṣafī (1813), Muḥammad Riẓā, a nobleman of Patna, examined the traditional families of six rāgas and their rāgiṇīs and concluded that they had no basis in the music of his time; he proposed instead to classify rāgas by their scales, taking the scale of Bilāval, with all its notes natural, as the standard. His proposal anticipates by a century the thāṭ system of Bhatkhande, who knew his work (Bor et al. 2010; Schofield 2010).

docs.title: 6.7 From Prabandha to Dhrupad and Kṛti
docs.text:
The treatises describe theory; they also allow the historian to follow, at least in outline, how the forms of composed song changed between the age of the prabandha and the modern repertoire. The story is not one of simple descent, since the medieval prabandhas themselves are lost and the names of forms often outlived the forms, but certain principles persist.

The first is the refrain. Śārṅgadeva’s dhruva, the section of a prabandha that must never be omitted, became in the following centuries the organising principle of vernacular devotional song. The songs of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda (twelfth century) each have a refrain, marked in the manuscripts as dhruva, to which the singer returns after every stanza; the pads of the north Indian saint-poets, the abhaṅgs of Maharashtra and the kīrtanas of the Haridāsas and of Annamācārya are all built on a refrain and a series of stanzas. In the north, the dhrupad (dhruvapada, “refrain-verse”) that emerged at the courts of the fifteenth century took its name from this principle and kept a four-part form whose last section, the ābhog, recalls the terminology of the prabandha (Chapter 7).

The second is the movement from text to music. The devotional song of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries was text-centred: its music served the words, and a singer might set the same words to different melodies. In the south, the songs of the Tāḷḷapāka composers, Annamācārya and his descendants at Tirupati, already show the division into a refrain (pallavi) and stanzas (caraṇa), and a Telugu work on the composition of such songs, the Saṅkīrtanalakṣaṇamu, is attributed to the family. The Haridāsas of Karnataka composed, besides their kīrtanas, the sūḷādi, a long devotional composition passing through a series of sections in different tālas, whose name links it to the sālagasūḍa of the treatises. Over the following centuries, and decisively in the generation of the Karnatak Trinity, the kīrtana became the kṛti, in which the music is as important as the text, the melody is fixed by the composer, and the composition provides the material for elaboration (Chapter 8).

The third is the place of the solfa and the drum syllable. The prabandha theory’s svara and pāṭa limbs anticipate the passages of solfa in the varṇam, the svarajati and the ciṭṭasvara of the kṛti, and the combination of drum syllables and meaningless vocables in the tillāna and tarānā; the dance traditions, which kept the recitation of drum syllables as part of their technique, preserved this element most fully (Chapter 13). The fourth, finally, is the ideal of the vāggeyakāra, the composer of both words and music, which the treatises formulated and which the great composers of both traditions — the Haridāsas, the dhrupad composers of Gwalior, the Trinity, Svāti Tirunāḷ — realised.

These continuities should not be overstated. The modern kṛti and khayāl are not prabandhas, and the treatises after Śārṅgadeva often describe the old forms long after they had disappeared, while saying little about the genres actually sung in their authors’ time. But the analytical vocabulary of the treatises shaped the way musicians named and thought about the parts of a composition, and it allowed the new forms of each age to be understood, by their makers and patrons, as continuations of an ancient art.

docs.title: 6.8 Colonial Encounters and the Making of Modern Theory
6.8.1 Orientalists and their informants
docs.text:
European interest in the theory of Indian music began with Sir William Jones’s essay “On the Musical Modes of the Hindus”, written in 1784 and published in Asiatic Researches in 1792. Jones read the Sanskrit and Persian treatises with the help of Indian scholars and tried to relate their rāgas to the modes of ancient Greek music; like many later Orientalists, he looked for the “true” Indian music in the ancient texts rather than in the music of contemporary performers. N. Augustus Willard, an officer in the service of the Nawab of Banda, took the opposite view in his Treatise on the Music of Hindoostan (1834), insisting that the texts must be judged against the practice of living musicians. The tension between the two approaches, textual and practical, ran through all later writing (Farrell 1997).

In Calcutta in the later nineteenth century, Indian scholars took up the subject on their own terms. Sourindro Mohun Tagore (1840–1914) founded the Bengal Music School (1871), published collections of Sanskrit and other texts on music and books on Indian instruments, and presented Indian music to European audiences as a learned art comparable to that of Europe. In the early twentieth century the question of the twenty-two śrutis became a subject of intense debate. K. B. Deval’s The Hindu Musical Scale and the Twenty-two Shrutees (1910), E. Clements’s Introduction to the Study of Indian Music (1913) and A. H. Fox Strangways’s The Music of Hindostan (1914) tried, by measurement and by reasoning from the texts, to establish the exact sizes of the śrutis; the debate was never resolved, and the modern understanding of śruti as a flexible framework rather than a fixed set of pitches is described in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 6.8.2 Bhatkhande and the new śāstra
docs.text:
Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande (1860–1936) brought the history of the treatises to its modern conclusion. Between about 1904 and 1909 he travelled through southern, western, central and eastern India, collecting manuscripts, interviewing musicians and meeting scholars, among them Subbarāma Dīkṣitar at Ettayapuram. His study of the Sanskrit texts led him to a conclusion that earlier writers had avoided stating plainly: the theory of the ancient and medieval treatises could not be applied to the music of his day. The grāmas and jātis had disappeared; the śuddha (natural) scale of the texts, built on the ṣaḍja-grāma, was not the śuddha scale of modern Hindustani musicians, which is the scale of Bilāval; and the rāgas described under familiar names in the medieval works often had little in common with the rāgas that bore those names in practice (Bhatkhande 1934; Bakhle 2005).

His response was to write a new śāstra. In the Lakṣyasaṅgītam (1910), a Sanskrit treatise in verse published under the pen-name “Catura Paṇḍita”, he described the music of current practice in the traditional form and language of the texts, as if to give it a classical authority of its own; the Abhinavarāgamañjarī, also in Sanskrit, set out the rāgas. His Marathi Hindustānī Saṅgīt Paddhati (four volumes, 1910–1932) explained the theory in the form of dialogues, and the six volumes of the Kramik Pustak Mālikā gave the compositions he had collected in notation (Chapter 4). At the heart of the system were the ten thāṭs — Bilāval, Kalyāṇ, Khamāj, Bhairav, Pūrvī, Mārvā, Kāfī, Āsāvarī, Bhairavī and Toḍī — under which he classified the rāgas of the north, together with assignments of vādī and saṃvādī and a theory of the time of performance. His lecture to the first All-India Music Conference at Baroda in 1916, later published as A Short Historical Survey of the Music of Upper India, set out his reading of the history of the treatises (Bhatkhande 1910; Bhatkhande 1934).

Bhatkhande’s achievement was immense, and his thāṭs remain the framework in which Hindustani rāgas are taught. Its costs, discussed in Chapter 7, lay in the way it subordinated the knowledge of hereditary musicians to a textual system, and in its claim to finality. Musicians have always pointed out that many rāgas fit uneasily into the ten thāṭs, that the theory of vādī and saṃvādī misdescribes some of them, and that a rāga is defined by its phrases rather than its scale. In this respect Bhatkhande stands where Rāmāmātya and Muḥammad Riẓā stood before him: a theorist who, faced with the gap between the books and the music, chose to describe the music.

The south had no single figure comparable to Bhatkhande, in part because its mela system already offered a classification that connected theory and practice. Its modern theory was shaped instead by publications and institutions. Subbarāma Dīkṣitar’s Saṅgīta Sampradāya Pradarśini (1904) set out the rāgas in the tradition of Veṅkaṭamakhin together with the compositions that exemplified them (Chapter 4); Abraham Pandither’s Karuṇāmirta Sāgaram (1917) argued for a Tamil origin of the southern system (Chapter 8); and from 1929 the Music Academy of Madras held annual conferences at which experts debated the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of particular rāgas, the number and size of the śrutis and the readings of the old texts, publishing their papers and conclusions in the Academy’s journal. These debates turned the old relation between lakṣaṇa and lakṣya into a modern institutional practice, in which a committee of musicians and scholars, rather than a royal author, pronounced on the correct form of a rāga (Weidman 2006; Subramanian 2006).

docs.title: 6.9 Reading the Treatises Today
docs.text:
The modern scholarly study of the treatises began with the editions of the early twentieth century, many of them published in the series of the princely and institutional libraries of Trivandrum, Baroda and Adyar, and was transformed in the second half of the century by the work of scholars such as V. Raghavan, Prem Lata Sharma, R. K. Shringy, Mukund Lath, Emmie te Nijenhuis, Lewis Rowell and Richard Widdess (Nijenhuis 1977; Rowell 1992; Widdess 1995; Powers and Widdess 2001). Their work suggests several principles of interpretation.

First, the texts must be read historically. A statement in a seventeenth-century treatise may be a copy of a thirteenth-century source describing music that had long since changed; the most valuable passages are often those in which an author departs from his source to describe something new, as Śārṅgadeva did with his “current” rāgas, Rāmāmātya with his melas and Muḥammad Riẓā with his critique of the rāga families.

Secondly, the notations and the technical descriptions can be used as evidence for actual music, but only with care. Widdess’s analysis of the notated examples in Mataṅga, Nānyadeva and Śārṅgadeva showed that the early rāgas can be partly recovered, but the manuscripts are often corrupt, and the reconstructions depend on assumptions about intonation, ornament and rhythm that the texts do not fully specify (Widdess 1995).

Thirdly, the treatises are evidence for the social history of music as well as its theory. They show which arts were valued at which courts, how authors claimed the authority of the past, how Jain, Hindu and Muslim patrons and scholars shared a common learned culture, and how the theory of music was used to give prestige to new repertoires. Their silences are evidence too: the absence of women and low-caste musicians from the authorship of the texts, and the near-absence of the music of ordinary people except as deśī material to be classified, tell us whose knowledge the literature recorded.

Finally, the treatises are not the music. Indian musicians have always learned from teachers, not from books, and many great musicians of the past three centuries could not have read a Sanskrit treatise. The literature records how a learned elite understood and organised the music it patronised; the music itself lived in the practice of performers, whose knowledge reached the written record only partially, and often only through the books of reformers such as Bhatkhande. To read the treatises well is to read them alongside that practice, as the best of their authors did.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Nijenhuis (1977) is the standard survey of the Sanskrit literature on music, and Rowell (1992) the best introduction to its thought. Widdess (1995) analyses the early rāgas and notations, and Powers and Widdess (2001) surveys theory and practice. For the texts see Lath (1978) and Nijenhuis (1970) (Dattilam), Sharma (1992) (Bṛhaddeśī), Shringy and Sharma (1978) (Saṅgītaratnākara) and Nijenhuis (1992) (Saṅgītaśiromaṇi). On Bhatkhande and the modern reorganisation of theory see Bhatkhande (1934) and Bakhle (2005), and on the Persian literature Schofield (2010).

docs.title: Chapter 7: Hindustani Music
docs.text: “Hindustani” music is the art music of northern and central India and of Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal: the music of dhrupad and khayāl, of ṭhumrī and ghazal, of the sitār, sarod, sāraṅgī, bānsurī and tablā. It shares the theory of rāga and tāla with the Karnatak music of the south (Chapters 4, 5 and 8), but its genres, instruments, repertoire and social history are its own. Above all it is the product of a long encounter between the musical cultures of India and those of the Persianate world, carried on for six centuries at the courts of Muslim and Hindu rulers, at Sufi shrines and Hindu temples, in the salons of courtesans and the homes of hereditary musicians, and finally in the concert halls, radio stations and music colleges of the twentieth century. The history comes first, because the genres make sense only within it; then the genres themselves and the concert; and then two great devotional traditions that grew up beside the art music of the courts, the Sufi qawwālī and the kīrtan of the Sikh Gurus.

docs.title: 7.1.1 The Sultanate and the Sufis
docs.text:
The Turkish and Afghan rulers who established the Delhi Sultanate in the thirteenth century brought with them musicians, instruments and musical ideas from Iran and Central Asia, and the Sufi orders that came with them, above all the Chishtīs, made listening to music (samāʿ) part of their devotional practice. In this world the most celebrated figure was Amīr Khusrau (1253–1325), the Persian poet of the Delhi court and disciple of the Chishtī saint Niẓāmuddīn Awliyāʾ, who wrote also in the vernacular Hindavi and was himself a connoisseur of music (Sharma 2005). Later tradition credited him with an extraordinary range of musical inventions: the qawwālī, the tarānā, the khayāl, several rāgas with Persian names, and the sitār and tablā.

Did Amīr Khusrau invent the sitār and the tablā?

No. None of Khusrau’s own writings, and no source of his time, mentions either instrument. The sitār is first securely documented in the eighteenth century, and Allyn Miner’s study of its history shows that it developed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries from smaller long-necked lutes, with the decisive changes in construction and technique made by hereditary musicians in Delhi, Lucknow and elsewhere (Miner 1993). The tablā likewise emerges in the eighteenth century, probably in Delhi, as an instrument for accompanying the newer, lighter genres; James Kippen’s work on the Lucknow tradition traces its early lineages (Kippen 1988). The attribution of both instruments to Khusrau appears in nineteenth-century writing and may owe something to confusion with later musicians of similar name. Even the genres traditionally associated with him (qawl, tarānā, khayāl) are ascribed to him by later tradition, not by contemporary evidence; what is certain is his stature as a poet and his place in the Chishtī culture of samāʿ (Sharma 2005; Bor et al. 2010).

docs.title: 7.1.2 Dhrupad and the regional courts
docs.text: In the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries the regional sultanates and Rajput kingdoms of the north were centres of musical patronage. The Tomar king of Gwalior, Mān Siṃh (r. 1486–1516), is traditionally associated with the rise of dhrupad, a genre of song in the vernacular Braj Bhāṣā set to rāga and tāla in a formal four-part structure. Gwalior became the most famous school of singers in north India, and its musicians were sought by other courts (Sanyal and Widdess 2004).

docs.title: 7.1.3 The Mughal court
docs.text:
Under the Mughals, and especially at the court of Akbar (r. 1556–1605), dhrupad became the most prestigious form of art music. Akbar’s chronicler Abū’l Faẓl lists the musicians of the court, Hindu and Muslim, from Gwalior, Kashmir, Iran and Central Asia; the most famous was Tānsen (d. 1589), who came to Akbar from the court of Rewa and around whom legends gathered of lamps lit and rain brought by his singing. In one popular legend, Akbar, dressed as a commoner, went with Tānsen to Vrindavan to hear the ascetic singer Svāmī Haridās, whom tradition makes Tānsen’s teacher (Figure 7.1). Tānsen’s descendants, the Seniyas, were for centuries the most prestigious lineage of north Indian music. Mughal emperors and nobles patronised musicians, collected and commissioned treatises, and had music depicted in painting; Bonnie Wade’s study of Mughal paintings shows the instruments and ensembles of the court in detail (Wade 1998). Writers in Persian, beginning in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, translated and adapted Sanskrit musical theory and described contemporary practice, creating a bilingual music theory that shaped Hindustani music’s understanding of itself (Schofield 2010; Bor et al. 2010).

Figure 7.1. Svāmī Haridās (right) playing a long-necked stringed instrument for Tānsen (centre) and Akbar (left, in plain dress) at Vrindavan; Rajasthani painting, first half of the eighteenth century (National Museum, New Delhi). The meeting belongs to legend, not to the court chronicles. Unknown artist (Rajasthan, first half of the 18th century), National Museum, New Delhi, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 7.1.4 The eighteenth and nineteenth centuries
docs.text: The decline of Mughal power in the eighteenth century did not mean the decline of music. At the court of Muhammad Shāh “Rangīle” (r. 1719–1748) in Delhi, khayāl, a more flexible and ornate genre than dhrupad, rose to prominence, associated especially with the court musician Niyamat Khān, who composed under the pen-name Sadāraṅg, and his relative Adāraṅg. As Delhi declined, musicians dispersed to the successor states — Awadh (Lucknow), Rampur, Gwalior, Jaipur, Baroda, Hyderabad, the Maratha courts and the zamindari households of Bengal — and to the commercial cities. In Lucknow under the nawabs, and especially under Wājid ʿAlī Shāh (r. 1847–1856), the light classical ṭhumrī and the dance of Kathak flourished among courtesans (ṭawāʾif) and hereditary musicians (Chapter 16). The sitār, sarod and tablā took their modern forms in this period, and the hereditary musicians of the period founded the stylistic lineages (gharānās) of modern Hindustani music (Neuman 1980; Miner 1993).

docs.title: 7.1.5 Musicians and their communities
docs.text: For most of this history, art music in north India was the hereditary profession of particular communities, most of them Muslim: the kalāwants, who claimed descent from court dhrupad singers; the ḍhāḍhīs and mirāsīs, who were often accompanists and genealogists; and the qawwāls of the Sufi shrines. Professional women singers and dancers — the courtesans, whose households trained girls in music, dance and poetry — were the principal performers of ṭhumrī, dādrā and ghazal, and many of the great singers of the early twentieth century came from this background. Brahmin and other Hindu musicians also practised, and Hindu temples, especially the Kṛṣṇa temples of the Puṣṭimārga sect, maintained their own traditions of dhrupad-style singing (havelī saṅgīt). Daniel Neuman’s study of the social organisation of Hindustani music describes the distinction, still important in the twentieth century, between soloists and accompanists, and the role of kinship and discipleship in the transmission of the art (Neuman 1980).

docs.title: 7.2 Writing about Music in Persian
docs.text:
For more than five centuries the art music of north India was written about in Persian as well as in Sanskrit and the vernaculars. Historians who looked for the history of Indian music only in Sanskrit long neglected these writings; they are now recognised as some of the most important evidence for the music of the period between Śārṅgadeva and the nineteenth century (Schofield 2010; Bor et al. 2010).

The earliest known Persian treatise on Indian music, the Ghunyat al-Munya, was compiled in 1374–75, in the reign of the Tughluq sultan Fīrūz Shāh. Drawing on Sanskrit sources and on the knowledge of practising musicians, it explains the Indian concepts of note, rāga, tāla and instrument, and the qualities expected of singers, for Persian-reading patrons who wished to understand the music they heard and paid for. Similar works followed at the courts of the sultanates, among them a treatise associated with the court of Sikandar Lodī of Delhi (r. 1489–1517). These works were not simply translations: their authors selected, explained and compared, and they record features of the music of their own time.

Under the Mughals the literature grew. Abū’l Faẓl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī (1590s) lists the musicians of Akbar’s court and describes the genres and instruments of Hindustani music. The reign of Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707), often said to have been hostile to music, in fact produced two of the most important works: Faqīrullāh’s Rāg Darpan (1666), which adapts a Hindi treatise ascribed to the court of Mān Siṃh Tomar of Gwalior and adds an account of the musicians of the author’s own day; and Mīrzā Khān’s Tuḥfat al-Hind (c. 1675), an encyclopaedia of Indian learning composed for a Mughal prince, with long sections on music and dance. Katherine Butler Brown (now Schofield) has shown that the emperor’s personal renunciation of music late in his reign did not amount to a ban, and that music continued to flourish in the households of the nobility (Brown 2007). In the eighteenth century Dargāh Qulī Khān’s account of Delhi under Muhammad Shāh, the Muraqqaʿ-i Dihlī, describes the singers, instrumentalists, dancers and courtesans of the city with an observer’s eye; in the nineteenth century Muḥammad Karam Imām’s Maʿdan al-Mūsīqī (1856) describes the musical world of Awadh under Wājid ʿAlī Shāh.

The Persian sources show that Mughal connoisseurs, Muslim and Hindu, treated Hindustani music as a learned art with its own theory, canon and great masters; that they integrated the Sanskrit categories — the six rāgas and their rāgiṇīs, the śrutis and the tālas — with the aesthetic vocabulary of Persian literature; and that they recorded the names, lineages and genres of musicians in a way the Sanskrit texts seldom did. Schofield has argued that the elite of the Mughal period carried out its own “classicisation” of music, centuries before the nationalist reformers of the twentieth century, and that the reformers’ neglect of these sources was part of their project of giving Indian music a purely Sanskrit history (Schofield 2010).

docs.title: 7.3 The Gharānās
docs.text:
A gharānā (from ghar, “house”) is a stylistic lineage, centred on a family of hereditary musicians and their disciples, distinguished by its approach to voice production, the treatment of rāga and composition, and its repertoire of compositions. The term came into common use only in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries, when musicians who had left their patrons’ courts needed to establish their credentials in a wider market; Neuman argues that a gharānā required at least three generations of distinguished musicians and a recognisable style (Neuman 1980). Table 7.1 lists the principal vocal gharānās of khayāl.

Table 7.1. Some vocal gharānās of khayāl Gharānā Founding figures Characteristics (in brief) Gwalior Haddu Khān and Hassu Khān (19th c.) Regarded as the oldest khayāl lineage; balanced, straightforward exposition of composition Agra Ghagge Khudā Bakhsh (19th c.); later Faiyaz Khan (1886–1950) Strong dhrupad and dhamār influence; nom-tom ālāp; rhythmic play with the text Kirana Abdul Karim Khan (1872–1937), Abdul Wahid Khan Slow, note-by-note unfolding of the rāga; emphasis on tone and intonation Jaipur–Atrauli Alladiya Khan (1855–1946) Complex, rarely heard rāgas; intricate, interwoven tāns Patiala Ali Bakhsh and Fateh Ali Khan (19th c.) Rapid, florid tāns; ṭhumrī Rampur–Sahaswan Inayat Hussain Khan (1849–1919) Tarānā; synthesis of Gwalior and Rampur styles

Instrumental music has its own lineages: the Seniya descendants of Tānsen, who played the bīn (rudra vīṇā) and rabāb; the Imdadkhani lineage of sitār, named after Imdad Khan (1848–1920) and continued by Vilayat Khan (1928–2004); the Maihar lineage of Allauddin Khan, whose pupils included his son Ali Akbar Khan (sarod, 1922–2009), his daughter Annapurna Devi (surbahār, 1927–2018) and Ravi Shankar (sitār, 1920–2012); and the tablā gharānās of Delhi, Ajrāḍā, Lucknow, Farrukhābād, Banāras and the Punjab (Chapter 5).

docs.title: 7.4 Regional Centres
docs.text:
The gharānās bear the names of places, and the history of Hindustani music is in large part a history of regional centres, each with its own patrons, genres and audiences (Bor et al. 2010; Neuman 1980).

Gwalior and Rampur. Gwalior, the home of dhrupad under Mān Siṃh Tomar, remained a centre under the Scindia rulers in the nineteenth century, when the khayāl singers associated with Haddu and Hassu Khān made it the starting point of most later khayāl lineages. The nawabs of Rampur, in Rohilkhand, patronised the descendants of Tānsen; the bīn player Wazir Khan of Rampur was the principal teacher of Allauddin Khan, through whom the Seniya tradition of instrumental music passed to the Maihar lineage.

Bengal. In Bengal a tradition of dhrupad took root at Bishnupur in the eighteenth century. After the annexation of Awadh in 1856, Wājid ʿAlī Shāh lived in exile at Metiabruz, on the edge of Calcutta, until his death in 1887, and his household made the city a centre of ṭhumrī, Kathak, the sarod and the tablā. The zamindars and merchants of Calcutta, among them members of the Tagore family, patronised musicians, held music conferences and collected instruments (Chapter 10), and the Bengali song traditions of Rabindranath Tagore and Kazi Nazrul Islam drew freely on rāga.

Banaras. Banaras, a city of temples, pilgrims and patrons, was a centre of ṭhumrī, dādrā and the seasonal songs, of a tablā gharānā and of the śahnāī; Siddheshwari Devi, Girija Devi and Bismillah Khan carried its music into the twentieth-century concert hall.

Maharashtra and northern Karnataka. From the late nineteenth century khayāl took deep root in western India. Balkrishnabuwa Ichalkaranjikar brought the Gwalior style to Maharashtra; Alladiya Khan settled at the court of Kolhapur and later in Bombay; Abdul Karim Khan made his home at Miraj, whose annual festival at a Sufi shrine became a gathering of musicians. Bombay’s merchants and music circles, the Marathi musical theatre and the schools of the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya created a large audience, and the towns of the Dharwad region of northern Karnataka produced an extraordinary number of singers of the Kirana and Jaipur–Atrauli styles, among them Sawai Gandharva, Mallikarjun Mansur, Gangubai Hangal and Bhimsen Joshi. By the mid-twentieth century western India had become, with Bengal, the main home of Hindustani vocal music (Bakhle 2005).

The Deccan. The sultanates of the Deccan had their own courtly culture of music. Ibrāhīm ʿĀdil Shāh II of Bijapur (r. 1580–1627) composed the Kitāb-i Nauras, a collection of songs in Dakhni set to named rāgas, opening with praise of Sarasvatī as well as of the Sufi saints; the Qutb Shahi court of Golconda and later the court of the Nizams of Hyderabad patronised north Indian musicians.

The Punjab. The Punjab was the home of the Patiala and Shāmcaurāsī lineages, of the ṭappā, of Sufi music and of Sikh kīrtan. The Harivallabh festival at Jalandhar, held at a shrine since the late nineteenth century, is among the oldest continuing music festivals in India; after 1947 the musicians of western Punjab continued their traditions in Lahore and elsewhere in Pakistan (below).

docs.title: 7.5 Dhrupad
docs.text:
Dhrupad (from Sanskrit dhruvapada, “fixed verse” or “refrain”) is the oldest of the genres of Hindustani art music still performed. Its name links it with the dhruva, a song-type of the medieval treatises, but as a genre of vernacular song it emerges in the fifteenth century; claims that it is “Vedic” have no basis. A dhrupad performance begins with a long, unmetred ālāp sung to syllables such as nom, tom, re and nā, which unfolds the rāga slowly from the lower register and gradually acquires a pulse (joḍ) and speed. The composition that follows, accompanied by the barrel drum pakhāvaj, has four sections: sthāyī, antarā, sañcārī and ābhog. The singer elaborates it by reciting the text in rhythmic transformations (layakārī) and dividing it into rhythmic patterns (bol-bāṇṭ), rather than with the rapid melodic runs of khayāl. The principal tālas are Cautāl (twelve beats), Sūltāl (ten), Tīvrā (seven) and, for the related genre dhamār, sung especially at Holī, the fourteen-beat Dhamār (Sanyal and Widdess 2004).

Tradition speaks of four styles (vāṇī) of dhrupad — Gauharī, Ḍāgurī, Khaṇḍārī and Nauhārī — associated with musicians or places of Akbar’s time; by the twentieth century the distinctions were largely nominal. Dhrupad declined in the nineteenth century as khayāl took over the courts and concert stages, and was preserved by a few families, notably the Dagars, and by the Mallik family of Darbhanga in Bihar. Its revival from the 1960s owed much to the Dagar brothers — Nasir Moinuddin and Nasir Aminuddin Dagar, and later Nasir Zahiruddin and Nasir Faiyazuddin Dagar — and to the rudra vīṇā player Zia Mohiuddin Dagar (1929–1990), and it now has many younger exponents, among them the Gundecha brothers and Uday Bhawalkar (Sanyal and Widdess 2004).

The texts of dhrupad are in Braj Bhāṣā and include praise of gods and of royal patrons, descriptions of seasons and festivals, and discussions of music itself. Composers included Hindu and Muslim musicians, and Muslim singers sang compositions in praise of Hindu deities as a matter of course.

docs.title: 7.6 Khayāl
docs.text:
Khayāl (from Arabic and Persian khayāl, “imagination”) became the principal vocal genre of Hindustani music in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It allows the singer more freedom than dhrupad, with a lighter voice and richer ornamentation, rapid melodic runs (tān) and a larger role for improvisation. A full khayāl performance usually consists of two compositions (bandiś) in the same rāga: a “great” khayāl (baṛā khayāl) in slow tempo, often in Ektāl, Jhūmrā or Tīntāl taken very slowly, and a “small” khayāl (choṭā khayāl) in medium or fast tempo, usually in Tīntāl or Ektāl. Each composition has two parts, the sthāyī, in the lower and middle registers, and the antarā, which rises to the upper tonic. The opening phrase of the sthāyī (the mukhṛā), which leads to the sam, is the refrain to which the singer constantly returns (Ruckert 2004; Wade 1979).

The slow khayāl is developed through a gradual expansion of the rāga (baṛhat or vistār), sung to the words of the text or to vowels, followed by rhythmic play with the words (bol-bāṇṭ, bol-tān), melodic runs on the vowel “ā” (ākār tān) and passages sung to the names of the notes (sargam). The fast khayāl brings faster and more brilliant tāns and tihāīs, and the performance often ends with a tarānā, a fast composition sung to syllables such as tā, nā, dere, tom and dir. The balance of these elements, the treatment of the text, and the speed and shape of the tāns distinguish the gharānās and individual singers. Each singer reconstructs the rāga and the composition afresh at every performance; the composition is a point of departure, not a text to be reproduced (Neuman 1980).

The texts of khayāl compositions, mostly in Braj Bhāṣā and related dialects, are short — often only a few lines — and deal with love and longing, the play of Kṛṣṇa, the seasons, the praise of patrons, saints and gods, and music itself. Many carry the pen-name of their composers, among them Sadāraṅg and Adāraṅg in the eighteenth century and, in the twentieth, the composers of the Agra and Gwalior lineages.

docs.title: 7.7 Ṭhumrī and the Light Classical Genres
docs.text:
Ṭhumrī is a genre of love song, in Braj and the eastern dialects of Hindi, whose texts are usually sung in the voice of a woman longing for her lover, often identified with Kṛṣṇa. It developed in nineteenth-century Lucknow and Banaras in the milieu of the courtesans and of the Kathak dancers, for whom it was the main expressive song (Chapter 16). Its musical treatment emphasises the expressive elaboration of the words (bol-banāv), with a freer use of rāga than khayāl: a ṭhumrī may draw on notes from related rāgas and is usually sung in a small group of “light” rāgas such as Khamāj, Kāfī, Bhairavī, Pīlū and Tilaṅg, in tālas such as Dīpcandī, Jat and Kaharvā. Two styles are distinguished: the earlier, more rhythmic bandiś kī ṭhumrī, associated with dance, and the slower bol-banāv kī ṭhumrī developed for listening (Manuel 1989; Perron 2007).

Related genres, often grouped as “light classical” (upaśāstrīya), include dādrā; ṭappā, a fast and intricate genre derived from the songs of Punjabi camel-drivers and refined in the nineteenth century; and seasonal songs such as kajrī and jhūlā for the rainy season, caitī for spring and horī for the Holī festival. The ghazal, the lyric genre of Persian and Urdu poetry, was sung in the courts and salons of north India and became one of the most popular forms of the twentieth century through singers such as Begum Akhtar (1914–1974), Mehdi Hassan of Pakistan and Jagjit Singh.

The singers of ṭhumrī and ghazal in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries were mostly courtesans — Gauhar Jan, the first star of the Indian gramophone (Section 23.2), Rasoolan Bai, Siddheshwari Devi and others — and their art was the target of the anti-nautch campaigns that sought to remove women performers of courtesan background from respectable society. Later singers, including Girija Devi and Shobha Gurtu, and scholars such as Peter Manuel and Lalita du Perron, have restored the genre’s history and its debt to these women (Manuel 1989; Perron 2007; Morcom 2013).

docs.title: 7.8 Instrumental Music
docs.text: Hindustani instrumental music developed largely from the eighteenth century, as the sitār, sarod and later the surbahār, santūr and bānsurī entered the concert world (Chapter 10). An instrumental performance usually begins with ālāp, joḍ and jhālā, modelled on the ālāp of the bīn and of dhrupad, followed by one or more compositions (gat) accompanied by the tablā. The early sitār repertoire distinguished the slow Masītkhānī gat, associated with the eighteenth-century musician Masīt Khān, and the fast Razākhānī gat of the nineteenth-century Lucknow musician Ghulām Razā (Miner 1993). The twentieth century saw the development of a “vocal” style of playing (gāyakī aṅg), especially in the sitār of Vilayat Khan, which imitated the phrasing and ornaments of khayāl, and of a fuller, more elaborate approach to ālāp drawing on the bīn tradition, in the Maihar school of Ravi Shankar and Ali Akbar Khan. Instrumentalists such as the śahnāī player Bismillah Khan (1916–2006), the santūr player Shivkumar Sharma and the flautist Hariprasad Chaurasia made concert instruments of instruments once confined to ceremonial or folk use.

docs.title: 7.9 The Hindustani Concert
docs.text:
The settings of Hindustani music have changed greatly over the last two centuries. Before the twentieth century most performances took place in the intimate gathering called mahfil or majlis: a room in a palace, a noble’s house or a courtesan’s salon, where a few connoisseurs sat on the floor around the musicians and responded to every phrase. The public concert, ticketed and held in a hall before hundreds or thousands of listeners, spread from the 1910s with the music conferences organised by Bhatkhande and others and became the normal setting after independence. The large music festivals of the twentieth century, such as the Sawai Gandharva festival in Pune (from 1953), brought together many artists over several nights.

A vocal performance in the modern concert is typically accompanied by tablā and by either harmonium or sāraṅgī, with one or two tānpūrās providing the drone (Figure 7.2); a dhrupad singer is accompanied instead by the pakhāvaj. An instrumental performance is accompanied by tablā alone, with a tānpurā or an electronic drone.

Figure 7.2. A young vocalist at a music festival in Kanpur, with tānpūrā, tablā and harmonium — the usual accompaniment of khayāl — and an electronic drone box behind. The photographer’s title describes the performance as dhrupad, which is normally accompanied by the pakhāvaj; the photograph is used here for the setting of the modern concert, not to illustrate a genre. Photo: Ayushdw1998, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The soloist chooses the rāgas, usually in accordance with the time of day, and the evening proceeds from serious rāgas and slow, extended performances to lighter pieces. It is customary, though not obligatory, to end with Bhairavī, sung or played in a ṭhumrī, bhajan or light composition. The accompanists follow the soloist: the sāraṅgī or harmonium player shadows the singer’s phrases a fraction behind and fills the pauses, and the tablā player keeps the ṭhekā, answers the soloist’s rhythmic phrases and, in instrumental performances, takes solo passages of his own.

The audience is part of the performance. Listeners in the mahfil tradition express their appreciation aloud, with exclamations such as vāh and kyā bāt hai, especially at a well-made return to sam or a beautiful phrase, and musicians respond to such recognition. Neuman has described how the hierarchy of the musical world was visible in performance: in where the musicians sat, in who could interrupt whom, and in the deference expected of accompanists to soloists (Neuman 1980). The modern concert hall has formalised the event, but the expectation that listeners will engage actively with the music remains.

docs.title: 7.10 Persianate and Sufi Music: Samāʿ and Qawwālī
7.10.1 Samāʿ
docs.text: For the Chishtī order of Sufis, which became the most widespread Sufi order in north India from the thirteenth century, listening to music and poetry in a ritual gathering (samāʿ) was a means of approaching God. The practice was controversial among Muslim jurists, and the Chishtī masters defended it with conditions: the listeners had to be spiritually prepared, the poetry appropriate, and the gathering properly conducted under the authority of a Sufi master. The Chishtī shrines — of Muʿīnuddīn Chishtī (d. 1236) at Ajmer, of Niẓāmuddīn Awliyāʾ (d. 1325) in Delhi, and many others — became centres of devotional music, and the anniversary of a saint’s death (ʿurs) is still celebrated with music (Qureshi 1986).

docs.title: 7.10.2 Qawwālī
docs.text:
Qawwālī is the music of the Sufi assembly, performed by a group of hereditary professional singers (qawwāls) led by one or two soloists, with a chorus who clap and repeat refrains, and accompanied today by harmonium and ḍholak or tablā. The name derives from qaul, “saying”, the term for a song setting an Arabic saying of the Prophet, which traditionally opens a samāʿ assembly; the most famous qaul, beginning man kunto maulā, is ascribed by tradition to Amīr Khusrau. The repertoire comprises poetry in Persian, in the Hindavi of the Delhi region and of the east (pūrbī), in Urdu and in Punjabi — praise of God (ḥamd) and of the Prophet (naʿt), songs in honour of ʿAlī (manqabat) and of the saints, and mystical love poetry (ghazal) — by poets from Rūmī and Khusrau to Bulleh Shāh and modern Urdu writers.

Regula Qureshi’s study of qawwālī at Delhi shrines shows that it is music made to serve a spiritual purpose. The singers watch the listeners and adapt the performance to their states: they repeat a line that has moved a listener, insert verses from other poems (girah) to intensify its meaning, and accelerate or prolong the music as a listener enters a state of ecstasy (ḥāl). Listeners present offerings of money (nazrāna) to the singers through the master of the assembly. The music uses rāgas and tālas, often light ones, but its form is shaped by the text and the occasion, not by the rules of art music (Qureshi 1986).

In the twentieth century qawwālī moved from the shrine to the concert stage, the gramophone and the film studio. Pakistani performers such as the Sabri Brothers and Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan (1948–1997) brought it to audiences around the world, and in India it has been performed at shrines, in concerts and in Hindi film. The shrine tradition continues alongside the commercial one, as do other forms of Sufi music in South Asia: the kāfī of the Punjab and Sindh, sung to the poetry of Bulleh Shāh and Shāh ʿAbdul Laṭīf, and the songs of the Bāuls and fakirs of Bengal (Chapter 21).

docs.title: 7.11 Sikh Kīrtan
docs.text:
The Sikh tradition is, from its beginning, a tradition of sung scripture. Guru Nānak (1469–1539) composed his hymns to be sung, and according to the traditional accounts travelled with a Muslim companion, Bhāī Mardānā, who played the rabāb while the Guru sang. When the fifth Guru, Arjan, compiled the Ādi Granth in 1604, he arranged its hymns not by author but by rāga, so that the scripture itself prescribes the music of worship; its structure and the liturgy of the gurdwārā are described in Section 9.12 (Mann 2001; Singh 2000).

Singing the hymns (śabad kīrtan) is the central act of Sikh worship, and the history of its musicians is a history of the Punjab’s shared musical culture. For centuries the professional singers at the Harmandir included Muslim rabābīs, who claimed descent from Bhāī Mardānā, as well as Sikh rāgīs; most rabābīs left for Pakistan at the Partition of 1947. Traditional instruments included the rabāb, the bowed sarandā, tāūs and dilrubā, and the pair of drums called jōṛī; in the twentieth century the harmonium became the standard accompaniment. Since the late twentieth century a movement for gurmat saṅgīt has sought to restore the singing of the hymns in their prescribed rāgas and to revive the stringed instruments of the older tradition.

docs.title: 7.12 Other Devotional Music of the North
docs.text: Hindustani art music has always lived alongside, and drawn on, devotional song. In the temples of the Puṣṭimārga sect of Vallabhācārya, centred on Nāthdvārā in Rajasthan, havelī saṅgīt sets the poetry of Sūrdās and the other poets of the aṣṭachāp to dhrupad- and dhamār-style music according to the hours of the day and the festivals of the year. The songs (pad) of Kabīr, Mīrābāī, Tulsīdās and Sūrdās are sung throughout the north as bhajans, in styles ranging from village singing to concert performance. In Maharashtra the Vārkarī pilgrims sing the abhaṅgs of Jñāneśvar, Nāmdev and Tukārām, and the Marathi musical theatre (saṅgīt nāṭak) of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries produced a popular semi-classical repertoire (nāṭyasaṅgīt). In Bengal, the songs of Rabindranath Tagore (Rabīndrasaṅgīt) created a distinct art-song tradition that draws freely on rāga, folk song and Western melody. The congregational kīrtan of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas, with khol drum and cymbals, has deep roots in Bengal and Odisha and is related to the saṅkīrtana of Manipur (Chapter 18) (Henry 1988). These traditions, and the devotional music of the south, are described more fully in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 7.13.1 Reform, nationalism and the music college
docs.text:
In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Hindustani music was reshaped by the decline of court patronage, the rise of urban middle-class audiences, and the nationalist project of creating a “classical” Indian music worthy of comparison with that of Europe. Two reformers were central. V. N. Bhatkhande (1860–1936), a Brahmin lawyer from Bombay, collected compositions from hereditary musicians, published them in notation, devised the system of ten thāṭs (Chapter 4), organised the All-India Music Conferences from 1916 and helped found the Marris College of Music in Lucknow (1926). V. D. Paluskar (1872–1931) founded the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya in Lahore in 1901 and a network of schools that taught music to middle-class students in a devotional, Hindu idiom (Bakhle 2005; Bhatkhande 1910).

Their achievements were real: they made music teachable outside the hereditary families, created a body of notated repertoire and helped give music social respectability. But as Janaki Bakhle has shown, they did so in ways that marginalised the hereditary Muslim musicians on whom they depended for their material: Bhatkhande by subordinating their knowledge to a rationalised, textual theory; Paluskar by presenting music as a Hindu devotional art whose proper practitioners were respectable Hindu householders. The courtesans were excluded even more decisively. The “classicisation” of Hindustani music, which Katherine Butler Schofield compares with similar movements in the Mughal period, was thus also a redistribution of musical authority along lines of religion, caste, class and gender (Bakhle 2005; Schofield 2010).

docs.title: 7.13.2 Recording, radio and the concert
docs.text: The gramophone (from 1902), All India Radio (from 1936) and the public concert created new audiences and new careers. Radio policy was itself an instrument of the new classicism, most famously in the long exclusion of the harmonium from the air, and after Independence the government promoted classical music on the radio as a national art (Section 23.2). The Partition of 1947 divided the musical world of the north; many hereditary musicians moved to Pakistan, some, like Bade Ghulam Ali Khan (1902–1968), later returning to India. The great figures of the mid-twentieth century — among them Kesarbai Kerkar, Gangubai Hangal, Mallikarjun Mansur, Amir Khan, Kumar Gandharva, Bhimsen Joshi and Kishori Amonkar among singers; Ravi Shankar, Vilayat Khan, Ali Akbar Khan and Bismillah Khan among instrumentalists; and Alla Rakha and his son Zakir Hussain (1951–2024) on the tablā — came from both hereditary and non-hereditary backgrounds and performed for audiences across India and, increasingly, the world (Chapter 23) (Neuman 1980; Farrell 1997).

docs.title: 7.13.3 Women on the concert stage
docs.text:
The history of women in Hindustani music in the twentieth century is a history of transition from the world of the courtesans to that of the respectable concert artist. In the early decades of the century most professional women singers came from courtesan families, and their art was both admired and stigmatised. As the anti-nautch campaigns and the new ideal of respectability closed the salons, some of these singers found new careers in recording, radio, theatre and film, and some changed their names or concealed their origins; Akhtaribai Faizabadi became, after her marriage, Begum Akhtar. At the same time women from “respectable” families began to perform in public; Hirabai Barodekar (1905–1989), daughter of the Kirana master Abdul Karim Khan, was among the first of them to give ticketed public concerts. The great women khayāl singers of the mid-century came from both worlds. Kesarbai Kerkar (1892–1977) and Mogubai Kurdikar (1904–2001) belonged to the hereditary performing communities of Goa; Gangubai Hangal (1913–2009) was the daughter of a Karnatak singer from a hereditary family; and Mogubai’s daughter Kishori Amonkar (1932–2017) became one of the most admired singers of the later twentieth century. Others, such as Siddheshwari Devi (1908–1977) and Girija Devi (1929–2017), carried the ṭhumrī tradition of Banaras into the concert hall (Perron 2007; Bakhle 2005).

The transition had costs. The repertoire and expertise of the courtesans were partly absorbed into the new concert music and partly lost; and women performers of the new generation were often expected to avoid the genres and gestures associated with courtesans, or to present them in a sanitised form. Lalita du Perron, Peter Manuel and others have argued that the history of ṭhumrī cannot be written without recognising the women who created and sustained it, many of whose names survive only on early gramophone records (Perron 2007; Manuel 1989).

docs.title: 7.13.4 Beyond India’s borders
docs.text: Hindustani music is not an Indian national music alone. Its history belongs equally to Pakistan, where the musicians of Lahore and the radio stations of Karachi and Lahore sustained musicians of the Patiala, Shāmcaurāsī, Kirana and other lineages after 1947, and where singers such as Roshan Ara Begum (1917–1982) and the brothers Salamat Ali Khan and Nazakat Ali Khan were among the leading performers of their generation; and to Bangladesh, the home of Allauddin Khan, whose influence through the Maihar lineage reached across the subcontinent. Patronage of art music declined in Pakistan in the later twentieth century, and many traditions there are now carried by a small number of families and by the qawwālī and ghazal of the popular stage. In Nepal, the Rana court patronised Hindustani musicians in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Through emigration and touring, Hindustani music has also become part of the musical life of Britain, North America and other parts of the world (Chapter 23) (Farrell 1997; Lavezzoli 2006).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Neuman (1980) is the classic study of the social organisation of Hindustani music, and Bor et al. (2010) a collection of essays on its history from the thirteenth century. Wade (1979) and Ruckert (2004) are clear introductions to the music. On particular genres see Sanyal and Widdess (2004) (dhrupad), Manuel (1989) and Perron (2007) (ṭhumrī). Miner (1993) and Kippen (1988) are the essential studies of the sitār and tablā. Bakhle (2005) and Schofield (2010) discuss the politics of “classical” music, and Brown (2007) the place of music at the Mughal court under Aurangzeb; Schofield (2023) follows the musicians of the late Mughal world from 1748 to 1858, and Katz (2017) tells the history of Hindustani music from the side of a hereditary Muslim lineage. Qureshi (1986) is the standard study of qawwālī, and Sharma (2005) the best introduction to Amīr Khusrau. On Sikh scripture and its musical organisation see Mann (2001) and Singh (2000).

docs.title: Chapter 8: Karnatak Music
docs.text: Karnatak (Carnatic) music is the art music of South India — of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Kerala — and of the South Indian communities of Sri Lanka and the diaspora. Its name, from karṇāṭaka, a term used in medieval texts for the south, was adopted in the colonial period to distinguish it from the “Hindustani” music of the north. Compared with Hindustani music, it places greater weight on a large repertoire of fixed compositions, most of them devotional songs in Telugu, Sanskrit, Tamil and Kannada; it classifies its rāgas under a systematic scheme of seventy-two parent scales; it uses heavy ornamentation (gamaka) as an integral part of rāga; and its concerts follow a format shaped in the twentieth century in the city of Madras (Chennai). Each January, on the anniversary of Tyāgarāja’s death, hundreds of musicians sit together on the bank of the Kāvēri at Tiruvaiyaru to sing his five “jewel” songs in chorus: an image of a tradition that venerates its composers above all. Behind that image lies a longer and more contested history, of courts and temples, of a theory of seventy-two scales, and of a modern concert world that is both a celebrated national art and a subject of debate about caste and community.

docs.title: 8.1.1 Tamil music
docs.text: The earliest descriptions of music in the south are in Tamil. The Caṅkam poems and the epic Cilappatikāram (c. fifth–sixth century) speak of the harp (yāḻ), of the melodic modes called paṇ, of drums, of the dancing girl Mātavi and her training, and of the songs and dances of herdsmen and hunters; the epic is a rich, if poetic, source for the music and dance of its time (Parthasarathy 1993). The devotional hymns of the Śaiva Nāyaṉmār (sixth to ninth centuries), collected in the Tēvāram, were arranged by paṇ and have been sung in Śiva temples ever since by hereditary singers (ōtuvār); Indira Peterson’s study shows how the hymns were conceived as songs for congregational worship (Peterson 1989). The temple hymnody of the Tamil country is described further in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 8.1.2 Paṇ and yāḻ: the Tamil theory of music
docs.text:
The Tamil sources preserve a musical vocabulary of their own, independent of the Sanskrit treatises though in contact with them. The Caṅkam poems associate particular melodies (paṇ) and particular kinds of harp (yāḻ) with the landscapes (tiṇai) of Tamil poetics, so that a melody, like a flower or a bird, could evoke the hills, the forest or the seashore. The Cilappatikāram names the seven notes with Tamil terms — kural, tuttam, kaikkiḷai, uḻai, iḷi, viḷari and tāram — and in its episode of the cowherd women’s round dance (Āycciyar kuravai) seven girls, each given the name of one of these notes, stand in a circle to sing and dance. The commentators and modern scholars read the scene as a representation of the way in which new modes are obtained by taking each note of a scale in turn as the starting point, a procedure comparable to the mūrchanā of the Sanskrit texts (Chapter 4) (Parthasarathy 1993).

Much of the early theory survives only in the medieval commentary on the epic by Aṭiyārkkunallār, who quotes from Tamil works on music and dance that are otherwise lost and describes the arrangement of modes (pālai) in cycles and other figures. Later Tamil treatises on the performing arts, such as the Pañcamarapu ascribed to Aṟivaṉār, are of uncertain date. The hymns of the Tēvāram, arranged under some two dozen paṇs, are the main bridge between this early theory and living practice: the ōtuvārs who sing them today use melodies identified with modern Karnatak rāgas, but how far these identifications preserve the medieval melodies is uncertain (Peterson 1989).

In the twentieth century the Tamil sources became the basis of a Tamil history of music, written partly in reaction to accounts that derived all southern music from Sanskrit theory. Abraham Pandither’s Karuṇāmirta Sāgaram (1917) argued that the system of intervals and the art music of the south were of Tamil origin; Swami Vipulananda’s Yāḻ Nūl (1947) attempted to reconstruct the ancient harps and their tunings; and from the 1940s the Tamil Isai movement (below) sponsored research into the paṇs and their relation to the rāgas. Some of the claims made in this literature, for the great antiquity of Karnatak rāgas in particular, go beyond the evidence, but the Tamil sources it brought to light are an essential part of the history of Indian music, and the relation of the ancient paṇs to the later rāgas remains a live question (Weidman 2006; Subramanian 2006).

docs.title: 8.1.3 From Vijayanagara to Thanjavur
docs.text:
The Sanskrit treatises of the medieval period, above all the Saṅgītaratnākara (Chapter 4), were authoritative in the south as in the north. The Vijayanagara empire (1336–1565) and the Nāyaka and Maratha kingdoms that succeeded it at Madurai, Thanjavur and elsewhere were the great patrons of southern music. Three developments of this period laid the foundations of Karnatak music.

First, devotional song in the vernacular languages became a principal vehicle of art music. The Kannada Haridāsa poets, above all Purandaradāsa (1484–1564), composed songs (kīrtana, sūḷādi) for congregational singing; Purandaradāsa is also credited by tradition with devising the graded exercises in Rāga Māyāmāḷavagauḷa with which students still begin, and is called the “grandfather” (pitāmaha) of Karnatak music. In Telugu, Annamācārya (1408–1503), the poet of the Veṅkaṭeśvara temple at Tirupati, composed devotional songs (saṅkīrtana) of which several thousand survive inscribed on copper plates (tradition credits him with 32,000). In the seventeenth century Bhadrācala Rāmadāsu sang to Rāma, Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha composed the Sanskrit Kṛṣṇalīlātaraṅgiṇī, a narrative in song used also by dancers, and Kṣetrayya composed the Telugu padams of love addressed to the god Muvva Gopāla that became central to the repertoire of dancers (Chapters 3 and 15).

Second, theorists at Vijayanagara and Thanjavur reorganised the classification of rāgas under parent scales (mela), the work that led to the modern scheme of seventy-two (Section 8.3).

Third, the court of the Maratha kings of Thanjavur (1676–1855) became a meeting place of musicians, dancers, poets and scholars from many regions. The musicians of the court, and of the temples of the Kāvēri delta, developed the forms of composition — varṇam, kṛti, padam, jāvaḷi, tillāna — that make up the modern repertoire (Subramanian 2006).

docs.title: 8.2 The Trinity and the Kṛti
docs.text: Three composers, all born at Tiruvarur in the Kāvēri delta within thirteen years of one another, are revered as the “Trinity” of Karnatak music. Their works define the kṛti, the principal compositional form of the tradition.

docs.title: 8.2.1 Tyāgarāja (1767–1847)
docs.text:
Tyāgarāja, a Telugu-speaking Brahmin who spent most of his life at Tiruvaiyaru on the Kāvēri, composed several hundred songs, most of them in Telugu and addressed to Rāma. His songs range from simple devotional pieces to elaborate kṛtis whose melodic variations (saṅgatis) expand each line step by step; they express personal devotion, reflection on music as a spiritual path, and, at times, the composer’s loneliness and frustration. Among his best-known works are the five pañcaratna (“five jewel”) kṛtis, sung together by hundreds of musicians at the annual festival (ārādhana) on the anniversary of his death at Tiruvaiyaru. The pallavi of one of them, in Rāga Śrī, salutes all the great musicians:

Tyāgarāja, Endarō mahānubhāvulu (Rāga Śrī), pallavi

endarō mahānubhāvulu andarikī vandanamulu

“There are so many great souls; my salutations to all of them.”

docs.title: 8.2.2 Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar (1775–1835)
docs.text: Dīkṣitar composed mainly in Sanskrit, with the signature (mudrā) “Guruguha”. His kṛtis, often in slow tempo with weighty gamakas, are notable for their learned texts, their systematic groups — songs in praise of the deities of particular temples, the navāvaraṇa songs for the goddess Kamalāmbā of Tiruvarur in the Śrīvidyā tantric tradition, songs to the nine planets — and their use of rare rāgas from the older mela scheme of Veṅkaṭamakhin. He also set Sanskrit texts to European tunes heard from the band of the East India Company at Madras (the noṭṭusvara sāhitya), a small but telling sign of the musical encounters of the period.

docs.title: 8.2.3 Śyāmā Śāstri (1762–1827)
docs.text: The eldest of the three, Śyāmā Śāstri was a priest of the temple of Bangāru Kāmākṣī at Thanjavur and composed in Telugu, Sanskrit and Tamil, with the signature “Śyāmakṛṣṇa”. His relatively small output is admired for its rhythmic subtlety — he favoured Miśra Cāpu and other unusual tālas — and for its intense devotion to the goddess; his three svarajatis are among the most valued compositions in the repertoire.

docs.title: 8.2.4 The kṛti
docs.text:
A kṛti has three sections: the pallavi (refrain), the anupallavi, which usually rises to the upper register, and one or more caraṇams, which often carry the composer’s signature and return to the melody of the anupallavi at the end. Many kṛtis add composed melodic variations (saṅgatis), passages of solfa (ciṭṭasvara), or passages in which the solfa syllables themselves form words of the text (svarākṣara). The kṛti is the frame for improvisation: a singer may precede it with ālāpana and elaborate one of its lines with niraval and kalpana svara (below) (Viswanathan and Allen 2004). Figure 8.1 shows the usual order of its sections.

Figure 8.1. The sections of a Karnatak kṛti in their usual order. Many kṛtis have several caraṇams, each followed by the pallavi, and some add composed variations (saṅgati) or passages of solfa (ciṭṭasvara).

Other composers of the period and after enriched the repertoire: Svāti Tirunāḷ (1813–1846), the Maharaja of Travancore, who composed in Sanskrit, Malayalam, Telugu, Kannada and Hindustani; Gopālakṛṣṇa Bhārati (nineteenth century), whose Tamil musical narrative Nantaṉār Caritram tells the story of the Dalit saint Nantaṉār; Patnam Subramania Iyer (1845–1902); Mysore Vasudevachar; and, in the twentieth century, Papanasam Sivan (1890–1973), whose Tamil songs became popular through film as well as concert.

docs.title: 8.2.5 Composers in Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam
docs.text:
The dominance of Telugu and Sanskrit in the concert repertoire, a legacy of the Nāyaka and Maratha courts and of the Trinity, has sometimes hidden the fact that art music was composed in the other languages of the south throughout this period. In Tamil, three poet-composers of the period between the sixteenth and the eighteenth centuries — Muttuttāṇṭavar of Sirkazhi, Mārimuttāppiḷḷai and Aruṇācalakkavirāyar — were later honoured as a “Tamil Trinity”. Muttuttāṇṭavar and Mārimuttāppiḷḷai composed songs to Śiva as Naṭarāja of Chidambaram, the latter including songs of mock censure of the god; Aruṇācalakkavirāyar’s Rāma Nāṭakam retells the Rāmāyaṇa in a sequence of songs and verses that became widely popular. Tamil padams for dancers were composed by Ghanam Krishna Iyer and Vaidisvarankoil Subbarama Iyer in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and in the nineteenth century Gopālakṛṣṇa Bhārati and Nīlakaṇṭha Śivan composed songs that are still sung. In the twentieth century the songs of the poet Subramania Bharati (1882–1921), with their nationalist and devotional themes, entered both the concert and the popular repertoire, and Papanasam Sivan, Periyasamy Thooran and others composed new Tamil kṛtis for the concert platform. The demand of the Tamil Isai movement that concerts include more Tamil songs (below) drew on this heritage.

In Kannada, the dēvaranāmas of the Haridāsas remained the core of devotional song, and the court of Mysore supported composers of kṛtis and varṇams, among them Mysore Sadashiva Rao and Mysore Vasudevachar. In Malayalam, Svāti Tirunāḷ and the poets of his court composed songs for concert and dance, and Irayimman Tampi, the author of Kathakaḷi plays, composed the lullaby Ōmanattiṅkaḷ kiṭāvō, one of the best-known songs of Kerala. Many of these composers wrote in more than one language, and the multilingual repertoire of the south is better understood as a shared resource than as the property of one language community (Subramanian 2006; Weidman 2006).

docs.title: 8.3.1 The seventy-two melakartas
docs.text:
Karnatak theory classifies rāgas under seventy-two parent scales (melakarta). Each melakarta is a complete seven-note scale ascending and descending, with Sa and Pa fixed and one form each of Ri, Ga, Ma, Dha and Ni. The number seventy-two follows from the possible positions of the movable notes (Chapter 4):

  • Ma can be natural (śuddha, M1) or sharp (prati, M2): 2 possibilities.

  • Ri and Ga together can occupy the four semitones between Sa and Ma in six ways (R1G1, R1G2, R1G3, R2G2, R2G3, R3G3), because the second Ri and the first Ga, and the third Ri and the second Ga, coincide in pitch.

  • Dha and Ni can likewise occupy the four semitones between Pa and the upper Sa in six ways (D1N1 … D3N3).

There are therefore \(2 \times 6 \times 6 = 72\) scales (Figure 8.2).

Figure 8.2. The twelve note positions (svarasthāna) of the octave with their sixteen Karnatak names (above) and their Hindustani names (below; flat notes in lower case, Ma\('\) = tīvra Ma). Because R\(_2\) and G\(_1\), R\(_3\) and G\(_2\), D\(_2\) and N\(_1\), and D\(_3\) and N\(_2\) share a pitch, Ri and Ga can be chosen in six ways (orange = Ri, blue = Ga) and so can Dha and Ni (orange = Dha, blue = Ni); with the two forms of Ma this gives \(2 \times 6 \times 6 = 72\) melakartas. The Ri–Ga pair fixes the cakra (pairs 1–6 for cakras 1–6 with M\(_1\) and 7–12 with M\(_2\)), and the Dha–Ni pair the place of a scale within its cakra.

They are numbered systematically: the first thirty-six have M1 and the second thirty-six M2; within each half, the scales are arranged in six groups (cakra) of six, the cakra fixing the Ri–Ga pair and the position within it the Dha–Ni pair. In arithmetical terms, if \(m\) is 0 for M1 and 1 for M2, \(a\) (1–6) the number of the Ri–Ga pair and \(b\) (1–6) that of the Dha–Ni pair, the number of the melakarta is \(36m + 6(a - 1) + b\). Kīravāṇi, for example, with M1 (0), R2G2 (the fourth pair) and D1N3 (the third pair), is \(0 + 18 + 3 = 21\) (Viswanathan and Allen 2004; Krishna 2013).

docs.title: 8.3.2 History of the scheme
docs.text:
The scheme was the work of two centuries. Rāmāmātya’s Svaramelakalānidhi (Vijayanagara, 1550) had grouped the rāgas of its time under twenty melas, defined by the arrangement of the frets of the vīṇā (Section 6.6). Veṅkaṭamakhin, writing at Thanjavur in the mid-seventeenth century, demonstrated in his Caturdaṇḍīprakāśikā that seventy-two melas were possible, though only nineteen were in use in his time, and he named the melas by existing rāgas, many of which did not use all seven notes in a straight line. In the eighteenth century the theorist Govindācārya (in the Saṅgrahacūḍāmaṇi) completed the system in its present form, requiring every melakarta to be a complete (sampūrṇa) scale in ascent and descent and giving the seventy-two the names now used (Table 8.1). These names encode their numbers by the kaṭapayādi scheme, in which consonants stand for digits (ka, ṭa, pa, ya = 1; kha, ṭha, pha, ra = 2; and so on): the first two syllables of the name, read in reverse order, give the number. “Kharaharapriyā” begins kha (2) ra (2): 22. “Mecakalyāṇi” begins ma (5) ca (6): read in reverse, 65. In the names of a few melakartas a prefix was added to make the code work, as in “Dhīraśaṅkarābharaṇam” (dhī 9, ra 2: 29) (Krishna 2013).

The scheme is an elegant piece of theory, and the existence of names for all seventy-two scales has encouraged composers to write in previously unused melas; Koṭīśvara Iyer (1870–1936) and M. Balamuralikrishna composed sets of songs in all seventy-two. But it is a classification of scales, not of rāgas. Many important rāgas (Bhairavi, Kāmbhōji, Bēgaḍa) use notes or phrases that do not fit their assigned mela neatly, and their identity lies in phrases and gamakas that no scale can represent.

All other rāgas are “derived” (janya) from a melakarta: they may omit notes (in ascent, descent or both), use notes in zigzag (vakra) order, or add a note foreign to the parent (bhāṣāṅga rāgas). Table 8.2 gives some well-known examples.

docs.title: 8.3.4 Gamaka
docs.text: Karnatak musicians regard gamaka as the life of rāga. Most notes in most rāgas are sung or played not as steady pitches but with characteristic movements: oscillations (kampita), slides (jāru), stressed repetitions and approaches from neighbouring notes. Teachers use Tamil and Telugu terms such as kampitam, jāru, nokku, oḍukkal and orikkai for particular movements, alongside the older Sanskrit lists (Chapter 4). In Rāga Tōḍi, for example, the Ga and Dha are sung with wide, slow oscillations that make the rāga instantly recognisable; the same notes in another rāga would be sung differently. The density and style of gamaka have changed over time and differ between schools (bāṇi); twentieth-century recordings show a range of approaches (Viswanathan and Allen 2004).

docs.title: 8.4 Compositional Forms
docs.text:
The Karnatak repertoire comprises a graded series of forms, used both for teaching and in performance (Viswanathan and Allen 2004; Krishna 2013).

Exercises and gītam. Students begin with scale exercises (sarali, janṭa and dāṭu varisai) and patterns in the seven sūḷādi tālas (alaṅkāra), usually in Māyāmāḷavagauḷa, and then learn simple songs (gītam), several attributed to Purandaradāsa. Svarajati. An intermediate form alternating passages of solfa and text; the three svarajatis of Śyāmā Śāstri are concert pieces in their own right. Varṇam. A composition that sets out the essential phrases of a rāga in alternating sections of text and solfa, sung in two speeds. The concert (tāna) varṇam, such as Viribōṇi in Bhairavi by Pacchimiriyam Ādiyappayya (eighteenth century) or Evvarī bōdhana in Ābhōgi by Patnam Subramania Iyer, opens many concerts; the dance (pada) varṇam, with more text, is the centrepiece of the Bharatanāṭyam recital (Chapter 15). Kṛti and kīrtana. The main concert form, described above. Padam and jāvaḷi. Slow, expressive love songs, in Telugu and Tamil, composed for and long transmitted by the hereditary women performers of the courts and temples; the jāvaḷi, a nineteenth-century genre, is lighter and faster than the padam (Chapter 3). Tillāna. A lively composition of rhythmic syllables with a short passage of text, used to close concerts and dance recitals; its form was developed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and is related to the Hindustani tarānā. Rāgamālikā. A “garland of rāgas”, a composition passing through several rāgas in succession. Devotional songs. Dēvaranāmas of the Haridāsas, the abhaṅgs of Maharashtra, the Tamil Tiruppugaḻ of Aruṇagirinātar (fifteenth century) and many others are sung in the lighter, later part of concerts.

docs.title: 8.5.1 The kacēri
docs.text:
The modern Karnatak concert (kacēri) took shape in the early twentieth century, when concerts moved from temples, weddings and patrons’ homes to the halls of the urban music societies (sabhā) of Madras. Its format is credited especially to the singer Ariyakudi Ramanuja Iyengar (1890–1967).
