A typical concert of two to three hours opens with a varṇam, continues with several kṛtis of increasing weight, some preceded by short ālāpanas and followed by kalpana svaras, and reaches its centre in one or two major kṛtis with full improvisation. It may then include a rāgam–tānam–pallavi, followed by the percussion solo (tani āvartanam), and ends with lighter pieces — padams, jāvaḷis, tillānas, devotional songs — and a closing benediction (maṅgaḷam) (Viswanathan and Allen 2004; Weidman 2006).

The ensemble usually consists of the principal performer (a singer, or a player of vīṇā, violin, flute or other instrument), a violinist who shadows and answers the melody, the mṛdaṅgam, often a second percussionist (ghaṭam, kañjīrā or morsing), and a drone (tambūrā, today often electronic). The violin, adopted in the early nineteenth century — the brother of Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar, Bāluswāmi Dīkṣitar, is credited with introducing it — is played seated, with the scroll resting on the player’s foot, and has become indispensable.

docs.title: 8.5.2 Improvisation
docs.text: Improvisation (manodharma) in Karnatak music takes four main forms. Ālāpana is the unmetred exposition of the rāga. Tānam is a rhythmic but unmetred elaboration, sung to syllables such as ā, nam, ta. Niraval is the improvised melodic variation of a single line of the text, keeping the words and their position in the tāla. Kalpana svara are improvised passages sung to the names of the notes, returning each time to a chosen point of the composition, of increasing length and complexity, and often ending with elaborate calculated cadences. In the rāgam–tānam–pallavi, the most demanding concert item, the musician improvises ālāpana and tānam in a chosen rāga, then sings a single composed line (the pallavi), often in a complex tāla, and develops it through niraval, changes of speed and kalpana svara, sometimes in several rāgas (rāgamālikā) (Viswanathan and Allen 2004).

docs.title: 8.6 The Music of the Temple: Periya Mēḷam
docs.text:
Beside the concert music of the sabhās, South India has a great tradition of temple music performed by the “large ensemble” (periya mēḷam): one or two nāgasvarams, long double-reed instruments of great power, with the barrel drum tavil, a drone reed (ottu or, today, a śruti box) and small cymbals (tāḷam). The periya mēḷam plays at fixed points in the daily ritual of the larger Śiva and Viṣṇu temples, at festivals, and above all in the processions in which the image of the deity is carried through the streets; it also plays at weddings and other auspicious occasions, for which its sound is considered essential. Its repertoire includes the mallāri, a genre of rhythmic compositions specific to temple processions and rituals, as well as kṛtis and extended improvisations in rāgas. In procession, nāgasvaram players may develop a single rāga for an hour or more, and some of the most admired ālāpanas of the twentieth century were played on this instrument (Viswanathan and Allen 2004).

The players of the periya mēḷam belonged, like the dancers and dance masters of the “small ensemble” (ciṉṉa mēḷam), to hereditary non-Brahmin communities attached to the temples, and their history is closely bound up with the social changes described below. Great nāgasvaram players such as T. N. Rajarathnam Pillai (1898–1956) were celebrated far beyond the temple and became stars of the gramophone and the concert stage, but the community as a whole was kept in a subordinate position in the new musical institutions of Madras, a fact much discussed in recent writing on the tradition (Subramanian 2006; Krishna 2013).

docs.title: 8.7 Regions and Centres
docs.text:
Although Karnatak music is often identified with Tamil Nadu, and particularly with Chennai, it has always been a music of the whole of South India. In Karnataka, the court of the Wodeyars of Mysore was a major centre of patronage in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, associated with the vīṇā players of the Mysore school, such as Veena Sheshanna (1852–1926), and with composers such as Mysore Vasudevachar (1865–1961); the Kannada dēvaranāmas of the Haridāsas remain central to the devotional repertoire. In Kerala, the court of Travancore under Svāti Tirunāḷ and his successors patronised Karnatak music, which was absorbed into the Kerala temple and theatre music (sōpāna saṅgītam) used in Kathakaḷi and Mohiniyāṭṭam (Chapter 18); singers such as Chembai Vaidyanatha Bhagavatar (1896–1974) were among the most popular of the twentieth century. In Andhra Pradesh, the language of most of the classical repertoire, the traditions of Annamācārya, Kṣetrayya and Tyāgarāja’s disciples were maintained in the courts of Vizianagaram, Bobbili and elsewhere, and twentieth-century musicians such as M. Balamuralikrishna (1930–2016) combined performance with new composition.

Beyond India, Karnatak music has a long history among the Tamil communities of Sri Lanka, Malaysia and Singapore, and since the 1970s it has flourished in the diaspora in Britain, North America and Australia. The annual Tyāgarāja Ārādhana festival held in Cleveland, Ohio, since 1978 is one of the largest gatherings of Karnatak musicians outside India. Teaching by visiting and resident teachers, and more recently online, has made it possible for many students in the diaspora to study the music seriously (Chapter 23) (Weidman 2006).

docs.title: 8.8 Learning Karnatak Music
docs.text: Karnatak music has a well-defined graded curriculum, laid down in its essentials by the time of Purandaradāsa and systematised in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The student works through the graded forms described above, from the exercises to the varṇams, and only then learns kṛtis. Each new composition is learnt phrase by phrase from the teacher, with its saṅgatis and gamakas, and singing in two or three speeds is a basic discipline. Improvisation is learnt last, by imitation of the teacher’s ālāpanas and kalpana svaras and by long practice. In the older system the student lived with the teacher (gurukulavāsa); today most students learn in weekly lessons, music schools and university departments, supplemented by recordings, and a performing career usually requires years of advanced study with a senior musician. Amanda Weidman has shown how the ideal of the “authentic” voice and the devotional singer were cultivated in the twentieth-century pedagogy of Karnatak music, and how notation, the microphone and the recording changed what students heard and how they learnt (Weidman 2006).

docs.title: 8.9 The Social History of Karnatak Music
8.9.1 Courts, temples and hereditary musicians
docs.text: Before the twentieth century, music in the south was practised by many communities. The temple music of the nāgasvaram and tavil was the hereditary art of the non-Brahmin community later called the Iśai Vēḷāḷar, to which the dance-masters (naṭṭuvaṉārs) and many devadāsīs also belonged; the court and temple dancers (devadāsīs) were also singers and players and transmitted much of the repertoire of padams, jāvaḷis and varṇams; and Brahmin musicians, many of them Telugu-speaking families who had come south with the Nāyaka and Maratha courts, practised and taught vocal and instrumental music (Subramanian 2006; Soneji 2012). Women of devadāsī families were among the most admired musicians of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries: the vīṇā player Vīṇā Dhanammal (1867–1938), whose granddaughters included the singers T. Brinda and T. Mukta and the dancer Balasaraswati; and the singer Bangalore Nagarathnamma (1878–1952), who built the shrine over Tyāgarāja’s tomb at Tiruvaiyaru and fought for women’s right to sing at the festival there.

docs.title: 8.9.2 Madras and the making of “classical” music
docs.text:
In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, as Lakshmi Subramanian and Amanda Weidman have shown, the centre of Karnatak music moved from Thanjavur to colonial Madras, and its patrons from princes and temple trustees to an urban, largely Brahmin middle class. The Music Academy of Madras, founded in 1928 in the wake of the Indian National Congress session held in the city in 1927, became the leading institution of the new musical public; its annual conference and the concert “season” of December and January, which now includes hundreds of concerts by many sabhās, defined the canon and the conventions of performance. The music was presented as a spiritual, devotional “classical” art, the southern counterpart of European classical music and an expression of national culture (Subramanian 2006; Weidman 2006).

This process had costs. The campaign against the dedication of devadāsīs, culminating in the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act of 1947, removed the institutional basis of the women musicians and dancers of those families (Chapter 15); the nāgasvaram players, though honoured as artists, were socially subordinated in the Brahmin-dominated sabhās; and the repertoire was shaped by the tastes of the new patrons, favouring the Telugu and Sanskrit kṛtis of the Trinity. The Tamil Isai (Tamil music) movement of the 1940s, supported by the Tamil Isai Sangam founded in 1943, demanded that more Tamil songs be sung in concerts, and the debate drew in questions of language, caste and Tamil identity. In recent years the singer and writer T. M. Krishna has argued forcefully that the Karnatak world remains marked by caste exclusion and has called for the music to be opened to communities long kept out of it (Krishna 2013).

docs.title: 8.9.3 Women and the modern stage
docs.text: The twentieth century also changed the place of women on the concert stage, as women from both hereditary and non-hereditary backgrounds became leading performers. The most famous of all Karnatak singers, M. S. Subbulakshmi (1916–2004), came from a devadāsī family of Madurai (her mother, Shanmukhavadivu, was a vīṇā player), married into the Brahmin nationalist circles of Madras and became a national symbol of devotional music; she sang at the United Nations General Assembly in 1966 and received the Bharat Ratna in 1998. Her career, as Weidman notes, shows both the opportunities and the constraints of the new musical public: success required a carefully managed image of respectability (Weidman 2006). D. K. Pattammal (1919–2009), from a Brahmin family, was among the first women of her community to sing in public concerts and to sing rāgam–tānam–pallavi. Among other major figures of the twentieth century were the singers Semmangudi Srinivasa Iyer, G. N. Balasubramaniam and M. L. Vasanthakumari, the nāgasvaram player T. N. Rajarathnam Pillai, the violinist Lalgudi Jayaraman and the mṛdaṅgam player Palghat Mani Iyer.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Viswanathan and Allen (2004) is an excellent introduction to Karnatak music in practice. Subramanian (2006) and Weidman (2006) are the essential studies of its modern history, and Krishna (2013) a performer’s critical account of the tradition, its aesthetics and its social exclusions. Peterson (1989) translates and discusses the Tēvāram, and Parthasarathy (1993) the Cilappatikāram. Soneji (2012) and Peterson and Soneji (2008) discuss the hereditary performers of the Tamil country.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Devotional Music: Kīrtan, Bhajan and Sacred Song
docs.text:
Most of the music made in India, now as in the past, has been made in worship. Long before the concert hall and the radio, and alongside the art music of courts and salons, people sang the names and deeds of their gods, the hymns of their saints and the scriptures of their communities: in temples and gurdwārās, at Sufi shrines and in Shia mourning assemblies, on pilgrim roads, in village squares and in the homes of devotees. This devotional music is not a single genre. It includes the professional temple singer and the congregation that sings without training; the solo narrator who preaches through song and the chorus that repeats a single name for hours; music set to strict rāgas and music sung to the tunes of film songs. What unites it is that its purpose lies outside the music itself, in devotion, merit, remembrance or ecstasy, and that its participants judge it by that purpose.

Earlier chapters have touched on several of these traditions: the hymns of the Tamil saints (Chapter 8), qawwālī and Sikh kīrtan (Chapter 7), and the devotional theatres and dances of Assam and Manipur (Chapter 18). This chapter looks at devotional music as a whole. It explains the basic forms, and then describes the principal regional and religious traditions: the temple hymnody of the Tamil country, music as a ritual offering in the temples and the sopāna singing of Kerala, the bhajana and harikathā traditions of the south, the abhaṅg and kīrtan of Maharashtra, the temple music of the Puṣṭimārga, the padāvalī kīrtan of Bengal, the nām and borgīt of Assam, the songs of Kabīr, Mīrā and Ravidās as sung by the communities that keep them, the musical structure of the Sikh scripture, the devotional music of Indian Islam beyond the qawwālī, Christian devotional song, and the song of the Jains and of the Newar Buddhists of Nepal. The poetry of the saints, as literature, is treated in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

docs.title: 9.1 Kīrtan and Bhajan: Terms and Forms
docs.text:
Two words cover much of the field. Kīrtana (from the root kīrt, “to mention, to tell, to praise”) means the telling or singing of the names, qualities and deeds of a deity. Bhajana (from bhaj, “to share, to partake of, to worship”, the root of bhakti itself) means worship and, in musical usage, a devotional song or a session of devotional singing. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa lists kīrtana second, after hearing (śravaṇa), among the nine forms of devotion (7.5.23), and teaches that what was achieved in earlier ages by meditation, sacrifice and temple worship is achieved in the present age of Kali by the singing of the names of Hari (12.3.52). The saṅkīrtana, the singing of the name “together”, thus became for many devotional movements both a practice and a theology: the sound of the divine name was held to make the deity present (Beck 1993).

In practice, three broad forms can be distinguished, though most traditions combine them.

Congregational name-singing (nāma-kīrtan, nām-saṅkīrtan). A leader sings a short phrase, usually a name or a series of names of the deity, and the group repeats it. The music is simple and responsorial, and its power lies in repetition and in a gradual increase of tempo and intensity, often leading to dance or ecstatic states. Cymbals and a barrel drum keep the time; the harmonium has been added almost everywhere since the late nineteenth century. Devotional song. The bhajan, pad, abhaṅg or, in the southern sense, kīrtana: a composed song with a refrain, by a known or attributed saint-poet, sung by a soloist or a group. These songs carry the signature (mudrā, chāp, bhaṇitā) of their author in the last verse, and they form the largest body of devotional music in India. Narrative and preaching kīrtan. A single performer, often a Brahmin or a learned devotee, combines song, recitation, story-telling and commentary on a text, with a small group of accompanists. The harikathā of the south and the kīrtan of Maharashtra (below) are examples; the form is related to the epic recitation discussed in Chapter 21.

Devotional music has always stood in a two-way relation with art music. The great composers of Karnatak music were devotional poets, and the dhrupad of the north grew up partly in temple contexts; conversely, temple and congregational singers have drawn on the rāgas and tālas of the art traditions. Alongside both, the devotional singing of villages and neighbourhoods keeps genres and occasions of its own (below).

docs.title: 9.2 The Temple Hymns of the Tamil Country
docs.text:
The earliest body of devotional song in an Indian vernacular that is still sung is that of the Tamil saints. The Śaiva hymns of Campantar, Appar and Cuntarar (seventh to ninth centuries), gathered into the first seven books of the Śaiva canon, the Tirumuṟai, under the name Tēvāram, were composed as songs in ten-verse units (patikam) for singing in particular temples, and were arranged in the canon by paṇ (Chapter 8). Inscriptions of the Cōḻa period record endowments for singers of the hymns (piṭārar) and for the drummers who accompanied them in the great temples, and the hereditary singers called ōtuvār have sung them ever since, at the conclusion of the daily rites and on festival occasions. Indira Peterson’s study shows that the hymns were conceived from the start as songs for a community of worshippers moving from shrine to shrine, and that their musical setting was integral to their meaning (Peterson 1989). In the twentieth century the Śaiva monasteries (ātīṉam) such as Dharmapuram ran schools for ōtuvārs and sponsored research into the paṇs, and the ōtuvār became, with the temple musicians of the periya mēḷam (Chapter 8), one of the last hereditary custodians of a pre-modern temple music in the south.

The Vaiṣṇava counterpart is the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham, the “four thousand sacred compositions” of the twelve Āḻvārs, compiled according to tradition by Nāthamuni in the tenth century. Tradition also credits Nāthamuni with setting the hymns to music and teaching them to his nephews, the first araiyars. The hymns are recited in Śrīvaiṣṇava temples and homes, and their performance reaches its climax in the winter festival of recitation (adhyayanotsava) at Śrīraṅgam and other temples, during which the whole collection is recited before the deity over some three weeks. At Śrīraṅgam, Śrīvilliputtūr and Āḻvār Tirunagari the hereditary araiyars, wearing a tall conical cap and keeping time with cymbals, sing selected hymns and interpret them with gesture and enacted dialogue (araiyar cēvai), a combination of song, recitation and abhinaya that is among the oldest surviving forms of devotional performance in India. Vasudha Narayanan’s study of the festival shows how the Tamil hymns were placed on a par with the Sanskrit Veda and given a liturgical setting that mirrored the Vedic one (Narayanan 1994).

A third Tamil tradition is that of the Tiruppugaḻ of Aruṇagirinātar (fifteenth century), songs in praise of Murukaṉ whose dense patterns of rhyme and rhythm (cantam) make them an exacting test of a singer’s command of tāla. In the twentieth century groups devoted to singing them spread among Tamil devotees in India and the diaspora, an example of a medieval hymnody revived as congregational music.

docs.title: 9.3 Music in Temple Ritual: Āgama and Sopāna
docs.text:
In the great Hindu temples music was not only sung by devotees but offered to the deity as part of the ritual. The Āgamas and the ritual manuals that govern temple worship in the south list song (gīta), instrumental music (vādya) and dance (nṛtta) among the services (upacāra) offered to the deity in the daily and festival rites, alongside bathing, adornment, food and lamps, and the larger temples employed musicians and dancers for this purpose (Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama). The periya mēḷam of the Tamil temples (Chapter 8), the hymns of the ōtuvārs and araiyars, the dance of the temple women (Chapter 15) and the singing of the Gītagovinda before Jagannātha at Puri (Chapter 17) were all, in this sense, ritual services, with fixed times, places and hereditary performers.

Kerala preserves a distinctive form of such music, the sopāna saṅgītam, named after the steps (sopāna) that lead up to the sanctum. During the evening worship a singer from one of the hereditary temple-servant communities stands beside the steps and sings, accompanying himself on the hourglass drum iṭakka, above all the songs of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda, in a slow, ornamented style and in rāgas that have their own Kerala names and characteristics. The singing is part of the ritual sequence and ends when the sanctum is closed. In the second half of the twentieth century singers such as Njeralath Rama Poduval took sopāna music out of the temple to the concert stage, where it has been recognised as a regional tradition of art music in its own right. It shows how a Sanskrit lyric composed in eastern India in the twelfth century became, in the far south, the core of a ritual music with its own melodic system, much as the same text became the basis of Odissi music and of the aṣṭapadī singing of the southern bhajana (below).

docs.title: 9.4 The Bhajana Tradition of the South
docs.text:
In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries a distinct tradition of congregational singing took shape in the Kāvēri delta, under the influence of Brahmin teachers associated with the cult of the divine name. Bodhendra Sarasvatī and Śrīdhara Veṅkaṭeśa Ayyāvāḷ, both of the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, taught that the repetition of the name of God was the supreme means of salvation, and Marudanallur Sadguru Svāmī, active in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, is credited with fixing the order of service (paddhati) of what came to be called the southern bhajana sampradāya.

The bhajana is remarkable for its multilingual repertoire. A full service draws on Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Marathi and Hindi: the aṣṭapadīs of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda, the taraṅgas of Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha, the songs of Purandaradāsa and Bhadrācala Rāmadāsu, the abhaṅgs of the Marathi saints, the songs of Tyāgarāja, and nāmāvalis (litanies of names). Several of Tyāgarāja’s songs, the utsava sampradāya and divyanāma kīrtanas, were composed for exactly such worship and are simpler than his concert compositions. The great bhajanas culminate in the enactment of the marriage of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa or of Sītā and Rāma (Rādhā Kalyāṇam, Sītā Kalyāṇam), with songs for each stage of the wedding, and in the divyanāma saṅkīrtanam, in which the singers circle a lamp, singing and dancing (Singer 1972).

Milton Singer’s study of bhajana groups in Madras in the 1950s found that they had become an important institution of the new urban middle class. Meeting in homes and halls, they brought together people of different castes and occupations, at least among non-Dalit Hindus, and Singer argued that they allowed educated professionals to combine modern occupations with an intense religious life, and to express in song an egalitarian ideal that their social world did not always realise (Singer 1972). The presence of Marathi abhaṅgs in the southern bhajana reflects the period of Maratha rule at Thanjavur (1676–1855), and the movement of songs, saints and practices between Maharashtra and the Tamil country is one of the clearest examples of the circulation of devotional music across language boundaries.

docs.title: 9.5 Harikathā: The Story-Sermon of the South
docs.text:
The same Maratha connection produced the southern harikathā (“story of Hari”), also called harikathā kālakṣepam (“passing the time with the story of Hari”). In the nineteenth century performers in the Thanjavur region adapted the Marathi narrative kīrtan (below) to Tamil and Telugu audiences, and Tanjore Krishna Bhagavatar (1847–1903) is generally credited with giving the Tamil form its classic shape. A harikathā performer stands before the audience, keeping time with a pair of wooden clappers fitted with jingles (ciplā), accompanied by a supporting singer, a violinist or harmonium player and a mṛdaṅgam player. He — and from the early twentieth century occasionally she — tells a story from the epics, the Purāṇas or the lives of the saints, in prose that moves between learned exposition and colloquial humour, and punctuates it with songs: Sanskrit verses, Tamil hymns, Telugu kṛtis, Marathi abhaṅgs and Hindi bhajans, often in elaborate rāga settings. The performer must therefore be at once a scholar, a story-teller and a trained singer.

In Andhra, Ādibhaṭla Nārāyaṇa Dāsu (1864–1945), a scholar, poet and composer, made the Telugu harikathā a major art and composed many harikathās of his own; he is remembered as its foremost master. In the twentieth century harikathā was broadcast on the radio and performed at temple festivals, weddings and the music season of Madras, and it carried new themes as well as old: performers told the lives of nationalist leaders and of reforming saints, and the form provided one of the few public platforms on which a woman could speak at length before a mixed audience. Its decline in the late twentieth century, in the face of television and of the shorter attention of urban audiences, has been partly offset by its use in religious broadcasting and on the internet. Harikathā also shows how the boundary between music, theatre and preaching was drawn differently in India than in modern Western categories: a single performer could be at once singer, actor and teacher.

docs.title: 9.6.1 The Vārkarīs and their songs
docs.text:
The Vārkarī tradition of Maharashtra centres on the god Viṭhobā (Viṭṭhala) of Pandharpur and on a line of saint-poets whose songs are its scripture: Jñāneśvar (Jñānadev, late thirteenth century), Nāmdev (traditionally 1270–1350), Eknāth (sixteenth century) and Tukārām (seventeenth century), together with many others, among them the women Muktābāī and Janābāī and the Mahār (Dalit) saint Cokhāmeḷā. Their songs are mostly in the abhaṅg (“unbroken”) metre of Marathi, short stanzas with a refrain, composed to be sung. The tradition gave a voice to people of low caste and to women; the authority of Cokhāmeḷā and Janābāī among its saints, and the stories of the hardships they suffered at the hands of Brahmin priests, are part of its memory, though the tradition did not abolish caste in the society around it (Novetzke 2008; Hawley and Juergensmeyer 1988).

The defining practice of the tradition is the vārī, the pilgrimage to Pandharpur, made above all for the ekādaśī of the month of Āṣāḍha (June–July). Palanquins bearing the sandals of Jñāneśvar from Alandi and of Tukārām from Dehu set out for Pandharpur, a journey of some three weeks, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of pilgrims organised in singing groups (diṇḍī). Each group has its leader, who carries a vīṇā (here a drone instrument), a drummer with the mṛdaṅg or pakhāvaj, and many singers with small cymbals (ṭāḷ), and the pilgrims sing abhaṅgs and the names of the saints as they walk. At certain halts the pilgrims form great circles (riṅgaṇ) around which a horse runs, and they dance and play games in the manner of the cowherd boys of Kṛṣṇa’s childhood. Irawati Karve’s account of walking with the pilgrims, written in the 1950s, remains one of the best descriptions of the experience (Karve 1962).

docs.title: 9.6.2 Two kinds of kīrtan
docs.text:
Maharashtra developed two forms of narrative kīrtan. The Vārkarī kīrtan, which tradition traces to Nāmdev, is led by a kīrtankār who takes an abhaṅg as his text, sings it with a chorus of cymbal players and a drummer, and expounds it with stories and other songs, the chorus taking up the refrain. Christian Novetzke has shown that the memory of Nāmdev himself, as a saint and as the founder of kīrtan, has been carried for centuries less by manuscripts than by the performances of kīrtankārs, who tell his story and sing his songs, so that kīrtan is at once a form of devotion and a form of public history (Novetzke 2008).

The other form, called Nāradīya or Haridāsī kīrtan, is performed by a single kīrtankār (traditionally a Brahmin) standing before the audience, accompanied by harmonium and tablā. It has two parts: the pūrvaraṅg, an exposition of a philosophical or devotional text, usually a verse or an abhaṅg, and the uttararaṅg, a story (ākhyān) that illustrates it, told in prose, verse and song. Its songs draw freely on rāga music and on the musical theatre (nāṭyasaṅgīt), and its performers are expected to be scholars, story-tellers and singers at once. In the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries some kīrtankārs used the form for nationalist themes (rāṣṭrīya kīrtan), and the reformer Gadge Maharaj (1876–1956), himself from a low-caste background, used the Vārkarī kīrtan to preach cleanliness, education and the rejection of caste prejudice and animal sacrifice, showing how flexible a medium the form could be.

The abhaṅg also crossed into art music. Singers of the Marathi musical theatre recorded abhaṅgs in semi-classical style, and from the 1970s Bhimsen Joshi’s concerts of saints’ songs (Santavāṇī) made the abhaṅg part of the repertoire of a great khayāl singer. The same songs continue to be sung by pilgrims who have never heard of either.

docs.title: 9.7.1 Sevā and kīrtan in the Puṣṭimārga
docs.text:
The Puṣṭimārga (“path of grace”), founded by Vallabhācārya (1479–1531) and organised by his son Viṭṭhalnāth (1516–1586), worships Kṛṣṇa as a child and youth of Braj. Its temples are called havelī (“mansion”), because the deity is served as the master of a great household, and its worship (sevā) consists in caring for him through the day and the year: waking, dressing, feeding, entertaining and putting him to rest. Music is an essential part of this care. At each of the eight daily “viewings” (darśan) of the deity — maṅgalā at dawn, śṛṅgār, gvāl, rājbhog at midday, utthāpan, bhog, sandhyā-ārtī and śayan at night — temple singers (kīrtankārs) sing songs appropriate to the hour, the season and the festival, in rāgas prescribed for each occasion (Gaston 1997).

The songs are the pads of the aṣṭachāp, the “eight seals”: four poets associated with Vallabha — Sūrdās, Kumbhandās, Paramānanddās and Kṛṣṇadās — and four with Viṭṭhalnāth — Nanddās, Chītasvāmī, Govindsvāmī and Caturbhujdās — together with later poets of the sect. Their poems describe the life of Kṛṣṇa as the devotee imagines it at each hour: waking at dawn, going out with the cows, returning in the evening, and the festivals of the year, from the spring songs of Vasant and Holī to the swing songs of the rains. The music is in the style of dhrupad and dhamār, sung by a lead singer and others, accompanied by the pakhāvaj, cymbals and a drone, and in some temples by stringed instruments. Anne-Marie Gaston’s study of the temples of Nathdwara in Rajasthan, the principal seat of the sect since the image of Śrīnāthjī was brought there from Braj in the seventeenth century, shows a hereditary musical service organised by liturgical calendar and maintained by families of temple singers and drummers (Gaston 1997).

docs.title: 9.7.2 Havelī music and the art tradition
docs.text:
The relation of havelī music to Hindustani art music is close but debated. The repertoire and style of the temples preserve compositions in dhrupad and dhamār form, many attributed to the aṣṭachāp poets, and the system of assigning rāgas to the hours of worship parallels the time theory of rāga (Chapter 4). Some musicians and scholars see the temples as one of the sources of dhrupad; others regard havelī saṅgīt as a parallel tradition that borrowed from the court music of the period. What is clear is that the temples kept alive a body of composition and a style of performance that had otherwise largely disappeared, and that in the twentieth century singers such as Pandit Jasraj drew on it in their concert repertoire.

Other temples of Braj have their own traditions. In the samāj gāyan of the Rādhāvallabha and Haridāsī communities of Vrindavan, a group of men seated before the deity sings the pads of the sect’s poets, the leader singing each line and the others repeating it. The Haridāsī community traces its line to Svāmī Haridās, the sixteenth-century saint-musician whom later tradition made the teacher of Tānsen; the story cannot be confirmed, but it expresses the conviction, widespread in the north, that the highest art music had its roots in devotion (Beck 1993).

docs.title: 9.8 Bengal: Padāvalī Kīrtan
docs.text:
In Bengal and Odisha the devotional movement inspired by Caitanya (1486–1533) made congregational singing the centre of religious life. According to his biographers, Caitanya led processional singing of the names of Kṛṣṇa through the streets of Navadvīp (nagar-kīrtan), and the ecstatic saṅkīrtan with the clay barrel drum khol (also called mṛdaṅga) and hand cymbals (karatāl) became the hallmark of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism. Out of this practice grew a more elaborate art form, the padāvalī kīrtan or līlā kīrtan, which sets the lyric songs (pada) of Vidyāpati, Caṇḍīdās, Govindadās, Jñānadās and many others, in Bengali and in Brajabuli, a literary language mixing Bengali with Maithili forms (Hawley and Juergensmeyer 1988).

A padāvalī kīrtan performance presents an episode (pālā) of the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa — the first stirrings of love, the secret journey to the meeting place, the lovers’ quarrel, separation after Kṛṣṇa’s departure for Mathura — through a sequence of songs chosen and linked by the lead singer. It begins with a gauracandrikā, a song about Caitanya (Gaurāṅga) that introduces the mood of the episode, because the Gauḍīya tradition understands Caitanya as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one person and his life as a re-enactment of their love. The singer elaborates the songs with ākhar, improvised lines inserted between the lines of the text that draw out their meaning, so that a short poem may be sung for a long time; the khol player and the chorus respond, and the music uses long and intricate tāla cycles proper to the genre. Tradition holds that the style of this kīrtan was fixed at a great gathering of Vaiṣṇavas at Kheturi, in the late sixteenth century, organised by the poet and teacher Narottama Dāsa, and later writers distinguish several regional styles named after the districts in which they arose, among them the Garāṇhāṭī and the Manoharśāhī.

Kīrtan has remained a living art in Bengal, sung by professional singers, men and women, at religious festivals, in homes after a death and on the radio and recordings. It has also travelled further than any other Indian devotional music. The International Society for Krishna Consciousness, founded in New York in 1966 by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, made the congregational singing of the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra with mṛdaṅga and karatāl a familiar sight in cities around the world, and the participatory kīrtan has since become part of the devotional and “yoga” culture of Europe and North America. In Manipur the Gauḍīya saṅkīrtana developed into a distinctive art of song and drum dance (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 9.9 Assam: Nām and Borgīt
docs.text:
The Vaiṣṇava movement of Śaṅkaradeva in Assam (Chapter 18) made the singing of the name (nām) the centre of its religious life, and created a devotional music that is still practised in every Assamese village. Its two central texts are collections of verse for congregational singing and recitation: Śaṅkaradeva’s Kīrtana-ghoṣā, narrative poems in Assamese on the deeds of Kṛṣṇa and the incarnations of Viṣṇu, and Mādhavadeva’s Nām-ghoṣā, a collection of devotional verses. In the village prayer hall (nāmghar) and in the sattras, the congregational service (nām-prasaṅga) is led by a precentor who sings a line that the congregation takes up, clapping or playing cymbals, in a form of responsorial singing that can build to great intensity. These services, held daily in the sattras and on many occasions in the villages, are open to all members of the community, and they gave the Assamese peasantry a shared liturgy in its own language.

The borgīts (“great songs”) of Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva are a more learned form. Composed in Brajabuli and set to named rāgas, they are sung at the beginning of services and of dramatic performances (bhāonā), often with a long unmetred introduction exploring the rāga before the song proper, accompanied by the khol and cymbals. Tradition says that many of Śaṅkaradeva’s borgīts were lost in a fire and that only a few dozen survive. The musical tradition of the sattras — the borgīt, the drumming of the khol, the songs of the plays and the dances of the monks — was one of the main sources from which Sattriya dance was reconstructed for the stage (Neog 1980). Assam also has narrative forms in which a lead singer and chorus perform sacred stories with song and gesture, such as the ojāpāli, whose singers present episodes from the epics and from the cult of the snake goddess Manasā.

docs.title: 9.10 Songs of the Margins: Kabīr, Mīrā and Ravidās
docs.text:
Not all devotional music belongs to temples, sects with institutions, or professional singers. Some of the most widely sung devotional songs of north India belong to saints who stood outside or against the religious establishments of their time, and whose songs have been kept alive above all by communities of low caste.

Kabīr, the fifteenth-century weaver of Banaras, composed songs (pad), couplets (sākhī) and longer poems that attack ritual, caste, the authority of Brahmin and mullah alike, and the illusions of the world, and that speak of a formless (nirguṇ) divine reality found within. His songs were collected in several traditions — the Bījak of the Kabīr Panth, the Sikh scripture and the anthologies of the Dādūpanthīs of Rajasthan — but they have lived above all in oral performance. Linda Hess’s study of Kabīr singing in the Malwa region of central India describes groups (maṇḍalī) of singers, most of them from Dalit communities such as the Balāīs and Meghvāls, who meet to sing Kabīr’s bhajans through the night, accompanied by the tambūrā, ḍholak, kartāl and mañjīrā; their leading singer, Prahlad Singh Tipanya, became widely known in India and abroad from the 1990s. Hess shows how the songs work through the bodies and voices of the singers, how they are adapted and recombined in performance, and how, for Dalit singers, Kabīr’s critique of caste is a living message rather than a historical curiosity. The same Malwa tradition inspired the Hindustani singer Kumar Gandharva, who settled in Dewas and recorded nirguṇī bhajans that brought this music into the concert hall (Hess 2015).

Mīrābāī, the sixteenth-century Rajput princess who, according to tradition, defied her marital family to devote herself to Kṛṣṇa, is known chiefly through songs sung in her name. Parita Mukta’s study of the Mīrā traditions of Rajasthan and Saurashtra shows that her songs were preserved and sung above all by peasant and artisan communities, among them the Meghvāl weavers, who saw in her defiance of the Rāṇā a model of resistance to the powerful, while the Rajput elite long regarded her memory with unease; only in the twentieth century, through nationalist and middle-class appropriation, film and the concert stage, did she become a respectable figure of devotional womanhood (Mukta 1994). The songs of Ravidās (Raidās), a leather-worker saint of Banaras whose hymns are included in the Sikh scripture, are sung in the gatherings of the Ravidāsī communities of Punjab and Uttar Pradesh, for whom his songs and his memory have been central to a modern assertion of Dalit religious identity. These traditions show that devotional song in India was never only an expression of shared piety; it was also a means by which the marginal remembered their own saints and voiced their own claims.

docs.title: 9.11 Devotion in the Village: Name-Singing and Seasonal Song
docs.text:
Much devotional music in north India is made neither in temples nor in sectarian institutions but in villages and neighbourhoods, by groups of ordinary devotees. Edward Henry’s study of the Bhojpuri-speaking region of eastern Uttar Pradesh and western Bihar distinguishes the occasions and genres of this music with care. Groups of men gather for kīrtan and bhajan in the evenings and at festivals, singing the names of Rāma or Kṛṣṇa and the songs of the saints to harmonium, ḍholak and cymbals; for special occasions a village or a family sponsors continuous name-singing for a fixed period, often twenty-four hours (aṣṭayām) or longer, in which teams of singers take turns so that the chant never stops. Such performances are believed to bring merit and protection to the village, and they draw singers from neighbouring settlements, so that they also create networks of friendship and rivalry between villages (Henry 1988).

Alongside these, women sing their own devotional and ritual songs: songs to the goddess, songs for the festivals of the year, and the songs of the life-cycle — the sohar sung at a birth, the many songs of the wedding, among them teasing and abusive songs addressed to the bridegroom’s party — in which devotion, humour and social comment mix freely. The nirguṇ songs on death and the impermanence of the body, often attributed to Kabīr, are sung by professional and amateur singers alike. Henry shows that the villagers themselves classify this music by occasion and purpose rather than by musical style, and that a single tune may serve several genres; what makes a song devotional is the setting and the intention of its singers, not its musical form (Henry 1988). The same holds for much of the music described in this chapter, and it is a reminder that the categories of “classical”, “folk” and “devotional” music used in this volume are analytical conveniences rather than the categories of the people who make the music (Chapter 21).

docs.title: 9.12 The Rāgas of the Guru Granth Sahib
docs.text:
Chapter 7 introduced the Sikh tradition of śabad kīrtan. Its scripture is the only one of the great religious canons organised by musical mode, and its structure deserves a closer look (Mann 2001; Singh 2000).

The Guru Granth Sahib opens with texts for recitation and daily prayer — the Japjī of Guru Nānak, which is recited rather than sung, and the short collections used at evening and bedtime prayer — and then presents the main body of hymns in thirty-one sections, each named after a rāga. Within each rāga section the hymns are arranged first by poetic form — hymns of four stanzas (caupade), of eight (aṣṭapadī), longer songs (chant) and the ballads called vār — and within each form by author, beginning with Guru Nānak and continuing with the later Gurus, followed by the songs of the bhagats, saint-poets from outside the Sikh line such as Kabīr, Nāmdev, Ravidās and the Sufi Shaikh Farīd. The headings of the hymns carry further musical directions. Many bear the word ghar (“house”) with a number; its meaning is disputed, and it has been interpreted as indicating a tāla, a melodic variant of the rāga or a manner of performance. A few hymns are marked partāl, indicating a change of tāla during the song. Several of the vārs carry instructions that they are to be sung to the tune (dhunī) of a named heroic ballad of the Punjab, an indication that popular as well as art melodies shaped the music of the early community. The volume ends with a Rāgamālā, a list of rāgas and rāgiṇīs in a classification of the family type (Chapter 4), whose place in the scripture has been debated among Sikhs since the nineteenth century.

The rāgas of the scripture include many familiar from Hindustani music (Āsā, Gūjarī, Bilāval, Rāmkalī, Basant, Sāraṅg, Malār, Kalyāṇ) and some that are regional or distinctive to the Sikh tradition (Mājh, Vaḍahaṃs, Tukhārī). The choice of rāga was associated with mood and season: the hymns in Vaḍahaṃs include songs of mourning, and those in Basant are sung in spring. The liturgy of the gurdwārā follows the day: Āsā dī Vār, with interpolated hymns, in the early morning, the evening and night prayers at their hours, and at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar kīrtan by successive groups of professional singers (rāgī jathā) through most of the day.

Besides the rāgīs and the Muslim rabābīs who sang in the gurdwārās before 1947 (Chapter 7), the Sikh tradition has a third kind of musician: the ḍhāḍhīs, who sing heroic ballads (vārs) of the Gurus and of Sikh history to the small hourglass drum ḍhaḍḍ and the bowed sāraṅgī, a tradition associated with the court of the sixth Guru, Hargobind. Among Sikh groups, the Nāmdhārīs have been notable patrons of Hindustani art music in the twentieth century. The gurmat saṅgīt revival of recent decades (Chapter 7) has been accompanied by debates about authenticity and about the place of women, who have not been part of the regular kīrtan rota in the sanctum of the Harmandir Sahib, a restriction that has been publicly contested.

docs.title: 9.13 Devotional Music in Indian Islam
docs.text: The qawwālī of the Sufi shrines (Chapter 7) is the best-known devotional music of South Asian Islam, but it is not the only one, and in some respects it is untypical: Muslim religious scholars have always been divided about the use of music in worship, and much Islamic devotional performance avoids instruments and the word “music” altogether. Regula Qureshi has described the resulting distinction between sound that is recited or chanted, which is acceptable to all, and sound that is “music”, which some reject (Qureshi 1986, 1981).

docs.title: 9.13.1 The Shia majlis
docs.text: The most elaborate tradition of this kind is that of the Shia mourning assembly (majlis), held above all in the first ten days of the month of Muḥarram to commemorate the martyrdom of the Prophet’s grandson Ḥusain at Karbala in 680. Its genres are distinguished by their manner of performance. In soz, a lead singer, supported by two or more assistants who sustain the notes (bāzū), sings a lament in a rāga-based melody without instrumental accompaniment; the salām is a salutation to the martyrs; the marsiya, the long elegiac poem in Urdu brought to its height in nineteenth-century Lucknow by Mīr Anīs and Mirzā Dabīr, is declaimed by a reciter with gesture and vocal art; and the nauḥa is a rhythmic lament sung by a group to the beating of the breast (mātam). Qureshi’s analysis shows how the majlis uses the resources of Hindustani music — rāga, refined vocal technique, a listening public trained in the courtly arts — while keeping its distance from “music” as entertainment; many hereditary musicians of Lucknow were also accomplished soz singers (Qureshi 1981; Hyder 2006).

docs.title: 9.13.2 Other traditions
docs.text: Sunni devotion has its own sung genres: the naʿt in praise of the Prophet, sung or recited without instruments at gatherings and on the Prophet’s birthday (milād); the remembrance (dhikr) of the Sufi orders; and the songs of the shrines of the countryside. In Kashmir the Sufiyāna kalām or Sufiyāna mūsīqī, a learned art of Sufi poetry sung by an ensemble with the hammered dulcimer santūr, the bowed sāz-e Kashmīr, the setār and drums, uses a system of modes called maqām that is related to, but distinct from, the rāgas of the plains; the santūr of modern Hindustani music (Chapter 10) was adapted from this tradition. In Sindh and the Punjab the kāfī, and in Bengal the mārphatī and murśidī songs, carry Sufi teaching in the language of the countryside, close to the Bāul songs described in Chapter 21. These traditions show South Asian Islam as a creator of devotional music in many languages and styles, adapting local musical resources to its own purposes.

docs.title: 9.14 Christian Devotional Song
docs.text:
India’s Christian communities created devotional music that combined their own liturgical traditions with the musical languages of their regions. The ancient Syriac Christians of Kerala and the Catholic communities of Goa and the west coast, whose performance traditions are described in Chapter 21, preserved liturgical chant and developed vernacular hymns and paraliturgical songs. Protestant missions from the eighteenth century onwards introduced the European hymn, translated into Indian languages and sung to Western tunes, but Indian converts soon began to compose devotional songs in Indian forms.

The most important early figure was Vedanāyakam Śāstri (1774–1864) of Thanjavur, a Tamil Protestant poet associated with the court of the Maratha king Serfoji II, who composed hundreds of Tamil kīrtanais set to Karnatak rāgas and tālas, and a Christian dance-drama in the form of the Tamil kuṟavañci, the Bethlehem Kuṟavañci, modelled on the court dance-dramas of Thanjavur (Chapter 15). His songs, and the later Tamil Christian lyrics in the same style, are still sung in Tamil churches, alongside translated Western hymns. In Maharashtra the poet Narayan Vaman Tilak (1861–1919), a Brahmin convert, wrote Christian abhaṅgs and bhajans in the manner of the Vārkarī saints, and in Bengal and the Hindi-speaking region Christian bhajans and kīrtans were composed in the styles of the surrounding devotional music. After the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) the Catholic Church in India encouraged the use of Indian music, instruments and dance in worship, and Indian musical settings of the liturgy became common.

In north-east India, where large parts of the Khasi, Mizo and Naga peoples became Christian in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, missionaries introduced choral hymn-singing in four-part harmony, and the hymn and the choir became central to the musical life of these communities. Indigenous composers adapted the form, and in Mizoram a style of hymn-singing with drum and dance, drawing on older Mizo song, developed alongside the missionary hymn. The choirs of Shillong and Aizawl have since won recognition across India and abroad, an unexpected outcome of the missionary encounter. Christian devotional music thus displays, in a short history, the same processes of translation and adaptation that the older traditions show over many centuries.

docs.title: 9.15 Jain and Buddhist Song
docs.text:
The Jain community has a large literature of hymns (stotra, stavan) in Sanskrit, Prakrit and the regional languages, from classical Sanskrit hymns such as Mānatuṅga’s Bhaktāmara Stotra to the vernacular stavans of later centuries, and singing is part of temple ritual, of festivals and of the domestic religious life of lay Jains. Whitney Kelting’s study of Śvetāmbara laywomen in Pune describes the singing groups (maṇḍaḷ) in which women meet to sing stavans at rituals and gatherings, often to melodies taken from film songs and folk songs, and shows how the women, through their choice and performance of songs, shape a lay understanding of Jain teaching and devotion that differs in emphasis from that of the monks (Kelting 2001). The study is a reminder that much devotional music in India is made by women, in domestic and semi-public settings, and is easily overlooked by histories that concentrate on temples and professional singers.

Buddhism, which largely disappeared from the plains of India in the second millennium, kept its musical traditions in the Himalaya. Among the Newars of the Kathmandu valley, Vajrayāna Buddhist priests preserved a repertoire of esoteric songs (caryāgīti) often compared with the Buddhist songs of eastern India of the late first millennium, sung in rāgas and sometimes danced. The Newar towns also preserve a Hindu–Buddhist devotional tradition, the dāphā, in which groups of men meet regularly in public rest-houses and temples to sing hymns in Newari, Maithili and Sanskrit in named rāgas and tālas, accompanied by drums and cymbals. Richard Widdess’s study of dāphā singing in Bhaktapur shows that these groups preserve rāga names, song forms and performance conventions that go back to the medieval courts of the Malla kings, and offers a rare opportunity to study a pre-modern rāga tradition that developed outside the art music of the Indian plains (Widdess 2013). The ritual music and masked dance of Tibetan Buddhism in Ladakh, Sikkim and the eastern Himalaya are described in Chapter 22.

docs.title: 9.16 Devotional Music, Art Music and the Media
docs.text:
In the twentieth century devotional music moved between the temple, the concert hall and the mass media in ways that changed all three. Concert musicians made devotional songs a regular part of their recitals: the Hindustani concert often ends with a bhajan (Chapter 7), the Karnatak concert includes bhajans and abhaṅgs among its lighter items, and singers built careers on devotional repertoires. M. S. Subbulakshmi’s role as the saint Mīrābāī in the film Meera (1945) and her recordings of Sanskrit hymns made her voice the sound of devotion for millions; Kumar Gandharva’s recordings of the nirguṇī songs of Kabīr and the Nāth yogis of Malwa brought a rural devotional repertoire into the concert hall; and the abhaṅgs of Bhimsen Joshi and the havelī compositions sung by Pandit Jasraj did the same for Maharashtra and Braj.

The cassette revolution of the 1980s had an even larger effect. Peter Manuel has shown how cheap cassettes allowed devotional music in regional languages, sung by local performers in styles close to everyday practice, to reach audiences far beyond the reach of the film-dominated record industry, and how the producers of devotional cassettes became some of the most successful firms in the music business (Manuel 1993). Film melodies, in turn, became the tunes of new devotional songs, as Kelting’s Jain singers and countless bhajan groups show. Purists deplored the borrowing; for the singers, a familiar tune was a means of carrying devotion, as folk tunes had been for the saints.

Devotional music has also carried the social tensions of the communities that sing it. The bhakti movements gave a voice to women and to people of low caste — Cokhāmeḷā, Janābāī, Ravidās, Kabīr — and their songs have been sung in the twentieth century as songs of social protest as well as devotion. Yet the professional performance of devotional music in temples has often been the hereditary right of particular castes, and Dalits were long excluded from many of the temples whose music this chapter describes. Women have been central to domestic and congregational singing and largely absent from the professional temple rota. A history of devotional music, like the history of the other arts in this volume, must attend to who sang, where, and for whom, as well as to what was sung.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Beck (1993) discusses the theology of sacred sound and devotional song in Hinduism, and Hawley and Juergensmeyer (1988) introduces the saint-poets whose songs are sung. On particular traditions see Peterson (1989) (Tamil Śaiva hymns), Narayanan (1994) (the Śrīvaiṣṇava festival of recitation), Singer (1972) (southern bhajana), Novetzke (2008) and Karve (1962) (Maharashtra), Gaston (1997) (Nathdwara), Hess (2015) (Kabīr singing in Malwa), Mukta (1994) (the Mīrā traditions), Mann (2001) and Singh (2000) (the Sikh scripture), Qureshi (1986), Qureshi (1981) and Hyder (2006) (Islamic devotional music), Wolf (2014) (the drumming and lament of Muḥarram and other Islamicate traditions), Kelting (2001) (Jain women’s singing) and Widdess (2013) (Newar dāphā). Henry (1988) studies the devotional songs of a north Indian village, and Manuel (1993) the devotional music of the cassette era.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Musical Instruments
docs.text: India has one of the richest instrumental cultures in the world: hundreds of stringed, wind, membrane and solid instruments, ranging from the single-stringed drone of a wandering singer and the clay pots of village percussion to the vīṇā, sitār and mṛdaṅgam of the concert stage. Instruments appear in the earliest Indian literature and art, are classified in the Nāṭyaśāstra, are described in detail in medieval treatises and are depicted in the sculpture and painting of every period. They have also changed constantly. Most of the instruments of modern art music took their present form in the last three centuries, often in response to new genres, new patrons and contact with other musical cultures. The ancient fourfold classification is the natural place to begin, because it still organises the way Indian musicians think about their instruments; the principal instruments of art music, the instruments of ritual and temple, their makers and players, and the instruments now rare follow. Folk instruments are discussed further in Chapter 21.

docs.title: 10.1 The Four Classes of Instruments
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra (ch. 28 in Ghosh’s numbering) divides instruments (vādya or ātodya) into four classes:

Tata (“stretched”): stringed instruments, such as the vīṇā. Suṣira (“hollow”): wind instruments, such as the flute (vaṃśa). Avanaddha (“covered”): instruments with a stretched skin, the drums. Ghana (“solid”): instruments sounded by striking solid bodies, such as cymbals.

The chapters that follow describe the two principal vīṇās of the theatre — the nine-stringed vipañcī, played with a plectrum, and the seven-stringed citrā, played with the fingers — the flute, and three drums of the puṣkara group (mṛdaṅga, paṇava and dardura), with their strokes and the ways of tuning and playing them (Ghosh 1950; Rowell 1992). Śārṅgadeva’s Saṅgītaratnākara devotes a whole chapter to instruments and describes many more, including several kinds of vīṇā (among them the one-stringed ekatantrī, the ālāpinī and the kiṃnarī), wind instruments and drums (Shringy and Sharma 1978).

The four-fold scheme, based on the material that vibrates, is the oldest systematic classification of instruments known (Table 10.1). It was brought to the notice of European scholars in the nineteenth century, and the Belgian curator Victor-Charles Mahillon, whose catalogue of 1880 was the starting point for the classification by Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs (1914) now used in museums worldwide, is generally thought to have been aware of it; the four Indian classes correspond broadly to the chordophones, aerophones, membranophones and idiophones of the modern system (Deva 1978).

Table 10.1. Some instruments of Indian art, devotional and temple music by class Class Examples Tata (strings) Sarasvatī vīṇā, rudra vīṇā (bīn), sitār, surbahār, sarod, sāraṅgī, santūr, tānpūrā, violin, dilrubā and esrāj, rabāb, gōṭṭuvādyam (citravīṇā), ektārā Suṣira (wind) bānsurī and veṇu (flutes), śahnāī, nāgasvaram, śaṅkha (conch), kombu (horn), harmonium Avanaddha (drums) tablā, pakhāvaj, mṛdaṅgam, tavil, ḍholak, khol, pung, ceṇṭa, maddaḷam, miḻāvu, iḍakka, kañjīrā, ḍaph, naqqāra Ghana (solid) ghaṭam, mañjīrā and tāḷam (cymbals), jalataraṅg, morsing (jaw harp), ghaṇṭā (bell), kartāl, cimṭā

docs.title: 10.2 Instruments in the Medieval Treatises and at the Mughal Court
docs.text:
The sixth chapter of the Saṅgītaratnākara (Chapter 4) is the fullest medieval account of Indian instruments. Śārṅgadeva keeps Bharata’s four classes but describes many more instruments within each, with details of their construction, tuning and technique. Among his stringed instruments are several vīṇās of different kinds: the one-stringed ekatantrī; the seven-stringed citrā and nine-stringed vipañcī of the older texts; the many-stringed mattakokilā; the ālāpinī, a stick zither with a single gourd; and the kiṃnarī, a stick zither with gourds and frets, the ancestor of the later fretted vīṇās. Under the wind instruments he describes the flute (vaṃśa) in several sizes, horns and conches; under the drums, a long series of barrel, hourglass and frame drums, among them the mardala, the paṭaha and the hourglass huḍukkā, with their strokes and syllables; and under the solid instruments cymbals and bells. The account shows that the instrumentarium of the thirteenth century was already very different from that of the Nāṭyaśāstra: the arched harp had gone, the stick zither had taken its place, and the drums had multiplied (Shringy and Sharma 1978; Deva 1978).

The Persianate courts brought further instruments. Mughal paintings, as Bonnie Wade has shown, depict with care the instruments of the court and its ceremonies: the Indian bīn and pakhāvaj beside the Afghan and Persian rabāb and long-necked tanbūr, frame drums (daf), and the naubat, the ceremonial ensemble of kettledrums (naqqāra), long trumpets (karnā) and shawms (surnā) that played at palace gates and marked the hours (Wade 1998). Some of these instruments remained foreign to the art music; others, through the hands of hereditary musicians, became the ancestors of its modern instruments, as the rabāb did of the sarod. The history of Indian instruments is thus a history of continual adoption and adaptation, from the Central Asian lutes of the medieval period to the violin and harmonium of the colonial period (below).

docs.title: 10.3.1 The vīṇā: from harp to zither
docs.text:
The word vīṇā has meant different instruments at different times. In early Indian art — the reliefs of Bharhut, Sanchi and Amaravati (second century BCE to third century CE) and the gold coins on which the Gupta king Samudragupta (c. fourth century CE) is shown playing (Figure 10.1) — the vīṇā is an arched harp, held against the body and plucked with the fingers or a plectrum. The Tamil yāḻ of the Caṅkam poems was also a harp. From about the seventh century, sculpture shows a new instrument, the stick zither: a bamboo or wooden stick with one or more strings, supported by a gourd resonator held against the player’s shoulder or chest. The fretted stick zithers of the medieval period developed into the two great vīṇās of modern India, while the harp disappeared from art music (Deva 1978).

Figure 10.1. Gold coin of the ‘lyrist’ type of Samudragupta (c. fourth century), showing the king seated and playing an arched harp (vīṇā) held on his lap (National Museum, New Delhi). Photo: SpeakingArch, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The northern rudra vīṇā or bīn is a large stick zither: a tube of wood or bamboo with two large gourd resonators, high fixed frets, four main strings and drone strings. It was the most prestigious instrument of the Mughal and post-Mughal courts and of dhrupad, played by the Seniya and other hereditary lineages, and its music influenced the ālāp of the sitār and sarod. It has very few players today, among whom the Dagar family has been prominent (Chapter 7). Figure 10.2 shows a vīṇā of this type in a miniature painting.

Figure 10.2. Detail of a painting by Ruknuddin, Bikaner, 1690–1695 (Metropolitan Museum of Art), showing a stick-zither vīṇā of the bīn type, with a gourd resonator and a bird-shaped finial. Detail of 'Kedar Ragini' ragamala folio, Bikaner, 1690-1695, Metropolitan Museum of Art (open access, CC0), via Wikimedia Commons

The southern Sarasvatī vīṇā, the principal stringed instrument of Karnatak music, is a lute (Figure 10.3): a large resonating body carved from jackwood, a hollow neck with twenty-four brass frets set in wax, a second (often decorative) resonator under the neck, four playing strings and three side strings used for drones and rhythm. It developed in the Thanjavur region in the seventeenth century; its frets allow the player to produce the full range of Karnatak gamakas by deflecting the string. Its iconographic association with the goddess Sarasvatī has made it the emblem of Indian music in general. Great modern players include Vīṇā Dhanammal, Karaikudi Sambasiva Iyer, S. Balachander and Emani Sankara Sastri.

Figure 10.3. A Sarasvatī vīṇā from Chennai (Collection of Musical Instruments, University of Göttingen), showing the large wooden resonating body, the fretted neck with its carved animal-head finial, and the second, gourd-shaped resonator under the neck. Photo: Katharina Common (photograph), Collection of Musical Instruments, University of Göttingen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 10.3.2 The sitār
docs.text: The sitār is a long-necked lute with a gourd resonator, a long hollow neck with eighteen to twenty movable curved metal frets, six or seven main strings and eleven to thirteen sympathetic strings (tarab) beneath the frets, played with a wire plectrum (mizrāb) worn on the right index finger. Its name derives from the Persian sihtār, “three strings”. Allyn Miner has shown that it developed in the eighteenth century from smaller folk lutes, gaining frets, strings and sympathetic strings over the following century and a half, and that its modern repertoire was created by hereditary musicians, beginning with the Masītkhānī and Razākhānī styles (Miner 1993). The surbahār, a larger, deeper sitār developed in the nineteenth century, was used to play ālāp in the style of the bīn. In the twentieth century the instrument evolved further in the hands of Vilayat Khan, whose “vocal style” sitār has one fewer bass string, and of Ravi Shankar, who favoured a heavier instrument with bass strings for ālāp; Ravi Shankar’s international career made the sitār the best-known Indian instrument in the world (Chapter 23).

docs.title: 10.3.3 The sarod
docs.text:
The sarod is a fretless lute with a skin-covered wooden belly, a polished metal fingerboard, four or five main strings, drone and rhythm strings and sympathetic strings, played with a plectrum of coconut shell. It developed in the nineteenth century from the Afghan rabāb, brought to India by Pathan musicians who served as soldiers and courtiers, and was adapted to Hindustani music by their descendants (Miner 1993). The metal fingerboard allows long slides (mīṇḍ) by sliding the fingernails along the string. Its great modern exponents include Allauddin Khan’s son Ali Akbar Khan and the Bangash family of Hafiz Ali Khan and Amjad Ali Khan. Figure 10.4 shows a sitār, a surbahār and a sarod.

Figure 10.4. (a) A sitār and a surbahār, the larger and deeper instrument developed for ālāp (Musical Instruments Museum, Brussels); (b) a sarod by the maker Mohan Lal Sharma (Ethnological Museum, Berlin), with its skin-covered belly and metal fingerboard. Photo: Miguel Discart, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 10.3.4 The sāraṅgī and other bowed instruments
docs.text:
The sāraṅgī is a short, broad, bowed lute carved from a single block of wood, covered with skin, with three gut playing strings and up to thirty-five or more sympathetic strings. The player stops the strings not by pressing them against the neck but with the cuticles of the fingernails, which allows the continuous slides and inflections of the voice. The sāraṅgī was for two centuries the principal accompaniment of khayāl, ṭhumrī and Kathak, played by hereditary Muslim musicians whose close association with courtesans brought social stigma; in the twentieth century it was largely displaced by the harmonium, and only a few soloists, notably Ram Narayan, brought it to the concert stage as a solo instrument (Neuman 1980). Fretted bowed instruments, the esrāj and dilrubā, are used in Sikh kīrtan and in Bengal. The violin, adopted into Karnatak music in the early nineteenth century, is described in Chapter 8. Figure 10.5 shows a sāraṅgī beside the harmonium that displaced it.

Figure 10.5. (a) A sāraṅgī in performance: the bow crosses the playing strings, with the rows of pegs for the sympathetic strings beside them; (b) a portable harmonium of the kind played seated on the floor, its bellows at the back pumped by one hand while the other plays. Photo: Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 10.3.5 The santūr and other zithers
docs.text: The santūr is a trapezoidal hammered dulcimer with about a hundred strings, arranged in courses over movable bridges and struck with light wooden mallets. It was the instrument of the Sufi music (sūfiyāna kalām) of Kashmir and was brought to the Hindustani concert stage in the second half of the twentieth century, chiefly by Shivkumar Sharma. The slide-played gōṭṭuvādyam or citravīṇā of Karnatak music, and the vicitra vīṇā of Hindustani music, are fretless instruments played by sliding a solid object along the strings.

docs.title: 10.3.6 The tānpūrā
docs.text: The tānpūrā (Hindustani) or tambūrā (Karnatak) is a long-necked lute with four or five unfretted strings, tuned usually to Pa or Ma and three Sa’s and played in a continuous slow cycle to provide the drone against which all Indian art music is performed. Its characteristic shimmering sound comes from the jawārī, a broad, slightly curved bridge whose surface the vibrating string grazes, and from threads (jīvā) placed between string and bridge to adjust the effect; together they enrich and prolong the upper partials, so that the drone continuously sounds the harmonics against which a singer tunes. C. V. Raman studied the acoustics of the curved bridges of Indian stringed instruments in the early 1920s. The drone sets up the tonic and fifth (or fourth) that define the frame of every rāga; it is a practical and acoustical necessity, and though it has been interpreted symbolically as the unchanging ground against which change takes place, the interpretation is modern.

docs.title: 10.4.1 Flutes
docs.text: The transverse bamboo flute (vaṃśa, veṇu, bānsurī, kuḻal) is among the oldest Indian instruments and, as the instrument of Kṛṣṇa, among the most beloved. A simple tube with six to eight finger-holes, it produces the full range of Indian ornaments through the partial covering of holes and the control of breath and angle. In Karnatak music the flute was established as a concert instrument by T. R. Mahalingam (“Mali”, 1926–1986) and N. Ramani; in Hindustani music by Pannalal Ghosh (1911–1960), who designed a larger flute for ālāp, and later by Hariprasad Chaurasia.

docs.title: 10.4.2 Double-reed instruments
docs.text: The śahnāī of the north and the nāgasvaram (nādasvaram) of the south are conical double-reed instruments, related to the surnā family of shawms found from North Africa to China. They are the instruments of auspicious occasions: the śahnāī at weddings, festivals and royal ceremonies, played with drums (naubat) at court gates and shrines; the nāgasvaram, with the barrel drum tavil, in the daily rituals and processions of South Indian temples and at weddings. Both were the hereditary instruments of particular communities: Muslim musicians in the north, the non-Brahmin Iśai Vēḷāḷar community in the south. Bismillah Khan (1916–2006) of Banaras brought the śahnāī to the concert stage and received the Bharat Ratna in 2001; T. N. Rajarathnam Pillai (1898–1956) was the most celebrated nāgasvaram player of his time.

docs.title: 10.4.3 The harmonium
docs.text: The harmonium, a free-reed keyboard instrument, came to India from Europe in the nineteenth century; a portable, hand-pumped version suited to sitting on the floor was manufactured in Calcutta from the 1870s and spread rapidly through popular theatre, devotional singing and light classical music. Its fixed, tempered pitches cannot produce the slides and microtonal inflections of Indian music, and critics, among them Rabindranath Tagore, condemned it as unsuitable, a campaign that kept it off All India Radio for three decades (Section 23.2). Musicians nevertheless adopted it as the standard accompaniment for khayāl, ṭhumrī, qawwālī, Sikh kīrtan and much else, and players such as Govindrao Tembe and Appa Jalgaonkar developed a distinctive accompanying art. The harmonium’s history is a reminder that the instruments of Indian music have always been adopted from wherever they came.

docs.title: 10.5.1 The mṛdaṅgam and the pakhāvaj
docs.text:
The double-headed barrel drum is the oldest type of drum in Indian art music; the mṛdaṅga (“clay body”) of the Nāṭyaśāstra is its ancestor in name. The Karnatak mṛdaṅgam has a body of jackwood and two heads of layered skin. The right head carries a permanent black loading paste (soru or karaṇai) of iron oxide, rice and other materials; the left head is loaded before each performance with a temporary paste of wet semolina, which produces a deep bass. The northern pakhāvaj, the drum of dhrupad, temple music and Kathak, is similar in construction (Figure 10.6), with a paste of wheat dough on the left head. Both drums are tuned to the tonic of the performer by adjusting the tension of their leather braces and the rim (Deva 1978).

Figure 10.6. A pakhāvaj (Musical Instruments Museum, Brussels): a double-headed barrel drum whose heads are tensioned by leather braces passing over wooden tuning blocks. Photo: Miguel Discart, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 10.5.2 The tablā
docs.text:
The tablā is a pair of drums played with the fingers and palms: the right-hand drum (dāyāṃ), of wood, tuned to the tonic, and the left-hand drum (bāyāṃ), of metal or clay, which gives a deep bass that the player modulates by pressing the heel of the hand on the skin (Figure 10.7). Each has a composite head with a black loading patch (syāhī) of iron filings, rice paste and gum, built up in many thin layers. The tablā emerged in the eighteenth century, probably in Delhi, as an instrument suited to accompanying khayāl, instrumental music and dance; its repertoire developed in the hereditary lineages described in Chapter 5 (Kippen 1988). (On the later legends that credit Amīr Khusrau with inventing the tablā and the sitār, see Chapter 7.)

Figure 10.7. A pair of tablā drums: the wooden dāyāṃ and the metal-bodied bāyāṃ, with their leather braces, tuning blocks and black syāhī patches. Photo: ShubhanTelang, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 10.5.3 Drums with harmonic overtones: C. V. Raman
docs.text: Most drums produce overtones that are not in a harmonic relation to the fundamental, and so have no clear pitch. The physicist C. V. Raman showed, in a short note in Nature in 1920 written with Sivakali Kumar and in a fuller paper of 1934, that the loaded heads of the mṛdaṅgam and the tablā behave differently: the central patch of paste so modifies the vibration of the membrane that the first several overtones are nearly harmonic, giving these drums a definite pitch and a musical tone (Raman 1934). The finding applies to both drums, and to other Indian drums built on the same principle, not to the tablā alone, as is sometimes claimed. Raman’s acoustical work, begun in Calcutta before his Nobel Prize of 1930 for the Raman effect, is a fine example of a scientist taking Indian instruments seriously as objects of study.

docs.title: 10.5.4 Other drums
docs.text: India has a very large number of other drums: the ḍholak, a small barrel drum of north Indian folk and devotional song; the khol, a clay drum of the Vaiṣṇava kīrtan of Bengal, Odisha and Assam; the pung of Manipur (Chapter 18); the tavil, partner of the nāgasvaram; the frame drums ḍaph and kañjīrā, the latter a small tambourine used in Karnatak concerts; the kettledrums naqqāra of courts and shrines; and the temple drums of Kerala, among them the cylindrical ceṇṭa, played with sticks, the maddaḷam, the hourglass iḍakka, whose pitch can be varied to play melodies, and the great copper miḻāvu of Kūṭiyāṭṭam (Chapter 19).

docs.title: 10.6 Solid Instruments
docs.text: The ghaṭam of Karnatak music is a clay pot, made of a special mix of clay and metal powders (the pots of Manamadurai in Tamil Nadu are especially prized), played with the fingers, palms and wrists; the player varies the tone by pressing the mouth of the pot against the stomach. The jalataraṅg (“waves of water”) is a set of porcelain bowls tuned by the amount of water they contain and struck with light sticks. The morsing is a jaw harp, used in Karnatak ensembles for its buzzing rhythmic sound. Cymbals of many sizes — mañjīrā, tāḷam, jhāñj — keep time in devotional singing and dance; the naṭṭuvaṉār who conducts a Bharatanāṭyam recital beats the rhythm on a pair of small cymbals (Chapter 15); and bells (ghaṇṭā) and gongs mark the times of worship in temples.

docs.title: 10.7 Instruments in Ritual and Temple
docs.text:
Many instruments have ritual functions independent of art music. The conch (śaṅkha) is blown in worship and was once blown in war; its sound is considered auspicious. Temple bells are rung by worshippers. In South India the nāgasvaram and tavil (maṅgaḷa vādyam, “auspicious instruments”) accompany the daily rituals and festival processions of temples, and each hour and ritual traditionally had its own repertoire. The temple orchestras of Kerala are among the most spectacular musical ensembles in India: the pañcavādyam (“five instruments”: timila, maddaḷam, ilattāḷam, kombu and iḍakka) and the ceṇṭa mēḷam, played by dozens of drummers and horn and cymbal players at festivals such as the Thrissur Pūram. In the north, the naubat of drums and śahnāīs played at palace gates and Sufi shrines marked the hours, and the havelī temples of the Puṣṭimārga have their own instrumental traditions (Chapter 7).

The Yājñavalkya Smṛti (3.115) says that one who knows the art of playing the vīṇā, is learned in śrutis and jātis and understands tāla reaches the path of liberation without effort. The verse expresses an idea that runs through Indian thought about music, that the disciplined practice of sound can be a spiritual discipline; it is often quoted by musicians.

docs.title: 10.8 Makers and Players
docs.text:
Instrument making in India has been the work of specialised artisans, often hereditary. The vīṇā makers of Thanjavur, whose instruments carry a geographical indication, carve the body and neck from jackwood and set the frets by ear; the sitār and tānpūrā makers of Miraj in Maharashtra, many of them from Muslim families of the Shikalgar community, supply musicians throughout India; tablā and pakhāvaj makers work in Banaras, Delhi, Mumbai and elsewhere; and ghaṭams are made by potters of Manamadurai. Their knowledge — the choice and seasoning of wood and gourd, the curving of a jawārī, the application of syāhī — is empirical, transmitted in workshops, and rarely written down (Deva 1978).

The social status of instruments and their players has varied greatly. Instruments associated with hereditary low-status communities (the sāraṅgī, the drums of many regions, the nāgasvaram) were long valued musically and despised socially, while instruments associated with high-status patrons and amateurs (the vīṇā, in the twentieth century the sitār) acquired prestige. The adoption by middle-class musicians of instruments once played by hereditary specialists has been one of the main processes of modern Indian musical history.

docs.title: 10.9 New Instruments and New Sounds
docs.text:
The adoption of foreign instruments did not end with the violin and the harmonium. In the twentieth century Indian musicians took up a whole series of instruments from outside the tradition and made them vehicles of rāga music, usually by modifying their construction and technique to allow the slides and ornaments that Indian music requires. In Karnatak music, U. Srinivas (1969–2014) made the electric mandolin a concert instrument, playing kṛtis and rāgam–tānam–pallavi on it from childhood; Kadri Gopalnath (1949–2019) adapted the saxophone, modifying its keys to produce gamakas; and the keyboard, the clarinet and the guitar have all found Karnatak exponents. In Hindustani music, the violin, long associated with the south, was taken up by players such as V. G. Jog and N. Rajam, the latter developing a vocal style of playing; the slide guitar, transformed by Brij Bhushan Kabra and by Vishwa Mohan Bhatt, whose “Mohan vīṇā” adds sympathetic and drone strings to a Western guitar, became a concert instrument; and the cello, the saxophone and the electric guitar have been used in fusion and experimental music (Chapter 23) (Farrell 1997; Lavezzoli 2006).

Technology has also changed the sound of the traditional ensemble. The electronic tānpūrā and the śruti box, first manufactured in India in the late twentieth century, have largely replaced the human-played drone in practice and in many performances; amplification has altered the balance between instruments and voices, favouring soft instruments such as the vīṇā and the flute in large halls; and recording and broadcasting have spread the sounds of particular instruments and players far beyond their original audiences. The harmonium, once banned from the radio, is now heard in almost every kind of Indian music, from khayāl to film song.
