Every generation of Indian musicians has adapted its instruments to its music; the process continues.

docs.title: 10.10 Collections and the Study of Instruments
docs.text:
The systematic study of Indian instruments began in the colonial period. Collectors, scholars and Indian patrons assembled instruments for museums and exhibitions; the Bengali scholar and patron Sourindro Mohun Tagore (1840–1914) published works on Indian music and sent collections of Indian instruments as gifts to institutions in Europe and elsewhere, which helped to make them known to Western students of music. The great museum collections of Indian instruments in Kolkata, Chennai, London, Brussels and New York date largely from this period. In independent India, the Sangeet Natak Akademi’s collection and its documentation of folk and classical instruments, the work of scholars such as B. C. Deva, and the archives of All India Radio have extended the record (Deva 1978).

Instruments are also important evidence for the history of music. Their appearance in sculpture and painting, their names in texts, and their surviving examples allow historians to trace the replacement of the harp by the stick zither, the arrival of Persian and Central Asian lutes and drums, and the development of the modern sitār, sarod and tablā. Bonnie Wade’s study of Mughal paintings, for example, uses their careful depiction of instruments and ensembles to reconstruct the music of the court; Allyn Miner’s history of the sitār combines written sources, paintings and surviving instruments (Wade 1998; Miner 1993). The acoustical study of instruments, begun by C. V. Raman, has been continued by physicists and engineers interested in the jawārī, the loaded drumhead and the voice; it is one of the few areas in which Indian music has been the subject of sustained scientific investigation, and its results are modest and precise rather than sensational.

docs.title: 10.11 Rare and Endangered Instruments
docs.text: Several instruments of Indian art music have become rare. The rudra vīṇā has only a handful of serious players, though it has attracted renewed interest; the surbahār and the sursiṅgār, a nineteenth-century fretless instrument used for dhrupad-style ālāp, are now seldom heard; the vicitra vīṇā has very few exponents; and the sāraṅgī, though still played, has lost much of its role as an accompanist and many of the families who played it have left the profession. The Tamil yāḻ, a harp described in Caṅkam poetry, has been the subject of scholarly reconstructions since the 1940s. Many folk instruments are also threatened by changes in the communities and occasions for which they were played (Chapter 21). Documentation by archives and broadcasting organisations, and the work of individual musicians and makers, have preserved some of what might otherwise have been lost.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Deva (1978) is the standard survey of Indian musical instruments. Miner (1993) is the authoritative history of the sitār and sarod, and Kippen (1988) of the tablā tradition of Lucknow. Raman (1934) is Raman’s paper on the Indian drums. On the ancient instruments see Rowell (1992); on instruments in Mughal painting, Wade (1998).

docs.title: Chapter 11: Song in the Modern Languages: Rabīndrasaṅgīt, Nazrulgīti and Their Contemporaries
docs.text:
Between the art music of the concert hall and the anonymous song of the village lies a large body of music that the earlier chapters have met only in passing: the authored song of the modern Indian languages. From the late nineteenth century poets and composers in Bengal, Maharashtra, Assam, the Tamil and Kannada country and the Urdu-speaking north wrote songs in their own languages, set them to melodies drawn from rāga, devotional and folk music and, at times, from European tunes, and published them with their names attached. These songs were sung in homes, schools, political meetings and theatres, carried by the gramophone and the radio, and learnt by millions who never attended a classical concert. Some became the anthems of nations. In Bengal the songs of Rabindranath Tagore and Kazi Nazrul Islam form genres of their own, Rabīndrasaṅgīt and Nazrulgīti, with their own teachers, institutions and standards of correct performance.

This chapter describes that body of song. It begins with what was new about it, then turns to Bengal, where it took shape first and most fully: the song before Tagore, Tagore’s own songs, the other song-makers of his generation, Nazrul, and the modern and political song of the twentieth century. It then describes the stage song and the lyric song of Maharashtra, the modern song of Assam, the lyric traditions of the south, the popular song of Gujarat and the Punjab, and the Urdu ghazal as a popular song, then the songs of the national movement, and ends with the questions of authorship, notation and fidelity that these traditions share. Film song, which grew out of the same world and soon overshadowed it, is treated in Chapter 23; the poetry of these writers, as literature, in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā.

docs.title: 11.1 What Was New about Modern Song
docs.text:
Song with a named author was not new in India. The vāggeyakāra, the composer who wrote both words and music, is described in the Saṅgītaratnākara, and the kṛtis of Tyāgarāja and the pads of the Puṣṭimārga poets carry their makers’ names (Chapters 6, 8 and 9). What changed in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries was the setting in which such songs were made and heard. Four changes stand out.

The first was the urban, educated, largely middle-class public of the colonial cities — Calcutta, Bombay, Pune, Madras, Guwahati, Lahore — which wanted songs in its own language that were neither the rustic song of the village nor the courtly art of the hereditary musician, and which was suspicious of the courtesan’s salon where much light classical music was heard (Section 7.7). The second was print. Song texts were printed in collections, and from the late nineteenth century melodies too were printed in the new staff-less notations of Bengal and Maharashtra, so that a song could be learnt from a book and its correct form fixed in writing. The third was the new machinery of sound: the harmonium, cheap and easy to play, which became the domestic instrument of the new song (Chapter 10); the gramophone record, whose three-minute side suited the song exactly; and, from the 1930s, the radio. The fourth was politics. Many of the songs were written for the reform movements and for the nationalist struggle, and the movement against the partition of Bengal in 1905, in particular, produced a flood of patriotic songs in Bengali that were sung in processions and meetings.

The result was a kind of song that its makers and listeners regarded as art but not as śāstrīya (classical) music. Its value lay first in the union of word and melody: the singer was expected to make the words clear and to render the melody as its composer had fixed it, not to improvise. In the language of All India Radio, which created units for it after Independence, it was “light music” (sugam saṅgīt); in Bengali it was simply gān, song, distinguished by its author.

docs.title: 11.2 Bengal before Tagore
docs.text:
The song of nineteenth-century Calcutta was varied. Rāmnidhi Gupta, known as Nidhu Babu (1741–1839), adapted the Hindustani ṭappā to Bengali love lyrics and made it the fashionable song of the city’s wealthy households; his songs, short, intricate in ornament and frankly secular, were sung for a century. Popular contests of improvised verse (kavigān), in which rival poet-singers answered each other before large audiences, the pāṃcālī narrative songs and the music of the jātrā theatre (Chapter 20) formed the popular end of the spectrum, while the kīrtan of the Vaiṣṇavas remained the great devotional tradition of the countryside (Chapter 9).

A new kind of song came from religious reform. For the services of the Brahmo Sabha, which he founded in 1828, Rammohan Roy (1772–1833) wrote hymns (brahmasaṅgīt) in Bengali on the formless God of the Upaniṣads, set in the manner of dhrupad, the most dignified of the Hindustani genres; Brahmo services were sung by trained musicians, and the Brahmo hymn became a model of serious, unostentatious song in the mother tongue. The Tagore family of Jorasanko, leading members of the Brahmo community, made their house one of the musical centres of the city. Its members heard and studied Hindustani music with professional musicians — among them the dhrupad singer Jadu Bhatta (Jadunath Bhattacharya, 1840–1883) of the Bishnupur tradition — and also heard European music; Jyotirindranath Tagore (1849–1925), Rabindranath’s elder brother, composed songs and devised the ākārmātrik notation, which writes the notes in Bengali letters with signs for duration above them and was later used for most Bengali song (Som 2009).

docs.title: 11.3.1 The songs and their arrangement
docs.text: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) wrote and set to music more than two thousand songs over some sixty years, from his teens until the last months of his life. He regarded them as his most lasting work, and they are the part of it that is most alive in Bengal and Bangladesh today. He collected them in the Gītabitān, first published in 1931–32 with the songs in chronological order; for the revised edition of 1941 he rearranged them not by date but by theme (paryāy), and the collection was completed after his death: songs of worship (pūjā), of the homeland (svadeś), of love (prem), of nature and the seasons (prakṛti), miscellaneous songs (vicitra) and songs for ceremonies (ānuṣṭhānik), with sections for the songs of the plays and dance-dramas. The categories overlap in a characteristic way: many of the “worship” songs are addressed to a divine beloved and many love songs can be read as songs of the divine, and the seasonal songs, above all those of the rains and of spring, carry the deepest feeling of all (Som 2009).

docs.title: 11.3.2 Sources of the music
docs.text:
Tagore’s melodies came from many sources, which scholars have traced through the phases of his work. In his early years he wrote many songs on the model of Hindustani compositions, often keeping the melody and metre of a known dhrupad or khayāl and replacing its words with Bengali ones; such songs are called bhāṅgā gān (“broken” or “adapted” songs). His musical plays of the early 1880s, Vālmīki-pratibhā (1881) and Kāl-mṛgayā (1882), mixed rāga-based songs with tunes drawn from European, especially Irish and Scottish, melodies he had heard during his stay in England; the best-known song with a European source, Purāno sei diner kathā, follows the melody of “Auld Lang Syne”. From the 1890s, when he managed the family estates in rural east Bengal, he drew increasingly on the kīrtan of the Vaiṣṇavas and on the songs of the Bāuls (Chapter 21), whose mystical idiom and plain melodies he admired; the tune of Āmār sonār Bāṃlā is taken from a song of the Bāul Gagan Harkara.

Out of these sources he made a style of his own. A Tagore song usually has a short refrain (sthāyī) and a contrasting middle section (antarā), often followed by further stanzas that return to the refrain, in the manner of the Hindustani composition; but the melody follows the shape and stress of the Bengali words closely, ornament is restrained, and the elaboration of the rāga by improvised passages, which the concert singer of khayāl took for granted, is excluded. Many songs use a rāga only as a point of departure, mixing notes of two or more rāgas for expressive effect. Tagore also devised several tālas of his own, among them jhampak, ṣaṣṭhī, rūpakaḍā, navatāl, ekādaśī and navapañcatāl, asymmetrical cycles without the “empty” beat (khālī) of the Hindustani tālas (Chapter 5), designed to follow the rhythm of his verse.

His essays and conversations on music, collected after his death, show him arguing for this ideal against two opponents: the Hindustani virtuoso, for whom words were a pretext for display, and the singer who took liberties with his tunes. In a well-known exchange with the singer Dilip Kumar Roy (1897–1980), who argued for the performer’s right to embellish, Tagore insisted that his songs be sung as written. He also condemned the harmonium as a crude, tempered instrument unsuited to Indian melody, and it was long excluded from the teaching of his songs at Santiniketan (Sections 10.4.3 and 23.2).

docs.title: 11.3.3 Plays, dance-dramas and the seasons
docs.text: Song was at the centre of Tagore’s theatre. His plays are full of songs, and in his last years he created a new form, the dance-drama (nṛtyanāṭya), in which the story is told entirely through song and dance: Citrāṅgadā (1936), Caṇḍālikā (1938), on the love of an untouchable girl for a Buddhist monk, and Śyāmā (1939). The dances drew on Manipuri, which he had brought to Santiniketan from 1919, on Kathakaḷi and on other forms (Chapter 18); his earlier play Naṭīr pūjā (1926), in which a girl of the school danced the role of a court dancer, was a landmark in making dance acceptable for girls of educated Bengali families. At Santiniketan he also created seasonal festivals — the festival of spring (Vasantotsav) and the welcome of the rains (Varṣāmaṅgal) — in which songs, recitation and dance were performed by students and teachers; these festivals, and the spring festival in particular, are still held and widely imitated.

docs.title: 11.3.4 Anthems
docs.text: Two of Tagore’s songs are national anthems. Jana-gaṇa-mana, first sung at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress in December 1911, was adopted in its first stanza as the national anthem of India in January 1950; Āmār sonār Bāṃlā, written during the agitation against the partition of Bengal in 1905, was adopted by Bangladesh at its independence. The national anthem of Sri Lanka was written and composed by Ananda Samarakoon, a former student at Santiniketan; claims that Tagore wrote or set it are disputed and rest on no direct evidence. The tune of Jana-gaṇa-mana as now sung is close to the version Tagore taught in 1919 at Madanapalle in south India, where Margaret Cousins wrote it down in staff notation.

docs.title: 11.3.5 Transmission, ownership and fidelity
docs.text:
Tagore’s songs were transmitted from the beginning both orally and in notation. His grandnephew Dinendranath Tagore (1882–1935), a singer of prodigious memory, learnt and notated a large part of them and taught them at Santiniketan; the notations were published in the many volumes of the Svarabitān, and the institution Tagore founded, Visva-Bharati, held the copyright in his works until the end of 2001. A music board of Visva-Bharati approved recordings of the songs, and its insistence on the published notations made Rabīndrasaṅgīt one of the most closely regulated song traditions in the world. The policy preserved the songs from casual distortion; it also led to conflicts with singers whose interpretations departed from the norm, of which the best known involved Debabrata Biswas (1911–1980), whose free and dramatic style was popular with listeners and repeatedly questioned by the board.

The great singers of the twentieth century — Santidev Ghosh (1910–1999), who had learnt directly from Tagore, Kanika Bandyopadhyay (1924–2000), Suchitra Mitra (1924–2011), Debabrata Biswas, and the film singers Pankaj Mullick and Hemanta Mukherjee, who brought the songs to the cinema and the radio — created distinct “schools” of interpretation within the limits of the notation. Since the copyright lapsed, new arrangements with Western instruments and popular styles have multiplied, to the delight of some listeners and the distress of others.

In East Pakistan, Tagore’s songs became a political question. When the government of Pakistan discouraged the celebration of his birth centenary in 1961 and later restricted his songs on state radio, Bengali intellectuals and musicians in Dhaka defended them as part of their own heritage; the cultural organisation Chhayanaut, founded in 1961, made the teaching of Rabīndrasaṅgīt and the celebration of the Bengali new year central to a Bengali identity that fed into the movement for independence. Rabīndrasaṅgīt is thus a national tradition of two countries, sung by Hindus and Muslims alike (Som 2009).

docs.title: 11.4 The Other Song-Makers of Bengal
docs.text:
Tagore was not alone. Bengali tradition groups three other poet-composers with him and with Nazrul as the five makers of the modern Bengali song, each with a recognisable musical personality.

Dvijendralāl Rāy (1863–1913), a civil servant who studied agriculture in England, wrote plays on historical subjects whose songs were sung throughout Bengal, comic and satirical songs (hāsir gān) that mocked the anglicised Bengali and the hypocrite, and patriotic songs, of which Dhana-dhānya-puṣpa-bharā (“filled with wealth, grain and flowers”) remains one of the best loved. His melodies are vigorous and often choral, with a directness that he admired in English and Scottish song; his son Dilip Kumar Roy became a singer and a writer on music.

Rajanīkānta Sen (1865–1910), a lawyer of Rajshahi, wrote mainly devotional songs of great simplicity and intensity, and during the agitation of 1905 the patriotic song Māyer deoyā moṭā kāpaṛ (“the coarse cloth given by the mother”), which urged Bengalis to wear Indian-made cloth. His songs are still sung as kāntagīti.

Atulprasād Sen (1871–1934), a barrister who spent most of his working life in Lucknow, wrote some two hundred songs whose melodies show the influence of the ṭhumrī, dādrā and ghazal he heard there, joined to Bengali kīrtan and Bāul melody. He introduced the lilting manner of the north Indian light classical song into Bengali, and his song in praise of the Bengali language, Moder garab moder āśā, became an anthem of the language movement in East Bengal.

docs.title: 11.5.1 The poet as composer
docs.text: Kazi Nazrul Islam (1899–1976) was born into a poor Muslim family of Churulia in the Bardhaman district of Bengal, sang as a boy with the leṭo troupes, a rural Muslim song-and-theatre form of western Bengal, served in a Bengali regiment of the British Indian army at the end of the First World War, and became famous overnight in 1922 with his poem “The Rebel” (Bidrohī; see Volume 8). In the following two decades he wrote and composed songs on a scale without parallel in modern Bengali: estimates of his output range from about three thousand to more than four thousand songs, many of them made for the gramophone and the radio. His working life as a composer ended in 1942, when he was struck by an illness that left him unable to speak or write for the remaining thirty-four years of his life. In 1972 the new state of Bangladesh brought him to Dhaka, where he died in 1976 and is honoured as the national poet; his marching song Cal cal cal became the military march of Bangladesh.

docs.title: 11.5.2 Range and style
docs.text:
Nazrul’s songs cover almost every genre known in Bengal, and several that he introduced. He brought the Persian and Urdu ghazal into Bengali, with its couplets, refrain and imagery of the nightingale and the rose, and his Bengali ghazals, sung in a light classical style close to that of the Urdu ghazal singers, were among the most popular records of the late 1920s and 1930s. With the singer Abbasuddin Ahmed (1901–1959) he created a repertoire of Islamic devotional songs in Bengali, of which the song for the end of the fast of Ramaḍān, O man ramjāner oi rojār śeṣe (1931), is still sung throughout Bangladesh at Īd; there had been little such song in Bengali before, and it gave Bengali Muslims a devotional music in their own language. At the same time he wrote many hundreds of songs to the goddess Kālī (śyāmāsaṅgīt) and to Kṛṣṇa, in the manner of the Bengali Śākta and Vaiṣṇava traditions, so that his work as a whole crosses the line between the communities in a way that both Indian and Bangladeshi admirers have emphasised.

Nazrul was also a serious student of Hindustani music, and many of his songs are rāga-based compositions in the manner of khayāl or ṭhumrī. For a series of radio programmes in Calcutta around 1940 he composed songs in new rāgas of his own, with Bengali names such as Dolan-cāṃpā, Veṇukā and Sandhyā-mālatī; accounts of the number of such rāgas vary. He drew too on folk song, on Middle Eastern and Latin American dance rhythms heard on records, and on marching songs; several of his books of revolutionary poems and songs were banned by the colonial government. He worked for the Gramophone Company in Calcutta as a composer and trainer of singers from the late 1920s, wrote and directed music for the early Bengali sound cinema, and composed for the Calcutta station of the radio.

docs.title: 11.5.3 Notation and authenticity
docs.text: Because Nazrul’s songs were made quickly, for the record industry, and his illness came before he could supervise their publication, their texts and melodies survive in many variants. The singers who had learnt from him — among them the composer Kamal Dasgupta (1912–1974) and the singer Feroza Begum (1930–2014), both of whom later settled in Dhaka — became the authorities for correct versions. In Bangladesh the Nazrul Institute, founded in Dhaka in 1985, has published standardised notations and recordings, and the question of authentic versions, as with Tagore’s songs, is debated between those who would fix the songs and those who value the variety of their performance.

docs.title: 11.6 Modern Song, Mass Song and After in Bengal
docs.text:
The gramophone and the radio created, from the 1930s, a third category beside the songs of the great poet-composers: the “modern song” (ādhunik gān), written by professional lyricists and set by professional composers for recording. Its first masters included the composer Himangshu Dutta (1908–1944), Kamal Dasgupta, and Sachin Dev Burman, who sang Bengali songs before he became a composer of Hindi film music in Bombay; and Pankaj Mullick (1905–1978), who as a composer and singer worked across Tagore songs, film and radio, and whose music for the dawn programme Mahiṣāsuramardinī, broadcast every year since the early 1930s on the morning that begins the Durgā Pūjā season, remains one of the best-loved radio programmes in Bengal. The decades after Independence were the high period of ādhunik gān: the singers Hemanta Mukherjee (1920–1989), Manna Dey (1919–2013) and Sandhya Mukherjee (1931–2022), the lyricist Gauriprasanna Majumdar and many others produced the songs released each autumn for the Pūjā season, a commercial calendar that shaped Bengali popular music for half a century.

A different strand came from the left. The Indian People’s Theatre Association (Chapter 19) created in Bengal a “mass song” (gaṇasaṅgīt) for choirs and political meetings. Jyotirindra Moitra’s song-cycle Navajībaner gān on the Bengal famine of 1943–44, the songs of Hemanga Biswas (1912–1987), who drew on the folk music of Assam and Sylhet, and those of Salil Chowdhury (1925–1995), who combined folk melody, Western harmony and choral writing and later became one of the most original composers of the Hindi and Bengali cinema, made the political song an art in its own right. In East Pakistan the songs of the language movement after 1952 and of the liberation war of 1971, broadcast by the clandestine radio of the independence movement, played a similar role.

From the 1970s a younger generation reacted against the conventions of both ādhunik gān and the film song. The Calcutta band Moheener Ghoraguli, founded in 1975, set Bengali poetry to a mixture of rock, Bāul and folk music, and in 1992 Suman Chattopadhyay (later Kabir Suman) released Tomāke cāi, an album of songs about city life sung to his own guitar, which began a movement of “songs about life” (jībanmukhī gān) and of Bengali bands that continues today.

docs.title: 11.7.1 The stage song
docs.text:
The Marathi musical drama (saṅgīt nāṭak), described as theatre in Chapter 19, produced the most important body of semi-classical song in western India. Its songs, called pads, were the main attraction of the plays, and audiences demanded encores that could extend a performance far into the night. Annasaheb Kirloskar’s Saṅgīt Śākuntal (1880) and Saṅgīt Saubhadra (1882) set their songs mainly to the tunes and metres of the Marathi kīrtan (Chapter 9), the lāvaṇī and other popular forms — the sākī, diṇḍī and āryā metres of the kīrtankārs were sung in recognisable melodies. With Govind Ballal Deval’s Saṅgīt Śāradā (1899), a play against the marriage of young girls to old men, and above all in the plays of the early twentieth century, the songs moved closer to Hindustani art music. Composers took their melodies from the bandiśes of khayāl, ṭhumrī and ṭappā and from Karnatak songs heard from touring companies, and shaped them into short, memorable pads that a trained actor-singer could decorate with tāns. Govindrao Tembe (1881–1955) composed the music of K. P. Khadilkar’s Saṅgīt Mānāpamān (1911), and the singer Bhaskarbuwa Bakhle (1869–1922), trained in the Gwalior, Agra and Jaipur styles, that of Saṅgīt Svayaṃvar (1916) (Ranade 1986).

The singer-actors became the stars of Marathi public life. Bal Gandharva (1888–1967), whose own company, the Gandharva Natak Mandali, was founded in 1913, sang women’s roles in a voice of great sweetness, with Master Krishnarao Phulambrikar as his composer; Keshavrao Bhosale (1890–1921) of the Lalitkaladarsh company and Master Dinanath Mangeshkar (1900–1942), the father of Lata Mangeshkar, were his rivals. The stage song spread far beyond the theatre through the gramophone, and nāṭyasaṅgīt became, as Ashok Ranade has shown, one of the main bridges by which Hindustani music reached a mass Marathi audience (Ranade 1986). The coming of sound cinema in the 1930s ruined the companies, but the songs survived on record and on the concert platform; in the 1960s the composer Jitendra Abhisheki (1929–1998) gave the form a new lease of life with the music of Katyār kāḷjāt ghusalī (1967), and nāṭyasaṅgīt is still a standard part of the repertoire of Marathi classical singers.

docs.title: 11.7.2 Bhāvgīt and the radio
docs.text: The lyric song (bhāvgīt), a setting of a modern Marathi poem for solo voice and small ensemble, grew from the 1920s and 1930s with the gramophone and the radio, and became one of the main forms of Marathi light music. Its most celebrated work is a radio series. The Gīt Rāmāyaṇ, fifty-six songs on the story of Rāma by the poet G. D. Madgulkar (1919–1977), set to music and sung by Sudhir Phadke (1919–2002), was broadcast weekly by All India Radio, Pune, from April 1955 to April 1956; it drew huge audiences, was published and recorded, and has been performed on stage ever since. Later composers, among them Hridaynath Mangeshkar, set the poetry of the Marathi saints and of modern poets with equal success, and the bhāvgīt became a model for the light music of other languages on the radio.

docs.title: 11.8 Assam: Jyotiprasad, Bishnu Rabha and Bhupen Hazarika
docs.text:
In Assam the modern song is closely tied to three artists whose names have become the names of genres. Jyotiprasad Agarwala (1903–1951), playwright, poet and film-maker, directed the first Assamese film, Joymatī (1935), and wrote songs that combined the borgīt and folk melodies of Assam (Chapter 9) with Western and Bengali influences; they are sung as Jyoti-saṅgīt. Bishnu Prasad Rabha (1909–1969), revolutionary, painter, dancer and musician, called Kalāguru (“master of the arts”), studied the music of the Bodo, Rabha, Mising and other peoples of the Brahmaputra valley and brought their melodies into his songs, which are sung as Bishnu Rabha saṅgīt. The poet Parbati Prasad Baruva (1904–1964) wrote lyrics of great delicacy for the same tradition.

Bhupen Hazarika (1926–2011), who sang as a child in Jyotiprasad’s second film, studied in Banaras and at Columbia University in New York, where he met the singer Paul Robeson, and returned to Assam to become the most popular singer and composer of the north-east. Working with the Indian People’s Theatre Association, he wrote songs of the Brahmaputra and its boatmen, of tea-garden labourers, of the unity of the valley’s peoples and of human solidarity; his best-known song, Bistīrṇa pārare, on the indifference of the great river to the suffering on its banks, takes its idea and its melody from Robeson’s “Ol’ Man River”. He composed for Assamese, Bengali and Hindi films, received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award for 1992 and was awarded the Bharat Ratna posthumously in 2019. The modern Assamese song as a whole, carried after Independence by the radio station at Guwahati, became a central part of Assamese identity (Chapter 22).

docs.title: 11.9 The South: Bharati and the Lyric Song
docs.text:
In the Tamil country the poet Subramania Bharati (1882–1921) wrote patriotic, devotional and philosophical songs that he indicated for singing in named rāgas and tālas, in a Tamil far simpler than that of classical poetry. His songs of the nation, of Śakti, of Kṛṣṇa as child, lover and friend, and of the liberation of women were taken up after his death by the nationalist movement and by concert singers — D. K. Pattammal, for one, was known for singing them — and set again and again for the cinema; in 1949 the government of Madras bought the rights to his works and placed them in the public domain. The Tamil Isai movement (Section 8.9) drew on Bharati’s example, and composers such as Papanasam Sivan (1890–1973) wrote Tamil kṛtis for the concert stage and songs for the Tamil cinema, where Tamil song soon found its largest audience.

In Karnataka the lyric song of modern Kannada poetry (bhāvagīte) became, through the radio, a genre called sugama saṅgīta. P. Kalinga Rao (1914–1981) was among its first popular singers and composers, and Mysore Ananthaswamy (1936–1995) and C. Ashwath (1938–2009) set the poems of Kuvempu, D. R. Bendre, K. S. Narasimhaswamy and others for voice and small ensemble, creating a repertoire sung at festivals, in schools and on stage. Kuvempu’s poem Jaya Bhārata jananiya tanujāte (1924) was declared the state song of Karnataka in 2004, and the choice between the musical settings of Ananthaswamy and Ashwath became a public controversy, reaching the High Court of Karnataka in 2022 — a sign of how seriously the authorship of a tune is taken in this tradition. The radio stations of Andhra and Kerala fostered similar genres, Telugu lalita saṅgītam and Malayalam lalitagānam, whose composers and singers were often trained in Karnatak music.

docs.title: 11.10 Gujarat and the Punjab
docs.text:
In Gujarat the modern song grew from two roots: the devotional pads of Narsinh Mehta and the other saint-poets, and the songs of the garbā, the circle dance of the Navarātri festival (Chapter 21). The Gujarati theatre companies of Bombay and the Gujarati cinema from the 1930s added their own repertoire, and the composer Avinash Vyas (1912–1984), who wrote and set hundreds of songs for Gujarati films and for the stage, composed many garbā songs that became the standard repertoire of the festival. After Independence the radio station at Ahmedabad fostered a Gujarati sugam saṅgīt of settings of modern poets, and its composers and singers — Purushottam Upadhyay among them — carried it to the concert stage. The vast urban garbā of today, with its professional singers and amplified bands, draws much of its music from these composed songs rather than from village tradition.

Punjabi popular song developed largely outside the cinema. On records from the 1930s and, after Partition, on both sides of the new border, singers adapted the folk genres of the Punjab — the wedding songs, the bolīs of the giddhā and bhāṅgṛā, the māhiyā and ṭappe couplets, the ballads of lovers such as Hīr and Rāṃjhā — for urban audiences. In India, Surinder Kaur (1929–2006), often singing with her sister Prakash Kaur, made the Punjabi wedding and folk song a respectable recorded genre; Lal Chand Yamla Jatt popularised the one-stringed plucked tumbī; and Asa Singh Mastana was among the most popular male singers of the 1950s and 1960s. In the 1970s and 1980s a style of earthy, often bawdy male–female duets, performed at village gatherings (akhāṛā) and sold on records and cassettes, made Amar Singh Chamkila the most popular Punjabi singer of his time; his murder in 1988, during the violence of that decade, has made him a subject of continuing debate about the morality and the social world of Punjabi song. In Pakistan, Alam Lohar, who accompanied himself on the tongs (cimṭā) and made the jugnī song famous, and the singer Reshma, of a nomadic community, carried the Punjabi and Rajasthani folk song to national audiences. The Punjabi song of the diaspora, transformed into a dance music in Britain, is described in Chapter 23.

docs.title: 11.11 The Urdu Ghazal as Popular Song
docs.text: In the Urdu-speaking north the ghazal was already a sung form in the salons of the courtesans (Section 7.7). In the twentieth century, as Peter Manuel has shown, it became a popular song in a series of stages: the gramophone records of the courtesan singers of the 1900s; the theatre and early cinema, which used ghazals as songs; the light classical concert ghazal of Begum Akhtar in India and of Mehdi Hassan (1927–2012) in Pakistan, sung with harmonium, sāraṅgī and tablā and elaborated with the techniques of ṭhumrī; and, from the 1970s, a simplified “pop ghazal” with guitar, violins and electronic instruments, sung by Jagjit Singh (1941–2011) and others, whose album The Unforgettables (1976), with Chitra Singh, opened a large new market (Manuel 1988). The ghazal-song carried Urdu poetry, and with it an idiom of love, longing and irony, to audiences who no longer read the script. It also carried politics: Faiz Ahmad Faiz’s poem Ham dekheṅge, sung by Iqbal Bano at a concert in Lahore in 1986 under the military government of Zia ul-Haq, became an anthem of protest on both sides of the border. The Hindi gīt and the Punjabi song had similar histories on the radio and on record, and the songs of the Partition generation, like the ghazal, remain a shared repertoire of India and Pakistan (Chapter 23).

docs.title: 11.12 Songs of the Nation
docs.text: Many of the songs described in this chapter were made for, or taken up by, the national movement, and song was one of its most effective instruments. Meetings opened and closed with song, processions sang through the streets, and a song could be learnt and repeated by people who could not read the pamphlets and newspapers of the movement. The colonial government recognised the danger: song-books were among the publications proscribed under the press laws, plays and jātrās with patriotic songs were censored under the Dramatic Performances Act of 1876 (Chapter 19), and singers such as the jātrā poet Mukunda Das (Chapter 20) and Nazrul were imprisoned.

docs.title: 11.12.1 Vande Mātaram
docs.text: The first great song of the movement was Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s hymn to the motherland as goddess, Vande Mātaram, written in a Sanskritised Bengali in the 1870s and placed in his novel Ānandamaṭh (1882), whose story of ascetic rebels made the song a call to arms (see Volume 24). Tagore set it to music and sang it at the Calcutta session of the Congress in 1896, and during the agitation against the partition of Bengal in 1905 its first words became the slogan of the movement throughout India. It was sung to many tunes, regional and rāga-based, and the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya singer V. D. Paluskar made a point of singing it at Congress sessions; a well-known account describes him insisting on singing it in full at the Kakinada session of 1923, despite the objection of the Congress president, Maulana Mohammad Ali, to music at the session. The later stanzas of the song, which identify the motherland with Durgā and other goddesses, were objected to by many Muslims, and in 1937 the Congress recommended that only the first two stanzas be sung at national gatherings. When the Constituent Assembly adopted Jana-gaṇa-mana as the national anthem in January 1950, Vande Mātaram was declared the national song, to be honoured equally with it. The history of the song shows how a devotional idiom could carry national feeling and, by the same token, divide those who did not share the devotion.

docs.title: 11.12.2 Gandhi and the bhajan
docs.text: Gandhi made congregational singing a daily discipline of the movement. The prayer meetings of his ashrams at Sabarmati and Wardha, and later the public prayer meetings of his tours, were built around the singing of devotional songs from many traditions, collected in the Āśram Bhajanāvalī. The music was in the charge of Narayan Moreshwar Khare, a pupil of Paluskar, who taught at the Sabarmati ashram and set the hymns to simple melodies for congregational singing. Two songs became inseparable from Gandhi’s name: Narsinh Mehta’s Gujarati Vaiṣṇava jana to, which defines the true devotee as one who feels the pain of others, and the chant Raghupati Rāghava Rājā Rām, in the version sung at his meetings with the line declaring that Īśvara and Allāh are names of one God. The morning procession through a town singing such songs (prabhāt pherī) became a common nationalist practice in the 1920s and 1930s. Gandhi’s choice was deliberate: the bhajan drew on the shared devotional culture of village India (Chapter 9), required no training, and made every participant a singer.

docs.title: 11.12.3 Anthems, marches and laments
docs.text:
The movement had many other songs. Muhammad Iqbal’s Sāre jahāṅ se acchā (1904), on the beauty of India, was sung in schools and at meetings, and is still played by Indian military bands (see Volume 8). In south-east Asia, Subhas Chandra Bose’s Indian National Army adopted Śubh sukh cain, a Hindustani version of Jana-gaṇa-mana, with music arranged by Captain Ram Singh Thakuri, who also composed its march Qadam qadam baṛhāye jā. The Punjabi revolutionaries of the Ghadar movement circulated their poems in printed collections to be sung and recited, and in every region the forms of folk song — the Marathi povāḍā, the Bengali jātrā song, the Tamil songs of Bharati — were turned to political use. After Independence the patriotic song passed largely to the cinema and the radio: Ai mere vatan ke logo, written by the poet Pradeep and composed by C. Ramchandra, sung by Lata Mangeshkar at a public function in Delhi in January 1963 in memory of the soldiers who died in the war with China, is the best-known example of a film-industry song that became a national lament.

The national song had its limits. It spoke in the idiom of the communities that made it — often an upper-caste Hindu idiom of the motherland as goddess — and the controversy over Vande Mātaram shows that the same song could unite some listeners and exclude others. Dalit, Ādivāsī and regional movements produced songs of their own, from the Ambedkarite jalsās of Maharashtra (Chapter 20) to the songs of the Jharkhand and north-eastern movements, in which the nation of the anthems was not always the community that mattered most.

docs.title: 11.13 Authors, Notations and the Problem of Fidelity
docs.text:
Table 11.1 lists some of the makers of the modern song described in this chapter. Several features unite their traditions.

Table 11.1. Some makers of modern song in the Indian languages Composer or poet Language Known for Rāmnidhi Gupta (Nidhu Babu), 1741–1839 Bengali Bengali ṭappā Rabindranath Tagore, 1861–1941 Bengali Rabīndrasaṅgīt; dance-dramas; two national anthems Dvijendralāl Rāy, 1863–1913 Bengali Theatre songs, comic and patriotic songs Rajanīkānta Sen, 1865–1910 Bengali Devotional and svadeśī songs Atulprasād Sen, 1871–1934 Bengali Songs in a north Indian light classical manner Kazi Nazrul Islam, 1899–1976 Bengali Bengali ghazal; Islamic and Śākta songs; new rāgas Salil Chowdhury, 1925–1995 Bengali, Hindi Mass song; film music Govindrao Tembe, 1881–1955 Marathi Music of the stage play Mānāpamān Sudhir Phadke, 1919–2002 Marathi Bhāvgīt; the radio Gīt Rāmāyaṇ Jyotiprasad Agarwala, 1903–1951 Assamese Jyoti-saṅgīt; first Assamese film Bishnu Prasad Rabha, 1909–1969 Assamese Songs drawing on the music of the valley’s peoples Bhupen Hazarika, 1926–2011 Assamese, Bengali Songs of the Brahmaputra; film music Subramania Bharati, 1882–1921 Tamil Patriotic and devotional songs in named rāgas Mysore Ananthaswamy, 1936–1995 Kannada Sugama saṅgīta settings of modern poetry

The first is the idea of the song as a fixed work. Unlike the bandiś of the Hindustani singer, which is a framework for improvisation, a song of Tagore, Nazrul or the Gīt Rāmāyaṇ is a finished composition in which words, melody and rhythm belong together, and the singer’s task is to realise it faithfully. Notation, copyright and the authority of institutions — Visva-Bharati, the Nazrul Institute, the radio — were the means by which this idea was enforced, and the tension between fidelity and interpretation, which no notation can resolve, runs through the history of all these traditions.

The second is their social base. The modern song was made largely by and for the educated middle class, and it allowed women of “respectable” families to sing in public, on record and on the radio at a time when the professional woman singer was still associated with the courtesan. Many of the most admired singers of Rabīndrasaṅgīt and bhāvgīt were such women. At the same time the songs drew constantly on the music of others — the courtesan’s ṭhumrī and ghazal, the Bāul’s song, the kīrtan, the tribal melody — and the history of these borrowings, like that of the classical revival, raises questions about whose music was being made respectable.

The third is the bond between song and political community. The modern song gave each of the major languages an emblem of itself, sung at its festivals and its protests, and several of its songs became the anthems of nation-states. That it could do so is a measure of how central song, rather than the instrumental or the classical art, has been to the public life of modern South Asia.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On Tagore’s songs see Som (2009), a musical biography with translations. On the Marathi stage song see Ranade (1986), and on the Urdu ghazal-song Manuel (1988); Manuel (1989) places the ghazal among the light classical genres. The recording industry, the radio and the cinema, through which most of these songs reached their listeners, are discussed in Chapter 23; Kinnear (1994) lists the earliest records, and Manuel (1993) describes the cassette era. The poetry of Tagore, Nazrul and Bharati is treated in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā, and Tagore’s thought in Volume 24, Samanvaya.

docs.title: Chapter 12: The Abhinayadarpaṇa and the Later Dance Treatises
docs.text: The Nāṭyaśāstra was followed by a long series of treatises that dealt with dance, either as part of a larger account of music (saṅgīta) or on its own. Some were encyclopaedic works written at royal courts; others were short manuals for teachers and performers. The best known of the latter, and in the twentieth century the most influential of all Sanskrit texts on dance, is the Abhinayadarpaṇa (“Mirror of Gesture”) ascribed to Nandikeśvara. A short Sanskrit manual of uncertain date thus became, in the twentieth century, the classroom text of a whole family of dance forms, and the question how far it, and the longer treatises of the medieval courts, describe what dancers actually did runs through what follows. The hand gestures of the Abhinayadarpaṇa, its most famous contribution, are treated together with those of the Nāṭyaśāstra and the Kerala manuals in Chapter 14; the four means of acting (abhinaya) that frame all these texts are described in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 12.1.1 Nandikeśvara
docs.text: Nandikeśvara, “lord of Nandi” or “Nandi the lord”, is the name of Śiva’s attendant and gatekeeper, and in Indian tradition an authority on music and dance; Abhinavagupta and Śārṅgadeva cite a Nandikeśvara among the early theorists. Several works are ascribed to him, among them the Abhinayadarpaṇa and the Bharatārṇava, a larger treatise on dance known in an incomplete form. Whether these works have anything to do with the early authority, or with each other, is uncertain. The Abhinayadarpaṇa as we have it is a compact manual of a few hundred verses whose date has been placed by different scholars anywhere between the early centuries CE and the thirteenth century or later; most recent writers prefer a date later than the Nāṭyaśāstra, but there is no secure evidence (Ghosh 1957; Bose 1991). It survives in manuscripts from the south, and differences between them, in the number of verses and in the lists of gestures, show that it was adapted by its users.

docs.title: 12.1.2 Editions and translations
docs.text: The text became widely known through two works. In 1917 the art historian Ananda K. Coomaraswamy, with the Telugu scholar Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya, published The Mirror of Gesture, an English translation of the Abhinayadarpaṇa with an introduction that presented Indian dance as a spiritual and classical art (Coomaraswamy and Duggirala 1917). Manomohan Ghosh published the Sanskrit text with an English translation in 1934 and in revised editions thereafter, and his text and numbering are used here (Ghosh 1957). In the twentieth century the Abhinayadarpaṇa became the textbook of the reconstructed Bharatanāṭyam and of the other southern dance forms: students learn its lists of hands and of head, eye and neck movements by heart, and its verses are recited in the classroom.

docs.title: 12.1.3 The invocation
docs.text:
The Abhinayadarpaṇa opens with a celebrated verse in which Śiva is described as the embodiment of the four kinds of acting:

Abhinayadarpaṇa 1

āṅgikaṃ bhuvanaṃ yasya vācikaṃ sarvavāṅmayam āhāryaṃ candratārādi taṃ numaḥ sāttvikaṃ śivam

“We bow to the auspicious one, the embodiment of sattva, whose bodily acting is the world, whose verbal acting is all language, and whose costume is the moon and the stars.”

The verse expresses in a single couplet the idea, central to the devotional understanding of Indian dance, that the dance of the performer is a reflection of the dance of the god. It also neatly names the four means of acting described in the Nāṭyaśāstra: bodily (āṅgika), verbal (vācika), extraneous (āhārya) and inner (sāttvika).

docs.title: 12.2 Drama, Dance and Pure Dance
docs.text: After a short account of the origin of drama, retold from the Nāṭyaśāstra, the Abhinayadarpaṇa distinguishes three kinds of performance. Nāṭya is drama, the representation of a traditional story. Nṛtta is dance that has no expression of mood or meaning, consisting of pure movement. Nṛtya is dance that expresses rasa and bhāva, the emotions and their states. The distinction, which goes back in this form to texts of the late first millennium, became the basis of the modern analysis of the dance forms into passages of pure and expressive dance; it is discussed in Chapter 13. The text recommends that nṛtta and nṛtya be performed especially at the coronations of kings, at festivals, processions and weddings, and on other auspicious occasions — a reminder of the courtly and ceremonial world for which it was written.

docs.title: 12.3.1 The assembly
docs.text: The Abhinayadarpaṇa imagines the performance as taking place before an assembly (sabhā) presided over by a king or patron. It compares the assembly to a wish-fulfilling tree, of which the Vedas are the branches, the sciences the flowers and the learned the bees, and it describes the qualities of the patron (sabhāpati): wealth, intelligence, discrimination, generosity, knowledge of music and dance. It prescribes the seating: the patron in the centre, his ministers and poets around him, the musicians placed so as to be heard, and the dancer in front of the assembly.

docs.title: 12.3.2 The dancer and the accompanists
docs.text:
The dancer is called the pātra (“vessel” or “character”), and the text assumes that she is a woman. It describes her as young, beautiful, graceful, confident, knowledgeable about rhythm and music, and responsive to the mood of the assembly, and it lists the qualities, physical and moral, that disqualify a dancer. It names ten “vital elements” (prāṇa) of the dancer: speed (javana), steadiness (sthiratā), line or grace of form (rekhā), turning (bhramarī), glance (dṛṣṭi), endurance (śrama), intelligence (medhā), devotion or commitment (śraddhā), speech (vacana) and song (gīta). It also describes the accompanists — the leader who keeps time with cymbals, the drummer, the flautist, the singers — and even the dancer’s ankle bells, which are to be of bronze and well tuned (Ghosh 1957; Coomaraswamy and Duggirala 1917).

Read historically, these passages describe the court and temple dance of the medieval and early modern south, performed by professional women dancers before male patrons, with male teachers and musicians. They are thus important evidence for the social world of the dancers who were later called devadāsīs (Chapter 15), and their emphasis on the dancer’s beauty and youth reflects that world’s assumptions as clearly as its aesthetic ideals.

docs.title: 12.3.3 Hand, eye, mind and feeling
docs.text:
Two verses of the Abhinayadarpaṇa (numbered 36–37 in common editions) state the principle of expressive dance more memorably than any other text:

Abhinayadarpaṇa 36–37 (Ghosh’s numbering)

kaṇṭhenālambayed gītaṃ hastenārthaṃ pradarśayet cakṣurbhyāṃ darśayed bhāvaṃ pādābhyāṃ tālam ācaret yato hastas tato dṛṣṭir yato dṛṣṭis tato manaḥ yato manas tato bhāvo yato bhāvas tato rasaḥ

“The song should be sustained by the throat, the meaning shown by the hands, the feeling shown by the eyes, and the rhythm kept by the feet. Where the hand goes, there the eyes go; where the eyes go, there goes the mind; where the mind goes, there is feeling; where there is feeling, there is rasa.”

The first verse describes the older practice, in which the dancer herself sang the song she interpreted; in the modern forms the singing is usually done by a vocalist. The second makes the coordination of hand and eye the foundation of expression, and is perhaps the most quoted verse in Indian dance teaching.

docs.title: 12.4 The Movements of the Body
docs.text: The Abhinayadarpaṇa’s analysis of the body is simpler than the Nāṭyaśāstra’s (Chapter 2). Its lists are short enough to be memorised and practised, which explains much of its popularity as a teaching text.

docs.title: 12.4.1 Head, eyes and neck
docs.text:
The text describes nine movements of the head (śirobheda), eight glances (dṛṣṭibheda) and four movements of the neck (grīvābheda), each with a list of uses (Table 12.1). The head may be held level (sama), raised (udvāhita), lowered (adhomukha), rolled in a circle (ālolita), shaken from side to side (dhuta), nodded up and down (kampita), turned away (parāvṛtta), turned and raised (utkṣipta) or moved from side to side like a fan (parivāhita). The lowered head expresses shame, sorrow or bowing; the shaken head denial or reluctance; the nodded head calling, questioning or threatening; the rolled head drowsiness, intoxication or possession. The eight glances range from the level gaze (sama) through the sidelong glance (sāci), the half-closed eye of meditation (nimīlita), the upward and downward glances (ullokita, avalokita) and the gaze that follows the hand (anuvṛtta). The four neck movements are the side-to-side glide (sundarī), the movement like a snake (tiraścīna), the sideways turn (parivartita) and the forward-and-back movement like a pigeon’s (prakampita); the gliding sundarī and prakampita are characteristic of Bharatanāṭyam and Kathakaḷi.

Table 12.1. Movements of the head, eyes and neck in the Abhinayadarpaṇa (Ghosh’s text) Part No. Names Head (śiras) 9 sama, udvāhita, adhomukha, ālolita, dhuta, kampita, parāvṛtta, utkṣipta, parivāhita Eyes (dṛṣṭi) 8 sama, ālokita, sāci, pralokita, nimīlita, ullokita, anuvṛtta, avalokita Neck (grīvā) 4 sundarī, tiraścīna, parivartita, prakampita Hands (hasta) 28 + 23 single and combined hands, with further sets for gods, planets, relations and others (Chapter 14)

These lists are much shorter than those of the Nāṭyaśāstra, which gives thirteen head movements, thirty-six glances and nine neck movements, together with movements of the eyebrows, eyelids, eyeballs, nose, cheeks, lips and chin. Later teachers often supplement the Abhinayadarpaṇa from the older text, and in practice dancers use many more facial movements than either text names; the training of the eyes in Kathakaḷi and Kūṭiyāṭṭam, for example, is far more elaborate (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 12.4.2 Postures, leaps, turns and gaits
docs.text:
The Abhinayadarpaṇa treats the lower body under several heads. It describes ten postures (maṇḍala), among them sthānaka (standing), āyata (with the knees bent outwards and the heels together, the basis of the half-seated position called araimaṇḍi in Bharatanāṭyam) and the lunges ālīḍha and pratyālīḍha; six standing positions (sthānaka), such as samapāda, ekapāda (on one foot) and nāgabandha; five leaps (utplavana); seven kinds of turn (bhramarī), including turns on one foot and turns in the air; eight movements of the feet (cārī); and ten gaits (gati), named after the swan, the peacock, the deer, the elephant, the horse, the lion, the snake and the frog, together with the gaits of the hero and of an ordinary man (Ghosh 1957).

These categories give the teacher a vocabulary rather than a technique. The Abhinayadarpaṇa does not describe the aḍavus of Bharatanāṭyam, the footwork of Kathak or the steps of Odissi, which belong to the living traditions and were systematised by twentieth-century teachers (Chapters 13, 15 and 16). Its gaits, however, are still taught, and its descriptions of the walks of animals and characters are used in dance-drama.

docs.title: 12.5 The Later Dance Treatises
docs.text:
Between the eleventh and eighteenth centuries a series of works in Sanskrit, and later in the regional languages, described dance as it was performed in the courts and temples of their authors’ time. Their general pattern is the same: they repeat, and sometimes reinterpret, the categories of the Nāṭyaśāstra (the “classical” or mārga dance), and then describe new, “regional” (deśī) forms, movements and items that the older text did not know. They are thus evidence both for the prestige of the ancient tradition and for the constant creation of new dance (Bose 1991; Vatsyayan 1968).

Mānasollāsa (1131). An encyclopaedia of royal pleasures compiled at the court of the Cāḷukya king Someśvara III in Karnataka, with sections on music and dance. Saṅgītaratnākara (first half of the thirteenth century). Śārṅgadeva’s seventh chapter, on dance (nartana), was the most influential post-Nāṭyaśāstra account of the subject (below). Nṛttaratnāvalī (1253–54). Composed by Jāya Senāpati, a general of the Kākatīya king Gaṇapatideva in Andhra, this work describes the mārga tradition and then, in detail, the deśī dances of its time, including regional dances with names such as peraṇi, prekhaṇa, carcarī, rāsaka, daṇḍarāsa and kolāṭa, several of them group and stick dances that survive in some form in folk practice. V. Raghavan’s edition revealed the richness of medieval Andhra dance (Raghavan 1965). Saṅgītadāmodara (fifteenth century). A work by Śubhaṅkara from eastern India, dealing with music and dance. Nartananirṇaya (late sixteenth century). Puṇḍarīka Viṭṭhala, a southern scholar who worked at northern courts, describes forms of dance current in his time, including composed (baddha) and free (anibaddha) dance and items that have been compared with the later repertoire of Kathak. Saṅgītasārāmṛta (eighteenth century). A work on music and dance attributed to the Maratha king Tulajā of Thanjavur, important for the history of southern dance before the modern repertoire was fixed. Hastalakṣaṇadīpikā. An anonymous Kerala manual of hand gestures, of uncertain date, which provides the gesture vocabulary of Kūṭiyāṭṭam and Kathakaḷi (Chapter 14). Abhinayacandrikā. An Odia manual attributed to Maheśvara Mahāpātra, of uncertain date (probably eighteenth century), used in the reconstruction of Odissi (Chapter 17).

docs.title: 12.5.1 The Saṅgītaratnākara on dance
docs.text: Because of its comprehensiveness and its authority in both north and south, Śārṅgadeva’s account of dance deserves a closer look. The seventh chapter of the Saṅgītaratnākara begins, like the Nāṭyaśāstra, with the origin of dance, and then defines nāṭya, nṛtta and nṛtya. It describes the movements of the major and minor limbs, largely following Bharata, and then gives the karaṇas, aṅgahāras and cārīs of the mārga tradition. What distinguishes it from the older text is the space it gives to deśī practice: postures (sthāna), cārīs and dance items that are not in the Nāṭyaśāstra and that Śārṅgadeva presents as current in his own time. It also discusses the qualities of the dance teacher (nāṭyācārya) and of male and female dancers, the composition of the troupe (sampradāya) with its singers, drummers and instrumentalists, and the faults to be avoided in performance (Shringy and Sharma 1978; Bose 1991). The commentaries of Siṃhabhūpāla and Kallinātha on this chapter show how later readers related its categories to the dance they knew.

docs.title: 12.5.2 The Nṛttaratnāvalī and the Kākatīya world
docs.text: Jāya Senāpati’s Nṛttaratnāvalī is the most detailed surviving account of medieval regional dance. Its first four chapters deal with the mārga tradition of the Nāṭyaśāstra; the last four describe deśī postures, cārīs, movements and complete dance items, many of them group dances performed at festivals. Among these is the peraṇi, a vigorous dance performed by men before Śiva. The Kākatīya temple at Palampet (Rāmappa), built in 1213, carries dancing figures on its bracket figures and pillars that correspond in a general way to the dances Jāya Senāpati describes. In the late twentieth century the dancer and scholar Nataraja Ramakrishna used the text and the sculptures to create a modern Peraṇi Śivatāṇḍavam, an example, like Padma Subrahmanyam’s karaṇas, of the creative reconstruction of dance from texts and images.

docs.title: 12.6 Dance in Literature, Sculpture and Painting
docs.text: The treatises are only one kind of evidence for the history of dance in India, and they have to be read with other kinds.

docs.title: 12.6.1 Literary evidence
docs.text: Sanskrit and Prakrit literature is full of dancers. In Kālidāsa’s play Mālavikāgnimitra (c. fourth–fifth century) the plot turns on a dance contest: two rival dance masters, Gaṇadāsa and Haradatta, each present a pupil before the king, and the heroine Mālavikā wins the contest with a difficult composition, while a learned nun acts as judge; in the first act the dance master Gaṇadāsa praises drama as a single entertainment for people of different tastes. Harṣa’s Ratnāvalī (seventh century) opens with the spring festival, in which townspeople dance the group dance called carcarī in the streets. Court poetry describes dancers in palace halls and temple festivals, and Buddhist and Jain literature describes courtesans whose accomplishments included dance and music (Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā). In Tamil, the Cilappatikāram (c. fifth–sixth century) describes the seven years of training of the dancer Mātavi under masters of dance, music, poetry and drumming, her debut before the Cōḻa king on a stage whose dimensions it records, and a series of eleven dances (patiṉoru āṭal) she performs at a festival, each associated with a god or a mythological episode (Parthasarathy 1993). These passages are literary and idealised, but they show that dance was a recognised profession with its own training, patrons and conventions in the early centuries CE.

docs.title: 12.6.2 Sculpture and painting
docs.text:
Visual art provides a continuous, if difficult, record. The small bronze figure from Mohenjo-daro of the third millennium BCE, popularly called the “dancing girl”, may or may not represent a dancer; the name is modern. From the second century BCE onwards, the reliefs of Bharhut and Sanchi show celestial dancers and musicians, some labelled by name; the paintings of Ajanta (fifth century CE) show dancers at courts and festivals; and from the sixth century, beginning with the many-armed dancing Śiva of Cave 1 at Badami (Figure 12.1), the dancing god becomes a major subject of Indian sculpture, culminating in the Cōḻa bronzes of Naṭarāja (Chapter 1). Medieval temples throughout India carry dancers on their walls and pillars: the karaṇa series of Thanjavur and Chidambaram (Chapter 2), the musicians and dancers of the dance hall at Konark, the bracket figures of Hoysaḷa temples, and the dancing figures of Khajuraho. Mughal and Rajput painting depicts court dancers and the dance of Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd women (Vatsyayan 1968).

Figure 12.1. The many-armed dancing Śiva carved at the entrance of Cave 1 at Badami, Karnataka, sixth century, with small figures of Gaṇeśa and a drummer beside his feet. Photo: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts showed how these sources can be read together with the treatises, and how the postures and movements described in the texts can be recognised in sculpture. Her method has been immensely productive, but it has limits. Sculptors had their own conventions, and a frozen pose does not tell us how a dancer moved into it or out of it; and a sculpture that resembles a modern dance pose does not prove a continuous tradition between them. Much modern writing on Indian dance, especially in the context of the twentieth-century revival, has treated temple sculpture as a direct record of the dances that later dancers performed. It is more accurate to say that the sculptures, the texts and the modern forms all draw, in different ways and at different times, on a shared vocabulary of movement and image (Vatsyayan 1968; Bose 1991).

docs.title: 12.7 Texts and Practice
docs.text:
How far did the dancers of any period actually follow these texts? Mandakranta Bose’s study of the Sanskrit dance treatises shows that each of them combines inherited categories with descriptions of contemporary practice, and that the balance shifts over time: the later texts devote more and more space to the deśī, the regional and current, and less to the mārga of Bharata (Bose 1991). The texts were written by scholars, often at royal courts, and they record what their authors considered worth classifying; they were not instruction manuals from which dancers learnt their art. Dancers learnt from teachers, and the hereditary teachers of the south — the naṭṭuvaṉārs — had their own oral and written traditions in Tamil and Telugu, much of which has been lost.

In the twentieth century the relation between text and practice was reversed. The reformers who reconstructed the court and temple dance of the south as “Bharatanāṭyam”, and the founders of the other classical forms, sought authority in the Sanskrit texts, which were newly available in print. The Abhinayadarpaṇa, because it was short, practical and available in English, became the canonical text of the new forms; its lists were taught in the new institutions; and performers began to describe their art as the living embodiment of the Nāṭyaśāstra and the Abhinayadarpaṇa. This was a creative and in many ways productive use of the texts. But it also obscured the immediate history of the dances, which lay in the repertoire and teaching of the hereditary performers whose authority the reformers were displacing (Chapter 15) (Soneji 2012; Meduri 1988).

docs.title: 12.8 Comparisons
docs.text: The Abhinayadarpaṇa and its relatives have often been compared with other systems of gesture and movement: the sign languages of deaf communities, the codified gestures of Japanese and Chinese theatre, the dance of Southeast Asia, and modern research on non-verbal communication. Some comparisons are illuminating — like sign languages, the hand gestures combine a limited number of shapes with location and movement to produce many meanings, and like spoken words they are polysemous and depend on context — but they should be made with care. The hasta vocabulary is not a language with its own grammar, and the claim that it “anticipated” modern sciences of communication confuses a performer’s code with a scientific theory. The dance traditions of Southeast Asia share themes and some gestures with Indian dance, but the direct influence of the Abhinayadarpaṇa on them has not been demonstrated. Claims that dance gestures have therapeutic effects are discussed, and qualified, in Chapter 23.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Coomaraswamy and Duggirala (1917) and Ghosh (1957) are the standard translations of the Abhinayadarpaṇa. Bose (1991) is the essential study of the Sanskrit dance treatises from the Nāṭyaśāstra to the eighteenth century, and Vatsyayan (1968) relates them to sculpture, painting and literature. Shringy and Sharma (1978) translates the Saṅgītaratnākara, and Parthasarathy (1993) the Cilappatikāram. On the twentieth-century use of the texts see Soneji (2012) and Meduri (1988).

docs.title: Chapter 13: Nṛtta, Nṛtya and Nāṭya
docs.text: Indian writing on dance distinguishes three modes of performance: nṛtta, pure or abstract dance, in which movement is organised by rhythm and has no representational content; nṛtya, expressive dance, in which the dancer conveys the meaning and feeling of a song or verse; and nāṭya, drama, in which performers enact a story with characters. The distinction is a theoretical one — most dance forms combine all three, often within a single item — but it has proved remarkably useful, both to the medieval theorists who formulated it and to the twentieth-century teachers who organised the classical repertoires around it. Watch a Bharatanāṭyam varṇam and the three modes alternate before one’s eyes: a passage of rhythmic footwork to the teacher’s recited syllables, then a line of the song interpreted through gesture and face, then, perhaps, a few moments in which the dancer becomes a character in a story. The history of the distinction, the units and compositions of pure dance, the song-based items of expressive dance and the conventions of dance-drama are taken in turn, followed by the modern recital and the gendered pairing of tāṇḍava and lāsya, a pairing that has shaped the discussion of Indian dance more than its history warrants.

docs.title: 13.1 The History of the Distinction
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra speaks of drama (nāṭya) and of dance (nṛtta). Its chapter on the tāṇḍava explains that nṛtta, unlike drama, does not depend on the meaning of a text; it is added to the performance because it creates beauty and because it is auspicious and loved by the gods (Chapter 2). The expressive mode that later writers called nṛtya is implicit in Bharata’s treatment of acting and of the songs (dhruvā) and dance-items (lāsyāṅga) of the stage, but it is not a separate category.

The threefold distinction appears in the dramaturgical and dance literature of the late first and early second millennia. Dhanañjaya’s Daśarūpaka (late tenth century), a handbook of drama, distinguishes nṛtya, which “rests on feeling” (bhāvāśraya), from nṛtta, which “rests on rhythm and tempo” (tālalayāśraya), and both from drama, which rests on rasa. The Abhinayadarpaṇa defines nāṭya as the enactment of a traditional story, nṛtta as dance devoid of mood and expression, and nṛtya as dance that expresses rasa and bhāva (Chapter 12). Śārṅgadeva’s Saṅgītaratnākara (thirteenth century) adopts the three categories and cross-classifies nṛtta and nṛtya as either vigorous (tāṇḍava) or delicate (lāsya) (Bose 1991; Shringy and Sharma 1978). In twentieth-century writing, beginning with Coomaraswamy and Kapila Vatsyayan, the three terms became the standard framework for describing the classical forms (Vatsyayan 1968, 1974).

docs.title: 13.2.1 The aesthetics of pure dance
docs.text: In nṛtta the body creates patterns in space and time: lines of the arms and legs, symmetrical and asymmetrical postures, paths across the floor, and above all the articulation of rhythm by the feet in relation to the music. Its pleasure is the pleasure of form and of rhythm — of precision, energy and the exact coincidence of movement with the beat. Writers have compared it with music without words or with geometry; the comparisons are apt as long as they are not taken as claims about mathematics.

docs.title: 13.2.2 Basic posture
docs.text: Each dance form has a basic stance from which its movement proceeds. In Bharatanāṭyam it is the half-seated araimaṇḍi (Tamil, “half-sitting”), with the knees bent outwards and the heels together, which corresponds to the āyata posture of the texts; Kuchipudi uses a similar position. Odissi alternates between the square, wide-legged cauka and the three-bend tribhaṅga, with the body curved at neck, waist and knee as in Odishan temple sculpture (Chapter 17). Kathak dancers stand upright, with the weight on flat feet, which allows rapid footwork and turns. Kathakaḷi actors stand with the feet apart and the weight on the outer edges of the feet, knees bent outwards, a stance derived from the training of Kerala’s martial art (Chapter 18). Manipuri dancers keep the knees soft and the movement continuous and rounded, with no sharp angles.

docs.title: 13.2.3 Units of movement
docs.text: The pure dance of each form is built from basic units. In Bharatanāṭyam these are the aḍavus (Tamil, “step” or “placing”), each a short combination of footwork, leg and arm positions and hand shapes performed to a rhythmic syllable pattern. They are grouped into families named after their characteristic action or syllables — among them taṭṭaḍavu (striking the feet), nāṭṭaḍavu (stretching the leg), kuditta meṭṭaḍavu (jumping and striking), tattimeṭṭaḍavu, sarikkal (sliding) and maṇḍi (kneeling) aḍavus — and each is practised in three speeds. The number of aḍavus taught, and their names, differ between schools; the systematic sequences taught today were organised by twentieth-century teachers, especially at Kalakshetra (O’Shea 2007). Kathak’s units are the patterns of footwork (tatkār) and turns (cakkar), Odissi’s the basic steps and sculptural poses (bhaṅgi) taught in the reconstructed curriculum of the 1950s, and Kathakaḷi’s the dance passages called kalaśam, which punctuate the sung text and end with characteristic leaps and turns.

docs.title: 13.2.4 Rhythmic compositions
docs.text:
Pure dance is organised by compositions of rhythmic syllables, recited by the dance master or drummer and articulated by the dancer’s feet and body (Viswanathan and Allen 2004; Kippen 1988). Table 13.1 compares the terms used in different forms.

In the southern forms, a jati is a passage of syllables (sollukaṭṭu) composed to fit the tāla and danced as a sequence of aḍavus; the term is unrelated to the jātis that classify the length of the laghu in tāla theory (Chapter 5). A passage of pure dance usually ends with a tīrmāṉam (“conclusion”) or aruḍi, a cadential phrase repeated three times so that its last syllable falls on the beat on which the song resumes. Longer cadences, korvais, combine several phrases. Their shapes can follow traditional designs called yati: in the “cow’s tail” (gopuccha) design the phrases become progressively shorter, in the “river” (srotovaha) design progressively longer, and in the “drum” (ḍamaru) and “mṛdaṅga” designs they first shrink and then grow, or the reverse.

In Kathak the compositions are those of the tablā and pakhāvaj — ṭukṛā, toḍā, paran, tihāī — recited (paḍhant) by the dancer before being danced, and many end with a tihāī or a chakkardār composition whose final stroke falls on sam. Kathak dancers also engage in rhythmic dialogue with the drummer, and in the most virtuosic passages the dancer’s footwork becomes a percussion instrument (Chapter 16).

Table 13.1. Some terms for the elements of pure dance in different forms Form Basic units Rhythmic compositions and cadences Bharatanāṭyam aḍavu families; araimaṇḍi jati, sollukaṭṭu, tīrmāṉam, aruḍi, korvai Kuchipudi aḍugus (steps), jumps jatis, tīrmāṉams Odissi basic steps and bhaṅgis (sculptural poses); cauka, tribhaṅga bols, ukuṭa (syllables recited) Kathak tatkār, cakkar toḍā, ṭukṛā, paran, tihāī, chakkardār Kathakaḷi stance and exercises from kaḷarippayaṯṯu kalaśams (dance interludes) Manipuri cholom (vigorous) and soft movement drum compositions of the pung

docs.title: 13.2.5 The dance master and the musicians
docs.text: Pure dance is inseparable from its music. In Bharatanāṭyam the naṭṭuvaṉār, the dance master, conducts the performance by reciting the rhythmic syllables and beating time on a pair of small cymbals (tāḷam); the art of conducting, naṭṭuvāṅgam, was for centuries the hereditary profession of men of the families whose women were the dancers, and is now often practised by the dancer’s teacher, male or female (Chapter 15). The mṛdaṅgam player follows the dancer’s feet and the naṭṭuvaṉār’s syllables. In Kathak the tablā or pakhāvaj player and the dancer are partners in a rhythmic dialogue. In Kathakaḷi the drummers on ceṇṭa and maddaḷam accompany every movement of the actor’s body and hands. In Manipuri the drummer may himself dance, as in the pung cholom (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 13.3.1 Dancing a song
docs.text:
In nṛtya the dancer interprets the words of a song or verse through gesture, facial expression and movement. The dancer uses the hand gestures (Chapter 14) to show the objects and actions named in the text, the eyes and face to convey the feelings, and the movement of the whole body to embody the character speaking — most often a woman addressing her lover, her confidante or a god. The principles are those of abhinaya described in Chapter 3.

A line of text is rarely shown only once. In the southern forms the singer repeats each line many times, and the dancer interprets it differently on each repetition (sañcāri): first showing the literal meaning, then elaborating an image or an implied situation, then showing the emotion in a succession of transitory states. A line such as “the moon is burning me”, sung by a woman separated from her lover, may become in performance a scene of evening, the rising moon, the cool breezes that should soothe her and instead torment her, the memory of the lover’s last visit and her anger at his absence. This improvised elaboration (manodharma) is the highest test of an expressive dancer; Balasaraswati, by common consent the greatest Bharatanāṭyam dancer of the twentieth century, was celebrated for it (Knight 2010).

docs.title: 13.3.2 The genres of expressive dance
docs.text:
Each form has its expressive genres. In Bharatanāṭyam and Kuchipudi they include the śabdam, a song of praise with short descriptive passages; the varṇam, the long central item that alternates pure dance and expression; the slow love-songs called padam, among them the Telugu padams of Kṣetrayya (seventeenth century); the lighter jāvaḷis of the nineteenth century; and Sanskrit verses (ślokas) and devotional songs. Odissi’s main expressive texts are the songs (aṣṭapadī) of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda and Odia devotional poetry. Kathak dancers interpret ṭhumrī, bhajan and ghazal, often seated or standing almost still, in an improvised style (bhāv batānā, “showing the feeling”) developed by the courtesans and hereditary dancers of nineteenth-century Lucknow and Banaras. Mohiniyāṭṭam uses Malayalam and Sanskrit songs, many composed at the court of Travancore in the nineteenth century, and Sattriya the devotional songs (borgīt) of the Assamese Vaiṣṇava saints.

Much of this repertoire was the property of hereditary women performers, created for them by court poets and composers and transmitted by them. Its frank eroticism, which the devotional tradition read as a language for the love of god, was one of the reasons why twentieth-century reformers attacked the women who performed it and why the reconstructed classical forms “purified” parts of it (Chapters 3 and 15) (Soneji 2012).

docs.title: 13.3.3 Expressive elaboration in the Kerala theatre
docs.text: The Kerala theatres developed the most elaborate techniques of expressive elaboration in India. In Kūṭiyāṭṭam, an actor may take a single verse of a Sanskrit play and spend an hour or more developing it: before speaking the verse he enacts, in gesture alone, the situation behind it, the memories it evokes and the actions it implies. In the technique called pakarnnāṭṭam (“transformed acting”) a single actor plays several characters in turn, showing each by a change of stance and expression; the battle between Rāvaṇa and Jaṭāyu, or the lifting of Mount Kailāsa, may be performed by one actor representing all the participants. Kathakaḷi actors use similar techniques in the passages of free elaboration called iḷakiyāṭṭam, in which an actor departs from the sung text to describe a scene, a memory or a reflection — the beauty of a forest, the sight of a pond, the lament of a bird — before returning to the play (Chapters 18 and 19) (Zarrilli 2000; Richmond et al. 1990).

docs.title: 13.3.4 Abhinaya with the whole body
docs.text: Expressive dance is not only a matter of hands and face. Dancers use the gaits and postures of characters (the swaying walk of a woman, the swagger of a hero), the direction of the eyes to establish where an imagined person or object is, and the movement of the whole body to create a scene: rowing a boat across a river, plucking flowers from a tree, bathing in a pond, churning butter. They also move between characters and narrator within a single song, now speaking as the heroine, now showing the absent lover, now describing the scene from outside. This fluid shifting of role and viewpoint, which requires no change of costume, is one of the most distinctive features of Indian solo dance and one of the hardest to learn.

docs.title: 13.4 Space and the Group
docs.text:
Most of the modern classical recital forms are solo forms, and much writing on Indian dance treats the solo dancer as the norm. Historically, however, group dance was common. The Nāṭyaśāstra describes group formations (piṇḍībandha) in the preliminaries of the theatre; the medieval treatises describe group dances such as the carcarī, the rāsaka and the stick dances (Chapter 12); the temple and court dancers of the south often danced in groups at festivals and processions; and the Rāsalīlā of Manipur and Braj, the group dances of Kerala and the dance-dramas are all ensemble forms. Folk and tribal dance is overwhelmingly communal, performed in circles and lines (Chapter 21).

The use of space also differs between forms. Bharatanāṭyam and Kuchipudi move along lines, diagonals and squares on a defined floor, often returning to centre-stage for cadences; Odissi traces curved paths; Kathak uses straight lines towards and away from the audience and turns on the spot; Kathakaḷi and Kūṭiyāṭṭam act on a small square stage before a lamp.
