The twentieth-century proscenium stage, with its frontal audience, lighting and curtains, changed the spatial practice of all these forms: it encouraged the frontal presentation of the solo dancer, and it made possible the large group choreographies of the dance-dramas created from the 1930s by Rukmini Devi at Kalakshetra, by Uday Shankar and by others, which drew on the vocabulary of the classical forms to tell stories with many dancers (Meduri 2005; Purkayastha 2014).

docs.title: 13.5 Dance and the Martial Arts
docs.text:
Several of India’s dance and theatre forms are closely related to its martial traditions, and the relation illuminates how the dancing body has been trained. The Nāṭyaśāstra already describes the standing positions of archery and the movements of combat among its cārīs and maṇḍalas, and stage fights were an important part of the theatre it describes (Chapter 2). In Kerala, the martial art kaḷarippayaṯṯu, practised in training halls (kaḷari) by the Nāyar warriors and other communities, supplied Kathakaḷi with much of its training regime: its kicks, jumps, stretches and body-preparation exercises, its massage, and its emphasis on the control of breath and the concentration of energy in the lower abdomen. Phillip Zarrilli’s studies show how the same body techniques serve both arts and how practitioners understand the inner energy they cultivate (Zarrilli 1998, 2000).

Other regions show similar links. The movement vocabulary of Chhau, especially in Mayurbhanj and Seraikela, draws on the martial exercises of the paika soldiers of Odisha and the surrounding region, and the dance was associated with martial displays at the courts that patronised it (Chapter 21). In Manipur, the sword and spear art thang-ta has influenced the vigorous male dances and the stage choreography of Manipuri dance, and the theatre of Ratan Thiyam has drawn on it extensively (Chapters 18 and 19). Many folk dances are or include stick and sword dances, which preserve the movements of combat in stylised form. In the twentieth century choreographers such as Chandralekha turned to kaḷarippayaṯṯu and yoga as sources of a strong, grounded movement that could be set against the decorative image of the classical dancer (Bharucha 1995).

The relation between dance and yoga is often asserted, but it should be stated carefully. The postural yoga taught today is largely a modern development, and the claim that the classical dance forms derive from yoga, or that particular dance movements correspond to particular āsanas, has no basis in the texts. What is true is that both dance and yoga, like the martial arts, belong to a culture in which the trained body was understood as a vehicle of concentration and transformation, and that many modern dancers practise yoga as part of their training (Volume 5, Yoga Taraṅgiṇī).

docs.title: 13.6 The Music of Dance
docs.text: Each form has its own musical ensemble, and its music is as much a part of its identity as its movement. Bharatanāṭyam is accompanied by the naṭṭuvaṉār with cymbals, a singer, the mṛdaṅgam, and usually violin, flute or vīṇā; its music is Karnatak, though the dance repertoire includes compositions (varṇams, padams, jāvaḷis, tillānas) that are rarely heard in concerts. Kuchipudi uses a similar ensemble, with songs mostly in Telugu. Odissi is accompanied by the mardala (a barrel drum), a singer, flute, violin or sitār and cymbals, playing a regional repertoire of rāgas and songs that its musicians have presented as a distinct “Odissi music”. Kathak uses Hindustani music, with tablā or pakhāvaj, sāraṅgī or harmonium, and a singer. Kathakaḷi has two singers, who sing the text of the play with cymbals and a gong, and drummers on the ceṇṭa, maddaḷam and iḍakka. Manipuri is accompanied by the pung drum, cymbals, flute and singers in the Vaiṣṇava devotional tradition. In every case the dancer must know the music thoroughly, and the best dancers are often also accomplished singers or drummers.

docs.title: 13.7.1 Dance-drama traditions
docs.text: In the nāṭya mode a group of performers enacts a story, each taking a character. Many of India’s performance traditions are dance-dramas of this kind: Kūṭiyāṭṭam, which preserves Sanskrit drama in a Kerala performance style; Kathakaḷi and its precursors Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam and Rāmanāṭṭam; the Kuchipudi yakṣagānas or dance-dramas such as Bhāmākalāpam; the Bhāgavata Mēḷa of the Tamil country; the Yakṣagāna of Karnataka; the Ankīyā Nāṭ of Assam; the Rāsalīlā of Manipur and of Braj; and the Rāmlīlā of north India (Chapters 17, 18 and 20). In these forms the performers are at once dancers, actors and, in some forms, singers; the drama is carried by song and narration as much as by dialogue; and the performance may last a whole night or, in Kūṭiyāṭṭam, many nights.

docs.title: 13.7.2 Conventions of dance-drama
docs.text: Dance-drama has its own conventions. Characters announce themselves at their entrance with a song (pravēśa daru in Kuchipudi) or a dance (the puṟappāṭu of Kathakaḷi); a stage manager or narrator (sūtradhāra, bhāgavata) introduces the story and links its episodes; characters are classified by type and costumed accordingly; and the stage is defined by convention rather than scenery, so that a walk around the stage can represent a journey and a curtain held by two attendants can mark an entrance. The relation between the conventional (nāṭyadharmī) and the naturalistic (lokadharmī) differs between forms. Kathakaḷi is at the conventional extreme, with silent actors who render every word of the sung text in gesture; Yakṣagāna allows its actors improvised spoken dialogue; Kuchipudi dance-dramas combine song, dance and speech.

docs.title: 13.8 The Recital
docs.text:
The modern solo recital, which presents pure and expressive dance in a fixed sequence of items, is itself a product of history. The order of the Bharatanāṭyam recital is traditionally credited to the Thanjavur Quartet in the early nineteenth century, though its present form was fixed in the concerts of the 1930s and after (Chapter 15); the Odissi recital was designed by the gurus who reconstructed the form in the 1950s; and the Kathak recital took its present shape in twentieth-century concerts. They share a common logic: the recital opens with an invocation and a display of pure dance, reaches its centre in an item combining pure and expressive dance, develops expression in a series of songs, and ends with a brilliant passage of pure dance and a benediction (Table 13.2).

Table 13.2. The order of items in three modern solo recitals (simplified) Stage Bharatanāṭyam Odissi Kathak Invocation puṣpāñjali or kauttuvam maṅgalācaraṇa vandanā Pure dance alārippu, jatisvaram baṭu (sthāyī) thāṭ, āmad, toḍās and ṭukṛās Pure and expressive śabdam, varṇam pallavī gat nikās, gat bhāv Expressive padam, jāvaḷi, śloka abhinaya (e.g. an aṣṭapadī) ṭhumrī, bhajan Climax and close tillāna, maṅgaḷam mokṣa tatkār and fast compositions

The recital format suited the concert hall, the proscenium stage and the urban audiences of the twentieth century. It also allowed dances that had been performed in very different contexts — temple rituals, court entertainments, processions, private salons — to be presented as unified “classical” arts with an internal logic, a feature that their founders often explained in spiritual terms, as a journey from the body to the soul. Such explanations express the meaning the forms have for many dancers today, but they are modern; the earlier contexts were far more varied and often far from spiritual (O’Shea 2007; Chakravorty 2008).

docs.title: 13.9 Tāṇḍava, Lāsya and Gender
docs.text:
Writers on Indian dance often describe its forms and movements in terms of the pairing of tāṇḍava, the vigorous dance of Śiva, with lāsya, the graceful dance of Pārvatī, and associate the first with men and the second with women. The pairing has textual roots (Chapter 2), and it captures a real contrast between vigorous and delicate qualities of movement. But as a description of the history of dance it is misleading. For most of recorded history, the professional dancers of the courts and temples were women, and their dances included vigorous pure dance as well as expressive items; the men of the same communities were teachers, musicians and conductors, while the all-male dance-drama traditions (Kathakaḷi, Kuchipudi, Yakṣagāna, Bhāgavata Mēḷa) cast men in women’s roles. In the twentieth century the meanings shifted again: the reformed classical forms were largely taken over by middle-class women performers, while male dancers had to justify their presence in what was now seen as a feminine art. The “natural” association of women with grace and men with vigour is thus a modern ideology as much as an ancient doctrine (O’Shea 2007; Chakravorty 2008).

The most radical modern critique of these categories came from the choreographer Chandralekha (1928–2006), who trained in Bharatanāṭyam and then, from the 1980s, created works that stripped the form of its devotional narratives and its decorative femininity to reveal the strength of its geometry, drawing also on yoga and Kerala’s martial art. Rustom Bharucha’s study of her work describes it as a sustained argument about the female body, sexuality and the nation (Bharucha 1995). Contemporary choreographers continue to work with and against the threefold classification (Chapter 23).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Vatsyayan (1968) and Vatsyayan (1974) give the classic account of nṛtta, nṛtya and nāṭya in the dance forms, and Bose (1991) traces the categories in the treatises. O’Shea (2007) and Chakravorty (2008) examine the modern recital and its ideologies in Bharatanāṭyam and Kathak; Knight (2010) describes expressive dance in Balasaraswati’s art; and Bharucha (1995) discusses Chandralekha’s critique.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Hastas: The Language of Gesture
docs.text: Of all the elements of Indian dance and theatre, the codified hand gestures (hasta, also called mudrā) are the most immediately distinctive. With a vocabulary of a few dozen basic hand shapes, each with many conventional meanings, combined with movements of the arms, eyes, face and body, a performer can represent persons, gods, animals, objects and actions, narrate a story and express feelings. The hand gestures are described in the Nāṭyaśāstra, in the Abhinayadarpaṇa and in regional manuals such as the Kerala Hastalakṣaṇadīpikā; they are used, in different forms and to different degrees, in Kūṭiyāṭṭam and Kathakaḷi, in Bharatanāṭyam, Kuchipudi, Odissi and Mohiniyāṭṭam, and more sparingly in Kathak and Manipuri. How a few dozen hand shapes can carry so many meanings is the central question here. The answer lies partly in the systems of the three main texts, partly in the conventions by which one gesture serves many purposes, and partly in the teaching through which a dancer learns them; the dance hasta must also be distinguished from the ritual and iconographic mudrā, with which it is often confused.

docs.title: 14.1 Hasta and Mudrā
docs.text: The Sanskrit dance texts use the word hasta, “hand”, for a gesture of the hand; the word mudrā, “seal” or “sign”, is used in the Kerala tradition and has become common in modern speech for all such gestures. In Hindu and Buddhist ritual and iconography, however, mudrā has a more specific meaning: the gestures made by priests and practitioners in worship and meditation, and the gestures of images of gods and Buddhas — the raised open palm of reassurance (abhaya), the lowered open palm of giving (varada), the joined thumb and forefinger of teaching (vitarka, jñāna), the Buddha’s touching of the earth (bhūmisparśa). Dance gestures and iconographic gestures overlap — a dancer may show the abhaya gesture to represent a god, and sculptors used dance poses — but they are different systems with different purposes: one is a means of representation in performance, the other a ritual and symbolic sign. Statements that dance gestures “are” yogic or tantric mudrās, or that they act on the body’s energies, confuse the two.

docs.title: 14.2 The Hands in the Nāṭyaśāstra
docs.text:
Chapter 9 of the Nāṭyaśāstra (in Ghosh’s numbering) describes three groups of hands (Ghosh 1950):

  • twenty-four single hands (asaṃyuta), each formed by one hand: patāka, tripatāka, kartarīmukha, ardhacandra, arāla, śukatuṇḍa, muṣṭi, śikhara, kapittha, kaṭakāmukha, sūcyāsya, padmakośa, sarpaśiras, mṛgaśīrṣa, kāṅgūla, alapadma, catura, bhramara, haṃsāsya, haṃsapakṣa, sandaṃśa, mukula, ūrṇanābha and tāmracūḍa;

  • thirteen combined hands (saṃyuta), formed by both hands together: añjali, kapota, karkaṭa, svastika, kaṭakāvardhamānaka, utsaṅga, niṣadha, dola, puṣpapuṭa, makara, gajadanta, avahittha and vardhamāna;

  • a further group of “dance hands” (nṛtta-hasta), positions and movements of the hands and arms used for their beauty in pure dance rather than to convey meaning, such as caturasra, udvṛtta, talamukha, svastika, latā and karihasta. Their number is given as twenty-seven in some editions and as twenty-nine or thirty in others.

The text also describes the ways in which the hands move (upwards, downwards, sideways, towards and away from the body) and the qualities with which gestures should be performed, and it insists that hand gestures must be accompanied by appropriate movements of the eyes, brows and face. It gives each gesture a list of uses: patāka, for example, can show striking, driving away, joy, pride, heat, rain or a shower of flowers, according to how it is moved and with what expression.

docs.title: 14.3 The Hands in the Abhinayadarpaṇa
docs.text:
The Abhinayadarpaṇa’s list, which is the basis of modern teaching in Bharatanāṭyam and several other forms, differs from the Nāṭyaśāstra’s in both number and names (Tables 14.1 and 14.2) (Ghosh 1957; Coomaraswamy and Duggirala 1917).

How many hands?

The counts differ between texts and teaching traditions, and this is a frequent source of confusion.

  • Nāṭyaśāstra: 24 single, 13 combined, and a group of 27–30 dance hands.

  • Abhinayadarpaṇa (Ghosh’s text): 28 single and 23 combined; some recensions and teachers add a twenty-fourth combined hand (avahittha), and many teachers add four further single hands, bringing the number to 32.

  • Hastalakṣaṇadīpikā (Kerala): 24 basic hands, combined to form several hundred signs.

All the figures in this chapter refer to these sources.

docs.title: 14.3.1 The single hands
docs.text:
Each single hand is defined by the position of the fingers and thumb and is followed in the text by a verse listing its applications (viniyoga). Table 14.1 gives the twenty-eight single hands of the Abhinayadarpaṇa with a selection of their applications, and Figure 14.1 shows twelve of them, with four of the combined hands.

docs.text:
The twenty-three combined hands of Ghosh’s text (Table 14.2) include gestures of greeting and respect (añjali, kapota), gestures that show objects or creatures by imitation (the fish, tortoise, boar and Garuḍa used in depicting Viṣṇu’s incarnations), gestures for divine attributes (the conch and discus of Viṣṇu, the liṅga of Śiva) and gestures for actions (swinging the arms, offering flowers, embracing).

docs.title: 14.3.3 One hand, many meanings
docs.text:
The principle that makes this small vocabulary expressive is viniyoga, “application”: each hand is used for many things, and the meaning is made clear by the context — the words of the song, the movement and position of the hand, the other hand, the eyes and face, the posture. The patāka, the flat hand, can show the beginning of a dance when raised before the face, a cloud when moved above the head, a river when moved sinuously at waist height, waves when the fingers ripple, a horse when moved in galloping rhythm, and silence or an oath when held before the lips or raised. A single hand can thus serve as noun, verb or attribute.

The meanings fall into a few types. Some gestures imitate the shape of an object (the sarpaśīrṣa for a snake’s hood, the mṛgaśīrṣa for a deer’s head, the combined matsya for a fish). Some show an action by miming it (kaṭakāmukha for drawing a bow or picking a flower). Some are conventional signs whose meaning must simply be learnt (śikhara for a husband, kapittha for Lakṣmī). Expert dancers combine these resources, using a gesture to show an object and then, with a change of expression, the feeling it arouses; and they sometimes devise new uses where the lists say nothing, within the logic of the system.

docs.title: 14.4 Special Sets of Hands
docs.text:
The Abhinayadarpaṇa and the teaching tradition that follows it add a number of special sets, formed by combining single hands in fixed ways (Ghosh 1957):

  • Hands for the gods (devahasta): fixed pairs of gestures for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sarasvatī, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya, Kāma, Indra, Agni, Yama and others, usually showing the god’s characteristic attribute (the discus and conch of Viṣṇu, the deer and axe of Śiva, the elephant head of Gaṇeśa).

  • The ten incarnations of Viṣṇu (daśāvatāra): sequences that show the fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, dwarf, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa and Kalki.

  • The nine planets (navagraha): gestures for the sun, moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu and Ketu.

  • Relations (bāndhava): gestures for husband and wife, mother and father, son, brother and others.

  • Social classes (jāti): gestures for the brahmin, the kṣatriya, the vaiśya and the śūdra.

  • Famous rivers, trees and creatures: gestures for the Ganges and other rivers, for particular trees and for animals and birds.

The precise forms of these gestures vary in different manuscripts and teaching lineages, and the lists in modern handbooks are often expanded. They show how closely the dance vocabulary was tied to the religious culture of its audiences, and — in the gestures for the four varṇas — how naturally the social hierarchy entered the representational code.

docs.title: 14.5 The Kerala Tradition: Hastalakṣaṇadīpikā
docs.text:
In Kerala, the gesture language of Kūṭiyāṭṭam and Kathakaḷi is based not on the Abhinayadarpaṇa but on the Hastalakṣaṇadīpikā, an anonymous manual of uncertain date. It describes twenty-four basic hands (mudrā): patāka, mudrākhya, kaṭaka, muṣṭi, kartarīmukha, śukatuṇḍa, kapittha, haṃsapakṣa, śikhara, haṃsāsya, añjali, ardhacandra, mukura, bhramara, sūcīmukha, pallava, tripatāka, mṛgaśīrṣa, sarpaśiras, vardhamānaka, arāla, ūrṇanābha, mukula and kaṭakāmukha. Many names are shared with the Sanskrit texts, but the shapes and uses often differ. Each basic hand can be made with one hand or with both, held in different positions and moved in different ways, and the combinations yield a vocabulary of several hundred signs (Zarrilli 2000; Richmond et al. 1990).

In Kathakaḷi and Kūṭiyāṭṭam the actor “speaks” with the hands: the text of the play, sung by the singers in Kathakaḷi or spoken by the actor in Kūṭiyāṭṭam, is rendered word by word in gesture, including grammatical words, with the eyes following and the face expressing the emotion. The gestures are larger and more forceful than those of Bharatanāṭyam, suited to the scale of the characters and the lamplit stage, and they are performed with a precise relationship to the rhythm of the drums. Kathakaḷi students spend years mastering them (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 14.6 Other Regional Traditions
docs.text: Each of the dance forms has its own gestural practice. Odissi draws on the Abhinayacandrikā and on the gestures of Odishan temple sculpture; its hands are held softly and in curved lines that match the tribhaṅga posture of the body (Chapter 17). Kuchipudi and Mohiniyāṭṭam follow the Abhinayadarpaṇa and the Kerala manuals respectively, with their own conventions. Kathak, shaped in the courts of north India where the expressive repertoire centred on the improvised interpretation of songs, uses a much smaller and less codified set of gestures, often closer to naturalistic mime, alongside the formal hand positions of its pure dance; Manipuri uses soft, rounded hand movements that rarely form the sharp shapes of the southern forms. Even within Bharatanāṭyam, teachers of different lineages (Pandanallur, Vazhuvoor, Thanjavur, Kalakshetra) differ in the shapes and uses of particular hands, and the “standard” forms taught in institutions represent the choices of twentieth-century teachers.

docs.title: 14.7 Hands in Pure Dance
docs.text: In passages of pure dance (nṛtta) the hands do not represent anything; they complete the lines of the body and articulate the rhythm. Bharatanāṭyam dancers use a small set of hands for this purpose, especially patāka, tripatāka, ardhacandra, kaṭakāmukha, alapadma, haṃsāsya and mṛgaśīrṣa, placed at the hips or chest or extended in straight lines from the shoulder; Odissi and Kuchipudi have their own conventions. The nṛtta-hastas of the Nāṭyaśāstra were movements of the arms and hands for the same purpose. The distinction between “meaningful” and “decorative” hands is not absolute — a pure-dance passage may include a gesture with a meaning, and an expressive passage depends on the beauty of line — but it reflects the basic division of Indian dance into pure and expressive modes (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 14.8 Movement, Placement and Sequence
docs.text:
A hand shape is only the beginning of a gesture. The Nāṭyaśāstra describes four basic movements of the wrist and fingers that accompany gestures — winding inwards (āveṣṭita), unwinding outwards (udveṣṭita), turning back (vyāvartita) and turning round (parivartita) — and the directions in which the hands can move. Dancers learn that the same shape means different things at different heights and distances from the body: a hand held high may indicate the sky, a god or something lofty; at the chest, the self or the heart; at the side, something beside or behind. The quality of movement matters too: a slow, sinuous patāka is a river, a quick, rippling one waves, and a sharp, cutting one a sword.

In performance, gestures form sequences that narrate an action. To show Kṛṣṇa lifting Mount Govardhana to shelter the cowherds from Indra’s storm, a dancer might show Kṛṣṇa with the flute, the gathering clouds and falling rain, the frightened people and cattle, the god raising the mountain on one finger and holding it aloft, and the people taking shelter beneath — each image a gesture or brief combination, linked by changes of posture, gaze and expression. Experienced dancers vary such sequences from performance to performance, and two dancers of the same school may interpret the same line in quite different ways.

docs.title: 14.9 Gesture in Sculpture
docs.text: Indian sculptors drew on the same vocabulary. The bronze images of Śiva Naṭarāja made in the Cōḻa period show one right hand raised in the gesture of reassurance (abhaya) and one left arm thrown across the body in the position the Nāṭyaśāstra calls karihasta or gajahasta, the “elephant’s trunk” arm, pointing to the raised foot; the other hands hold the drum of creation and the fire of destruction. Images of gods frequently show the kaṭakāmukha hand holding a flower, the kapittha or śikhara hands holding weapons, and the patāka hands of blessing. The overlap between the dancer’s and the sculptor’s vocabulary has encouraged the reconstruction of dance from sculpture (Chapters 2 and 12), but it should not be overstated: sculptors chose gestures for clarity of symbolic meaning in a single, static image, dancers for clarity in movement and in a sequence (Vatsyayan 1968; Smith 1996).

docs.title: 14.10 Learning the Hands
docs.text:
In the classical forms, students learn the hands early, usually by reciting the verses of the Abhinayadarpaṇa (or the Kerala manual) while forming each hand, and then by learning their applications in verses and simple songs. Expressive use develops later, through the learning of compositions in which each word of the text has its gesture, and through the guidance of a teacher who shows several ways of interpreting the same line. In Kathakaḷi the training is longer and more intensive: students practise the hands daily with the eye exercises, and learn the vocabulary as part of learning the plays.

The goal of this training is not the mechanical display of gestures. Teachers insist that a gesture should be “filled” with the feeling it conveys, that the eyes should follow the hand and the face express its meaning, and that the transitions between gestures matter as much as the gestures themselves — the principle expressed in the Abhinayadarpaṇa’s verse “where the hand goes, there the eyes go” (Chapter 12). Great performers of abhinaya have often used relatively few codified gestures, relying on the eyes and face and on subtle movements of the body.

docs.title: 14.11 Gesture Beyond the Stage
docs.text:
In the twentieth century the hand gestures of Indian dance became a symbol of Indian culture itself. Coomaraswamy’s The Mirror of Gesture presented them as a classical language comparable with the arts of Europe; they appeared on stamps, in posters and in public art; and, in a striking recent example, a wall of large sculpted hands forms the backdrop of the arrival hall at Delhi’s international airport (Figure 14.2). Their use as national emblems has made them familiar far beyond the audiences of dance.

Figure 14.2. Large sculptures of hand gestures (hasta, mudrā) on a wall of copper discs at Terminal 3, Indira Gandhi International Airport, New Delhi. Photo: Dev Jadiya, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Hand gestures have also been drawn into the modern wellness industry, which teaches “mudrās” claimed to affect health, energy and mood. These practices draw on the ritual and yogic mudrās described above rather than on the dance tradition, and their health claims have not been demonstrated.

Health and Safety Note

There is no reliable evidence that holding particular hand gestures treats illness, whether the explanation offered is “energy”, mirror neurons or acupressure points. The general point about therapeutic claims for the arts is made in Section 4.13; “mudrā therapy” is not a substitute for medical care.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The hand gestures of the Abhinayadarpaṇa are described and translated in Coomaraswamy and Duggirala (1917) and Ghosh (1957), and those of the Nāṭyaśāstra in Ghosh (1950). Vatsyayan (1968) and Bose (1991) discuss gesture in the dance texts and in sculpture. For the Kerala tradition see Zarrilli (2000) and Jones and Jones (1970).

docs.title: Chapter 15: Bharatanāṭyam
docs.text: Bharatanāṭyam, the dance associated with Tamil Nadu, is today the most widely practised Indian dance form in the world, taught in thousands of schools in India and the diaspora and performed on stages from Chennai to Toronto. It is also the form whose history has been most contested. Its practitioners have often described it as an ancient temple art, continuous with the dance of the Nāṭyaśāstra and the sculptures of Cōḻa temples. Historians have shown that its immediate ancestor was the court and temple dance called sadir or dāsiyāṭṭam, performed by hereditary women dancers — the women later called devadāsīs — and their male teachers, and that the form known as Bharatanāṭyam was created in the 1930s and 1940s when this dance was reconstructed for the concert stage, largely by and for middle-class performers, in the same years in which the hereditary performers were legally and socially dispossessed. Both histories matter, and so does the art itself, whose technique, repertoire, music and institutions are described after the history. The account draws especially on the work of Amrit Srinivasan, Saskia Kersenboom, Avanthi Meduri, Matthew Allen, Janet O’Shea, Davesh Soneji, Douglas Knight and Leslie Orr.

docs.title: 15.1.1 The medieval evidence
docs.text: Tamil inscriptions from the ninth century onwards record women attached to temples, called by terms such as tēvaraṭiyāḷ (“servant of the god”) and taḷiccēri peṇṭukaḷ (“women of the temple quarter”). The most famous record is the inscription of the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I at the great temple of Thanjavur (completed c. 1010), which lists some four hundred women transferred to the temple from other temples, each given a house and a share of the temple’s revenue. Some of these women danced and sang in the temple’s rituals and festivals; dance was one of the services (with singing, the waving of lamps and the carrying of offerings) that temples maintained. Leslie Orr’s study of the inscriptions has shown, however, that the medieval “temple women” were a varied group — donors, devotees and servants as well as performers — and that most inscriptions say nothing about dance or about sexual relationships; the composite figure of the “devadāsī” as a dedicated temple dancer and courtesan is a later and partly colonial construction projected back onto this earlier history (Orr 2000).

docs.title: 15.1.2 The early modern world
docs.text:
The direct ancestors of Bharatanāṭyam belong to the Nāyaka and Maratha courts of Thanjavur, Madurai and Pudukkottai (sixteenth to nineteenth centuries) and to the temples they patronised. In this world, professional women performers served both temples and courts. They were dedicated, often as girls, in a ceremony in which a tāli (marriage emblem) was tied in the name of the deity; as “wives of the god” they could not be widowed, were regarded as auspicious (nityasumaṅgalī, “ever-auspicious women”), performed ritual duties in the temple and danced in its festivals and processions (Kersenboom-Story 1987). They also performed at courts, at the weddings and festivals of wealthy patrons, and in private salons. Their households were matrilineal: daughters inherited property and the profession, and many women formed long-term relationships with patrons outside marriage. The men of the same communities were musicians — nāgasvaram players, drummers — and the dance masters (naṭṭuvaṉārs) who taught the women and conducted their performances. The ensemble of dancer, naṭṭuvaṉār and musicians was called the “small ensemble” (ciṉṉa mēḷam), in contrast to the “big ensemble” (periya mēḷam) of nāgasvaram and tavil (Srinivasan 1985; Soneji 2012).

These women were neither the chaste temple nuns of some modern accounts nor simply the prostitutes of colonial ones. They were highly trained professional artists, among the few literate women of their time, with considerable economic independence, who also lived outside the norms of conjugal respectability; their status and their art depended on patronage relationships that were at once economic, artistic and sexual. Many women of these communities were not dancers at all, and the communities themselves were internally stratified. None of these facts can be dropped to make the story simpler (Soneji 2012; Srinivasan 1985).

docs.title: 15.1.3 The Thanjavur court and the Quartet
docs.text:
At the court of the Maratha king Serfoji II (r. 1798–1832) the four brothers known as the Thanjavur Quartet — Ciṉṉayya, Poṉṉayya, Civāṉantam and Vaṭivēlu, from a hereditary family of naṭṭuvaṉārs and disciples of the composer Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar — composed much of the repertoire of the dance: varṇams, padams, jatisvarams, śabdams and tillānas, many in Telugu and addressed to the gods or to the king. Tradition credits them with arranging the items of a dance recital in the sequence still followed today. Vaṭivēlu later served at the court of Travancore, where he is associated with the development of Mohiniyāṭṭam and of violin playing in Karnatak music; Ciṉṉayya went to Mysore. The descendants and disciples of the Quartet, among them the Pandanallur family of Meenakshisundaram Pillai (1869–1964), were the principal teachers of the dance into the twentieth century (Peterson and Soneji 2008).

The repertoire of the court and temple dancers included more than the solo items of the modern recital. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries they also performed dance-dramas called kuṟavañci, in which a fortune-teller woman of the hill tribes (kuṟatti) foretells the union of a heroine with a god or king; one of the best known, the Tirukkuṟṟālak Kuṟavañci by Tirikūṭa Rācappa Kavirāyar, was composed in the early eighteenth century, and others were composed for the Thanjavur temple. The women also sang and danced in the Telugu and Marathi court theatre of Thanjavur (Peterson and Soneji 2008).

docs.title: 15.2.1 The anti-nautch movement
docs.text:
From the 1890s Christian missionaries, Indian social reformers and colonial officials campaigned against the “nautch” (from Hindustani nāc, dance), the performance of professional women dancers at weddings, festivals and official receptions, which they condemned as immoral. The campaign became a campaign against the dedication of girls to temples. Its leading figure in the Madras Presidency was Muthulakshmi Reddy (1886–1968), the first woman member of the Madras Legislative Council and herself the daughter of a woman from the hereditary community, who regarded dedication as a form of sexual exploitation of girls. The reformers were supported by the non-Brahmin Self-Respect movement and by many members of the hereditary communities themselves, some of whom formed caste associations, adopted the name Iśai Vēḷāḷar and sought social respectability by renouncing the profession. Other women of the community, notably the singer Bangalore Nagarathnamma, opposed legislation that would deprive them of their livelihood and their art. After decades of campaigning, the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act of 1947 made dedication illegal and declared invalid the customary rights attached to it (Srinivasan 1985; Soneji 2012).

The law ended a system that had made many women and girls vulnerable to exploitation. It also, as Amrit Srinivasan’s classic article argued, destroyed the economic and social basis of a community of women artists without providing them with any alternative, and left them stigmatised: their dance was now respectable only if others performed it (Srinivasan 1985).

docs.title: 15.2.2 The making of Bharatanāṭyam
docs.text:
While the reformers attacked the dancers, a group of nationalist cultural activists in Madras set out to “save” the dance. The lawyer and freedom fighter E. Krishna Iyer (1897–1968), who had learnt sadir and performed it in women’s costume, campaigned for its recognition as an art, and in the early 1930s the Madras Music Academy began to present dancers from the hereditary families at its annual conferences. In these years the name “Bharatanāṭyam” was adopted for the dance, connecting it with Bharata’s Nāṭyaśāstra and with a pan-Indian classical heritage (on the folk etymology bhāva–rāga–tāla, see Chapter 2) (Meduri 1988; Allen 1997).

The decisive figure was Rukmini Devi Arundale (1904–1986), a Brahmin woman from a Theosophist family, married to the British Theosophist George Arundale. Inspired partly by the ballet of Anna Pavlova, she learnt dance from Mylapore Gauri Ammal and Pandanallur Meenakshisundaram Pillai, gave her first public performance in 1935, and in 1936 founded at Adyar the International Academy of the Arts, later called Kalakshetra. There she created a new institutional form for the dance: a residential school with a fixed curriculum, teaching Brahmin and other middle-class girls and boys; a new costume and stage design based on temple sculpture; a repertoire from which she removed or reinterpreted items she considered erotic, emphasising devotion (bhakti) and spiritual purity; and a series of large-scale dance-dramas on Sanskrit and Tamil themes, beginning in the 1940s (Meduri 2005; Allen 1997).

Scholarly Note: The reconstruction debate

Rukmini Devi’s work has been read in sharply different ways. For her admirers, and for the official history of Indian culture, she rescued a dying art from disrepute and made it a national treasure; Avanthi Meduri’s edited volume presents her as a visionary institution-builder (Meduri 2005). For Amrit Srinivasan, Matthew Allen and Davesh Soneji, the “revival” was also an appropriation: the art of a low-status community of women was taken over by upper-caste performers, renamed, “purified” of its sexuality and given a new history that erased the people who had created it (Srinivasan 1985; Allen 1997; Soneji 2012). Janet O’Shea shows how later dancers have negotiated between these histories in a global art (O’Shea 2007). The debate is not settled. Rukmini Devi did build the institutions through which the dance survived and spread; the cost of that survival was borne by the community from which it was taken.

docs.title: 15.2.3 Balasaraswati
docs.text: The great counter-example to the narrative of rescue was T. Balasaraswati (1918–1984). Born into the family of the vīṇā player Vīṇā Dhanammal, one of the most distinguished musical families of the hereditary community, she learnt dance from the naṭṭuvaṉār K. Kandappa Pillai and music from her family, and began performing as a child. She was celebrated above all for her abhinaya, the depth and spontaneity of her interpretation of padams and jāvaḷis, and for her integration of music and movement. She insisted that the erotic repertoire was itself devotional, that the dance needed no purification, and that the hereditary tradition was its true repository; she resisted the stylistic changes of Kalakshetra. Her career, which included teaching in the United States from the 1960s, is described in Douglas Knight’s biography (Knight 2010). That she was for a long time the most famous representative of her community on the concert stage shows both the strength of her art and how few others from that community were able to continue.

docs.title: 15.2.4 The afterlife of the hereditary tradition
docs.text: The hereditary performers did not simply disappear. Some continued to teach as naṭṭuvaṉārs to the new middle-class dancers; some women continued to perform in private or in rural contexts, in Tamil Nadu and in coastal Andhra, where the kalāvantula tradition persisted into the late twentieth century, and where the dancer Swapnasundari has, since the late twentieth century, presented the repertoire she learnt from kalāvantula women under the name Vilāsini Nāṭyam, a revival that raises, as the earlier ones did, the question of who may claim and present the art of the hereditary dancers; and many of their descendants left the arts and sought other livelihoods. Davesh Soneji’s ethnography of these communities records their memories of performance and the shame and loss that accompanied the transformation of their art into “Bharatanāṭyam” (Soneji 2012). Recent scholarship and some contemporary dancers have sought to acknowledge this history openly, and to perform the old repertoire with credit to those who preserved it.

docs.title: 15.3.1 Posture and line
docs.text:
Bharatanāṭyam’s movement is built on the half-seated araimaṇḍi, with the knees turned out and the heels together (Figure 15.1), from which the dancer steps, stamps, jumps and turns while keeping the torso upright. Its aesthetic emphasises clear lines — of the arms extended from the shoulders, of the legs in the araimaṇḍi and in extended positions, of the body in sculptural poses held at the end of phrases — and the precise articulation of rhythm by the feet, whose ankle bells (salaṅkai) make every stamp audible. The full squat (muḻumaṇḍi) and kneeling positions are used in some aḍavus and poses.

Figure 15.1. Bharatanāṭyam dancers, disciples of Saroja Vaidyanathan, at a youth festival in 2012; the dancer at the centre stands with knees bent and turned outwards in araimaṇḍi. Photo: Sumita Roy Dutta, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 15.3.2 Aḍavus
docs.text: The pure-dance vocabulary is taught through the aḍavus (Chapter 13), grouped in families according to their characteristic action or syllables: taṭṭaḍavu (striking the feet), nāṭṭaḍavu (stretching a leg and striking the heel), viśāru aḍavu (sweeping movements), tattimeṭṭaḍavu (alternating flat foot and heel), kuditta meṭṭaḍavu (jumping), sarikkal (sliding), maṇḍi aḍavu (kneeling and squatting) and tīrmāṉa aḍavu (cadential). Each is practised in three speeds. The number and naming of the aḍavus vary between schools; the systematic sequences taught today were organised largely in the twentieth century.

docs.title: 15.3.3 Abhinaya
docs.text: The expressive technique of Bharatanāṭyam combines the hand gestures of the Abhinayadarpaṇa (Chapter 14), the movements of eyes, brows, head and neck, and the conventions of character and situation described in Chapter 3. The dancer usually plays a woman — the heroine, her confidante, or a devotee — and moves between the roles of narrator and characters. In the expressive items the dancer elaborates each line of the text through repeated interpretations (sañcāri), and the finest performers improvise their elaborations in response to the music. The expressive repertoire of padams and jāvaḷis is the art’s richest inheritance from the hereditary performers, and the art in which Balasaraswati excelled.

docs.title: 15.3.4 Styles (bāṇi)
docs.text: Bharatanāṭyam is transmitted in stylistic lineages called bāṇi, named after the villages or institutions of their teachers. The Pandanallur bāṇi, associated with Meenakshisundaram Pillai and his successors, is known for its geometric clarity and restraint; the Vazhuvoor bāṇi of Ramaiah Pillai (1910–1991) for its flowing movement and dramatic flair; the Thanjavur bāṇi for its continuity with the Quartet’s family; and the Kalakshetra style, developed from the Pandanallur tradition by Rukmini Devi and her teachers, for its precision, its angular line and its large-scale choreography. Bharatanāṭyam also had a distinct history in the Mysore court, where dancers performed until the mid-twentieth century. Contemporary dancers often combine elements from several lineages.

docs.title: 15.4 The Recital
docs.text:
The solo recital (mārgam) follows a sequence traditionally attributed to the Thanjavur Quartet and adapted in the twentieth century (O’Shea 2007; Kothari 1979):

Puṣpāñjali or kauttuvam. An invocation. The kauttuvam, a short composition in praise of a deity, belongs to the temple repertoire of the hereditary dancers; the puṣpāñjali, an offering of flowers, is a modern addition widely used today. Alārippu. A short piece of pure dance, danced to drum syllables in a simple tāla, which progressively brings the eyes, neck, shoulders, arms and legs into movement; its name is often explained as “flowering”. Jatisvaram. Pure dance to a composition of solfa syllables (svara) in a rāga, alternating with rhythmic passages (jati). Śabdam. The first expressive item: a song, often in Telugu, praising a god or a patron, with short descriptive passages and pure-dance links. Varṇam. The centrepiece, lasting half an hour or more. Its first half has a pallavi and anupallavi interpreted expressively, each followed by passages of pure dance (jatis) danced to rhythmic syllables, and a muktāyi svaram; its second half (caraṇam) alternates a refrain with passages of solfa (eṭṭugaḍa svarams), each danced and then interpreted expressively. The varṇam demands stamina, rhythmic precision and expressive depth, and tests the dancer more than any other item. Padam and jāvaḷi. Slow expressive songs of love; the padams of Kṣetrayya and the Tamil padams of Subbarāma Iyer and others are among the masterpieces of the repertoire. Tillāna. A brilliant pure-dance item to a lively composition of rhythmic syllables, ending with a short passage of text. Maṅgaḷam or a closing verse.

The music of the recital is Karnatak, but the dance repertoire — especially the pada varṇams, padams and jāvaḷis — forms a body of music partly distinct from the concert repertoire, and many compositions survive only because dancers and their musicians preserved them.

docs.title: 15.5.1 The ensemble
docs.text: The dancer is accompanied by a naṭṭuvaṉār, who recites the rhythmic syllables and keeps time with cymbals; a vocalist; a mṛdaṅgam player; and one or more melodic instrumentalists, usually on violin, flute or vīṇā. In the hereditary tradition the naṭṭuvaṉār was the teacher and leader of the performance, and in the early decades of the twentieth century the dancer sang as well as danced; in the modern concert the dancer is silent, and the dancer’s teacher, male or female, often conducts. The art of conducting, naṭṭuvāṅgam, is now taught to women as well as men.

docs.title: 15.5.2 Costume and jewellery
docs.text: The costume of Bharatanāṭyam was redesigned in the 1930s and 1940s. The dancers of the hereditary tradition performed in a sari, sometimes with trousers beneath; Rukmini Devi and her collaborators designed a tailored costume of silk, with a fan of pleats between the legs that opens in the araimaṇḍi, and adopted a set of “temple jewellery” modelled on the ornaments of sculpture, many of them made by craftsmen of Nagercoil and other towns. The set typically includes the head ornaments representing the sun and moon, a forehead ornament (neṯṯi cuṭṭi), earrings (jimikki), a nose stud, necklaces, armlets (vaṅki), a waist belt (oṭṭiyāṇam), an ornament for the plaited hair (jaṭai nākam) with flowers, and the ankle bells. The hands and feet are painted with red dye (ālta) to make their movements visible. Two styles of costume are common, one with trousers (“pyjama”) and one resembling a draped sari (O’Shea 2007).

docs.title: 15.5.3 Stage and temple
docs.text: The modern dance is performed on the proscenium stage of the concert hall, often with a small image of Naṭarāja placed at the side and a lamp lit before the performance. Many dancers speak of the stage as a temple and of the performance as an offering. The image is a twentieth-century convention, part of the effort to present the dance as a temple art; the dance of the hereditary performers was performed in many settings, sacred and secular. Some contemporary dancers have returned to temple festivals as venues, now as invited artists rather than as ritual servants.

docs.title: 15.6 Training, the Araṅgēṯṯam and the Institutions
15.6.1 Training
docs.text: A Bharatanāṭyam student begins with the aḍavus, practised daily, together with the hand gestures and the head, eye and neck movements of the Abhinayadarpaṇa; then learns the items of the recital in order of difficulty, from the alārippu to the varṇam; and finally learns the expressive repertoire. The training lasts many years and was traditionally conducted in the teacher’s home, the student living or spending long hours there; today most students learn in classes, often once or twice a week, alongside school or work, while professional dancers train in institutions such as Kalakshetra or with a senior teacher. Universities in India and abroad offer degrees in dance. The training of the body and of the mind’s understanding of music and poetry go together; the best dancers are also musicians and readers of the texts they interpret.

docs.title: 15.6.2 The araṅgēṯṯam
docs.text: The araṅgēṯṯam (Tamil, “ascending the stage”) is the formal debut of a dancer, in which the student performs a full recital before an invited audience, with the teacher conducting. In the hereditary tradition it marked a young woman’s entry into the profession; in the twentieth century it became a rite of passage for middle-class girls, a demonstration of accomplishment and of the family’s cultural capital, and in the diaspora a major social event. The elaborate and expensive araṅgēṯṯam has been criticised by teachers who feel that it marks the end of serious study rather than its beginning, and by scholars as an emblem of the class transformation of the art (O’Shea 2007).

docs.title: 15.6.3 Institutions
docs.text: The institutions that shaped modern Bharatanāṭyam include Kalakshetra (now a national institution), the dance school of the Madras Music Academy, the Darpana Academy founded in 1949 at Ahmedabad by Mrinalini Sarabhai (1918–2016), and many private schools in India and abroad. The Sangeet Natak Akademi, founded in 1952–53, recognised Bharatanāṭyam as one of the “classical” dances, gave awards to its leading teachers and dancers, and supported festivals and documentation (Chapter 23).

docs.title: 15.7 Dancers and Teachers of the Twentieth Century
docs.text:
The history of modern Bharatanāṭyam is often told through two women, Rukmini Devi and Balasaraswati, but it was made by many more. The naṭṭuvaṉārs of the hereditary families — among them Meenakshisundaram Pillai of Pandanallur, Ramaiah Pillai of Vazhuvoor, Kandappa Pillai, and K. P. Kittappa Pillai, a descendant of the Thanjavur Quartet who taught and published the Quartet’s compositions — trained most of the dancers of the new generation, and their lineages are the bāṇis of today. Women of the hereditary families, such as the Mysore court dancer K. Venkatalakshamma, transmitted repertoire and abhinaya to new performers, often with little public recognition (Soneji 2012; Kothari 1979).

Among the dancers of the new middle-class generation, some became national figures. Kamala, trained in the Vazhuvoor style, became famous as a child dancer in films and later as a performer and teacher in the United States; Vyjayanthimala combined a career as a film star with serious Bharatanāṭyam performance; Mrinalini Sarabhai founded the Darpana Academy and created dance-dramas on contemporary themes; Yamini Krishnamurthy (1940–2024), equally celebrated in Kuchipudi, toured widely. Later generations included scholars and choreographers as well as performers: Padma Subrahmanyam, who reconstructed the karaṇas of the Nāṭyaśāstra from texts and temple sculpture (Chapter 2); Chandralekha (1928–2006), who used the vocabulary of Bharatanāṭyam and of yoga and martial arts to create contemporary work critical of the form’s conventions; and dancers such as Alarmel Valli, Malavika Sarukkai and Leela Samson, who developed distinctive individual approaches to the classical repertoire. Men also returned to the form after the 1930s, among them Ram Gopal, the Kalakshetra-trained V. P. Dhananjayan and C. V. Chandrasekhar, and many younger dancers in India and abroad (O’Shea 2007; Bharucha 1995).

The shift from hereditary to middle-class performers also changed the position of the teacher. In the early twentieth century the naṭṭuvaṉār was usually a man of the hereditary community, who taught, composed, conducted and arranged performances, and whose authority rested on his family’s knowledge. By the later twentieth century many teachers were women dancers from non-hereditary backgrounds who had studied with such men and then opened their own schools, and many of them conducted the performances of their students. The professional dance school, run by a celebrated dancer, became the characteristic institution of the art, and the hereditary teachers, with a few notable exceptions, faded from public view (O’Shea 2007; Soneji 2012).

docs.title: 15.8 Bharatanāṭyam in the Modern World
docs.text:
From the mid-twentieth century Bharatanāṭyam spread far beyond Tamil Nadu. It was taken up by dancers from every region and community of India, became a staple of school and college cultural programmes and a symbol of Indian culture in official presentations abroad, and travelled with the Tamil and wider South Asian diasporas to Sri Lanka, Malaysia, Singapore, Britain, North America, Australia and elsewhere. Janet O’Shea’s study shows how dancers in different places have used the form to make claims about national, regional, religious and diasporic identity, and how the meanings of “tradition” shift accordingly (O’Shea 2007).

Within India the repertoire itself has widened. Dancers have set Tamil Caṅkam poetry, the hymns of the Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉmārs and modern poetry in many languages; Padma Subrahmanyam presents her reconstruction of the karaṇas as a distinct style, Bharatanṛtyam; and contemporary choreographers have used the vocabulary of the form against its devotional and gendered conventions (Chapters 13 and 23).

At the same time the form remains marked by its history. Debates continue about caste and access — whether the dance remains the preserve of particular communities, how the descendants of the hereditary performers are acknowledged, and how far the devotional framing adopted in the 1930s excludes other meanings. Bharatanāṭyam is best understood neither as an unchanged ancient art nor as a simple invention, but as a living tradition that was radically reshaped in the twentieth century and continues to change (Soneji 2010; Gaston 1996).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Soneji (2010) collects the key essays on Bharatanāṭyam’s history and practice, including Srinivasan (1985) and Allen (1997). Soneji (2012) is the essential study of the hereditary performers and their afterlife, Orr (2000) the major study of medieval temple women, and Kersenboom-Story (1987) an account of the ritual role of the devadāsī. Meduri (2005) and Knight (2010) present the two great figures of the twentieth century, and O’Shea (2007) the global history of the form. Gaston (1996) and Kothari (1979) describe technique and repertoire, and Krishnan (2019) shows how early Tamil cinema shaped the modern form.

docs.title: Chapter 16: Kathak
docs.text: Kathak is the classical dance of north India and of Pakistan, known for its rapid, intricate footwork, its spins, its rhythmic dialogue with the drum, and its subtle interpretation of songs. Its name is usually derived from kathā, “story”, and from the kathakas, story-tellers who recited sacred narratives. Like Bharatanāṭyam, Kathak has an official history and a more complicated real one. The official history, formulated in the mid-twentieth century, traces it from ancient temple story-tellers through the devotional dance-dramas of Kṛṣṇa to the Mughal courts, where it is said to have been “secularised”, and back to the temple in its modern revival. Recent scholarship, especially Margaret Walker’s history and Pallabi Chakravorty’s ethnography, has shown that the dance we know as Kathak took shape mainly in the courts and salons of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, in the hands of hereditary male dancers and of professional women performers, the courtesans; that the name “Kathak” for this dance and its classical status were established only in the twentieth century; and that the narrative of temple origins played an important part in that classicisation. The art that emerged from that history — its lineages, technique, repertoire, music and costume, and its modern institutions and performers — is described after the history itself.

docs.title: 16.1.1 Kathakas and the story of origins
docs.text:
Sanskrit literature mentions kathakas, reciters of stories, and medieval north Indian society had many kinds of professional narrators and singers who performed religious and heroic stories with song and gesture. Modern Kathak dancers have traced their art to such performers, and in particular to a hereditary community called Kathak, settled in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Banaras, some of whose families became the principal dance teachers of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The Lucknow family of Birju Maharaj traced its origin to Handia near Allahabad. The connection between this community and ancient story-tellers is plausible in a general sense but cannot be documented in detail (Walker 2014; Kothari 1989).

The devotional dance-dramas of Kṛṣṇa (rāslīlā) performed in Braj, the region of Mathura and Vrindavan, from the sixteenth century onwards share many themes with Kathak’s expressive repertoire, and the twentieth-century narrative often presented the rāslīlā as Kathak’s direct ancestor. The two forms have influenced each other, but the rāslīlā is a distinct tradition of Brahmin-led troupes of boy actors, and the claim of direct descent is part of the modern story rather than an established fact (Walker 2014).

docs.title: 16.1.2 Dance at the courts
docs.text:
The dance that became Kathak developed above all in the courts of north India in the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries: the Mughal court and its nobility, the Rajput courts of Rajasthan, the nawabs of Awadh at Lucknow, and the smaller courts and wealthy households of the region. In these settings dance was performed by professional women — the courtesans (ṭawāʾif), whose households trained girls in singing, dance and poetry and who entertained in the mahfil, the evening gathering of music and conversation — and by hereditary male dancers and musicians, who taught them and also performed themselves. Mughal and Rajput paintings show women dancers in long skirts and jackets turning, with musicians playing sāraṅgī and drums; European visitors described the “nautch” performances of dancing women at courts, festivals and receptions (Walker 2014; Morcom 2013).

The court of Wājid ʿAlī Shāh, the last nawab of Awadh (r. 1847–1856), occupies a special place in Kathak’s history. The nawab was himself a poet, composer and performer, staged dance-dramas (rahas) on the theme of Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd women, and patronised musicians and dancers; the ṭhumrī, the lyrical song genre central to Kathak’s expressive repertoire, flourished at his court (Chapter 7). Tradition names Ṭhākur Prasād as the nawab’s dance teacher and Kālkā Prasād and Bindādīn, younger members of the same family, as the founders of the Lucknow lineage; Bindādīn is remembered as the composer of many ṭhumrīs. After the British annexation of Awadh in 1856, the nawab’s household moved to Calcutta, and the musicians and dancers of Lucknow dispersed among other patrons (Kothari 1989; Walker 2014).

docs.title: 16.1.3 The anti-nautch campaigns and the classical revival
docs.text:
From the late nineteenth century the courtesans became the target of the same anti-nautch campaigns that attacked the temple dancers of the south (Chapter 15). Reformers condemned their art as immoral; their aristocratic patrons disappeared; and many women abandoned dance, turned to singing for the gramophone and the radio, or later found work in the film industry. The hereditary male dancers, meanwhile, became teachers to new middle-class students.

In the 1930s and after, Kathak was reconstructed as a “classical” art. Dancers such as Madame Menaka (Leila Sokhey, 1899–1947) created Kathak ballets for the stage; the hereditary families of Lucknow and Jaipur taught in the new schools of Bombay, Delhi and Calcutta; and after Independence the Sangeet Natak Akademi recognised Kathak as one of India’s classical dances. The name “Kathak” itself, which had referred to the hereditary community, was now applied to the dance. As Margaret Walker shows, this classicisation was accompanied by a new history: the dance was said to have begun in Hindu temples, to have been “degraded” at the Muslim courts and by the courtesans, and to have been restored to its spiritual roots by the revival. Pallabi Chakravorty and Anna Morcom have shown how this narrative excluded the courtesans and other professional women performers, whose art the classical form had absorbed, and how “respectable” Kathak has continued to define itself against them (Walker 2014; Chakravorty 2008; Morcom 2013).

Scholarly Note: Hindu and Muslim in Kathak

Kathak is often described as a “synthesis” of Hindu devotional and Muslim courtly culture. The description is apt in that its repertoire includes both songs about Kṛṣṇa and the salāmī (salutation) of the Mughal court, both bhajan and ghazal, and in that its makers included Hindus and Muslims. But it can also suggest two separate cultures that met, whereas the courtly culture of north India was itself shared: Muslim patrons commissioned songs about Kṛṣṇa, Hindu dancers performed at Muslim courts, and the courtesans and musicians who created much of the art belonged to communities that crossed religious lines. The more recent tendency to present Kathak as essentially Hindu and its court history as a deviation is as much a modern construction as the synthesis (Walker 2014; Chakravorty 2008).

docs.title: 16.2 The World of the Ṭawāʾif
docs.text:
Because the courtesans were written out of the history of classical dance, it is worth describing their world more fully. In the cities of north India in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries — Delhi, Lucknow, Banaras, Patna, Agra, Hyderabad and others — the most accomplished professional women performers lived in households, often headed by an older woman, that trained girls in singing, dance, Urdu poetry and the manners of courtly society. Their salons (koṭhā) were places of music, conversation and poetry where young men of good family were sent to acquire refinement, and their patrons included nobles, merchants and officials. The leading courtesans were wealthy, owned property, commissioned and composed poetry and music, and were among the principal patrons of the male musicians and dancers who taught and accompanied them. Their relationships with patrons were often sexual, and the profession included women of very different status, from celebrated artists to women in poverty and dependence (Morcom 2013; Perron 2007).

The courtesans’ art centred on the song — ṭhumrī, dādrā, ghazal — interpreted through expressive movement and gesture, with passages of rhythmic dance. Much of what is now the expressive repertoire of Kathak, including the seated interpretation of songs (bhāv batānā), was their creation or was developed in their salons. From the late nineteenth century the colonial state, Indian reformers and the new nationalist culture combined to stigmatise them as prostitutes: the courtesans lost their patrons, their property and their social standing, and their art was taken over, in modified form, by middle-class dancers who sought to distance themselves from it. Anna Morcom has traced the afterlife of the courtesan tradition among women performers in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, in the shadow of the “respectable” classical arts and of Bollywood (Morcom 2013). Recognising the courtesans’ contribution does not require romanticising their world; it requires including them in the history of the art they helped to create.

docs.title: 16.3 The Gharānās
docs.text:
Like Hindustani music, Kathak is transmitted in stylistic lineages called gharānās, centred on hereditary families of teachers (Kothari 1989; Walker 2014).

Lucknow. Associated with the family of Ṭhākur Prasād, Kālkā Prasād and Bindādīn, and in the twentieth century with Kālkā Prasād’s sons Acchan Maharaj (1883–1946), Lacchu Maharaj (1901–1978) and Shambhu Maharaj (1910–1970), and Acchan Maharaj’s son Birju Maharaj (1938–2022). It is known for grace and delicacy (nazākat), for the subtle interpretation of ṭhumrī and for refined, rounded movement. Jaipur. Associated with dancers who served the courts of Rajasthan, among them the brothers Jailal and Sundar Prasad and their families. It is known for vigorous, complex footwork, long compositions in difficult tālas, powerful parans derived from the pakhāvaj, and fast turns. Banaras. Associated with the lineage traced to Jānakīprasād and with the naṭvarī style of rhythmic syllables; Sitara Devi (1920–2014), daughter of the Banaras teacher Sukhdev Maharaj, became one of the most celebrated performers of the twentieth century. Raigarh. A shorter-lived lineage created at the court of Raja Chakradhar Singh of Raigarh (in present-day Chhattisgarh) in the 1930s and 1940s, where dancers and musicians from Lucknow and Jaipur were brought together and new compositions and treatises were produced.

The distinctions between gharānās are real but have been blurred by modern teaching, in which students often learn from teachers of different lineages.

docs.title: 16.4.1 Stance and footwork
docs.text: The Kathak dancer stands upright, with the weight evenly distributed on flat feet and the knees straight or slightly flexed, the posture of the courtly mahfil rather than of the half-seated southern forms. The basic stance (thāṭ) is a graceful pose with one arm raised and the head and eyes slightly inclined. The feet produce rhythm through rapid striking of the heel, the ball and the flat of the foot, and through the ankle bells (ghuṅgrū), often more than a hundred on each ankle, which the dancer can sound loudly, softly or with a single isolated bell. The basic footwork pattern (tatkār), recited to the syllables tā thei thei tat, ā thei thei tat, is practised in Tīntāl at increasing speeds and in many variations; in performance the dancer improvises series of variations (laḍī, “chain”) on a footwork pattern, building to a climax.

docs.title: 16.4.2 Turns
docs.text:
The cakkar (“turn”) is Kathak’s most spectacular movement. The dancer spins on the heel or ball of one foot, or with alternating feet, the arms held out or close to the body, completing a turn in each beat or half-beat, and often ends a series of turns in a held pose on the sam. Dancers perform long series of turns — sometimes dozens — at high speed; the spreading skirts of women dancers make them visually striking (Figure 16.1). The suggestion that Kathak’s turns derive from the whirling of Sufi dervishes is speculative; turning is a common element of north Indian dance.

Figure 16.1. Two Kathak dancers in spins (cakkar), their skirts flaring with the turn. Photo: Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 16.4.3 The upper body and the hands
docs.text: Kathak uses the hands, arms and upper body in long curving lines and soft, rounded movements, with the wrists and fingers often finishing a phrase in a delicate gesture. Its gestures are less codified than those of the southern forms: in the expressive repertoire the dancer relies more on naturalistic mime, on the eyes and face, and on small movements of the head, neck and shoulders than on a fixed vocabulary of hand signs (Chapter 14). The eyebrows, eyes and neck — the sideways glide of the neck, the play of a glance — are used with great subtlety, especially in the Lucknow style.

docs.title: 16.5.1 Pure dance
docs.text:
Kathak’s pure dance (nṛtta) is built on rhythmic compositions that the dancer usually recites (paḍhant) before dancing them, so that the audience hears the rhythmic pattern and then sees and hears it executed (Kothari 1989):

Thāṭ. An opening in slow tempo, in which the dancer explores poses and small movements of the eyes, neck and wrists within the tāla, marking the sam with a pose. Āmad. An “entrance” composition (from Persian āmad, “arrival”), often with the syllables of speech rather than of the drum. Salāmī. A composition ending in a salutation, a survival of the court mahfil. Ṭukṛā and toḍā. Short compositions (“pieces”), usually ending in a tihāī on the sam. Paran. A composition in the heavy, resonant syllables of the pakhāvaj (dhā, kiṭa, taka, dhumakiṭa), danced with powerful footwork. Kavitt. A poem, often in Braj Bhāṣā and on a devotional theme, set to rhythm and danced with gestures illustrating the words. Primalu. A composition made of the names of gods set to rhythm. Chakkardār compositions. Compositions repeated three times so that their final syllable falls on sam (Chapter 5). Tatkār and laḍī. Extended improvised footwork. Jugalbandī. An improvised rhythmic dialogue between dancer and drummer, in which each answers and extends the other’s phrases, often ending with a shared tihāī.

docs.title: 16.5.2 Gat
docs.text: The gat (“gait” or “movement”) is a distinctively Kathak genre. In gat nikās (“bringing out the gait”) the dancer, moving with a gliding walk around the stage in Tīntāl, presents a character with a few stylised gestures — a young woman with a veil, a woman carrying a water pot, Kṛṣṇa with his flute, a deer — and returns to the starting point on the sam. In gat bhāv the dancer develops such a character into a short narrative, without words, through mime and movement: Kṛṣṇa stealing butter, the encounter of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa at the riverbank, the “teasing at the well” (panghaṭ), episodes from the epics. In these pieces the dancer may play several characters in rapid alternation, identifying each by a characteristic gesture, stance or way of wearing the veil.

docs.title: 16.5.3 Expressive dance
docs.text: Kathak’s expressive genre is the interpretation of songs: ṭhumrī, dādrā, bhajan and ghazal. In the style called bhāv batānā (“showing the feeling”), the dancer, seated or standing almost still, interprets each line of a song sung by a vocalist, elaborating it through successive interpretations in the manner described in Chapter 3. This art was developed by the courtesans and by the hereditary male dancers of Lucknow and Banaras, among whom Bindādīn and Kālkā Prasād’s descendants were especially celebrated; in the twentieth century Shambhu Maharaj and Birju Maharaj were renowned for it. Much of its repertoire consists of love songs in which the heroine addresses Kṛṣṇa or an unnamed beloved, expressing longing, reproach or the joy of meeting.

docs.title: 16.5.4 The recital
docs.text: A modern Kathak solo recital usually begins with an invocation (vandanā) and a section of pure dance in Tīntāl — thāṭ, āmad, ṭukṛās and toḍās, parans, kavitts — often with gat nikās and gat bhāv; continues with expressive items such as a ṭhumrī or bhajan; and ends with fast footwork, turns and a jugalbandī with the drummer. Dancers sometimes perform in other tālas (Jhaptāl, Dhamār, Rūpak) or in compositions of unusual length to display their rhythmic skill. The tempo of the pure-dance section rises gradually, as in Hindustani music, from slow to very fast (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 16.6.1 Music
docs.text: Kathak is accompanied by Hindustani musicians: a tablā player (and sometimes a pakhāvaj player), a singer, and an instrumentalist playing sāraṅgī, sitār, flute or harmonium, who plays a repeated melodic cycle (lahrā or nagmā) that marks the tāla during the pure dance. The relation between dancer and drummer is central: the drummer must follow every nuance of the dancer’s footwork, and the two improvise together. The dancer is also expected to be a skilled reciter of rhythmic syllables, and often a singer.

docs.title: 16.6.2 Costume
docs.text: Two styles of costume are common. In the “Mughal” style, women wear a long fitted jacket with a flared skirt (aṅgarkhā or anārkalī) over close-fitting trousers (cūṛīdār), with a cap or veil; in the “Hindu” style, a full skirt (lahãgā or ghāgrā) with a bodice and a long scarf (oṛhnī or dupaṭṭā) used expressively to represent a veil, a cradle or a river. Men wear a long aṅgarkhā or kurtā with cūṛīdār or a dhotī. Both styles are modern stage costumes based on the dress depicted in court painting; the difference between them, like many aspects of modern Kathak, reflects the twentieth-century debate about the dance’s “Hindu” and “Muslim” identities.

docs.title: 16.7 Institutions and Performers
docs.text:
After Independence Kathak was taught in new institutions: the Bharatiya Kala Kendra in Delhi (1952), where Lacchu Maharaj’s brother Shambhu Maharaj and later Birju Maharaj taught; the Kathak Kendra, established in Delhi in 1964 as a national institute under the Sangeet Natak Akademi; dance departments of universities; and many private schools. The hereditary teachers trained middle-class women from many regions, who became the principal performers of the form, and men from non-hereditary backgrounds also took it up (Chakravorty 2008; Kothari 1989).

Among the leading performers and teachers of the twentieth century were Birju Maharaj, who combined the Lucknow tradition with a remarkable gift for choreography and teaching and received the Padma Vibhushan in 1986; Sitara Devi of Banaras, famous for her energy and her performances in early Hindi cinema; Damayanti Joshi; Gopi Krishna, who also worked in film; Rohini Bhate of Pune, a scholar and teacher; and Kumudini Lakhia, who founded the Kadamb school in Ahmedabad in 1967 and created group choreographies that broke with the solo format and the conventional themes of the form (Katrak 2011).

docs.title: 16.8 Training a Kathak Dancer
docs.text: Training in Kathak begins with the basic stance and with tatkār, practised daily in Tīntāl at slow, medium and fast tempos until the feet can produce clean, even strokes at every speed, and with the recitation of the syllables of the ṭhekā and of simple compositions while keeping the tāla with the hands. The student learns the hand and arm movements called hastak together with the footwork, then the turns, first single and then in series, and gradually a repertoire of ṭukṛās, toḍās, parans and tihāīs from the teacher’s lineage. Rhythmic recitation (paḍhant) is an essential skill, since the dancer must recite each composition clearly before dancing it. Expressive dance is taught later, through gats and the interpretation of bhajans and ṭhumrīs, and the art of improvising expressive variations is acquired, if at all, only after many years. In the institutions founded after Independence, this training was organised into graded courses and examinations, while many students continued to learn privately in the households of hereditary teachers (Chakravorty 2008; Kothari 1989).

docs.title: 16.9 Kathak beyond India
docs.text: Kathak is not only an Indian art. In Pakistan, dancers of Kathak and related forms continued to perform and teach after 1947, and state cultural institutions supported dance in the 1950s and 1960s; but under the military government of the late 1970s and 1980s public dance was officially discouraged, and several leading dancers left the country or performed mainly abroad. Nahid Siddiqui, a pupil of the Pakistani teacher Maharaj Ghulam Hussain Kathak and later of Birju Maharaj, became the most internationally prominent Pakistani Kathak dancer, working for long periods in Britain. In Bangladesh, Kathak is taught alongside other classical and folk dances. In the South Asian diaspora, especially in Britain and North America, Kathak has become one of the most widely studied Indian dance forms, taught in community schools and in some universities, and British dancers such as Akram Khan have made it the starting point for contemporary choreography that has reached audiences far beyond South Asian communities (Chapter 23) (Katrak 2011; Chakravorty 2008).

docs.title: 16.10 Kathak and Film
docs.text: Hindi cinema has drawn heavily on Kathak and on the courtesan dance from which it grew. Classic films set in courtesan milieus, such as Pakeezah (1972) and Umrao Jaan (1981), and historical spectacles such as Mughal-e-Azam (1960), whose famous dance sequence was choreographed by Lacchu Maharaj, presented Kathak-based dance to vast audiences; Birju Maharaj choreographed for several films, among them Devdas (2002). Film has popularised Kathak and provided a livelihood for many dancers, but it has also perpetuated the image of the courtesan dancer that the classical form sought to escape, and the boundary between “classical” Kathak and film dance remains a matter of concern among teachers and critics (Morcom 2007; Chakravorty 2008).

docs.title: 16.11 Kathak and Bharatanāṭyam Compared
docs.text: The two most widely practised classical forms differ in almost every technical respect — Kathak’s upright stance against Bharatanāṭyam’s half-seated one, its turns against Bharatanāṭyam’s lines, its Hindustani music against Bharatanāṭyam’s Karnatak, its relatively uncodified gestures against Bharatanāṭyam’s vocabulary of hastas. Their histories are strikingly parallel. Both grew out of the art of professional women performers and the hereditary male teachers who trained them; both suffered from the anti-nautch campaigns; both were reconstructed in the twentieth century as “classical” arts with ancient, devotional histories, largely by and for middle-class performers; and in both cases the women whose art was reconstructed were marginalised in the process. The comparison shows that the history of Indian dance in the modern period is in large part a single history, played out in different regions and idioms (Chapter 1).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Walker (2014) is the essential critical history of Kathak, and Chakravorty (2008) an ethnography of Kathak, women and modernity. Morcom (2013) discusses the professional women performers excluded from “classical” dance, and Morcom (2007) the music and dance of Hindi film. Kothari (1989) is a well-illustrated account of the gharānās, technique and repertoire. For the music see Chapter 7 and Manuel (1989).

docs.title: Chapter 17: Odissi and Kuchipudi
docs.text: Two dances of eastern and south-eastern India reached the concert stage by very different routes. Odissi, from Odisha, is known for its sculptural poses and flowing movement, its basis in the songs of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda, and its links with the great temple of Jagannātha at Puri; it was reconstructed in the 1950s by a group of teachers and scholars from the surviving traditions of temple women and boy dancers, from sculpture and from texts. Kuchipudi, from coastal Andhra, grew out of a tradition of devotional dance-drama performed by the Brahmin men of a single village and was transformed in the twentieth century into a solo concert form performed mainly by women. The comparison between a dance rebuilt from fragments and a theatre turned into a concert dance runs through the account of each form’s technique, repertoire, music and costume and of the people who shaped it.

docs.title: 17.1.1 Early evidence
docs.text:
Odisha has a long record of dance in inscriptions and sculpture. The Hāthīgumphā inscription of the Jain king Khāravela of Kaliṅga (first century BCE), carved above a cave at Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar, records that the king entertained his capital with festivals of music and dance. A relief in the nearby Rāṇī Gumphā cave shows a woman dancing to the accompaniment of women musicians. From the ninth century, the temples of Bhubaneswar and later the Sun Temple at Konark (thirteenth century), whose dance hall (nāṭamaṇḍapa) is carved with dancers and musicians (Figure 17.1), carry innumerable figures of dancers in the curved postures that modern Odissi has made its own. These sculptures show that dance was cultivated in Odisha over many centuries and that sculptors shared a vocabulary of poses with dancers; they do not, by themselves, demonstrate a continuous tradition from the first century BCE to the present, as is sometimes claimed (Vatsyayan 1968; Kothari and Pasricha 1990).

Figure 17.1. Two dancing drummers, each with a barrel drum at the waist, in relief panels on the Sun Temple at Konark, thirteenth century. Photo: Kinkiniroy2012, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 17.1.2 The mahārīs of Puri
docs.text: The most important institutional home of dance in medieval and early modern Odisha was the temple of Jagannātha at Puri. Its women servants, the mahārīs (also called devadāsīs), were ritually married to the deity and performed dance and song as part of his daily and festival rituals: they danced at the time of the god’s morning meal and sang the songs of the Gītagovinda at the ritual of putting him to sleep, and they had duties in the great annual festivals. Frédérique Apffel Marglin’s study of the mahārīs, based on fieldwork with the last women of the institution in the 1970s, describes their ritual roles, their place in the temple’s system of purity and auspiciousness, and their relationships with the king, the priests and their patrons (Marglin 1985). Their numbers declined in the twentieth century; dedication ended, and the last mahārīs died in the early twenty-first century.
