Their dance, performed in the temple rather than for the public, contributed relatively little directly to the reconstructed form, though some mahārīs taught the reformers and some items, such as songs of the Gītagovinda, were part of their repertoire.

docs.title: 17.1.3 The gotipuas
docs.text:
From about the sixteenth century, according to tradition, groups of young boys dressed as girls — the goṭipuas (“single boys”) — performed dance and song outside the temple, at festivals and processions and for the households of patrons, especially in the service of Vaiṣṇava institutions. Their dance, which combined lyrical songs in Odia with acrobatic poses and backbends (Figure 17.2), was more widely accessible than the mahārīs’, and several of the gurus who reconstructed Odissi in the twentieth century, among them Kelucharan Mohapatra and Pankaj Charan Das, had trained as goṭipuas or in the closely related popular theatre. The goṭipua tradition survives in villages near Puri, notably Raghurajpur, alongside the classical form (Kothari and Pasricha 1990).

Figure 17.2. Goṭipua dancers, boys dressed as girls, forming an acrobatic group pose in a performance at Puri, 2018. Photo: Rangan Datta Wiki, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 17.2 The Making of Odissi
docs.text:
The name “Odissi” and the form now known by it date from the 1950s. In those years, as the new state government and the cultural elite of Odisha sought recognition for the region’s arts, a group of gurus and scholars met in Cuttack and Bhubaneswar to define and systematise a classical dance. The group, known as Jayantika, included the gurus Kelucharan Mohapatra, Pankaj Charan Das, Deba Prasad Das and Mayadhar Raut, the scholar Kalicharan Patnaik, and others. They drew on the goṭipua and theatre traditions in which several of them had trained, on what they could learn from the mahārīs, on the poses of temple sculpture, and on texts such as the Abhinayacandrikā, an Odia manual of dance (Chapter 12). They devised a basic vocabulary of steps and poses, a sequence of items for the solo recital, and a body of choreographies, many of which are still danced. After considerable debate, the Sangeet Natak Akademi accepted Odissi as a classical dance (Kothari and Pasricha 1990).

The reconstruction was a creative act. Like the reconstruction of Bharatanāṭyam, it drew on living traditions but also selected, refined and in places invented, and like it, it was carried out largely by men for the benefit of a new generation of women performers from educated middle-class families, who replaced the temple women and boy dancers of the earlier traditions. Different gurus developed distinct styles: Kelucharan Mohapatra’s lyrical and intricate style became the most widespread, while Pankaj Charan Das and Deba Prasad Das, the latter drawing more on folk and tribal elements, developed their own lineages.

docs.title: 17.3.1 Cauka and tribhaṅga
docs.text: Odissi is built on two basic stances. The cauka (“square”) is a symmetrical stance with the knees bent and turned out, the feet apart and the arms held out at shoulder height and bent at the elbows, forming a square; it is associated with Jagannātha and with vigorous movement. The tribhaṅga (“three bends”) is an asymmetrical stance in which the head, torso and hips are deflected in opposite directions, so that the body forms a gentle S-curve; it is associated with Kṛṣṇa and with lyrical grace. Much of the movement of Odissi consists of passages from one to the other. The terms of Indian iconography for bodily inclination — abhaṅga (slight bend), samabhaṅga (straight), atibhaṅga (extreme bend) and tribhaṅga — are used in teaching (Kothari and Pasricha 1990; Vatsyayan 1974).

docs.title: 17.3.2 Movement
docs.text: The characteristic quality of Odissi lies in its transitions: the torso moves independently of the hips in sideways deflections, the movement flows in curves rather than straight lines, and the dancer passes from one sculptural pose (bhaṅgi) to another, holding each briefly. The footwork, performed with ankle bells, is less percussive than that of Bharatanāṭyam or Kathak, but complex rhythmic passages are danced in the pure-dance items. The hand gestures follow the Abhinayadarpaṇa and the Abhinayacandrikā but are held softly, in curved lines (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 17.4.1 The recital
docs.text:
The solo recital devised in the 1950s and later refined by Kelucharan Mohapatra and others consists of (Kothari and Pasricha 1990):

Maṅgalācaraṇa. An invocation, beginning with an offering of flowers and a salutation to the earth (bhūmi praṇām), followed by a verse in praise of a deity, often Jagannātha or Gaṇeśa. Baṭu or sthāyī. A pure-dance item, associated with Śiva as Baṭukeśvara, that presents the basic poses and movements of the form in a sequence of increasing complexity. Pallavī. An item of pure dance in which a melody in a particular rāga is elaborated by both musicians and dancer, with increasingly intricate movement and rhythm. Abhinaya. One or more expressive items, interpreting a song from the Gītagovinda or from Odia devotional poetry. Mokṣa. A concluding item of fast pure dance, said to represent liberation, ending in stillness.

Choreographers have also created dance-dramas and new items, and a short item called tarijham is sometimes added between pure and expressive dance.

docs.title: 17.4.2 The Gītagovinda
docs.text: Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda, a Sanskrit poem of twelve cantos with twenty-four songs (aṣṭapadīs) on the love of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, composed in the twelfth century, has a special place in Odisha. Jayadeva is claimed by Odia tradition as a native of the region, the poem has been sung in the Jagannātha temple for centuries, and an order of King Pratāparudradeva inscribed in the temple about 1500 required that its songs be sung and danced before the god. In Odissi, songs of the Gītagovinda are the principal vehicle of expressive dance. Among the most often danced are lalita-lavaṅga-latā (the third song), which describes spring in the forest where Kṛṣṇa plays with the cowherd women; yāhi mādhava (the seventeenth), in which Rādhā dismisses the unfaithful Kṛṣṇa when he comes to her at dawn; and priye cāruśīle (the nineteenth), in which Kṛṣṇa begs her forgiveness. The poem’s frank eroticism was understood in the Vaiṣṇava tradition as an expression of the love between the soul and god (Chapter 3; Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā).

docs.title: 17.4.3 Odissi music
docs.text: Odissi is danced to music sung in a regional style that its exponents call “Odissi music”, drawing on the tradition of Odia devotional song and on treatises written in Odisha, such as the seventeenth-century Saṅgītanārāyaṇa. The ensemble includes a singer, a player of the mardala (a barrel drum), a flute or violin and cymbals. Besides the Gītagovinda, the repertoire uses the Odia songs of poets such as Upendra Bhañja and Kavisūrya Baladeva Ratha, and genres such as the campū (alternating prose and verse) and the cautiśā, an acrostic poem in which each stanza begins with a successive letter of the Odia alphabet. Whether Odissi music should be classed as a third system beside Hindustani and Karnatak music, or as a regional variety of Hindustani music, has been debated since the mid-twentieth century.

docs.title: 17.4.4 Costume
docs.text:
The Odissi dancer wears a silk sari of Odishan weave, often a Sambalpuri or Bomkai, draped and stitched to allow movement; silver jewellery in the filigree style of Cuttack; and a crown-like headpiece of white pith (tāhiā) set into a bun of hair and flowers, said to resemble the spire of a temple (Figure 17.3). The jewellery and headpiece were adopted in the 1950s and after, partly from the costume of the goṭipuas and of temple sculpture.

Figure 17.3. An Odissi dancer at the closing ceremony of the International Odissi Festival 2018, Bhubaneswar, in a stitched silk costume with a belt of metal ornaments and the spire-like headpiece (tāhiā) set in her hair. Photo: Prateek Pattanaik, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 17.5 Dancers and Teachers
docs.text: Kelucharan Mohapatra (1926–2004), who had begun as a goṭipua and a percussionist in the popular theatre, became the most influential teacher and choreographer of Odissi; his choreographies of pallavīs and Gītagovinda songs are danced throughout the world. Among the first generation of women performers were Priyambada Mohanty, Minati Mishra and Sanjukta Panigrahi (1944–1997), who as a girl from a Brahmin family scandalised her community by becoming a professional dancer, studied Bharatanāṭyam at Kalakshetra and Odissi with Kelucharan Mohapatra, and became one of the best-known Odissi dancers in the world; she also worked with the theatre director Eugenio Barba in the International School of Theatre Anthropology. Indrani Rahman and Sonal Mansingh helped bring Odissi to national and international audiences, and later dancers such as Madhavi Mudgal, Kumkum Mohanty, Aruna Mohanty, Ratikant Mohapatra and Ileana Citaristi have taught and choreographed widely. Odissi is now taught in many countries (Kothari and Pasricha 1990).

docs.title: 17.6 Odissi Today: Debates and Directions
docs.text:
Odissi’s rapid rise from a regional reconstruction to an internationally performed classical form has generated debates of its own. One concerns its relation to its sources. The reconstruction of the 1950s drew on the goṭipuas and on popular theatre at least as much as on the temple, yet the official history of the form emphasised the temple and the mahārīs, and the goṭipua tradition was for a long time regarded as a “folk” relative rather than a parent. Since the 1990s scholars and dancers have paid more attention to the goṭipuas and to the surviving mahārīs, and some dancers have tried to learn and present what remained of the mahārīs’ temple repertoire; such presentations raise the same questions about the transfer of ritual practice to the stage that arise in Bharatanāṭyam (Chapter 15) (Marglin 1985; Kothari and Pasricha 1990).

A second debate concerns style. Kelucharan Mohapatra’s style became so dominant that it came to be identified with Odissi itself, while the lineages of Pankaj Charan Das and Deba Prasad Das, the latter with its stronger links to the tribal and folk dances of Odisha and to Śākta and Tantric themes, were less widely known; their students have since worked to give them greater visibility. A third concerns innovation: choreographers have created group works, dance-dramas and contemporary pieces using Odissi’s vocabulary, and the question of how far the form can be extended without losing its identity is discussed among teachers, critics and audiences. The Odisha state government and its institutions, the Odissi Research Centre in Bhubaneswar among them, have supported documentation and research, and festivals at the temples of Konark and Mukteśvara present the form in settings that recall the sculptures from which much of its imagery derives.

Odissi’s international spread began early. Indrani Rahman performed it abroad in the 1960s, Sanjukta Panigrahi’s work with Eugenio Barba brought it into the experimental theatre of Europe, and dancers from many countries — among them the Italian-born Ileana Citaristi, who settled in Odisha — have studied and taught it. Like Bharatanāṭyam and Kathak, it is now taught in the South Asian diaspora and beyond (Chapter 23) (Kothari and Pasricha 1990; Katrak 2011).

docs.title: 17.7 Kuchipudi: The Village and Its Theatre
17.7.1 Kuchipudi village
docs.text: Kuchipudi takes its name from a village in the Krishna district of Andhra Pradesh, whose Brahmin families — the Bhāgavatulu — performed devotional dance-dramas (yakṣagānas or kalāpas) in Telugu. According to tradition, the village was granted to the performers as an endowment by Abul Hasan Tana Shah, the last Qutb Shahi sultan of Golconda, in the late seventeenth century, after he had seen them perform. The troupes travelled through the Telugu country, performing at temple festivals and for patrons; their plays lasted through the night, combined song, dance, mime and spoken dialogue, and were performed entirely by men, with men taking the women’s roles (Kothari and Pasricha 2001).

docs.title: 17.7.2 Siddhendra Yogi and the Bhāmākalāpam
docs.text: The founder of the tradition, according to its own account, was Siddhendra Yogi, a Vaiṣṇava ascetic whose date is uncertain (he is often placed in the seventeenth century). He is said to have composed the Bhāmākalāpam, the dance-drama of Satyabhāmā, Kṛṣṇa’s proud and jealous queen, which became the most famous work of the repertoire, and to have required the boys of the village to learn to perform it. The role of Satyabhāmā, with its long entrance song and its expression of pride, love, anger and longing, was the supreme test of the village’s actors; in the twentieth century Vedantam Satyanarayana Sarma (1935–2012) was especially celebrated in it. Other plays of the repertoire include the Gollakalāpam, a dialogue between a milkmaid and a Brahmin on philosophical and social questions, the Prahlāda Caritram, Uṣāpariṇayam and Śaśirekhāpariṇayam.

docs.title: 17.7.3 The Bhāmākalāpam in performance
docs.text:
The Bhāmākalāpam shows the conventions of the village theatre clearly. Performances traditionally took place in the open air, on a temporary stage lit by torches, before an audience that sat through the night. The sūtradhāra, who sang, conducted the drummers and spoke as narrator and as interlocutor of the characters, opened the play with invocations and introduced each character. A character entered behind a curtain held by two attendants, presented himself or herself through an entrance song (pravēśa daru) that described his or her qualities, and was revealed when the curtain was lowered. Satyabhāmā’s entrance is the most famous of all: she announces herself as the proud and beautiful queen of Kṛṣṇa, and the scene, extended by repetition and improvisation, could last for hours. The play then follows Satyabhāmā through her quarrel with Kṛṣṇa, her separation, her messages through her confidante Mādhavi, and her eventual reconciliation, giving the actor of her role scope for every shade of pride, jealousy, longing and love (Kothari and Pasricha 2001).

Spoken dialogue, in Telugu prose and verse, alternated with song and dance; the actor of Satyabhāmā both sang and danced the songs and spoke the dialogue, often improvising exchanges with the sūtradhāra that drew laughter from the audience. The performers were Brahmin men, and the female roles were played by men who specialised in them, a convention that survives in the village and in the Bhāgavata Mēḷa. The combination of devotional subject, sophisticated poetry, theatrical improvisation and an all-male cast is characteristic of the Telugu dance-drama and quite different from the solo women’s dance that Kuchipudi later became.

docs.title: 17.7.4 Related traditions
docs.text: Kuchipudi belongs to a family of Telugu devotional dance-dramas that also includes the Bhāgavata Mēḷa of Melattur and neighbouring villages in the Thanjavur region of Tamil Nadu, where Telugu-speaking Brahmin families perform plays by Melattur Veṅkaṭarāma Śāstri (eighteenth to nineteenth century), such as Prahlāda Caritram, at the festival of Narasiṃha each year; and the Telugu court theatre of the Thanjavur Nāyakas. It is more distantly related to the Yakṣagāna of Karnataka (Chapter 20). These traditions share the role of the sūtradhāra or bhāgavata, the narrator-singer who introduces and links the scenes; the entrance songs (pravēśa daru) with which characters present themselves; and the alternation of song, dance and dialogue (Richmond et al. 1990).

docs.title: 17.8 From Dance-Drama to Solo Dance
docs.text:
In the twentieth century Kuchipudi was transformed. Vedantam Lakshminarayana Sastry (1886–1956), a master of the village tradition, began to teach women and to develop solo items extracted from the dance-dramas. After debates at the Sangeet Natak Akademi in the late 1950s, in which advocates such as the scholar Banda Kanakalingeswara Rao argued for its classical character, Kuchipudi was recognised as a classical dance. The decisive figure in its transformation was Vempati Chinna Satyam (1929–2012), a member of one of the village families, who founded the Kuchipudi Art Academy in Madras in 1963. He trained women dancers in large numbers, standardised the technique, choreographed a solo repertoire and many new dance-dramas for women and men, and made Kuchipudi a pan-Indian and international concert form. Yamini Krishnamurthy (1940–2024), Raja and Radha Reddy and Swapnasundari were among the dancers who brought it to national prominence (Kothari and Pasricha 2001).

The transformation had costs comparable to those of the other classical forms. The village tradition of all-male dance-drama declined, though the village and some of its families continue to perform; the theatrical skills of the old repertoire — speech, improvisation, the playing of women’s roles by men — became marginal to a form centred on the solo female dancer; and the debate between those who regard the dance-drama as Kuchipudi’s true essence and those who emphasise the solo concert continues.

docs.title: 17.9.1 Technique
docs.text: Kuchipudi shares much of its basic vocabulary with Bharatanāṭyam — the half-seated posture, the aḍavus (Telugu aḍugus), the hand gestures of the Abhinayadarpaṇa — but it moves with greater fluidity and speed, with quick, darting movements, jumps, turns and a playful, dramatic quality inherited from the dance-drama. Its expressive style is more openly theatrical, and dancers often sing or speak lines in performance, as in the old plays.

docs.title: 17.9.2 Repertoire
docs.text: The modern solo recital typically includes an invocation, often to Gaṇeśa; a pravēśa daru, the entrance song of a character such as Satyabhāmā, presented as a solo; jatisvarams and tillānas of pure dance; expressive items, among them the padams of Kṣetrayya, the Telugu songs of Annamācārya (1408–1503), the poet of the Tirupati temple, and Sanskrit verses; and the taraṅgam. The taraṅgam sets passages from Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha’s Sanskrit song-cycle on the life of Kṛṣṇa, the Kṛṣṇalīlātaraṅgiṇī (seventeenth century), to dance; in modern performance it usually ends with the dancer dancing on the rim of a brass plate, sometimes with a pot of water on the head, a feat whose origin is unclear and which has no basis in Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha’s text (Kothari and Pasricha 2001). Group dance-dramas, old and new, remain an important part of Kuchipudi practice.

docs.title: 17.9.3 Music and costume
docs.text:
Kuchipudi is accompanied by Karnatak musicians — a naṭṭuvaṉār, singer, mṛdaṅgam player and violinist or flautist — and most of its songs are in Telugu. Its solo costume and jewellery resemble those of Bharatanāṭyam (Figure 17.4), with differences in the cut of the costume; the dance-dramas use character costumes, crowns and make-up for gods, demons and heroes.

Figure 17.4. Kuchipudi dancers, disciples of Raja, Radha and Kaushalya Reddy, at the Youth Festival, 2012. Photo: Sumita Roy Dutta, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 17.10 Two Paths to Classical Status
docs.text: Odissi and Kuchipudi show how differently “classical” Indian dance forms came into being. Odissi was assembled in the 1950s from temple, popular and sculptural sources by a group of gurus and scholars; Kuchipudi was adapted from a living village theatre by its own hereditary masters. Odissi replaced the temple women and boy dancers of its past with middle-class women; Kuchipudi replaced the Brahmin men of its village with women from many communities. Both found their authority in Sanskrit texts and temple sculpture as well as in their own traditions, and both were recognised by a national institution, the Sangeet Natak Akademi, after debates about whether they were sufficiently “classical”. The forms that resulted are now among the most admired in India, and their histories show that the classical canon was made, not simply inherited (Chapter 1).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Kothari and Pasricha (1990) and Kothari and Pasricha (2001) are well-illustrated accounts of the two forms, their history, technique and repertoire. Marglin (1985) is the essential study of the mahārīs of Puri. Vatsyayan (1968) and Vatsyayan (1974) relate Odissi to sculpture and to the other classical forms. For the Telugu dance-drama traditions see Richmond et al. (1990).

docs.title: Chapter 18: Kathakaḷi, Mohiniyāṭṭam, Manipuri and Sattriya
docs.text: A Kathakaḷi performance begins at dusk with drumming and lasts until dawn, lit in the old way by a single large oil lamp at the front of the stage; a Manipuri rāsa is danced in the courtyard of a temple to Kṛṣṇa. Four of the dance forms now recognised as classical come from two regions at opposite ends of India. From Kerala come Kathakaḷi, the dance-drama of epic heroes and demons performed by men in spectacular make-up and costume, and Mohiniyāṭṭam, a solo dance of women in white and gold. From the north-east come Manipuri, the devotional dance of the Meitei people of the Manipur valley, centred on the Rāsalīlā of Kṛṣṇa, and Sattriya, the dance of the Vaiṣṇava monasteries of Assam. The four forms have very different histories, but they share a close relation with religious institutions and with regional languages, music and martial traditions, and all four were reshaped in the twentieth century by new institutions and by their recognition as national “classical” arts.

docs.title: 18.1.1 Precursors
docs.text: Kathakaḷi (Malayalam, “story-play”) took shape in the second half of the seventeenth century in the courts of central Kerala. It drew on several older traditions. Kūṭiyāṭṭam, the Kerala performance of Sanskrit drama by the Cākyār actors in temple theatres, provided a refined technique of acting with gesture and eye (Chapter 19). Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam, a cycle of eight plays on the life of Kṛṣṇa composed in Sanskrit in the mid-seventeenth century by Mānavēdan, the Zamorin of Calicut, and performed in the Guruvayur temple, provided a model of the dance-drama with elaborate costumes and masks. Rāmanāṭṭam, plays on the Rāmāyaṇa composed in Malayalam by the ruler of Kottarakkara, is traditionally regarded as Kathakaḷi’s direct ancestor: by using Malayalam songs instead of Sanskrit it made the action intelligible to wider audiences. The training and body of the actors owed much to the martial art of Kerala, kaḷarippayaṯṯu, practised by the Nāyar warriors from whom most of the actors came (Zarrilli 2000; Jones and Jones 1970).

docs.title: 18.1.2 Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam at Guruvayur
docs.text: Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam survives as a temple art at the Kṛṣṇa temple of Guruvayur. Its text, Mānavēdan’s Sanskrit Kṛṣṇagīti, a song-poem modelled on Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda, is divided into eight plays covering the life of Kṛṣṇa from his birth to his ascent to heaven — Avatāram, Kāḷiyamardanam, Rāsakrīḍa, Kaṃsavadham, Svayaṃvaram, Bāṇayuddham, Vividavadham and Svargārohaṇam — which are performed on successive nights as offerings commissioned by devotees; by custom the cycle is not allowed to end with the death of Kṛṣṇa, and the first play is performed again after the last. The songs are sung by singers while the actors, who do not speak, dance and mime, some of them wearing painted wooden masks; the make-up and costumes resemble those of Kathakaḷi, which may have borrowed from them. Since the mid-twentieth century the troupe has been maintained by the temple administration, and performances take place in the temple precincts, where entry has been restricted to Hindus (Zarrilli 2000; Richmond et al. 1990).

docs.title: 18.1.3 The literature of Kathakaḷi
docs.text: A Kathakaḷi play is called an āṭṭakkatha (“story for performance”). It consists of Sanskrit verses (ślokas) that narrate the action, sung by the singers, and Malayalam songs (padams) that give the words of the characters, which the actors render in gesture. Among the most celebrated authors are the Kottayam Tampurān (late seventeenth century), whose four plays on episodes of the Mahābhārata — Bakavadham, Kalyāṇasaugandhikam, Kirmīravadham and Nivātakavacakālakeyavadham — set standards for the form; Uṇṇāyi Vāriyar (eighteenth century), whose Naḷacaritam, in four parts, is regarded as the masterpiece of Kathakaḷi literature; and Irayimman Tampi (1783–1856), author of Kīcakavadham and other plays. Other favourites include Duryodhanavadham, Kirātam and Uttarāsvayaṃvaram. The repertoire is drawn from the epics and the Purāṇas, and its plays are performed in selected scenes rather than complete (Zarrilli 2000).

docs.title: 18.1.4 The Kalamandalam
docs.text: By the early twentieth century Kathakaḷi had lost much of its royal and aristocratic patronage. The Malayalam poet Vallathol Narayana Menon (1878–1958), with Manakkulam Mukunda Raja, founded the Kerala Kalamandalam in 1930 to train actors and musicians in a residential school, recruiting the leading teachers of the time. The Kalamandalam standardised training, built a new audience for the form, sent troupes abroad and made Kathakaḷi internationally famous; it also, as critics have noted, tended to establish its own style as the norm at the expense of other lineages. Among the great actors of the twentieth century were Pattikkamthodi Ravunni Menon, a celebrated teacher, Kalamandalam Krishnan Nair, Kalamandalam Ramankutty Nair and Kalamandalam Gopi (Zarrilli 1984, 2000).

docs.title: 18.1.5 Caste and gender
docs.text: Kathakaḷi was created in a hierarchical society. Its patrons were kings, Nampūtiri Brahmin landlords and temples; its actors were mostly Nāyar men; and its audiences, until the twentieth century, were largely drawn from the upper castes, since performances took place in temple and household compounds from which lower castes were excluded. Women did not act. In the twentieth century the Kalamandalam and other schools opened training to students of other communities, and women’s Kathakaḷi troupes have performed since the 1970s, but the form’s social history remains a subject of discussion in Kerala (Zarrilli 2000).

docs.title: 18.2.1 Make-up and costume
docs.text:
Kathakaḷi’s make-up (vēṣam) classifies characters into types, each recognisable at once (Figure 18.1):

Pacca (“green”): noble heroes and gods, such as Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Arjuna and Naḷa, with green faces framed by a white ridge of rice paste and lime (cuṭṭi) that projects from the jaw. Katti (“knife”): arrogant and ambitious characters of royal rank, such as Rāvaṇa, Duryodhana and Kīcaka, with green faces marked by upturned red “knife” patterns on the cheeks and white knobs on the nose and forehead. Tāḍi (“beard”): the red-bearded (cuvanna tāḍi) evil and violent characters, such as Duśśāsana; the white-bearded (veḷḷa tāḍi), especially Hanumān; and the black-bearded (karutta tāḍi), forest-dwellers such as the hunter. Kari (“black”): demonesses and other savage characters. Minukku (“polished”): women, sages, Brahmins and messengers, with a simple yellowish-orange make-up.

The costume consists of a large, layered skirt over a padded frame, a jacket, ornaments, and an elaborate head-dress (kirīṭam) whose shape also indicates the character type. Applying the make-up takes several hours; senior actors lie on their backs while make-up artists build up the cuṭṭi. Actors redden the whites of their eyes for performance by placing a seed (cuṇṭappū) under the eyelid.

Figure 18.1. A Kathakaḷi actor in pacca (green) make-up and costume, the type used for noble heroes and gods. Photo: Niraksharan, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 18.2.2 Gesture and expression
docs.text: The actors do not speak. Their words are sung by two singers, the principal (poṉṉāni) and the second (śiṅkiṭi), and the actor renders each word in gesture, using the twenty-four basic hand gestures of the Hastalakṣaṇadīpikā in combination (Chapter 14), with the eyes and face expressing the emotion. Kathakaḷi’s facial technique is among the most elaborate in the world: actors practise daily exercises of the eyes, brows, cheeks and lips, and can show the transitory states of emotion (Chapter 3) in rapid succession or sustain a single state for many minutes. Between sung passages, the actors perform passages of pure dance (kalaśam) to the drums, and in passages of free elaboration (iḷakiyāṭṭam) they depart from the text to describe a scene or reflect on their situation.

docs.title: 18.2.3 Music
docs.text: The singers sing in a style derived from the Kerala temple music called sōpānam, using Karnatak rāgas with particular conventions; the principal singer keeps time with a gong (cēṅṅala) and the second with cymbals (ilattāḷam). The drummers play the cylindrical ceṇṭa, struck with sticks, which accompanies male characters and scenes of violence; the barrel-shaped maddaḷam, played with the hands; and, for female characters and gentle scenes, the hourglass iḍakka. The drumming follows every movement of the actor’s body and hands.

docs.title: 18.2.4 The structure of a performance
docs.text: A traditional Kathakaḷi performance begins at dusk with drumming (kēḷikoṭṭu) that announces the night’s performance to the surrounding villages, and continues through the night by the light of a large oil lamp at the front of the stage. Before the play come preliminary items: the tōṭayam, an invocatory dance performed behind a hand-held curtain (tiraśśīla); a benediction; the puṟappāṭu, a dance of entrance; and the mēḷappadam, a display of the musicians, in which a song from Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda is sung. The scenes of the play follow, each beginning with the dramatic lowering of the curtain held by two attendants, and the performance ends at dawn with a short closing dance. Modern performances in theatres are usually much shorter (Zarrilli 2000; Jones and Jones 1970).

docs.title: 18.2.5 Training
docs.text: Kathakaḷi training is famously rigorous. Students traditionally begin as boys, live at the school and train for many years. The day begins before dawn with exercises for the eyes and face and with physical exercises derived from kaḷarippayaṯṯu, including kicks, jumps and stretches; during the rainy season students receive a full-body massage with the feet (uḻiccil) by the teacher, intended to make the body supple. They then practise the basic steps and positions, the hand gestures and the dances and roles of the plays. Phillip Zarrilli’s studies of kaḷarippayaṯṯu and Kathakaḷi describe how this training produces a body in which the actor’s inner energy and concentration become visible (Zarrilli 1998, 2000).

docs.title: 18.2.6 A play in performance: Naḷacaritam
docs.text: Uṇṇāyi Vāriyar’s Naḷacaritam shows what Kathakaḷi literature and acting can achieve. Based on the story of Naḷa and Damayantī in the Mahābhārata, it is divided into four parts, each traditionally performed on a separate night. The first tells of the love of Naḷa and Damayantī, awakened by the reports of a golden swan who carries messages between them, and of their marriage despite the rivalry of the gods; the second of Naḷa’s loss of his kingdom at dice, possessed by the demon Kali, and of his desertion of Damayantī in the forest; the third of Naḷa’s transformation by the serpent Kārkoṭaka into the misshapen charioteer Bāhuka and his service at the court of Ṛtuparṇa; and the fourth of the reunion of the couple. The play is admired for the psychological depth of its characters, above all Naḷa and Damayantī in separation, and for the opportunities it gives actors to show complex and changing states of mind: the scene in which Naḷa, unable to bring himself to abandon his sleeping wife, leaves and returns several times is a celebrated test of acting. Its poetry, in a Sanskrit-rich Malayalam, is regarded as among the finest in the language (Zarrilli 2000).

docs.title: 18.2.7 Kathakaḷi in the modern world
docs.text: In the twentieth century Kathakaḷi became an emblem of Kerala and of Indian theatre. The Kalamandalam’s tours from the 1960s took it to Europe, the Soviet Union and the United States, and it attracted the interest of Western theatre practitioners, who saw in its training and its stylised acting an alternative to European realism. New plays were composed on subjects outside the epics — among them episodes from the Bible, Kerala history and Western literature — and the most famous of these experiments, a Kathakaḷi King Lear created in 1989 by the French dancer Annette Leday and the Australian playwright David McRuvie with Kalamandalam artists, was performed in Europe and at Shakespeare’s Globe in London, and provoked debate in Kerala about the limits of the form. Women’s troupes, short performances for tourists, and the use of Kathakaḷi imagery in advertising and in Kerala’s tourism promotion have all changed the form’s place in society, while the all-night performance in a temple compound before a village audience, though less frequent, continues (Zarrilli 2000).

docs.title: 18.3.1 History
docs.text:
Mohiniyāṭṭam, “the dance of the enchantress”, takes its name from Mohinī, the beautiful woman whose form Viṣṇu assumed to deceive the demons at the churning of the ocean. It is a solo dance performed by women. References to dance by this name occur in Malayalam literature of the eighteenth century, and the form flourished at the court of Travancore in the early nineteenth century, especially under the composer-king Svāti Tirunāḷ (1813–1846), who wrote songs for it and whose court was visited by Vaṭivēlu of the Thanjavur Quartet (Chapter 15). Like the court and temple dance of the Tamil country, it was performed by professional women whose way of life was condemned by reformers, and by the early twentieth century it had largely disappeared from respectable performance (Venu and Paniker 1983).

Its modern form was created at the Kerala Kalamandalam, where Vallathol introduced it in the 1930s. Teachers such as Thottassery Chinnammu Amma, one of the few remaining performers of the older style, taught there, and the dancer Kalamandalam Kalyanikutty Amma (1915–1999) did much to establish the form through her performance, teaching and writing. Like the other reconstructed forms, modern Mohiniyāṭṭam combines surviving traditions with new choreography and a new, “purified” image; its emphasis on restraint and devotional grace was in part a response to the stigma attached to the dance in the early twentieth century (Venu and Paniker 1983).

docs.title: 18.3.2 Technique and repertoire
docs.text: Mohiniyāṭṭam is characterised by a gentle, swaying movement of the torso from side to side (sometimes compared to the swaying of palm leaves or of a swing), soft, circular movements of the arms, a half-seated stance less deep than that of Bharatanāṭyam, and gliding footwork. Its basic steps (aṭavus) are taught in four groups, called taganam, jaganam, dhaganam and sammiśram. Its expressive technique draws on Kathakaḷi and on Kerala’s hand gestures, as well as on the vocabulary shared with Bharatanāṭyam. The repertoire includes a coḻkeṭṭu (an invocatory item of pure dance), jatisvaram, varṇam, padams and tillāna, many of them songs from Svāti Tirunāḷ’s court, in Malayalam (often in the Sanskrit-mixed style called Maṇipravāḷam), Sanskrit and Telugu. The music is Karnatak, sung in a manner influenced by the sōpānam style, with maddaḷam, iḍakka, violin and flute (Venu and Paniker 1983).

docs.title: 18.3.3 Costume and modern dancers
docs.text:
The dancer wears the white or off-white cotton sari of Kerala with a gold border (kasavu), arranged in pleats, with gold jewellery and the hair tied in a bun on the left side of the head and encircled with jasmine (Figure 18.2). The costume, which differs strikingly from the coloured silks of the other southern forms, was established in the twentieth century. Besides the Kalamandalam teachers, dancers such as Kanak Rele in Mumbai, Bharati Shivaji in Delhi and Kalamandalam Kshemavathy have developed and taught the form.

Figure 18.2. Mohiniyāṭṭam dancers, disciples of Jaya Prava Menon, at the Youth Festival, Delhi, 2012, in the white and gold kasavu costume, with jasmine round the hair-knot. Photo: Sumita Roy Dutta, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 18.3.4 Women’s performance in Kerala
docs.text: Mohiniyāṭṭam belongs to a wider world of women’s performance in Kerala. In Kūṭiyāṭṭam, women of the Nampyār community, the Naṅṅyārs, play the female roles and perform a solo genre, Naṅṅyār kūttu, in which an actress narrates and enacts episodes of the life of Kṛṣṇa (Chapter 19). Women’s group dances such as tiruvātirakkaḷi, performed in a circle at the festival of Tiruvātira, are part of domestic and community celebration. Some writers have suggested links between these forms and Mohiniyāṭṭam; the historical relations are uncertain, but together they show that Kerala women performed in many settings before the twentieth century.

docs.title: 18.4.1 The Meitei world
docs.text:
Manipur, in the far north-east of India on the border with Myanmar, was an independent kingdom of the Meitei people until 1891, when it came under British control, and became part of India in 1949. The Meitei had their own religion, centred on the worship of ancestral and local deities (lai), with priests (maibā) and priestesses (maibī). Its great ritual festival, Lai Haraoba (“the pleasing of the gods”), includes dances in which the maibīs, in trance, enact the creation of the world and the human body and the story of the god and goddess, and in which the community dances in procession. These dances, which survive, are an essential part of the background of Manipuri dance (Doshi 1989).

The hills around the Manipur valley are home to many other peoples, among them the Naga and Kuki-Chin communities, with their own dances, music and festivals, which are not part of “Manipuri” dance in the classical sense but are equally part of the region’s performing arts (Chapter 21).

docs.title: 18.4.2 Vaiṣṇavism and the Rāsalīlā
docs.text: In the eighteenth century the Meitei kings adopted Vaiṣṇavism, at first under King Pamheiba (Garib Niwaz, r. 1709–1748), and then in its Bengali Gauḍīya form, the devotion of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa taught by the followers of Caitanya, under King Bhāgyacandra (Ching-Thang Khomba, r. 1763–1798, with interruptions). Bhāgyacandra is credited with creating the Manipuri Rāsalīlā, the dance of Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā and the cowherd women on autumn and spring nights, in which the movement vocabulary of the Meitei ritual dances was combined with Vaiṣṇava songs and themes; tradition says that the form was revealed to him in a dream. Several kinds of rās are performed — among them the Mahārās, Vasantarās and Kuñjarās — on particular festival nights, in the courtyards of temples such as the Govindajī temple in Imphal, before the image of the god. Kṛṣṇa is played by a boy, and Rādhā and the cowherd women by girls and women (Doshi 1989).

docs.title: 18.4.3 Saṅkīrtana and the drum dances
docs.text:
The other great pillar of Manipuri performance is the saṅkīrtana (Nata Saṅkīrtana), the congregational singing of Vaiṣṇava songs by male singers who dance as they sing, accompanied by drummers playing the pung, a barrel drum, and players of large cymbals. The saṅkīrtana is performed at life-cycle ceremonies and festivals and in temples, and has a central place in Meitei religious and social life; it was inscribed by UNESCO on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013. Within it, the drummers’ dance (pung cholom) and the cymbal players’ dance (kartāl cholom) are virtuoso displays of leaps, turns and acrobatic movement performed while playing (Doshi 1989).

Manipur also has a martial art, thang-ta (sword and spear), whose movements have influenced dance, and popular dances such as the circle dance thabal chongba, performed on moonlit nights during the spring festival of Yaoshang.

docs.title: 18.4.4 Technique and costume
docs.text:
Manipuri movement is rounded and continuous, with the knees soft, the feet placed gently and without the percussive stamping of the southern forms, the body turning in spirals and the arms moving in curves. The vigorous male style (cholom) of the drum dances contrasts with the gentle movement of the Rāsalīlā. The costume of the cowherd women in the Rāsalīlā is one of the most striking in Indian dance: a stiff, cylindrical skirt (kumil), embroidered and decorated with mirrors, worn with a fine transparent veil over the face; Kṛṣṇa wears a peacock-feather crown and a yellow garment (Figure 18.3).

Figure 18.3. (a) A Manipuri Rāsalīlā: Kṛṣṇa, in a yellow garment and crown, among cowherd women in the stiff cylindrical skirt (kumil) and veil; (b) a drummer dancing the pung cholom with the pung slung at his waist. Both photographed in 2007. Photo: Matsukin (Flickr), CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 18.4.5 Tagore and the modern Manipuri
docs.text: Manipuri became known in the rest of India through Rabindranath Tagore, who saw a Manipuri dance performance at Sylhet (now in Bangladesh) in 1919 and invited Manipuri teachers to his school at Santiniketan, where the dance was taught from 1919–20 and later used in Tagore’s dance-dramas. In the following decades teachers from Manipur taught in Calcutta, Bombay and elsewhere; the Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy was founded at Imphal in 1954; and Guru Bipin Singh (1918–2000), working with the Jhaveri sisters of Bombay, developed a concert repertoire drawn from the Rāsalīlā, the saṅkīrtana and the Lai Haraoba. As with the other classical forms, the move to the concert stage involved selection and adaptation, and debates continue in Manipur about the relation between the ritual performances and the stage repertoire, and about the place of the older Meitei traditions within a dance identified as Vaiṣṇava (Doshi 1989).

docs.title: 18.5.1 Śaṅkaradeva and the sattras
docs.text:
Sattriya is the dance of the sattras, the monasteries of the Assamese Vaiṣṇava movement founded by Śaṅkaradeva and his disciple Mādhavadeva (traditional dates 1449–1568 and 1489–1596). Śaṅkaradeva’s “religion of one refuge” (ekaśaraṇa dharma) taught exclusive devotion to Kṛṣṇa expressed above all through hearing and singing his name and deeds (nām-kīrtana); it rejected the ritualism and caste exclusiveness of Brahmanical religion, opened devotion to people of all castes and to the tribal peoples of the Brahmaputra valley, and replaced image worship in many contexts with the scripture placed in the prayer hall (nāmghar). Śaṅkaradeva was a poet, composer, playwright and painter, and he made the performing arts the principal vehicle of his teaching (Neog 1980).

His one-act plays (aṅkīyā nāṭ), written in Brajabuli, a literary language mixing Assamese with Maithili and Braj forms, dramatise episodes from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa and the Rāmāyaṇa; their performance, called bhāonā, is led by a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and narrates, and includes music, dance, masks and processions. His devotional songs, the borgīts (“great songs”), set in particular rāgas, are still sung in the sattras and at the beginning of performances. The sattras, established throughout the Brahmaputra valley and especially on the river island of Majuli, became the custodians of this art. For centuries the dances were performed by celibate monks (bhakats) as part of the daily and festival rituals, in the nāmghar (Neog 1980).

docs.title: 18.5.2 The dances
docs.text:
The sattra repertoire includes the dances that form part of the bhāonā — the dance of the sūtradhāra, the dances of the characters such as Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd women — and independent dances such as the gāyan-bāyan (the dance of the singers and drummers who open performances, playing the khol drum and cymbals while dancing), the cāli (a graceful dance), the jhumurā, the nādu bhaṅgī and the dances of the Rās festival. Its technique is built on basic exercises called māṭi ākhorā (“ground exercises”); the basic stance, orā, has a masculine (puruṣa) and a feminine (prakṛti) form; and its movement combines vigorous and graceful qualities. The khol, a barrel-shaped clay drum, and cymbals (tāl) provide the rhythm, with their own repertoire of compositions (Figure 18.4).

Figure 18.4. Sattriya dancers, women and men, at the Khajuraho Dance Festival, Madhya Pradesh, 2026. Photo: Suyash Dwivedi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 18.5.3 From the monastery to the stage
docs.text: In the twentieth century the dances of the sattras began to be performed outside them, at first by monks and then by trained lay dancers, including women. After a long campaign by Assamese scholars and artists, the Sangeet Natak Akademi recognised Sattriya as a classical dance in 2000. Recognition brought support, teaching institutions and national and international audiences, and also the questions familiar from the other forms: which sattra’s style should be considered standard, how far the solo stage repertoire should depart from the monastic contexts, and how women should perform a tradition created by and for monks. Some sattras have welcomed the new practice; others insist on the separation of their ritual from the concert stage. The erosion of Majuli by the Brahmaputra, which threatens several of the most important sattras, adds to the urgency of documenting and sustaining the tradition (Neog 1980).

docs.title: 18.6 Common Themes
docs.text: These four forms illustrate, in different ways, the relation between dance and religious institutions in India: the temple and court in Kerala, the royal Vaiṣṇava state in Manipur, the monastery in Assam. In each case, devotion did not exclude other dimensions: Kathakaḷi’s plays are full of violence and comedy, Mohiniyāṭṭam’s songs of erotic longing, and the Manipuri Rāsalīlā is at once a ritual, a festival and a social occasion; and in each case the regional language, music and martial tradition gave the dance its character and made it a focus of regional identity. The twentieth-century institutions described above standardised training, created concert repertoires and opened the forms to new performers (in Kathakaḷi and Sattriya, to women), while raising questions about the relation between the stage forms and the communities and rituals from which they came.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Zarrilli (2000) is the best introduction to Kathakaḷi, its history, training and plays; Zarrilli (1984) and Jones and Jones (1970) are earlier studies, and Zarrilli (1998) describes the martial art on which Kathakaḷi training draws. Venu and Paniker (1983) describes Mohiniyāṭṭam. Doshi (1989) is a collection of essays on the dances of Manipur. Neog (1980) is the classic study of Śaṅkaradeva and the Assamese Vaiṣṇava movement. On the Kerala theatre see also Richmond et al. (1990).

docs.title: Chapter 19: Theatre Traditions
docs.text: India’s theatre is as old as its literature and as varied as its languages. Its oldest layer, the Sanskrit drama of the classical period, survives as literature and as theory, but only one tradition, the Kūṭiyāṭṭam of Kerala, still performs it; how the plays were staged, and what Kūṭiyāṭṭam can and cannot tell us about that, are the first concerns here, followed by the puppet theatres and the modern theatre of the nineteenth to twenty-first centuries. Sanskrit drama as literature is treated in Volume 8 of this series, Kāvya Kalpalatā; here the emphasis is on performance. The regional popular theatres are described in Chapter 20, the dance-dramas of Kerala, Andhra and Assam in Chapters 17 and 18, and ritual and folk performance in Chapter 21.

docs.title: 19.1.1 Conventions
docs.text: Sanskrit drama, as described in the Nāṭyaśāstra (Chapter 2) and practised by the playwrights of the first millennium CE, had distinctive conventions. Plays opened with a benediction and a prologue in which the director (sūtradhāra) introduced the play and the author. They mixed languages: kings, Brahmins and other high-status men spoke Sanskrit, while women, children and men of low status spoke Prakrit dialects, so that the social hierarchy was audible. They mixed prose dialogue with verse, sung or recited. They were divided into acts, with interludes (praveśaka, viṣkambhaka) in which minor characters reported events not shown on stage. The theory forbade the representation on stage of certain actions — death, battle, eating, sleeping and some others — which were reported rather than shown, and the great plays ended in the fulfilment of the hero’s aim rather than in catastrophe; “tragedy” in the Greek sense was not a Sanskrit genre. The vidūṣaka, the hero’s Brahmin jester, was a stock comic figure (Keith 1924; Raghavan 1993).

docs.title: 19.1.2 The dramatists
docs.text:
The earliest Sanskrit dramas of which fragments survive are Buddhist plays by Aśvaghoṣa (first or second century CE), found in manuscripts from Central Asia. Of the playwrights whose works survive complete, the most important are (Keith 1924):

Bhāsa. Known for centuries only by reputation — Kālidāsa names him as a famous predecessor — Bhāsa preceded Kālidāsa, though his date is uncertain. In 1909–10 T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī found in Kerala manuscripts of thirteen anonymous plays which he attributed to Bhāsa and published from 1912. The attribution remains debated: the plays may be acting versions transmitted and adapted by the Cākyār actors of Kerala. They include Svapnavāsavadatta, a romantic drama of King Udayana; Pratijñāyaugandharāyaṇa, a play of political intrigue; and short plays on episodes of the Mahābhārata, among them Ūrubhaṅga, which shows the dying Duryodhana on stage, an exception to the convention against showing death. Kālidāsa (c. fourth–fifth century CE). The greatest Sanskrit poet wrote three plays: the Mālavikāgnimitra, a court comedy about King Agnimitra and the dancer Mālavikā (Chapter 12); the Vikramorvaśīya, on King Purūravas and the nymph Urvaśī; and the Abhijñānaśākuntala, the story of King Duṣyanta and Śakuntalā, whose fourth act, in which Śakuntalā leaves her foster-father’s hermitage, an anonymous traditional verse singles out as the finest thing in all literature. Śūdraka (third–fifth century CE). The Mṛcchakaṭika (“The Little Clay Cart”), a ten-act prakaraṇa, tells of the love of the poor Brahmin merchant Cārudatta and the courtesan Vasantasenā against a background of gamblers, thieves, a corrupt royal brother-in-law, a trial and a political revolution; it is the liveliest picture of urban society in Sanskrit drama. Viśākhadatta (date uncertain; proposals range from the fifth to the ninth century). The Mudrārākṣasa is a political drama of the struggle between the ministers Cāṇakya and Rākṣasa. Harṣa (r. 606–647), king of Kanauj, is credited with two court comedies, Ratnāvalī and Priyadarśikā, and the Buddhist drama Nāgānanda. Bhavabhūti (early eighth century) wrote the Mālatīmādhava and the Uttararāmacarita, which dramatises Rāma’s banishment of Sītā with a depth of pathos (karuṇa) that later critics admired. Later playwrights. The tradition was continued by such works as the Veṇīsaṃhāra of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa, the Bālarāmāyaṇa and the Prakrit Karpūramañjarī of Rājaśekhara (c. 900), and the allegorical Prabodhacandrodaya of Kṛṣṇamiśra (eleventh century), and Sanskrit plays were written until modern times, increasingly as literary works rather than for performance.

docs.title: 19.1.3 Four plays
docs.text:
A brief look at four plays shows the range of the classical theatre. Kālidāsa’s Abhijñānaśākuntala (“Śakuntalā recognised by a token”) opens with King Duṣyanta, out hunting, entering a hermitage and falling in love with Śakuntalā, the foster-daughter of the sage Kaṇva, whom he first observes as she tries to escape a bee. They marry secretly, and the king returns to his capital, leaving her his signet ring. The irascible sage Durvāsas, neglected by the distracted Śakuntalā, curses her: her husband will forget her until he sees a token. In the fourth act, the most celebrated in Sanskrit drama, Śakuntalā takes leave of the hermitage, its trees, its creepers and its fawn; at court the king, under the curse, rejects her, for she has lost the ring. When a fisherman finds the ring in a fish, the king’s memory returns, and after long remorse he is reunited with Śakuntalā and their son in a celestial hermitage. The play’s blend of love, nature and pathos made it the most famous Sanskrit work in Europe after William Jones’s English translation of 1789, which Goethe and many others admired (Keith 1924).

Śūdraka’s Mṛcchakaṭika could hardly be more different. Its ten acts move between the house of the impoverished Brahmin Cārudatta, the mansion of the wealthy courtesan Vasantasenā, the streets of Ujjayinī and the court of law, with a gambler who becomes a Buddhist monk, a thief who steals for love, a vain and brutal royal brother-in-law, and a revolution that overthrows the king. Its humour, its realism and its sympathy for people of every class have made it a favourite of modern directors, who have staged it in many languages.

Bhavabhūti’s Uttararāmacarita takes up the most painful episode of the Rāma story, his banishment of the pregnant Sītā in deference to public opinion. In its third act Sītā, made invisible by the grace of the river goddess, watches Rāma as he revisits the forest where they once lived together and laments her loss; she hears his grief and he feels her presence, but they cannot meet. Unlike the epic, the play ends in reconciliation, through a play-within-the-play. Later critics regarded it as the supreme expression of the pathetic rasa (karuṇa), and Bhavabhūti himself declared that pathos is the one rasa of which the others are transformations.

Harṣa’s Nāgānanda (“The Joy of the Serpents”) is a Buddhist drama. Its hero, the prince Jīmūtavāhana, offers his own body to the divine bird Garuḍa to save the serpent who was to be Garuḍa’s victim that day, and is restored to life by the goddess Gaurī. Its blend of romantic comedy in the first acts with self-sacrifice in the last, and its religious inclusiveness, made it one of the few plays to enter the Kūṭiyāṭṭam repertoire (below). Together these plays show that the classical theatre could be courtly or urban, comic or tragic in mood, Hindu or Buddhist in inspiration, and that it addressed audiences who appreciated both poetry and spectacle (Keith 1924; Raghavan 1993).

docs.title: 19.1.4 Types of play
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra and Dhanañjaya’s Daśarūpaka (late tenth century) classify plays into ten types (rūpaka) according to the source of the plot, the type of hero, the dominant rasa and the number of acts (Table 19.1). Later writers added a large number of “minor” types (uparūpaka), among them the nāṭikā, a four-act court comedy such as Harṣa’s Ratnāvalī, and the saṭṭaka, written entirely in Prakrit, such as Rājaśekhara’s Karpūramañjarī; several uparūpakas were forms of dance-drama and song (Keith 1924).

Table 19.1. The ten types of play (daśarūpaka) Type Acts Characteristics nāṭaka 5–10 Well-known story; royal or divine hero; love or heroism dominant (e.g. Abhijñānaśākuntala) prakaraṇa 5–10 Invented story; hero a Brahmin, minister or merchant; heroine may be a courtesan (e.g. Mṛcchakaṭika) samavakāra 3 Gods and demons; several heroes; tumult and deceit ḍima 4 Violent action involving gods, demons and other beings īhāmṛga 4 A hero’s pursuit of a divine woman, with conflict vyāyoga 1 A martial episode not concerned with love aṅka (utsṛṣṭikāṅka) 1 Pathos; lamentation after battle bhāṇa 1 Monologue of a rake (viṭa) addressing imaginary companions prahasana 1 Farce satirising ascetics, Brahmins and others vīthī 1 A short piece for one or two characters

docs.title: 19.1.5 The structure of the plot
docs.text:
Sanskrit dramaturgy analysed the plot of a full play in three overlapping ways. The hero’s action passes through five stages (avasthā): beginning (ārambha), effort (prayatna), prospect of success (prāptyāśā), certainty of success (niyatāpti) and attainment of the goal (phalāgama). The plot consists of five elements (arthaprakṛti): the seed (bīja) from which the action grows, the drop (bindu) that carries it forward after interruptions, the extended episode (patākā), the brief episode (prakarī) and the denouement (kārya). And the play is divided into five junctures (sandhi) — opening (mukha), progression (pratimukha), development (garbha), pause or crisis (vimarśa) and conclusion (nirvahaṇa) — each with numerous sub-divisions (the Daśarūpaka lists sixty-four). The four dramatic styles (vṛtti) described in Chapter 2 characterise the tone of a play or scene (Keith 1924; Byrski 1974).

The system was used by critics to analyse the great plays, and its categories are a remarkable early analysis of dramatic form. Its value for understanding actual performance is more limited: it describes the ideal structure of a literary play, and most of the regional theatres described below were shaped by quite different principles.

docs.title: 19.1.6 The handbooks of dramaturgy after Bharata
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra was followed by a long series of handbooks on drama. Their literary side — the classification of plots, heroes and heroines and the theory of rasa — is treated in Volume 8; for the history of performance they matter chiefly for what they reveal about the forms of theatre and dance current in their authors’ time. Dhanañjaya’s Daśarūpaka, written at the Paramāra court of Mālava in the late tenth century, with the commentary of Dhanika (probably his brother), became the standard digest of dramatic theory and the source of most later discussions of the ten types of play. The Nāṭakalakṣaṇaratnakośa of Sāgaranandin, of uncertain date, was known only from quotations until Sylvain Lévi found a manuscript in Nepal in the early twentieth century. The Nāṭyadarpaṇa of Rāmacandra and Guṇacandra, two Jain pupils of Hemacandra in twelfth-century Gujarat, is notable for its independence: it holds that rasa may be painful as well as pleasurable, and it describes genres of performance that the older texts ignored. Śāradātanaya’s Bhāvaprakāśana (thirteenth century) and the Rasārṇavasudhākara of Siṃhabhūpāla (Śiṅgabhūpāla), the Recharla king who also commented on the Saṅgītaratnākara (Chapter 6), gather a great deal of information about minor dramatic forms and the music and dance of drama; Viśvanātha’s Sāhityadarpaṇa (fourteenth century, Odisha) gives the classic list of eighteen “minor” types (uparūpaka); and in the sixteenth century Rūpa Gosvāmin’s Nāṭakacandrikā adapted the theory to the devotional drama of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas, for which he himself wrote plays on the life of Kṛṣṇa (Keith 1924; Raghavan 1993).

The minor types are of special interest for the history of performance, because many of them were forms of dance and song rather than of spoken drama. The hallīśaka is a circular dance of women around a single man, the rāsaka and nāṭyarāsaka are danced and sung entertainments, and other forms in the lists are monologues, song-recitals or mimed episodes. V. Raghavan, who studied these lists in detail, argued that they record a large world of court and popular dance-drama, related to the deśī dances of the music treatises, which the classical theory had not recognised, and that several of them are the ancestors, at least in type, of the circle dances and dance-dramas of later regional tradition (Raghavan 1993). The handbooks thus document, in their own categories, the same movement from mārga to deśī that the treatises on music record (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 19.1.7 Language, caste and gender on the Sanskrit stage
docs.text: Sanskrit drama built social hierarchy into its form. Its heroes were kings and Brahmins; its women and servants spoke Prakrit; its comedy often turned on the low status of characters — the jester’s greed, the courtesan’s mercenary mother, the lower-caste executioners of the Mṛcchakaṭika. At the same time some plays gave remarkable prominence to women and to people of low status: the courtesan Vasantasenā is one of the most admirable characters of the Mṛcchakaṭika, whose plot ends with a cowherd made king. The actors themselves were of low status in the society that admired their art (Chapter 2), and women performers, who played the female roles, were often courtesans. Volume 8 discusses these questions further.

docs.title: 19.2 The Sanskrit Play in Performance
docs.text: The Sanskrit plays survive as literary texts, copied and commented upon by scholars, and they are usually studied as literature. But they were written for the stage, and their stage directions, their prologues and the prescriptions of the Nāṭyaśāstra allow something of their performance to be reconstructed. The limits of the evidence must be stated at once: no eyewitness account of the staging of a complete classical play survives from the first millennium, no theatre building of the period has been securely identified (Chapter 2), and the only continuous performance tradition, the Kūṭiyāṭṭam of Kerala (below), is a regional tradition of the second millennium, not a fossil of the theatre of Kālidāsa.

docs.title: 19.2.1 Occasions and audiences
docs.text: The prologues of the plays name the occasions on which they were performed and the audiences for whom they were intended. Plays of Kālidāsa and of Harṣa were, according to their prologues, presented at spring festivals before assemblies of connoisseurs; Bhavabhūti’s plays were staged at the festival of the god Kālapriyanātha; and many prologues praise the discernment of the audience (pariṣad) and the director’s anxiety to satisfy it. The theatre of the classical plays was thus a festival theatre of courts and temples, addressed to an educated audience who knew the conventions and the theory. One rare outside witness is the Kuṭṭanīmata (“The Bawd’s Counsel”), a satirical poem by Dāmodaragupta, a minister of the eighth-century Kashmiri king Jayāpīḍa, which describes in some detail a performance of the first act of Harṣa’s Ratnāvalī given in a temple at Varanasi, with comments on the acting and the audience’s response. Its description shows that the plays continued to be performed, in excerpts and at temple festivals, long after their composition (Keith 1924; Raghavan 1993).

docs.title: 19.2.2 The conventions of the stage
docs.text: The stage directions reveal a theatre of convention rather than illusion, the nāṭyadharmī mode of the Nāṭyaśāstra (Chapter 2). Characters enter and leave through a curtain (yavanikā or tiraskariṇī) at the back of the stage; an entry “with a toss of the curtain” (apaṭīkṣepeṇa) marks a hurried or agitated arrival. Actions are performed in mime: the stage direction nāṭayati or nāṭyena (“by acting”) accompanies the watering of plants, the plucking of flowers, the opening of a door or, in the first act of the Abhijñānaśākuntala, the driving of a chariot at speed, which the king and his charioteer represent by their movements alone. A journey is shown by walking round the stage, and the zones of the stage (kakṣyā) allow different places to be represented at once. Speech, too, is conventional. A character may speak “to himself” (svagatam) in the hearing of the audience but not of the other characters; “apart” to one character (janāntikam), screening the others with a hand gesture (tripatāka); “turning away” to share a secret (apavāritam); or “to the sky” (ākāśabhāṣitam), answering an unseen speaker whose words he repeats (“What do you say? …”). These conventions demanded an audience trained to read them, and they gave the actor’s body and voice, rather than scenery, the task of creating the world of the play (Keith 1924; Tarlekar 1975).

docs.title: 19.2.3 Song and music in the play
docs.text:
Music ran through the performance. The Nāṭyaśāstra places the musicians (kutapa) on the stage between the two doors of the dressing room, with singers, a vīṇā, a flute and drums, and its chapter on the songs of the stage (dhruvā) prescribes five kinds of song according to their function: songs of entry (prāveśikī), songs of exit (naiṣkrāmikī), songs that mark a change of mood or tempo (ākṣepikī), songs that soothe or please after an emotional climax (prāsādikī), and songs that fill an interval in the action (āntarā). The dhruvās were sung by the singers of the ensemble rather than by the actors, mostly in Prakrit, and they often introduced a character or a situation indirectly, by an image — a swan on a lake, an elephant in rut, the moon among clouds — that the audience was expected to apply to what it saw. They are the earliest documented instance of a principle that runs through Indian theatre: that song frames, comments on and intensifies the action (Ghosh 1950; Rowell 1992).

The manuscripts of the plays seldom record the dhruvās, which belonged to the musicians’ repertoire rather than to the author’s text, but several plays include songs within the action. In the second act of Kālidāsa’s Mālavikāgnimitra the heroine performs a song and dance before the king as a test of her teacher’s skill (Chapter 12); in the fifth act of the Abhijñānaśākuntala a song in Prakrit, sung offstage by one of the king’s queens, reminds him of a love he has forgotten; and the fourth act of the Vikramorvaśīya, in which the maddened king searches the forest for Urvaśī, contains in some recensions a series of songs in Apabhraṃśa with directions for their musical and danced performance, whose authenticity is disputed but which show how a later stage elaborated the play in music and dance.

docs.title: 19.2.4 Speech and the actor’s voice
docs.text: The Nāṭyaśāstra treats the delivery of the spoken and recited text (pāṭhya) as a branch of acting (vācika, Chapter 3), and analyses it in musical terms: the notes, registers and pitch contours of the voice, the intonation (kāku) that distinguishes a question from a statement and irony from sincerity, and the tempo appropriate to each rasa. Verses were not merely spoken but delivered in a heightened, partly chanted manner, and the actor’s voice was trained as carefully as his body. The mixture of languages was a performing as well as a literary convention (Volume 8): an actor had to command Sanskrit and the Prakrit appropriate to his role, and manuscripts of the plays, especially from the south, often supply a Sanskrit paraphrase (chāyā) of the Prakrit passages, a sign that by the second millennium Prakrit was no longer understood without help. The Kerala actors, who still speak the Prakrit of the plays on stage, learn it with such paraphrases and deliver it in a characteristic intoned style.

docs.title: 19.2.5 The vidūṣaka on stage
docs.text: The vidūṣaka, the Brahmin jester and companion of the hero (Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā), was above all a performer’s role. The Nāṭyaśāstra describes his stage appearance in comic terms — short, bald, with protruding teeth and a distorted face, carrying a crooked staff — and assigns him an eastern Prakrit; his comedy lay in his greed for sweets, his cowardice, his misuse of learned language and his deflation of the hero’s romantic rhetoric. He also has a place in the ritual preliminaries: the Nāṭyaśāstra’s pūrvaraṅga includes a comic three-way dialogue (trigata) between the director, his assistant and the jester. F. B. J. Kuiper argued from this and other evidence that the jester descended from a ritual antagonist in a cosmogonic contest enacted in the preliminaries, and David Shulman has explored, in the South Indian traditions, the jester as the comic double of the king, who exposes the limits of royal and sacred authority (Kuiper 1979; Shulman 1985). Whatever his origins, the vidūṣaka became the actor closest to the audience, and it is in his role that the Kerala theatre developed its most elaborate improvisations (below).

docs.title: 19.2.6 The classical plays on the modern stage
docs.text: Outside Kerala, the Sanskrit plays returned to the stage in the colonial period as part of the rediscovery of a classical heritage. Translations and adaptations of the Abhijñānaśākuntala were among the first productions of the new theatres in the regional languages: Annasaheb Kirloskar’s Marathi musical Śākuntal of 1880 (below) was the founding work of the Marathi musical stage. In independent India the plays have been staged both in Sanskrit and in translation. The annual Kālidāsa festival at Ujjain, held since the late 1950s, presents productions of Kālidāsa’s plays; Habib Tanvir’s Hindustani version of the Mṛcchakaṭika, Miṭṭī kī Gāṛī, first staged in the 1950s and later revived with his company of Chhattisgarhi folk actors, became one of the classics of the modern Indian stage; and the plays attributed to Bhāsa, with their short length, epic subjects and unusual willingness to show violence and death on stage, attracted directors of the “theatre of roots” (below). K. N. Panikkar staged several of them in Sanskrit with his company in Thiruvananthapuram, drawing on Kūṭiyāṭṭam, Kathakaḷi and the martial art of Kerala, and Ratan Thiyam’s Manipuri Ūrubhaṅgam (1981), on the death of Duryodhana, made the play internationally known. These productions do not reconstruct ancient performance, which cannot be recovered; they are modern interpretations that use the conventions of the Sanskrit play — the narrator, the mime, the mixture of speech, song and dance — to create a theatre different from European realism, as the playwrights of the classical period had done in their own way (Dharwadker 2005).

docs.title: 19.3.1 History and community
docs.text: Kūṭiyāṭṭam (“combined acting”) is the performance of Sanskrit drama in Kerala, and the only living tradition of Sanskrit theatre. It is performed by the Cākyārs, a community of temple servants, who play the male roles; by women of the Nampyār community, the Naṅṅyārs, who play the female roles and sing; and by Nampyār men, who play the large copper pot-drum (miḻāvu). Its documented history goes back about a thousand years; tradition credits a Cēra king, Kulaśekhara, himself the author of two Sanskrit plays, with reforming it and introducing the use of Malayalam for the jester. For most of its history it was performed only in special temple theatres (kūttampalam) before audiences of upper-caste Hindus, as a form of temple service (Richmond et al. 1990; Brandon 1993).

docs.title: 19.3.2 Repertoire and technique
docs.text:
Kūṭiyāṭṭam does not perform whole plays. It stages single acts, over several nights, from a small repertoire of plays: works attributed to Bhāsa, Śaktibhadra’s Āścaryacūḍāmaṇi, Harṣa’s Nāgānanda, Kulaśekhara’s plays and a few others, following acting manuals preserved in Malayalam (below). The actor speaks the Sanskrit and Prakrit text in a chanting delivery, interpreting each word with gestures based on the Hastalakṣaṇadīpikā (Chapter 14; Figure 19.1), and elaborates the meaning of each verse at length, sometimes playing several characters in turn (pakarnnāṭṭam). The technique of the eyes and face (netrābhinaya) is extraordinarily refined; the actor Māṇi Mādhava Cākyār (1899–1990) became famous for it (Richmond et al. 1990).

Figure 19.1. A Kūṭiyāṭṭam performance: an actor in costume and make-up, seated on a stool beside the large oil lamp (nilaviḷakku); at the right are an iṭakka player and a miḻāvu drum in its wooden frame. Photo: Ramesh Lalwani, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (from Flickr)

docs.title: 19.3.3 The theatre and the ensemble
docs.text: The kūttampalam is a rectangular building within the temple enclosure, facing the shrine, with a raised square stage under its own roof, supported by pillars; the best known, such as that of the Vaṭakkunnāthan temple at Thrissur, are among the finest examples of Kerala’s timber architecture (Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa). A great bell-metal lamp (nilaviḷakku) stands at the front of the stage; behind the actor, the two miḻāvu drums sit in wooden frames, played by Nampyār drummers with the flat of the hands. The ensemble is completed by the hourglass drum iṭakka, whose pitch can be bent by tightening its lacing, a short double-reed pipe (kuṟumkuḻal), a conch and the small cymbals (kuḻittāḷam) played by the Naṅṅyār, who sits at the side of the stage and recites verses at fixed points. A performance is an offering: it is sponsored as a votive act, the stage is ritually prepared, and the lamp is lit as for worship. The audience traditionally sat on the floor of the hall, and in some temples the performance of certain acts was an annual obligation of the temple (Richmond et al. 1990; Jones 1984).

docs.title: 19.3.4 The shape of a performance
docs.text:
Because Kūṭiyāṭṭam stages single acts and elaborates them at great length, an act may occupy many nights. The performance of an act normally begins with the ceremonial entrance (puṟappāṭu) of its principal character, danced behind and then in front of a hand-held curtain. On the following nights the actor, alone on stage, presents the nirvahaṇam, the retrospective narration of the events that led to the act, in gesture and facial expression, often taking on the roles of several characters in turn. Only then is the text of the act itself performed, with the characters together on stage — the “combined acting” that gives the form its name. The actor first speaks or intones a line or verse of the text, then interprets it word by word in gesture, and then elaborates its situation and emotion in an improvisation (āṭṭam) that may last far longer than the recitation; a single verse can occupy an hour or more. The Malayalam manuals preserved in the actors’ families specify what is to be elaborated and how: the āṭṭaprakāram sets out the acting of each passage, and the kramadīpikā the order of the performance, the music and the ritual procedures. Clifford Reis Jones’s edition and translation of Śaktibhadra’s Āścaryacūḍāmaṇi together with its manuals made these texts available to scholars and showed how the written play, the manual and the actor’s knowledge combine in performance (Jones 1984).

Some acts became celebrated set pieces. In the Aṅgulīyāṅkam, the sixth act of the Āścaryacūḍāmaṇi, Hanumān brings Rāma’s ring to Sītā in Laṅkā, and the actor playing Hanumān narrates the whole story of the Rāmāyaṇa up to that point in gesture over many nights; in temples where it was performed as an annual ritual, the complete performance extended over several weeks. The Mantrāṅkam, the third act of the Pratijñāyaugandharāyaṇa attributed to Bhāsa, is famous for its long passages for the jester. Kerala’s own Sanskrit plays, the Subhadrādhanañjaya and Tapatīsaṃvaraṇa of King Kulaśekhara, are known with a commentary, the Vyaṅgyavyākhyā, which reflects the early practice of the Kerala stage, and the Pallava king Mahendravarman’s farce Mattavilāsa (Volume 8) is performed in an abbreviated, partly ritual form (Richmond et al. 1990).

docs.title: 19.3.5 The jester’s nights
docs.text: The vidūṣaka of Kūṭiyāṭṭam is the most developed jester of any Indian theatre. In the acts in which he has a major part he performs alone on several nights before the play proper. He speaks Malayalam as well as Sanskrit and Prakrit, translating and expounding the verses of the hero for the audience, and he presents comic disquisitions on the four “aims of man” of the jester — eating (aśana), serving the king (rājasevā), amusement (vinoda) and cheating (vañcana) — which parody the four aims of life of Brahmanical teaching. His improvisations range over the follies of every class, the pretensions of scholars and the conduct of the powerful, and the convention that he speaks the truth under licence made him a channel of social criticism within the temple itself (Shulman 1985; Richmond et al. 1990).

docs.title: 19.3.6 Cākyār kūttu and Naṅṅyār kūttu
docs.text: Two solo genres grew out of the same tradition. In Cākyār kūttu (also called prabandham kūttu), a single Cākyār in the costume of the vidūṣaka tells a story from the epics or Purāṇas, reciting Sanskrit verses from narrative poems in mixed prose and verse (campū and prabandha), many of them composed for this purpose by Kerala poets such as Mēlpputtūr Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri, and expounding them in Malayalam with witty asides at the expense of the audience, including its most eminent members, who by convention could not answer back. Māṇi Mādhava Cākyār and Painkulam Rama Chakyar were among the great twentieth-century exponents of the form. In Naṅṅyār kūttu, the female counterpart, a Naṅṅyār performs alone, over many nights, the story of Kṛṣṇa, presented as narrated by a maid of the heroine of Kulaśekhara’s Subhadrādhanañjaya, in gesture and expression to verses that are usually recited by a second Naṅṅyār keeping time with cymbals; the genre was revived in the late twentieth century after a period of decline. Both genres, like Kūṭiyāṭṭam itself, have been transformed by their move from the temple to public stages and schools, and both have attracted new performers, women and men, from outside the hereditary communities.

docs.title: 19.3.7 From temple to stage
docs.text: In the mid-twentieth century Kūṭiyāṭṭam began to be performed outside temples. Painkulam Rama Chakyar (1905–1980) and others took it to public stages and taught it at the Kerala Kalamandalam, where students from outside the Cākyār and Nampyār communities began to learn it, and the great actor Ammannur Madhava Chakyar (1917–2008) trained students at Irinjalakuda. In 2001 UNESCO proclaimed Kūṭiyāṭṭam a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, one of the first such proclamations. The opening of the art to new performers and audiences has saved it from extinction but has raised questions about its relation to the temple and to the communities who kept it for centuries.

docs.title: 19.4 Regional Theatres
docs.text: From the medieval period onwards the regional languages developed their own theatres, many of them combining song, dance, narration and improvised dialogue in all-night performances on religious and epic themes: Yakṣagāna in Karnataka, Terukkūttu in Tamil Nadu, Jātrā in Bengal, Tamāśā in Maharashtra, Nauṭaṅkī and its relatives in the north, Bhavāī in Gujarat, the Rāmlīlā and Rāslīlā of the Hindi-speaking region and many others. They are described in Chapter 20; the dance-dramas of Kerala, Andhra and Assam are described in Chapters 17 and 18.

docs.title: 19.5 Puppet Theatre
docs.text:
India has a rich tradition of puppet theatre. The word sūtradhāra (“holder of the string”) for the director of a play has led some scholars to suggest that drama itself developed from puppetry, a theory now generally regarded as unproven (Chapter 2). Four main kinds of puppet are used (Varadpande 1987; Blackburn 1996):

String puppets: the kaṭhputlī of Rajasthan, presented by itinerant Bhāṭ families; the gombeyāṭa of Karnataka; and others in Odisha, Andhra and Tamil Nadu. Rod puppets: the putul nāc of West Bengal and the rod puppets of Odisha. Glove puppets: the pāvakathakaḷi of Kerala, which uses the stories and costume conventions of Kathakaḷi, and glove puppet shows in Uttar Pradesh and Odisha. Shadow puppets: the tōlpāvakkūttu of Kerala, the tholu bommalāṭa of Andhra Pradesh with its large, coloured leather figures, the togalu gombeyāṭa of Karnataka and the rāvaṇachāyā of Odisha.

The tōlpāvakkūttu of central Kerala, studied by Stuart Blackburn, is performed in special theatres attached to temples of the goddess Bhadrakāḷī. Puppeteers of the Pulavar families present the story of Rāma, following the Tamil Irāmāvatāram of Kampaṉ, over many nights, behind a white screen lit by a row of oil lamps; the performance is said to be offered to the goddess, who missed the battle of Rāma and Rāvaṇa because she was herself fighting a demon.
