The puppeteers’ commentary, in a mixture of Tamil and Malayalam, explains and debates the meaning of the verses, so that the performance is also a form of learned exegesis (Blackburn 1996).

The other traditions are as varied as the regions. The kaṭhputlī string puppeteers of Rajasthan, itinerant families of the Bhāṭ community, perform above all the story of Amar Singh Rāṭhoṛ, a seventeenth-century Rajput noble at the Mughal court, with a cast of courtiers, dancers, jugglers and horsemen; the puppeteer gives the puppets their voices through a reed held in the mouth, while a woman of the family sings and plays the ḍholak and narrates the story. The tholu bommalāṭa of Andhra Pradesh uses large, jointed figures of translucent leather, painted in strong colours, which throw coloured shadows on the screen (Figure 19.2); its repertoire comes from the Telugu Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, and its pair of comic characters, a quarrelsome husband and wife, comment on the action and on village life. The related togalu gombeyāṭa of Karnataka uses similar figures, while the rāvaṇachāyā of Odisha uses small, unjointed, opaque figures of deer-skin and a sung Odia Rāmāyaṇa. The rod puppets (putul nāc) of Bengal perform the repertoire of the jātrā, and the glove-puppet pāvakathakaḷi of Kerala, revived in the second half of the twentieth century, presents Kathakaḷi stories with miniature Kathakaḷi costumes and music.

Figure 19.2. (a) Rajasthani kaṭhputlī string puppets before their booth, with a musician playing the ḍholak, Jaipur, 2009; (b) painted leather figures of the tholu bommalāṭa against a lit screen, Hyderabad, 2019. Photo: Ravikiran Rao, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Like other hereditary performers, the puppeteers suffered from the loss of patronage and the competition of cinema and television, and many families abandoned the art or turned to selling puppets to tourists. At the same time puppetry has been taken up by modern artists and educators: the Sangeet Natak Akademi and other bodies have supported traditional troupes, and urban companies such as Dadi Pudumjee’s Ishara Puppet Theatre in Delhi have combined traditional techniques with contemporary themes and international collaboration, while puppets have been widely used in education and public-health campaigns.

docs.title: 19.6.1 Colonial-era theatres
docs.text: Modern Indian theatre began in the colonial cities in the nineteenth century. In Calcutta, Bengali amateur and then professional theatres staged plays modelled partly on English drama, partly on Sanskrit and Bengali traditions; the Bengali public theatre, established from 1872, produced a vigorous commercial drama, and its leading figure Girish Chandra Ghosh and its star actress Binodini Dasi, a woman of courtesan background who left a remarkable autobiography, made it a major institution. Dinabandhu Mitra’s Nīl Darpaṇ (1860), which exposed the oppression of indigo cultivators, and later nationalist plays alarmed the colonial government, which passed the Dramatic Performances Act of 1876 to censor plays it considered seditious. In Bombay and western India the commercial Parsi theatre and the Marathi musical drama, beginning with Annasaheb Kirloskar’s Śākuntal (1880), created the popular stage described below (Dharwadker 2005; Bharucha 1983).

docs.title: 19.6.2 The Parsi theatre and the company theatres
docs.text:
The most widely seen theatre of colonial India was neither the folk theatre of the villages nor the literary drama of the educated elite, but the commercial “company” theatre. Its prototype was the Parsi theatre of Bombay. Parsi amateur clubs began staging plays in the 1850s — an early landmark was a Gujarati Rustam and Sohrab in 1853 — and by the 1870s professional companies owned by Parsi entrepreneurs, such as the Victoria and the Alfred theatrical companies, were performing in Gujarati, Urdu and Hindustani in purpose-built theatres. The companies took their models from the English stage of Bombay, with its proscenium, painted drop scenes and stage machinery, and from Indian sources: the Urdu musical drama Indar Sabhā, first performed at Lucknow in the 1850s, Persian romance, the epics and Purāṇas, and adaptations of Shakespeare. Their plays were full of songs set to rāgas and popular tunes, of spectacle and of melodrama, and they toured throughout India and to Southeast Asia and East Africa (Gupt 2005; Hansen 2011).

The companies employed actors, musicians and writers from many communities. Their most celebrated playwright, Agha Hashr Kashmiri (1879–1935), wrote Urdu and Hindi plays that were performed for decades; Narayan Prasad Betab and Radheshyam Kathavachak wrote mythological plays in Hindi. Women’s roles were long played by men, some of whom became famous for them, while the first actresses, often from Anglo-Indian or courtesan families, faced the stigma attached to women on the stage. Kathryn Hansen’s work on the autobiographies of Parsi theatre actors shows how the companies created a new kind of professional performer and a public that crossed lines of religion, language and class (Hansen 2011). When sound cinema arrived in 1931, the Parsi theatre supplied it with its first actors, writers, musicians, theatre owners and much of its dramatic idiom (Chapter 23).

Other regions developed their own company theatres. In Maharashtra the musical drama (saṅgīt nāṭak) reached its height in the first decades of the twentieth century with the singer-actor Bal Gandharva (1888–1967), who played women’s roles with a grace that set fashions for women in the audience; its songs, the nāṭyasaṅgīt, are described in Section 11.7. In the Tamil country, the touring “company drama” was shaped by Sankaradas Swamigal (1867–1922), who wrote and directed plays for “boys’ companies” of child actors; its singer-actors, among them K. B. Sundarambal and M. K. Thyagaraja Bhagavathar, became stars of early Tamil cinema, and from the 1940s Dravidian movement writers, among them C. N. Annadurai and M. Karunanidhi, used the stage and the screen to spread their political message. In Andhra the Surabhi family companies have performed mythological plays since the late nineteenth century, and the Telugu padya nāṭakam, in which actors sing verses in elaborate musical settings, remains popular. These theatres are often dismissed as commercial or derivative, but they were the theatre of most Indians for three generations, and much of the music, acting style and storytelling of Indian cinema descends from them (Dharwadker 2005).

docs.title: 19.6.3 After 1940
docs.text: The Indian People’s Theatre Association (IPTA), founded in 1943 and associated with the Communist Party, brought together writers, actors, musicians and dancers to create political theatre; its Bengali production Nabānna (1944) by Bijon Bhattacharya, about the Bengal famine, is a landmark. After Independence the state founded the National School of Drama in Delhi (1959), which under Ebrahim Alkazi’s direction (1962–1977) trained a generation of directors and actors. A modern theatre in the Indian languages flourished, with playwrights such as Mohan Rakesh in Hindi (Āṣāḍh kā ek din, 1958), Vijay Tendulkar in Marathi (Ghāshīrām Kotvāl, 1972), Girish Karnad in Kannada (Tughlaq, 1964; Hayavadana, 1971) and Badal Sircar in Bengali, who developed a “Third Theatre” of minimal means performed in open spaces outside the proscenium (Dharwadker 2005).

docs.title: 19.6.4 Theatre in the languages
docs.text: Modern Indian theatre is not one theatre but many, each with its own centres, audiences and history. In Bengal, the “group theatre” movement that grew out of IPTA after 1947 produced companies such as Sombhu Mitra’s Bohurupee, whose productions of Tagore’s plays, among them Raktakarabī, were landmarks, and the political theatre of Utpal Dutt; Kolkata’s amateur and semi-professional groups remain among the most active in India. In Maharashtra, a lively commercial and experimental theatre in Marathi, with playwrights from Vijay Tendulkar to Mahesh Elkunchwar and Satish Alekar and directors such as Vijaya Mehta, has coexisted with the popular Tamāśā and the musical drama. In Karnataka, the playwrights Girish Karnad and Chandrashekhar Kambar drew on myth and folk forms, and the rural theatre institute Ninasam at Heggodu, founded by K. V. Subbanna, created audiences for serious theatre in villages and small towns. In Kerala, G. Sankara Pillai and K. N. Panikkar developed a theatre rooted in Kerala’s ritual and performance traditions; in Manipur, Heisnam Kanhailal and Ratan Thiyam made Imphal one of the centres of experimental theatre in India; in Tamil Nadu, the popular “company drama” of the early twentieth century, which trained many of the stars of Tamil cinema, gave way to a smaller modern theatre and to Dalit and feminist groups. Hindi theatre, centred on Delhi, the National School of Drama and the cities of the Hindi belt, has been shaped by translation as much as by original writing, with plays from every Indian language and from world drama (Dharwadker 2005).

docs.title: 19.6.5 Theatre and tradition
docs.text:
From the 1960s many directors sought to create a modern Indian theatre that drew on traditional forms rather than on Western realism. Habib Tanvir (1923–2009) worked with folk performers from Chhattisgarh in his Naya Theatre, whose Charandas Chor (1975) became internationally known; B. V. Karanth used Yakṣagāna and other regional forms; K. N. Panikkar drew on Kerala’s performance traditions and Sanskrit drama; and Ratan Thiyam’s Chorus Repertory Theatre in Imphal used Manipuri martial arts and ritual. This “theatre of roots”, encouraged by state institutions, produced some of the most celebrated productions of the period. Critics such as Rustom Bharucha argued that it sometimes treated folk forms as raw material for urban audiences and the state’s cultural projects, detached from the communities who performed them (Bharucha 1993); Aparna Dharwadker places the movement in the longer history of post-Independence theatre (Dharwadker 2005).

Other strands of modern theatre have been more directly political. Street theatre, such as that of the Jana Natya Manch, whose founder Safdar Hashmi was killed during a performance in 1989, took plays to workers and slum-dwellers; Dalit theatre in Maharashtra and elsewhere, from the 1970s, staged experiences of caste oppression; and women directors and writers, among them Vijaya Mehta, Usha Ganguli, Anuradha Kapur and Amal Allana, have created theatre that questions the gender conventions of both traditional and modern forms. Festivals such as the National School of Drama’s Bharat Rang Mahotsav (from 1999) and institutions such as Ninasam in rural Karnataka and the Rangayana repertory in Mysore sustain a varied theatre culture in many languages.

docs.title: 19.7 Continuities
docs.text: Across this diversity some features recur: the narrator who stands between the play and the audience (the sūtradhāra of Sanskrit drama, the bhāgavata of Yakṣagāna, the Vivek of Jātrā, the clown of Tamāśā and Terukkūttu (Chapter 20), the puppeteer-commentator of tōlpāvakkūttu); the combination of song, dance and speech; the long, often all-night performance; the importance of improvisation within a fixed framework; and the close relation of performance to festival and ritual. These continuities should not be taken to mean that Indian theatre is unchanging or that it all descends from the Nāṭyaśāstra. The regional forms grew out of their own languages, religious movements, patrons and audiences, and the modern theatre out of the colonial city and the nation. What links them is less a common origin than a shared repertoire of stories and techniques, adapted again and again to new circumstances.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Richmond et al. (1990) is the best introduction to India’s traditional theatres, and Brandon (1993) places them in an Asian context. Keith (1924) and Raghavan (1993) remain standard on Sanskrit drama, and Byrski (1974) and Lidova (1994) discuss its religious context; Kuiper (1979) and Shulman (1985) interpret the jester. Jones (1984) edits a Kūṭiyāṭṭam play with its acting manuals, and Blackburn (1996) studies the Kerala shadow puppets; for the regional theatres see Chapter 20. For modern theatre see Dharwadker (2005), Bharucha (1983) on the political theatre of Bengal and Bharucha (1993) on intercultural theatre and the “theatre of roots”; Lal (2004) is a reference companion to the whole field. For the Parsi theatre Gupt (2005) and Hansen (2011); Varadpande (1987) gives a general history.

docs.title: Chapter 20: Regional and Popular Theatres
docs.text:
From the late medieval period onwards each of India’s major languages developed theatres of its own. Most of them combine song, dance, narration and spoken dialogue; most are performed in the open air, often through the night, at festivals or fairs; and most were, until recently, the work of hereditary or professional troupes drawn from particular communities. They are usually called “folk” or “traditional” theatres, but neither word is quite right. Many have written texts, printed and sold in large numbers; many are professional and commercial; and several are not old, having taken their present forms in the nineteenth or twentieth century. What distinguishes them from the Sanskrit drama of the classical period (Chapter 19) is their use of the regional languages, their roots in particular religious movements and local patrons, and their audiences, which until the coming of cinema included most of the people of India.

Several regional theatres are described in other chapters: the dance-dramas of Kerala, Kathakaḷi and Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam (Chapter 18); the Kuchipudi and Bhāgavata Mēḷa dance-dramas of the Telugu tradition (Chapter 17); the aṅkīyā nāṭ of Assam (Chapter 18); the ritual theatres of Teyyam and Chhau and the bardic performances of the epics (Chapter 21); and the puppet theatres (Chapter 19). The theatres described here are the principal popular theatres of the other regions: Yakṣagāna of Karnataka, Terukkūttu of Tamil Nadu, Jātrā of Bengal, Tamāśā of Maharashtra, Nauṭaṅkī and its relatives in the north, Bhavāī of Gujarat and Bhāṇḍ Pāthar of Kashmir, the Rāmlīlā and Rāslīlā of the Hindi-speaking region, and several others. It ends with the performers themselves and with the place of these theatres in modern India.

docs.title: 20.1 The Regional Theatres at a Glance
docs.text:
Table 20.1 gives an overview of the forms discussed in this chapter (Richmond et al. 1990; Varadpande 1987), and Figure 20.1 places several of them, with the centres of the classical dances, on a map. They differ greatly in language, subject and style, but they share a family of features. Most of them have a figure who stands between the play and the audience — a singer-narrator, a director, a clown or a commentator — who introduces the characters, links the scenes and comments on the action. Most use music continuously, with a small ensemble of drums, cymbals and a melodic instrument; their texts are largely sung, and their actors must be singers. Most perform in an arena or on a simple platform, with the audience on three or four sides, and use few properties and little scenery. Most mix fixed text and improvisation: the songs are fixed, but the dialogue that expands them is made up afresh at each performance. And most, until the mid-twentieth century, were performed entirely by men, with female roles played by female impersonators, whose art was admired as one of the summits of the actor’s skill.

Table 20.1. Some regional theatre traditions Form Region Characteristics Yakṣagāna Coastal Karnataka Dance-drama on epic themes; singer-narrator (bhāgavata); improvised dialogue; spectacular costume Terukkūttu Tamil Nadu All-night street theatre on the Mahābhārata, linked with the cult of Draupadī Jātrā Bengal, Odisha, Assam Popular musical theatre on mythological, historical and social themes; open-air arena Tamāśā Maharashtra Popular theatre of song (lāvaṇī), dance and comic sketches Nauṭaṅkī Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Punjab Sung verse drama with the nagāṛā kettledrum Svāṅg, Khyāl Haryana, Rajasthan Verse dramas with music, related to Nauṭaṅkī Māc Madhya Pradesh Sung folk drama of the Malwa region Bhavāī Gujarat Satirical sketches (veṣa) performed at festivals of the goddess Bhāṇḍ Pāthar Kashmir Satirical theatre of hereditary performers Rāmlīlā North India Enactment of the Rāmāyaṇa over many days, especially at Ramnagar (Varanasi) Rāslīlā Braj Devotional dance-drama of Kṛṣṇa, performed by boy actors Special Nāṭakam Tamil Nadu Musical drama by actors hired individually for each night Pālā, Prahlāda Nāṭaka Odisha Sung narrative with chorus; devotional drama of Narasiṃha Shumang Līlā Manipur Courtyard theatre of social comedy and satire Ōṭṭan Tuḷḷal Kerala Solo sung and danced narration with social satire Figure 20.1. Centres associated with the classical dances and with some of the regional theatres described in this volume, each marked at a representative place: Thanjavur (Bharatanāṭyam), Thrissur district (Kathakaḷi, Mohiniyāṭṭam and Kūṭiyāṭṭam), Kuchipudi village (position approximate), Puri (Odissi), Lucknow and Jaipur (two centres of Kathak), Seraikela, Purulia and Mayurbhanj (the three styles of Chhau), Udupi (Yakṣagāna), the Kanchipuram region (Terukkūttu), Pune (Tamāśā), north Gujarat (Bhavāī, position approximate), Kanpur (Nauṭaṅkī), Vrindavan (Rāslīlā), Ramnagar near Varanasi (Rāmlīlā) and Kolkata (Jātrā). The forms are performed over much wider areas than a single point can show. Manipuri (Imphal) and Sattriya (Majuli) lie east of the frame, and Bhāṇḍ Pāthar (Kashmir) north of it. Positions are plotted by latitude and longitude; the coastline is simplified, islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no political boundaries are shown.

These theatres were never isolated from one another or from the classical arts. Their music drew on rāgas and tālas as well as on regional song; their gestures and dance often echoed the codified dance traditions of their regions; and their stories came from the epics and Purāṇas, from the devotional poetry of the saints and from regional romances and legends. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries they borrowed from the Parsi and company theatres and from cinema, and in turn supplied cinema with actors, songs and conventions (Chapter 19).

docs.title: 20.2.1 History and texts
docs.text: Yakṣagāna (“song of the yakṣas”) is the theatre of coastal Karnataka, in the districts of Dakshina Kannada, Udupi and Uttara Kannada, with related forms in the plains of the Deccan. The word is found in Kannada and Telugu sources from about the sixteenth century, at first apparently as the name of a kind of song or sung composition. Its texts, called prasaṅgas (“episodes”), are verse plays in Kannada, composed in a range of song metres and set to named rāgas and tālas; several hundred survive, from the early modern period to the present, most of them on episodes of the Rāmāyaṇa, the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, with later additions from regional legend and history. Since the late twentieth century plays have also been composed in Tulu, the language of much of the coastal audience (Ashton and Christie 1977).

docs.title: 20.2.2 Performance
docs.text:
A Yakṣagāna performance is directed by the bhāgavata, the singer who sits at the back of the stage, sings the verses of the prasaṅga, keeps time with small cymbals and controls the pace of the whole performance. With the drummers he forms the himmēḷa (“back ensemble”): the barrel drum maddaḷe, played with the hands, and the cylindrical drum ceṇḍe, played with sticks, together with a drone. The actors, the mummēḷa (“front ensemble”), dance to the sung verses and then improvise the spoken dialogue (arthagārike) that interprets them. The best actors are celebrated for their eloquence: a scene of a few sung verses can become, in their hands, an extended debate on duty, devotion or politics, and the audience comes as much for the argument as for the dance.

Costume and make-up classify the characters. Kings and heroes wear tall, elaborate crowns and wide jewelled breastplates; demons and other fierce characters wear make-up in strong colours and patterns and huge headdresses; women’s roles, until recently, were played by men in saris and jewellery (Figure 20.2); and a clown (hāsyagāra) provides comedy and links the scenes. Two main styles are distinguished: the northern (baḍagu tiṭṭu) of Udupi and Uttara Kannada, and the southern (teṅku tiṭṭu) of Dakshina Kannada and the neighbouring Kasaragod district of Kerala, with differences in dance, costume and drumming. The performance traditionally begins with preliminaries, including songs of invocation and dances by young performers, before the play proper begins late in the evening, and it continues until dawn (Ashton and Christie 1977; Richmond et al. 1990).

Figure 20.2. A Yakṣagāna performance, 2022: an actor in a woman’s costume and make-up dances before the seated singers and drummers; another character stands at the right. Photo: Vandana bhat kaustubha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 20.2.3 Troupes and patrons
docs.text:
The professional troupes (mēḷa) traditionally belong to temples, such as those of Kaṭīl and Dharmasthala, and perform through the dry season, from the end of the monsoon to its return. Most performances are sponsored by devotees as votive offerings in fulfilment of a vow, so that the same play may be offered to the deity by different families night after night in different villages. In the twentieth century commercial troupes began to perform in tents for paying audiences, introducing new plays, including plays based on films and on social themes, and the old relation between troupe, temple and devotee came to coexist with a market in tickets and stars. A seated, costume-free variant, tāḷamaddaḷe, consists entirely of sung text and improvised debate, and is valued as an art of eloquence in its own right. In recent decades women have begun to perform Yakṣagāna, both in mixed and in all-women troupes.

The form also attracted modern artists. The novelist Shivarama Karanth studied and experimented with Yakṣagāna, creating new productions for the modern stage; the director B. V. Karanth and others drew on it in the “theatre of roots” (Chapter 19); and a tradition of string puppetry in the Yakṣagāna style shows its influence on other forms. Martha Ashton and Bruce Christie’s study remains the fullest account in English of its technique and repertoire (Ashton and Christie 1977).

docs.title: 20.3 Terukkūttu
docs.text:
Terukkūttu (“street theatre”) is the all-night theatre of the villages of northern Tamil Nadu. Its performers prefer the name Kaṭṭaikkūttu, after the carved wooden ornaments (kaṭṭai) worn by the principal characters, and they reject “street” as a slighting description of an art that, in its own view, is a demanding discipline. The troupes are professional, made up of men from several non-Brahmin agricultural and artisan castes, and they perform mainly in the dry season, engaged by village festival committees (Bruin 1999).

The repertoire is dominated by the Mahābhārata, in versions derived from Tamil retellings of the epic, and its performance is bound up with the cult of the goddess Draupadī. In many villages of the region Draupadī is worshipped as a goddess, and her festival, lasting up to eighteen days, combines daytime recitation and exposition of the epic by a learned reciter with night-long kūttu performances of its episodes, in a sequence that follows the story from Draupadī’s marriage through the dice game and her humiliation to the war and the death of Duryodhana. Some episodes involve the whole village: in the play of Arjuna’s penance, the actor playing Arjuna climbs a tall pole, singing as he goes, and on the last day of the festival the death of Duryodhana is enacted beside a great clay image of the fallen king. Alf Hiltebeitel’s study of the Draupadī cult shows how the festival reinterprets the epic, making Draupadī its central figure and the Pāṇḍavas her devotees (Hiltebeitel 1988).

A kūttu performance begins with preliminaries behind a hand-held curtain and the entry of the kaṭṭiyakkāraṉ, the clown and master of ceremonies, who introduces the play, announces the characters and banters with the audience and the actors. The main characters make their entrance behind the curtain, which is lowered to reveal them in a burst of song and dance (Figure 20.3). The text consists of songs, sung by the actors and repeated by a chorus seated with the musicians, and of improvised dialogue in prose. The ensemble includes a harmonium, the double-headed mirutaṅkam, cymbals and the mukavīṇai, a small double-reed instrument. Richard Frasca’s study analyses the structure of performance in detail, and Hanne de Bruin’s work, based on long collaboration with the performer and teacher P. Rajagopal, shows how flexible the tradition is: its performers constantly adjust plays, music and dialogue to occasion and audience (Frasca 1990; Bruin 1999).

Figure 20.3. A Terukkūttu actor in the painted make-up and ornamented headpiece of a principal role, 2020. Photo: TAPAS KUMAR HALDER, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

In the late twentieth century the form entered the modern theatre. The Chennai group Koothu-p-pattarai, founded by the writer Na. Muthuswamy in 1977, made the training and techniques of kūttu the basis of a modern theatre, and the Kattaikkuttu Sangam, founded in 1990 by Rajagopal and de Bruin, created a school in which young people, girls as well as boys, are trained in the form, a significant change in a tradition that had been the preserve of men.

docs.title: 20.4 Jātrā
docs.text:
Jātrā (from Sanskrit yātrā, “journey”, “procession”, “festival”) is the popular theatre of Bengal, with related forms in Odisha and Assam. Its roots lie in the devotional processions and performances of the Vaiṣṇava movement inspired by Caitanya in the sixteenth century; according to his biographers, Caitanya himself took part in a dramatic performance on the life of Kṛṣṇa. The older kṛṣṇa-yātrā of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries was a sung drama of Kṛṣṇa’s life, with long stretches of song and little action (Richmond et al. 1990).

In the nineteenth century, under the influence of the new urban theatres of Calcutta (Chapter 19), jātrā became a professional, commercial theatre, with more dialogue, more varied subjects and companies that toured the countryside. Its subjects expanded from mythology to history, romance and contemporary society. Performed in an arena with the audience on all sides, it combined declamatory, melodramatic acting with songs and an orchestra that opened the performance with an overture. Its characteristic figure, the Vivek (“conscience”), appears at moments of crisis to comment in song on the moral meaning of the action, and a chorus of singers once commented similarly from the sides. In the early twentieth century the poet-performer Mukunda Das (1878–1934) created a nationalist jātrā whose songs and plays, supporting the svadeśī movement, were banned by the colonial government, and later playwrights wrote jātrās on political and social subjects, from peasant struggles to events abroad (Richmond et al. 1990).

The modern jātrā is a large industry. Its companies, many with offices on Chitpur Road in north Kolkata, sign contracts with village organisers and festival committees and tour through the season, which runs from the autumn festivals until the monsoon. From the mid-twentieth century women began to replace the male actors who had played female roles, and microphones, electric lighting and recorded or amplified music changed the style of performance. Odia jātrā, with its own companies and repertoire, has a similar history. In Assam the “mobile theatre” (bhrāmyamān) companies, the first of which was founded in 1963, tour with tents, stages, lights and large casts, staging plays that range from Assamese history to adaptations of world drama and Hollywood films for audiences of several thousand a night; they are among the most successful popular theatres in India.

docs.title: 20.5 Tamāśā
docs.text:
Tamāśā (from a Persian word meaning “spectacle” or “entertainment”) is the popular theatre of Maharashtra. It took shape in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, in the period of the Peshwas and after, in the camps of soldiers and the towns of the Deccan, and its songs drew on the lāvaṇī, the erotic and topical song form brought to a high art by poets (śāhīr) such as Rām Joshī, Anant Phandī and Honājī Bāḷā, and on the powāḍā, the ballad of heroic deeds. Two kinds of performance developed. In the saṅgīt bārī, women singer-dancers perform lāvaṇīs for seated audiences in theatres and halls; in the touring ḍholkī-phaḍ tamāśā, named after its principal drum, a troupe presents an evening of songs, dances and comic scenes ending in a play (vag) (Paik 2022).

The ḍholkī-phaḍ performance follows a set order: an invocation to Gaṇeśa (gaṇ); the gavḷaṇ, a comic and erotic scene of Kṛṣṇa teasing the milkmaids on their way to market, in which the clown plays Kṛṣṇa’s companion; songs and dances; and the vag, a play on a romantic, historical or social subject. The songāḍyā, the clown, is the heart of the performance, commenting satirically on the action and on society. The ensemble includes the ḍholkī, the halgī frame drum, the one-stringed tuntuṇe, cymbals and harmonium.

The performers came largely from low-caste and Dalit communities, among them the Mahārs, Māṅgs and Kolhāṭīs, and the women performers bore the stigma attached to women who danced in public. The form became a battleground of caste and gender politics. In the 1930s and after, Ambedkarite troupes adapted its structure in the jalsā, replacing the erotic gavḷaṇ with songs of social reform and the message of Ambedkar, and in the 1940s and 1950s the Dalit writer Annabhau Sathe and the cultural troupes of the left used its forms in the movement for a united Maharashtra. At the same time Dalit leaders urged their communities to abandon performance that they regarded as degrading. Shailaja Paik’s study of Dalit women in Tamāśā shows how these women negotiated the charge of “vulgarity” that attached to their art, and how questions of caste, sexuality and respectability were fought out on their bodies (Paik 2022). Tamāśā remains popular in rural Maharashtra, and the lāvaṇī (Chapter 21) has entered the Marathi cinema and the concert stage.

docs.title: 20.6 Nauṭaṅkī and the Sung Theatres of the North
20.6.1 Nauṭaṅkī
docs.text:
Nauṭaṅkī, the subject of Kathryn Hansen’s major study, is a sung verse theatre of north India, with centres in western Uttar Pradesh and around Kanpur, and an audience across the Hindi-speaking region. It developed in the nineteenth century from the older svāṅg (or sāṅgīt), sung dramas performed in open arenas at fairs and festivals. Its name comes from one of the most popular stories of the repertoire, the tale of the princess Nauṭaṅkī, so delicate that she weighed only “nine ṭaṅks”, who was won by a young hero disguised as a woman (Hansen 1992).

The plays are written in a sequence of verse metres — above all the dohā, the caubolā and the daur — each with its own melodic treatment, and are sung by the actors in powerful, high voices that carry to large open-air audiences, punctuated by the thunder of the nagāṛā kettledrums. The drummer’s virtuosity is one of the pleasures of the form. Two styles developed: that of Hathras, associated with lineages of poets and performers organised in akhāṛās and with the writer and publisher Natharam Sharma Gaur, whose printed plays circulated widely; and that of Kanpur, associated with Shrikrishna Pahalwan and his company, which put more emphasis on prose dialogue and on dramatic action. The plays were printed in cheap chapbooks, sold at fairs and railway stations, and Hansen’s study of these texts shows a repertoire of romances (Lailā–Majnūṃ, Śīrīṃ–Farhād), legends of devotion and sacrifice (Rājā Hariścandra), tales of heroes and bandits (Sultānā Ḍākū) and, from the early twentieth century, nationalist and social themes (Hansen 1992).

Women began to perform in Nauṭaṅkī in the twentieth century. Gulab Bai of Kanpur (1926–1996) became its most famous actress and later ran her own company. Hansen shows how the theatre’s portrayal of heroic women, female impersonation and the presence of women performers allowed it to explore questions of gender, desire and honour, and how its stories of Hindu and Muslim heroes and its mixed Hindi–Urdu language reflected a shared popular culture that crossed religious lines. In the second half of the twentieth century the form declined in the face of cinema and video, and its companies increasingly turned to song-and-dance shows; it has been revived in adapted forms by urban theatre directors and by the National School of Drama (Hansen 1992).

docs.title: 20.6.2 Svāṅg, Khyāl and Māc
docs.text: Nauṭaṅkī has close relatives. In Haryana the sāṅg (svāṅg) was given a large new repertoire in the early twentieth century by the poet-performer Pandit Lakhmi Chand (1903–1945), whose plays are still performed and whose songs are among the best-known in Haryanvi. In Rajasthan the khyāl (khel, “play”) developed regional styles, such as the Kuchāmaṇī, Shekhāwāṭī and Jaipurī, each associated with particular troupes and poets, with plays on Rajput heroes, saints and romances sung in powerful voices to drums. In the Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh the māc, performed on a high platform (māc, “stage”), developed in the nineteenth century around Ujjain, with plays on romantic and legendary themes. These forms share the sung verse, the open-air arena, the all-night performance and the drum ensemble of Nauṭaṅkī, and Hansen treats them as members of a single family of north Indian popular theatre (Hansen 1992; Varadpande 1987).

docs.title: 20.7 Satire and the Goddess: Bhavāī and Bhāṇḍ Pāthar
20.7.1 Bhavāī
docs.text:
Bhavāī, the theatre of Gujarat and parts of Rajasthan, is a sequence of short plays (veṣa) performed at night in village squares and temple courtyards, especially during the festival of the goddess at Navarātri. Its traditional performers, the Targālā (also called Bhavāiyā) and related communities, trace the form to a legendary founder, Asāita Ṭhākar, said to have been a fourteenth-century Brahmin who was outcasted for eating with a girl of a farming caste whom he had rescued from a powerful man, and who is credited by tradition with composing 360 veṣas. The story is a legend, but it expresses the performers’ sense of their own marginal status and their claim to a learned ancestry.

A Bhavāī performance opens with an invocation to the goddess and to Gaṇeśa, and its veṣas range from devotional and legendary episodes to sharp satire of social types: the miserly merchant, the corrupt official, the Brahmin, the foolish husband and the quarrelsome wife. A clown (raṅglo) comments and improvises; the music is dominated by the bhūṅgaḷ, a long copper trumpet, with drums and cymbals; and female roles are played by men. In the twentieth century Bhavāī was taken up by modern theatre-makers: the actress Dina Gandhi (later Pathak) won fame in the Bhavāī-based musical play Mena Gurjari, and Shanta Gandhi’s Jasma Odan (1968), produced for the National School of Drama, made the form known to urban audiences throughout India (Richmond et al. 1990; Varadpande 1987).

docs.title: 20.7.2 Bhāṇḍ Pāthar
docs.text: The Bhāṇḍ Pāthar of Kashmir is the theatre of the Bhāṇḍs, a hereditary community of Muslim performers who also served as musicians and entertainers at weddings and festivals. Its plays (pāthar, from Sanskrit pātra, “character”) are satirical sketches of social types and rulers — landlords, officials, foreign masters — performed in the open air with dance and music, led by the surnāī (shawm) and drums, with improvised dialogue in Kashmiri. Plays such as the Angrez Pāthar, satirising the British, show the form’s long tradition of mocking the powerful. Like other hereditary performers of the region, the Bhāṇḍs suffered from the decline of patronage and from the conflict in Kashmir after 1989, and efforts to document and sustain their art have been made by cultural organisations in Kashmir.

docs.title: 20.8.1 The Rāmlīlā of Ramnagar
docs.text:
The enactment of the Rāmāyaṇa as Rāmlīlā, based on Tulsīdās’s Hindi Rāmcaritmānas (late sixteenth century), takes place throughout north India in the weeks around the autumn festival of Dussehra. The most famous, at Ramnagar, across the Ganges from Varanasi, has been sponsored by the Mahārājas of Banaras since the early nineteenth century (Figure 20.4) and lasts about a month. It is one of the most remarkable theatre events in the world. The action moves through the town and its surroundings, where permanent sites represent Ayodhyā, Janakpur, Citrakūṭ, Paṃcavaṭī and Laṅkā, and the audience — thousands on the great days — follows the actors from place to place. The roles of Rāma, his brothers and Sītā are played by Brahmin boys who have not reached puberty; when they are in costume they are regarded as embodiments (svarūp) of the deities, and spectators bow before them. A priest-director (vyās) prompts the actors from the text, a group of chanters (rāmāyaṇī) sings the verses of the Rāmcaritmānas that each scene enacts, and the Mahārāja attends in state, on an elephant, as patron and as the representative of the king in the story (Kapur 1990; Schechner 1983).

Figure 20.4. “Ram Leela Mela, as performed at Ram Nugur before the Raja of Benares”: lithograph by Louis Haghe after a drawing by James Prinsep, 1834. The crowds, the elephants of the Mahārāja’s party and a giant effigy (right) fill the open-air site. James Prinsep (drawing) and Louis Haghe (lithograph), 1834; British Library, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Anuradha Kapur’s study of the Ramnagar Rāmlīlā examines its acting, in which the young actors speak their lines in a stylised, formal manner, and the way in which the performance makes the boundary between actor and god, theatre and worship, permeable; Richard Schechner’s essays describe the use of the whole town as an “environmental” theatre and the participation of the audience, among them the nemīs, devotees who attend every day of the cycle (Kapur 1990; Schechner 1983). Elsewhere Rāmlīlā takes many forms: neighbourhood productions on temporary stages organised by local committees, the great public Rāmlīlās of Delhi, and dance-drama versions created for the concert stage, among them that of the Shriram Bharatiya Kala Kendra in Delhi, performed annually since 1957. Indian emigrants took the Rāmlīlā to the Caribbean, Fiji and elsewhere, where it remains an important expression of community identity. UNESCO proclaimed the Rāmlīlā a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005 and inscribed it on its Representative List in 2008.

docs.title: 20.8.2 The Rāslīlā of Braj
docs.text: The Rāslīlā of Braj, the region around Mathura and Vrindavan, enacts the love and play of Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā and the cowherd women. Its troupes are led by a svāmī (rāsdhārī), a Brahmin who directs the performance and owns the costumes, and its actors are Brahmin boys who play Kṛṣṇa, Rādhā and the cowherd women. A performance has two parts. The rās is a circular dance of Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs, with songs from the devotional poets of Braj, which presents the eternal, unchanging play of the god; the līlā that follows enacts a particular episode, such as Kṛṣṇa’s theft of butter or his quarrel with Rādhā, in song and improvised dialogue. As at Ramnagar, the boys in costume are treated as svarūps, and devotees touch their feet. Braj tradition traces the form to the Vaiṣṇava revival of the sixteenth century, naming several saints as its founders; Norvin Hein’s study, based on fieldwork in the 1940s and 1950s, remains the classic account of the Rāslīlā and of the other religious plays of the Mathura region, from the Rāmlīlā to the tableaux (jhāṃkī) of the festivals (Hein 1972).

docs.title: 20.9.1 The Special Drama of Tamil Nadu
docs.text:
The “company drama” of the early twentieth century (Chapter 19) left a popular descendant in the Tamil countryside: the Special Nāṭakam or “Special Drama”, so called because its actors are engaged “specially” for each performance rather than belonging to a permanent company. Organisers of temple festivals and family celebrations book the actors individually, through actors’ associations based mainly in Madurai and other towns of southern Tamil Nadu; actors who may never have performed together meet on the night and perform, without rehearsal, one of a small number of standard plays — among them Vaḷḷi Tirumaṇam, the marriage of the god Murukaṉ to the tribal girl Vaḷḷi, and Hariścandra — whose songs, scenes and conventions they all know. The performance, which lasts through the night, opens with a long comic scene between a male clown (the “Buffoon”) and a female dancer, full of bawdy repartee and topical jokes, and continues with the play, in which songs in rāga-based Tamil styles alternate with improvised dialogue.

Susan Seizer’s ethnography of Special Drama artists shows how the actors, and above all the actresses, live with the stigma that attaches to people who perform on stage, especially women who perform in public at night and travel with men who are not their relatives. She describes the strategies by which actresses protect their respectability offstage — in how they travel, dress and speak — and the ways in which the comic scenes on stage both exploit and comment on the moral anxieties of the audience (Seizer 2005). Her work is one of the best studies of the social life of popular theatre performers in modern India.

docs.title: 20.9.2 The Konkan and the Deccan: Daśāvatāra and Gondhaḷ
docs.text:
On the Konkan coast of Maharashtra and in Goa, the Daśāvatāra (“ten incarnations”) is a theatre of temple festivals, performed through the night by troupes of male actors who tour the villages in the dry season. Its first part is a fixed preliminary sequence in which Gaṇeśa, the goddess Sarasvatī and other deities appear and dance, interrupted by a comic demon who provides the evening’s first laughter; its second part is a play (ākhyān) on an episode from the Purāṇas, usually one involving an incarnation of Viṣṇu, performed with songs to harmonium and drums and with improvised dialogue in Marathi or Konkani. The actors bring their own costumes and make-up, the female roles are played by men, and the dialogue is created afresh at each performance within the frame of a known story, much as in Yakṣagāna to the south.

The gondhaḷ of Maharashtra and the Deccan is a ritual performance in honour of the goddess — Tuḷjā Bhavānī of Tuljapur, Reṇukā of Mahur and others — performed at night after a wedding or another family ceremony by hereditary performers of the Gondhaḷī community. A lead singer, with companions playing the saṃbaḷ drum and the one-stringed tuntuṇe, invokes the goddess before a lamp and a sacred pot, and then narrates a story (ākhyān) in song and speech, with humour and topical comment. It stands between ritual and theatre: its purpose is the worship of the goddess on behalf of the family, but its narrative and its comedy make it one of the popular entertainments of the region, and its songs to the goddess have entered the wider repertoire of Marathi devotional and popular music.

docs.title: 20.9.3 Odisha: Pālā, Daskathia and Prahlāda Nāṭaka
docs.text: Odisha, besides its jātrā, has several distinctive forms of narrative and dramatic performance. The pālā is a sung narrative performed by a lead singer (gāyaka) with a chorus (pāliā) who play cymbals and a drum; it is associated with the worship of Satya Pīr or Satyanārāyaṇa, a figure revered by both Hindus and Muslims, and its singers are prized for their learning, quoting Sanskrit and classical Odia poetry, and for their wit in the comic exchanges with the chorus. In the daskathia, two performers, a singer and his companion, narrate devotional stories with song and with the rhythm of wooden clappers (kāṭhi) held in the hand. The Prahlāda Nāṭaka of southern Odisha, centred on the Ganjam district, enacts the story of the demon king Hiraṇyakaśipu, his devotee son Prahlāda and the man-lion avatar Narasiṃha, with songs in the rāgas of Odissi music, on a stage dominated by a tall structure representing the demon king’s throne; its text is attributed to a nineteenth-century local ruler. Their music draws on the same regional repertoire of rāgas and songs as the Odissi music that accompanies the classical dance of the region (Chapter 17).

docs.title: 20.9.4 Shumang Līlā
docs.text: In Manipur, the Shumang Līlā (“courtyard play”) is a popular theatre of social comedy, satire and melodrama performed in the courtyards of houses and in open spaces, with the audience on all sides and almost no scenery. It developed in the twentieth century from earlier comic entertainments, and its troupes are traditionally single-sex: in the all-male troupes men play the women’s roles, and in all-female troupes women play the men’s. Its plays deal with family life, social problems and politics, and it has been an important medium of public comment in a state where the political situation has often been tense. The more formal, proscenium-based Manipuri theatre that produced Heisnam Kanhailal and Ratan Thiyam (Chapter 19) grew up alongside it.

docs.title: 20.9.5 Ōṭṭan Tuḷḷal
docs.text: In Kerala, the eighteenth-century poet Kuñcan Nampyār created tuḷḷal, a solo form in which a performer in colourful costume and make-up sings and dances Malayalam verse narratives, accompanied by a singer, a drummer and a cymbal player. A traditional story says that Nampyār, a temple drummer, invented it after being mocked by a Cākyār for falling asleep while accompanying a Cākyār kūttu (Chapter 19), and that he set out to draw the audience away from his rival. Whatever the truth of the story, tuḷḷal is a popular counterpart to the learned Sanskrit theatre: it uses everyday Malayalam, tells stories from the epics and Purāṇas, and fills them with satire of contemporary society, including Brahmins, rulers and the foibles of every caste. Three forms are distinguished by costume and metre (ōṭṭan, śītaṅkan and paṟayan), of which ōṭṭan tuḷḷal is the most popular.

docs.title: 20.10 Performers, Patrons and the State
docs.text:
The regional theatres were sustained by particular social arrangements, and their recent history reflects the changes in those arrangements. Their performers were mostly hereditary specialists or members of particular castes and communities, many of them low in the caste hierarchy, and acting, like dancing in public, often carried social stigma. Their patrons were temples, landlords, merchants, village committees and devotees fulfilling vows, and the economics of performance ranged from ritual obligation to straightforward commerce. Female impersonation was a respected art: the female impersonators of Yakṣagāna, Nauṭaṅkī and the Parsi theatre, like Bal Gandharva on the Marathi stage (Section 11.7), were stars, and their departure from the stage when women began to perform was experienced in some traditions as a loss as well as a liberation.

From the 1950s the state took an interest in these theatres. The Sangeet Natak Akademi organised festivals and seminars on “traditional” and “folk” theatre and supported troupes and training; the Song and Drama Division of the central government’s Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, established in 1954, employed folk performers to carry messages about development, health and family planning to rural audiences, often in the forms of Nauṭaṅkī, Jātrā, Tamāśā or Burrakatha; and the “theatre of roots” movement of the 1970s and 1980s drew on regional forms to create a national modern theatre (Chapter 19). These interventions brought money and recognition, but they also raised questions — discussed by Rustom Bharucha and others — about who controls a tradition, about the selection of particular forms as representative of a region, and about the transformation of community performance into staged “heritage” (Bharucha 1993; Dharwadker 2005).

The greatest change, however, came from cinema, television and video, which from the 1950s onwards took over much of the audience and many of the functions of the popular theatres. Some forms declined sharply; others, such as Jātrā, the mobile theatre of Assam, Yakṣagāna and Tamāśā, adapted, adopting amplification, electric light, new repertoires and new business models, and remain large popular institutions. The regional theatres are therefore not survivals from an unchanging past but living, commercial and constantly changing arts, whose history over the last two centuries is as much a part of the history of Indian theatre as the Sanskrit drama of the first millennium.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Richmond et al. (1990) is the best general introduction to India’s regional theatres, Varadpande (1987) gives a general history, and Lal (2004) is a reference companion with entries on most of the forms. On particular forms see Ashton and Christie (1977) (Yakṣagāna); Frasca (1990), Bruin (1999) and Hiltebeitel (1988) (Terukkūttu and the Draupadī cult); Hansen (1992) (Nauṭaṅkī and the sung theatres of the north); Paik (2022) (Tamāśā and Dalit women); Seizer (2005) (the Tamil Special Drama); Kapur (1990) and Schechner (1983) (the Ramnagar Rāmlīlā); and Hein (1972) (the religious drama of Braj). Bharucha (1993) and Dharwadker (2005) discuss the place of traditional forms in modern Indian theatre.

docs.title: Chapter 21: Folk and Tribal Performance
docs.text: Most of the music, dance and drama performed in India has never been called “classical”. It is performed in villages and small towns, at festivals, weddings, harvests and pilgrimages, in shrines and sacred groves, by specialist hereditary performers or by whole communities, in hundreds of languages and dialects. No survey can do more than sample this field. The sample offered here moves from song in everyday life to the bards who sing oral epics, the dances of festivals and communities, the ritual performances in which performers become gods, the music and dance of the Ādivāsī (tribal) peoples and the instruments of folk music; but it begins by asking what the words “folk” and “tribal” mean, and it ends with how the performers have fared in modern India. Popular and regional theatre is treated in Chapter 20 and puppet theatre in Chapter 19; the wider knowledge systems of tribal and folk communities are the subject of Volume 23 of this series, Jana–Jāti.

docs.title: 21.1 The Idea of “Folk”
docs.text:
Indian music theory has long distinguished mārga, the canonical art described in the treatises, from deśī, the music and dance of the regions (Chapters 4 and 12). But deśī meant something different from the modern “folk”: the medieval theorists used it for the regional art music and dance of courts and temples as well as for popular forms, and much of what they called deśī later became “classical”. The modern categories of “folk” and “tribal” arts were shaped in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries by colonial ethnography, which classified Indian society into castes and tribes, and by nationalist and post-Independence cultural policy, which presented India’s “folk” arts as the expression of the nation’s rural soul and staged them at the Republic Day celebrations and in national festivals from the 1950s onwards (Vatsyayan 1976).

These categories are useful but must be used with care. “Folk” does not mean simple, anonymous or unchanging: many folk genres are highly skilled, professional arts with known lineages of performers and constantly changing repertoires. The line between folk and classical has always been crossed in both directions, as rāgas, rhythms, genres and stories moved between village, temple and court (Chapters 7 and 5). And “tribal” communities are not isolated survivals from the past but peoples with their own histories, many of them in long contact and exchange with their neighbours. Above all, folk and tribal performance must be understood on its own terms — in its own social and ritual contexts and for its own purposes — and not as the raw material from which “higher” arts were made.

docs.title: 21.2 Song in Everyday Life
docs.text:
Song accompanies almost every activity and stage of life in rural India. There are work songs for grinding grain, transplanting rice, rowing and herding; seasonal songs for the rains (kajrī, jhūlā), for spring (caitī, phāg) and for festivals; and songs for birth (sohar), marriage, and death. Much of this repertoire is sung by women, often in groups, and it gives voice to women’s experience — of marriage and separation from their natal families, of conflicts with in-laws, of desire and humour — with a frankness rarely found in literary or classical genres. In Maharashtra, thousands of women’s grinding songs (ovī) have been recorded; in the Bhojpuri-speaking region of Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, Edward Henry’s study showed how the songs of different occasions and social groups form a whole musical culture (Henry 1988).

Devotional song is equally widespread: the bhajans and kīrtans of village congregations; the abhaṅgs of the Vārkarī pilgrims to Pandharpur; the songs of the Sufi shrines; the Sikh śabad; and the songs of particular saints and cults (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 21.2.1 The Bāuls
docs.text: The Bāuls of Bengal, in both India and Bangladesh, are wandering religious singers whose songs express an esoteric spiritual path that draws on Vaiṣṇava, Sufi and Tantric ideas and rejects the authority of scripture, caste and religious institutions. Their songs speak of the “man of the heart” (moner mānuṣ), the divine within the body, in images of rivers, boats, birds and cages. The most famous Bāul poet, Lālan Fakir (traditionally c. 1774–1890), was claimed by both Hindus and Muslims. Bāuls accompany themselves on the one-stringed ektārā or the plucked drum khamak, often with a small drum and ankle bells. Jeanne Openshaw’s study shows the diversity of people and practices covered by the name, and the gap between the romantic image of the Bāul popularised by Rabindranath Tagore and the social realities of Bāul life (Openshaw 2002). UNESCO inscribed the Bāul songs, as nominated by Bangladesh, on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (proclaimed 2005).

docs.title: 21.2.2 Hereditary musicians of Rajasthan
docs.text: In western Rajasthan, the Manganiyār and Laṅgā communities, both Muslim, are hereditary professional musicians who for generations sang for patron families (jajmān) of Hindu Rajputs and other castes and of Muslim herders, performing at births, weddings and festivals the songs of the patrons’ genealogies, ballads, love songs and devotional songs. They accompany themselves on the bowed kamāicā (Manganiyār) and the sindhī sāraṅgī (Laṅgā), with the ḍholak and the clappers called khartāl. From the 1960s, documentation by folklorists and the interest of urban and international audiences brought some of these musicians to world stages, transforming the economy of the tradition while the old patronage relationships continued in the villages.

docs.title: 21.3 Bards and Epics
docs.text:
India has a rich tradition of oral epic, performed by professional bards for particular communities, often over many nights. The volume Oral Epics in India edited by Stuart Blackburn and others surveyed this tradition and showed how closely each epic is tied to the identity, religion and social position of the community that sponsors it (Blackburn et al. 1989).

Pābūjī kī paṛ. In Rajasthan, the epic of the hero-god Pābūjī is performed by a bhopā, a priest-singer of the Nāyak community, with his wife, before a long painted cloth (paṛ) that depicts the episodes of the story; the bhopā plays the bowed rāvaṇhatthā, and the bhopī holds a lamp to illuminate the part of the cloth being sung. The performance, which may last through the night, is an act of worship of Pābūjī as well as a story. John Smith’s edition and translation of the epic is one of the major works of Indian folklore scholarship (Smith 1991). A similar tradition, with a still larger cloth, celebrates Devnārāyaṇ, a god of the Gūjar herders. Ālhā. In Bundelkhand and the Gangetic plain, the epic of the brothers Ālhā and Ūdal, warriors of twelfth-century Mahoba, is sung during the rains, especially by and for agricultural communities. Pandvānī. In Chhattisgarh, a single performer narrates and enacts the Mahābhārata, holding a tambūrā decorated with peacock feathers that becomes, in performance, a mace or a bow; Teejan Bai made the vigorous standing style famous. Southern bow-songs and story-songs. In the Tamil country the villuppāṭṭu (“bow song”) is performed with a large musical bow struck with sticks; in Andhra the burrakatha is performed by a lead singer with two companions who joke and comment, and was adapted by political movements in the twentieth century to spread their messages.

docs.title: 21.4 Festival and Community Dances
docs.text:
Folk dance in India is overwhelmingly communal: it is danced in circles, lines and processions by the members of a community rather than by specialists for spectators, and it belongs to a festival, a season or a rite of passage. Its history in the last hundred years has been a history of what happens when such dances acquire spectators — in cities, on the stage, in the diaspora and on screen. A few examples show the range of what has happened (Vatsyayan 1976).

On each of the nine nights of the goddess (Navarātri) in Gujarat, women gather after dark around a lamp set in a perforated clay pot (garbo) or an image of the goddess and dance garbā: they move round the centre in a ring, clapping, turning and stepping together, while one of them leads a song to the goddess that the others take up. Later in the night men and women join in dāṇḍiyā rās, striking their sticks against those of their partners as the rings move. The dance needs no audience and no training beyond growing up within the community. In the last half-century the same festival has become a vast urban and diasporic event, with professional singers, amplified bands, rented grounds, passes and new steps learnt in classes before the season; UNESCO inscribed garbā on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2023. The communal form survives inside the spectacle, but the spectacle has changed who dances, where, and for whom.

Bhāṅgṛā travelled further. Originally a men’s dance of the harvest season in the Punjab, danced to the large drum (ḍhol) with leaps and shoulder movements and short verses (bolī) shouted or sung, it became a staple of college competitions in the twentieth century and, through the Punjabi diaspora in Britain from the 1980s, the basis of a popular music heard worldwide. The women’s giddhā, in which dance accompanies sung couplets that comment, often satirically, on family and social life, has remained closer to its domestic setting. The difference between the two says something about which dances can be turned into a public spectacle, and by whom.

Elsewhere the history of a dance is a history of caste and stigma. Lāvaṇī, the song-dance of Maharashtra performed by women singer-dancers to the ḍholkī drum, is known for its erotic and witty songs; it was part of the Tamāśā theatre (Chapter 20) and of private “sitting” performances (baiṭhakī lāvaṇī). Its performers came largely from communities such as the Kolhāṭī and from Dalit castes, and bore the stigma attached to women who performed in public; the genre is now also performed by middle-class dancers on stage and in film, often without acknowledgment of those who created it. In Tamil Nadu the paṟai, the frame drum played by Dalit drummers at funerals and festivals and long a mark of their low status, has in recent decades been taken up by Dalit activists and artists as an emblem of pride and resistance, and is now played by troupes at political meetings and cultural festivals as well as in its old settings.

Beside these stand a great many dances that have changed less, or whose changes are less visible: the women’s clapping dances (kummi), the stick dances (kōlāṭṭam) and the pot-balancing karakāṭṭam of Tamil temple festivals; the drummers’ ḍoḷḷu kuṇita of the Kuruba community of Karnataka; the women’s tiruvātirakkaḷi of Kerala; in Rajasthan the women’s turning dance ghūmar, the terah tālī of the Kāmaḍ women, who strike cymbals tied to their bodies, and the dance of the Kālbeliyā, which the dancer Gulabo Sapera brought to international stages and UNESCO inscribed in 2010; and in Kashmir the women’s rouf. The dances of Assam and of the north-eastern hills, from Bihu to the bamboo dance of the Mizos, are described in Chapter 22.

docs.title: 21.5 Chhau
docs.text:
Chhau is a dance-drama of eastern India in three regional styles, each named after the place where it grew up. Seraikela Chhau, of the former princely state of Seraikela in Jharkhand, uses delicate masks and refined, stylised movement; Purulia Chhau, of West Bengal, uses large, colourful masks with towering headdresses and vigorous, acrobatic movement (Figure 21.1); and Mayurbhanj Chhau, of Odisha, is danced without masks, so that its expression lies wholly in the body. The origin of the name is disputed: derivations proposed include chāyā, “shadow” or “image”, and chāuni, “military camp”. All three styles present episodes from the epics and Purāṇas and other stories — in Purulia the goddess Durgā’s killing of the buffalo-demon is a favourite — accompanied by drums and the double-reed śahnāī, and all were traditionally danced by men.

Figure 21.1. Purulia Chhau dancers in painted masks and towering headdresses, 2017. Photo: Diganta Talukdar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Their movement vocabulary draws on martial exercises with sword and shield and on the movements of animals and of daily life, and the basic training resembles that of a martial art more than that of a classical dance. The occasion was the spring festival of Caitra Parva, which in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the rulers of Seraikela and Mayurbhanj made a court festival: the princely families patronised troupes, and members of the Seraikela family were themselves celebrated dancers and choreographers. Purulia Chhau, by contrast, never had a court; it is danced through the night in village arenas by troupes drawn from many communities, Ādivāsīs among them, and its masks are made by the artisans of Charida village. After the princely states were merged into India, the state governments and the Sangeet Natak Akademi took over part of the patronage, and Chhau troupes have toured widely in India and abroad. UNESCO inscribed Chhau on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2010, and the Ministry of Culture includes it among India’s classical dances (Vatsyayan 1976).

Chhau is treated here rather than with the classical forms because, unlike them, it has no textual theory of its own and no tradition of solo concert performance; its history is that of princely and village patronage, and a fuller account would depend on ethnographic studies of the three styles. Its ambiguous position — “classical” in one official list and not in another — illustrates how institutional these categories are. So does the Gauḍīya Nṛtya of Bengal, which the dancer Mahua Mukherjee has, since the late twentieth century, reconstructed from medieval Bengali texts, temple sculpture and regional forms, and for which recognition as a classical dance has been sought: like Odissi in the 1950s (Chapter 17), it shows a classical form being made rather than found.

docs.title: 21.6 Ritual Performance
docs.text: In many parts of India performance is a means by which gods, goddesses, ancestors and spirits become present among the people. These performances are not “folk dance” in the sense of recreation, nor theatre in the sense of representation: the performer is understood to become, for the duration of the rite, the deity, who speaks, blesses, heals and judges.

docs.title: 21.6.1 Teyyam
docs.text:
In northern Kerala (Kannur and Kasaragod districts), the teyyam (from daivam, “god”) season runs from about October to May. In shrines and household compounds, performers from communities such as the Malayan, Vaṇṇān, Vēlan and Pulayan — castes and tribes that were long treated as low or untouchable — spend hours being dressed and painted (Figure 21.2), with spectacular headdresses that may tower several metres high, and then dance, to the drums, the story and character of one of several hundred deities, among them goddesses, deified heroes and ancestors, and the spirits of people who died tragic deaths. At the climax the performer is possessed by the deity and receives the worship of the community, including people of the highest castes, to whom he gives blessings and advice. Many teyyam stories speak of caste injustice, of low-caste heroes and women wronged by the powerful and deified after death. Scholars have debated how far the temporary reversal of hierarchy in teyyam challenges or reinforces the social order; in the twentieth century the tradition became both an emblem of Kerala culture and a site of claims by its performers to dignity and recognition.

Figure 21.2. A teyyam performer with painted face and headdress, a drummer behind him, at Muzhappilangad, Kannur district, Kerala, 2020. Photo: Shagil Kannur, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 21.6.2 Other ritual theatres
docs.text:
The bhūta kōla of the Tulu-speaking region of coastal Karnataka, performed by the Nalike, Parava and Pambada communities, similarly embodies spirits (bhūta) that protect villages and adjudicate disputes. In Kerala, muḍiyēṯṯu, a ritual drama of the goddess Kāḷī’s battle with the demon Dārika performed in Bhadrakāḷī temples (inscribed by UNESCO in 2010), and paṭayaṇi, with masks made from the sheaths of areca palms, are performed for the goddess. In the Garhwal Himalaya, the rammaṇ of the village of Saloor-Dungra, a festival of masked dances and recitations in honour of a local deity, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2009. The Rāmlīlā of north India and the Lai Haraoba of Manipur (Chapter 18) are also, in their different ways, rituals as well as performances.

The mountain regions have ritual traditions of their own, shaped by village deities who speak through mediums, by hereditary drummers of low caste whose ritual knowledge is indispensable, and, in Ladakh, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh, by Tibetan Buddhism. The rammaṇ of Saloor-Dungra belongs to this world; the possession rites of the jāgar and the Pāṇḍav līlā of Garhwal, the procession music of the deities of Himachal Pradesh, the masked dances (cham) of the monasteries and the lay music of Ladakh are described in Chapter 22.

docs.title: 21.7 Ādivāsī Music and Dance
docs.text:
India’s Ādivāsī (“original inhabitant”) peoples, officially classified as Scheduled Tribes, number several hundred communities with their own languages, religions and arts. Dance and song are at the centre of their communal life, marking the agricultural year, marriage and the cycle of life, and the worship of their deities and ancestors. Only a few examples can be given here; Volume 23, Jana–Jāti, treats tribal knowledge more fully (Vatsyayan 1976).

A Santal dance shows the pattern. At the festivals of flowers (Baha) and of the harvest (Sohrae), and at weddings, the women of a Santal village in Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha or Bihar dance in long lines, arms linked, moving with small steps, while the men play the drums (tamak, tumdak) and flutes; the line, not the individual dancer, is the unit of the dance, and anyone of the community may join it. The same principle governs the night-long dancing in circles and lines around a branch of the karam tree with which the Oraon, Munda, Gond, Baiga and other peoples of central and eastern India celebrate the karam festival. Other dances are more specialised: among the Raj Gonds of Telangana the gusāḍī dancers, in headdresses of peacock feathers, perform during the Dandārī festival, and the Warlis of the Sahyadri foothills of Maharashtra dance in spiral formations to the gourd-and-bamboo pipe tārpā, a dance that their paintings often depict. The Bhils of western India celebrate the bhagoriyā festival before Holi with dancing to drums and flutes.

Ādivāsī music and dance have suffered from the pressures that have transformed Ādivāsī life — displacement by dams, mines and forest policy, migration for work, and the cultural pressure of mainstream religion and media. They have also been staged, often out of context, as “tribal dances” at official functions, and adapted by urban choreographers. Many communities have responded by reasserting their arts as part of political and cultural movements for recognition, land and autonomy.

docs.title: 21.8 Beyond the Hindu Mainstream
docs.text:
Folk performance in India is often described as if it were exclusively Hindu, but every religious community of the subcontinent has its own traditions of song, dance and theatre, many of them the product of long interaction between communities.

The Christian communities of Kerala and Goa have performance traditions shaped by centuries of contact with Portuguese Catholicism as well as by local forms. In central Kerala, the Latin Catholic communities of the coast perform cavittu nāṭakam (“stamping drama”), a musical drama on Christian and European heroic subjects — the emperor Charlemagne, saints and martyrs — created in the period of Portuguese influence, in which the actors’ stamping on a wooden stage provides much of the rhythm; the Syrian Christians have mārgamkaḷi, a group dance in a circle around a lamp that retells the mission of the apostle Thomas. In Goa, the mando, a slow song-and-dance genre in Konkani of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, combines Western harmony and dance with Konkani poetry of love and social life, and the tiatr, a popular Konkani theatre that began in the 1890s, combines plays with topical songs and remains a vigorous commercial form.

Muslim communities have many traditions of their own. The Mappila Muslims of Kerala sing māppiḷappāṭṭu, a large body of songs in Arabic-Malayalam on religious, heroic and romantic themes, and perform group dances such as the women’s oppana at weddings and the men’s kōlkaḷi (stick dance) and duff muṭṭu, sung to frame drums. The Siddis of Gujarat and Karnataka, descendants of Africans who came to India over many centuries as soldiers, sailors and slaves, perform the dhamāl or goma, a drum-and-dance tradition associated with the shrines of their saints, which preserves elements of East African music. Across north India the processions of Muḥarram are accompanied by elegies (marsiya, nauḥa) and drumming, and the Sufi shrines are centres of qawwālī and other devotional music (Chapter 7).

In the Punjab, the ḍhāḍī singers perform heroic ballads, including ballads of Sikh history, to the small hourglass drum ḍhaḍḍ and the sāraṅgī; the kavīśars sing similar ballads unaccompanied. Jain communities sing devotional songs (stavan) in temples and at festivals, and Buddhist communities in Maharashtra and elsewhere, since the conversion led by B. R. Ambedkar in 1956, have created new devotional and political song traditions celebrating the Buddha and Ambedkar. These traditions are an essential part of the musical life of India, and their omission from accounts of “Indian” folk arts reflects the assumptions of those accounts rather than the realities of performance (Vatsyayan 1976; Manuel 1993).

docs.title: 21.9 Folk Instruments
docs.text:
Folk music uses a great variety of instruments, many of them made by the players or by local craftsmen from bamboo, gourd, wood, skin and metal (Table 21.1). Several, such as the ektārā and the rāvaṇhatthā, are among the simplest of instruments in construction yet capable of great expressive subtlety in the hands of skilled players (Deva 1978).
