docs.title: 21.10 Folk Performance in Modern India
docs.text:
The twentieth century transformed the world of folk performance. Colonial and post-colonial folklorists collected songs and stories; nationalist writers and artists, from Tagore to the theatre directors of the 1960s, drew inspiration from them; and the Indian state, through the Republic Day celebrations, the National Folk Dance Festival (from the 1950s), the Sangeet Natak Akademi, the regional Zonal Cultural Centres (from the 1980s) and state academies, presented folk arts as the heritage of the nation. Recordings, radio, cassettes and later the internet created new markets and audiences; folk songs and dances entered film music and popular culture; and some performers, such as the Manganiyārs, Bāuls and Kālbeliyā dancers, found international careers (Manuel 1993).

These changes have been double-edged. Patronage has shifted from local communities to governments, festivals, tourists and media; performances have been shortened and adapted for the stage; and the arts of low-caste and Ādivāsī communities have sometimes been celebrated as “heritage” while their performers remained poor and stigmatised. Some traditions have declined as their occasions disappeared; others have flourished in new forms. Documentation by archives and researchers has preserved recordings of many traditions, but the survival of a living art depends above all on the communities that practise it and on their ability to make a living and to be respected for it. Discussions of “endangered” folk arts are most useful when they take account of what the performers themselves want.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Vatsyayan (1976) surveys the folk dances of India and their relation to the classical forms. Blackburn et al. (1989) is the standard collection on oral epics, and Smith (1991) an edition and study of the Pābūjī epic. Henry (1988) studies Bhojpuri song, Openshaw (2002) the Bāuls, and Manuel (1993) the effects of cassette technology on popular and folk music. For instruments see Deva (1978).

docs.title: Chapter 22: Music and Dance of the North-East and the Himalaya
docs.text:
The mountain arc that runs from Kashmir through Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills to Arunachal Pradesh, and the hills and valleys of the north-east around the Brahmaputra, are home to a greater variety of peoples, languages and religions than any other part of India. Speakers of Indo-Aryan languages (Assamese, Bengali, Nepali, the Pahāṛī languages and Kashmiri), of many Tibeto-Burman languages (Meitei, the Naga languages, Mizo, Bodo, Garo, Kokborok, Ladakhi, Lepcha, Monpa and others) and of the Austroasiatic Khasi live side by side. Their religions include Vaiṣṇava and Śākta Hinduism, Tibetan Buddhism, Islam, Christianity, which became the majority religion of Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya in the twentieth century, and indigenous religions such as the Meitei worship of the lai, the Khasi Niam Khasi and the Donyi-Polo faith of Arunachal. Their music and dance are correspondingly diverse.

Earlier chapters have described the parts of this world that entered the national canon of “classical” dance — Manipuri and Sattriya (Chapter 18) — together with the devotional music of the Assamese sattras and nāmghars (Section 9.9). Seen from Delhi or Chennai these regions are margins; seen from Guwahati, Shillong or Leh they are centres, with performance traditions of their own and with neighbours across the borders in Bangladesh, Myanmar, Tibet, Bhutan and Nepal. The account that follows moves from Assam outside the sattras and Manipur beyond the classical stage to the hill states of the north-east and to Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills, then to the ritual music and masked dance of Tibetan Buddhism, the lay musicians of Ladakh and the Tibetan exiles, and finally to Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. The material culture, governance and ecological knowledge of the region’s Ādivāsī peoples are treated in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti, which also describes the Hornbill Festival of Nagaland and the log drums of the Naga villages.

docs.title: 22.1.1 Bihu
docs.text:
The three Bihu festivals of Assam mark the agricultural year: Bohāg or Rongālī Bihu at the Assamese new year in mid-April, before the sowing; Kātī or Kongālī Bihu in autumn, when the granaries are empty; and Māgh or Bhogālī Bihu in January, after the harvest. Bohāg Bihu is the festival of song and dance. Traditionally young men and women sang and danced in the fields and groves, away from the village, in the days of the festival, and bands of singers (husorī) went from house to house singing blessings and receiving gifts. The Bihu songs (bihugīt or bihunām) are short lyrical verses of love, longing, nature and village life, often frankly erotic, sung to a small number of melodies and capped by the cries of the dancers; Praphulladatta Goswami’s collection of some two hundred and sixty songs, with English translations, remains a basic source (Goswami 1957). The instruments are the double-headed ḍhol, played with a stick and the hand, whose rhythms drive the dance; the buffalo-horn pipe pepā; the bamboo jaw harp gogonā, traditionally played by women; small cymbals; the split-bamboo clapper ṭokā; and the clay whistle xutulī.

In the twentieth century Bihu moved from the fields to the public stage. Urban committees in Guwahati and other towns organised staged Bihu from the middle of the century, with competitions for dance troupes and for the “Bihu queen”; the dance was standardised into a sequence of steps and hip movements, and the songs entered the radio and the record industry. Purists regretted the loss of the field Bihu; the staged festival, for its part, made Bihu the emblem of Assamese identity, performed at every public occasion and in the diaspora.

docs.title: 22.1.2 Ojāpāli, Deodhanī and the narrative song
docs.text:
Assam has a long tradition of narrative singing in which a leader (ojā) and a chorus (pāli) present a sacred story with song, gesture and dance, the chorus keeping time with large cymbals. Two kinds of ojāpāli are distinguished. The sukanānnī ojāpāli sings the story of the snake goddess Manasā from the Assamese Padmāpurāṇa attributed to the poet Sukavi Nārāyaṇadeva, and is performed at the worship of the goddess; the byāha-gowā ojāpāli sings episodes from the epics and Purāṇas, with the ojā explaining the songs in prose and the dāināpāli (the chief assistant) adding humour. The form, strongest in the old district of Darrang, combines learned rāga-based singing, hand gestures and footwork; scholars have seen in it one of the sources of the dramatic and dance traditions of the sattras.

In the same worship of Manasā, the deodhanī is a woman possessed by the goddess who dances, with a sword and shield, to the drums and the songs of the ojāpāli; the dance, performed in trance, has been adapted for the stage as a “folk dance” of Assam. The worship of Manasā in the Brahmaputra valley and in Bengal is one of the main settings of ritual song in eastern India, and its singers preserve a large body of narrative poetry.

docs.title: 22.1.3 Islamic song: Zikir and Zārī
docs.text: The Muslims of the Brahmaputra valley sing devotional songs called zikir (from Arabic dhikr, remembrance), attributed by tradition to the Sufi Azan Fakir (Shāh Mīrān), who is believed to have come to Assam in the seventeenth century and settled near Sivasagar. The songs, in Assamese, use the melodies and imagery of Assamese folk and devotional song to express Islamic teaching and Sufi devotion; they are sung by a leader and chorus, with clapping, and have long been heard by Hindus and Muslims alike. The related zārī are songs of lament for the martyrs of Karbalā. Azan Fakir’s shrine at Saraguri Chapori near Sivasagar is a place of pilgrimage, and the annual commemoration there is attended by people of both communities.

docs.title: 22.1.4 Goālpārīyā and Kāmrūpīyā song
docs.text: The western districts of Assam have song traditions of their own. The Goālpārīyā songs (goālpārīyā lokagīt) of the old Goalpara district, in a dialect close to the Rajbanshi speech of north Bengal, include the songs of the mahouts and elephant-catchers (māhut bandhu re), of the buffalo herders, and of women waiting for absent lovers, sung to the long-necked plucked lute dotorā; the singer Pratima Barua Pandey (1934–2002), born into the family of the zamindars of Gauripur, who had themselves been famous elephant-catchers, made them known throughout Assam and beyond. The Kāmrūpīyā songs of the Kamrup district include devotional and seasonal songs and the songs of the boatmen. Bhupen Hazarika and other modern composers drew heavily on both (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 22.1.5 The peoples of the valley
docs.text: The Bodo, the largest of the Tibeto-Burman peoples of the plains of Assam, celebrate their new year festival, Bwisāgu, in mid-April with the bāgurumbā, a dance of women in long lines whose spreading shawls have earned it the name “butterfly dance”. Their great ritual is the kherāi, the worship of the supreme deity Bathou and the other gods, in which a priestess (doudinī) dances in trance through a long series of dances, each with its own rhythm, while musicians play the long bamboo flute siphuṅ, the drum khām, the bowed lute serjā and cymbals. The Mising, a riverine people of upper Assam, celebrate the spring festival of Ali-āye-ligāṅ, at the start of the sowing, with the dance gumrāg and with oinitom songs; Rabha, Tiwa, Karbi, Dimasa and other communities have their own festivals and dances. In the tea gardens of Assam, the descendants of labourers brought from Chotanagpur and central India in the nineteenth century maintain the jhumur songs and dances of their homelands, now a recognised genre of Assamese performance and an important part of the region’s popular music.

docs.title: 22.2 Manipur beyond the Classical Stage
docs.text:
Manipuri dance as it is seen on the national stage grew out of the Vaiṣṇava rāsalīlā and saṅkīrtana and the Meitei Lai Haraoba (Chapter 18). Behind it lies a wider Meitei musical culture. The pena, a fiddle with a body made from a half coconut shell and a bamboo neck, played with a bow strung with horsehair and hung with small bells, is the essential instrument of the Lai Haraoba: its player (penakhongbā) accompanies the maibī priestesses through the days of the festival, and the instrument was also used by bards to sing the Meitei epic and ballad repertoire, including the story of the lovers Khamba and Thoibi. In the Khongjom parbā, a singer accompanied by a small drum narrates the battle of Khongjom of 1891, in which the army of Manipur fought the British, and other episodes of Meitei history; the form, which grew up after the battle and the loss of independence, is a vehicle of Manipuri historical memory.

The Meitei martial art thang-ta (“sword and spear”, part of the larger tradition called huyen langlon) has ritual and demonstration forms performed to the drum, and its movements have been used by modern choreographers and theatre directors, notably Ratan Thiyam (Chapter 19); its history as a martial art is treated in Volume 20, Yuddha and Dhanurveda. The Shumang Līlā, the comic courtyard theatre of Manipur, is described in Chapter 20. The hill peoples of Manipur — Tangkhul, Mao, Kabui and other Naga communities, and the Kuki-Chin peoples — have festivals, dances and song traditions that belong with those of Nagaland and Mizoram, described below, rather than with the Meitei valley.

docs.title: 22.3.1 Nagaland
docs.text:
The Naga peoples — Angami, Ao, Chakhesang, Konyak, Lotha, Sema, Rengma, Phom and others in Nagaland, and related communities in Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh and Myanmar — had, before the twentieth century, a musical life organised around the agricultural cycle, the village and its men’s and women’s dormitories, feasts of merit, warfare and the rites of the dead. Songs accompanied work in the fields, often sung by groups in alternation, the celebration of the harvest and of feasts, courtship and mourning; dances were performed by men in full ornament with spears and shields, and by women in lines. Many Naga song traditions are polyphonic, with two or more voices moving in parallel or against a held note, and the Chakhesang li, sung by women, has been brought to wide audiences by modern performers (see Volume 23). Instruments include bamboo and buffalo-horn trumpets, bamboo flutes, the jaw harp, a one-stringed bowed fiddle and the great log drums of some villages.

The twentieth century transformed this world. American Baptist missionaries, active among the Ao from the 1870s, brought Christianity, literacy and the hymn, and by the end of the century most Nagas were Christian; the hymn and the church choir became the central musical institutions of village life, and many old songs, associated with headhunting, feasts of merit and the old religion, were abandoned. In recent decades churches, schools, the state government’s festivals and young musicians have revived and adapted older songs and dances, and Nagaland has also become known for its rock, gospel and folk-fusion musicians.

docs.title: 22.3.2 Meghalaya: Khasi, Jaintia and Garo
docs.text:
The Khasi and Jaintia (Pnar) of the central hills of Meghalaya speak Austroasiatic languages and follow matrilineal descent. Their great dances are religious. The Shad Suk Mynsiem (“dance of the joyful heart”), held each April in Shillong by followers of the indigenous Khasi religion, is a thanksgiving in which unmarried women in rich silks and gold ornaments dance with downcast eyes and small steps in the centre, while men with swords and fly-whisks dance around them in a protective outer circle. The Shad Nongkrem, held in autumn at Smit, the seat of the chief (syiem) of Hima Khyrim, is a five-day festival of thanksgiving and propitiation with dances of the same kind. The music is provided by drums (ksing), the double-reed pipe tangmuri, the small plucked lute duitara and flutes. The Garo of the western hills celebrate the harvest festival Wangala in honour of the sun god Saljong, with long lines of dancers moving to the beat of the long dama drums and the sound of brass gongs (rang) and buffalo-horn trumpets; since 1976 a “Hundred Drums Wangala” festival has been held near Tura, bringing village troupes together in competition.

The Welsh Calvinistic Methodist mission, which began work at Sohra (Cherrapunji) in 1841, gave the Khasi a written language and a hymnody, taught through the tonic sol-fa system of notation. Choral singing became one of the great passions of Khasi and Jaintia life, and Shillong developed a rich musical culture of church choirs, brass bands and, from the 1960s, rock and blues music sung in English and Khasi. The success of the Shillong Chamber Choir in a national television competition in 2010 drew national attention to this tradition.

docs.title: 22.3.3 Mizoram
docs.text: The Mizos, Kuki-Chin peoples of the southern hills, are known outside the region for the cheraw, in which dancers step nimbly in and out of pairs of horizontal bamboo poles clapped together and apart by seated men, now performed at the spring festival Chapchār Kūt and on every public occasion. Older Mizo music included many named song types for feasts, hunting, war, love and mourning, accompanied by gongs and the drum (khuang). Welsh and English Baptist and Presbyterian missionaries arrived in the 1890s, and a series of religious revivals from 1906 onwards made Mizoram almost wholly Christian. The revivals produced something unexpected: after an early period in which only translated Western hymns were sung, Mizo Christians began in the early decades of the twentieth century to compose hymns in a Mizo style, with indigenous melodic idioms, sung slowly and repeatedly to the drum at gatherings and wakes, and accompanied by a swaying dance of the congregation. These songs, sung in the practice called lengkhawm, became the heart of Mizo religious life and one of the most striking examples in India of a mission religion taking on a local musical form.

docs.title: 22.3.4 Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh
docs.text:
The Reang (Bru) of Tripura are known for the hojāgiri, a dance that turns balance into an art. Women dancers stand on earthen pots and move only from the waist down, so that the pitchers, lamps and bottles balanced on their heads stay still while the body below them sways, to the music of bamboo flutes, drums and cymbals; the dance has become the emblem of the community on the state’s stages. The Tripuri, whose dynasty ruled the former kingdom, celebrate the Garia festival in April with dances of their own.

Arunachal Pradesh, home to some twenty-six major peoples and many smaller groups, divides musically between west and east. In the west the Monpa and Sherdukpen are Buddhists of the Tibetan tradition, with monastic cham (below), the masked yak dance and the dance-drama Aji Lhamu, a regional form of the Tibetan opera. Among the Tani-speaking peoples of the centre and east — Adi, Apatani, Nyishi, Galo, Tagin — the central figure is the priest-singer (miri among the Adi), who chants long narratives of origin and migration at festivals and rites of healing; at the Adi harvest festival of Solung the women dance the ponung in a circle around a male leader who sings and keeps time with a sword fitted with jingles, so that the singer of narratives is also the leader of the dance. The Wancho and Nocte in the east, related to the Konyak Nagas, share many features of Naga music.

docs.title: 22.4 Sikkim and the Darjeeling Hills
docs.text:
Sikkim, a Buddhist kingdom under the Namgyal dynasty from the seventeenth century until it became part of India in 1975, and the hills of Darjeeling and Kalimpong, have three main communities: the Lepcha, the earliest inhabitants; the Bhutia, of Tibetan origin; and the Nepali-speaking majority, many of whose ancestors came from Nepal in the nineteenth century. The monasteries maintain the ritual music and cham of Tibetan Buddhism; the festival of Pang Lhabsol, held in late summer, honours the mountain deity of Kangchenjunga with a masked dance in which the deity and his attendants appear, and is associated with the oath of brotherhood between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples. The Lepchas have their own songs of origin and of the mountain landscape, and their bamboo flute and zither traditions.

The Nepali communities brought the music of the hills of Nepal: the maruni, danced at the festival of lights (Tihār) by dancers in women’s costume, accompanied by a clown; the frame drum ḍamphu and the selo songs of the Tamang; the pañcai bājā band of the Damai tailor-musicians at weddings; and the sung duets of men and women (dohorī) in which singers exchange improvised couplets. Darjeeling became, in the twentieth century, a centre of modern Nepali song: the composer Amber Gurung (1938–2016), who began his career there, later composed the music of the national anthem adopted by Nepal in 2007. The music of these hills is a reminder that the borders of the Indian state cut across musical worlds shared with Nepal, Bhutan and Tibet.

docs.title: 22.5.1 The monasteries of the Indian Himalaya
docs.text: The Buddhist monasteries of Ladakh (Hemis, Thiksey, Lamayuru and others), of Lahaul, Spiti and Kinnaur in Himachal Pradesh (among them Tabo, founded in 996, and Key), of Sikkim (Pemayangtse, Rumtek), and of the Monpa country of Arunachal Pradesh (Tawang, founded in 1680–81) belong to the Tibetan Buddhist tradition, whose music has been studied above all by Mireille Helffer (Helffer 1994). Music in these monasteries is liturgical. It accompanies the daily services, the long rituals of offering and of meditation on the deities (sādhanā), and the great annual festivals, and it is understood as an offering — the Tibetan word for the instrumental music of the rite, mchod rol, means “offering music” — to the buddhas, the protective deities and, in some rites, to the spirits who must be pacified. The Buddhist chanting of Ladakh was inscribed by UNESCO on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2012.

docs.title: 22.5.2 Chant and notation
docs.text: The core of the liturgy is chant. Much of it is recitation of texts on a single pitch or a narrow range, at varying speeds; the most solemn passages are sung in a melodic style (dbyangs), in which each syllable is stretched over long, slowly changing tones and subtle shifts of vocal colour. These melodies are written in a graphic notation (dbyangs yig), in which curved lines above the text show the rise and fall of the voice, with additional signs for timbre and ornament; the notation, which differs between monastic orders and monasteries, is an aid to a melody learnt from a teacher, not a score. The Gelug tantric colleges of Gyuto and Gyume, re-established in India after 1959, are famous for a deep chant in which each monk sings a very low fundamental and makes an overtone audible above it, so that a single voice seems to produce a chord.

docs.title: 22.5.3 The instruments
docs.text: The monastic ensemble has no strings. It consists of a pair of long telescopic copper trumpets (dung chen), which produce a deep fundamental and a few overtones; a pair of double-reed shawms (rgya gling), which play melodies; conch-shell trumpets (dung dkar) and, in some rites, the short trumpet made from a human thighbone (rkang gling); large frame drums on a handle (rnga); two kinds of cymbals, the flat sil snyan and the bossed rol mo; and the handbell (dril bu) and small hourglass drum (ḍamaru) used by the officiant. The instruments play in fixed sequences of entries, rolls and accelerating and decelerating strokes on the cymbals and drums, which mark the sections of the liturgy, invite the deities and accompany offerings; the shawm melodies, like the chants, are learnt orally with the help of notation. Within the monastery the musicians are monks; the music is part of a monk’s training rather than a profession (Helffer 1994).

docs.title: 22.6 Cham: The Masked Dance of the Monasteries
docs.text:
The best-known public performances of Tibetan Buddhism are the masked dances (’cham) performed by monks in the courtyards of the monasteries at annual festivals. A cham is not a play but a ritual: the dancers, wearing brocade robes and great painted masks, embody the deities of the monastery’s meditation and protective pantheon, and their movements, prescribed in choreographic manuals (’cham yig) and accompanied by the monastic orchestra, enact the subjugation of the forces hostile to the Dharma. The dances often culminate in the ritual destruction of an effigy (linga) of dough representing these forces, which is cut into pieces and offered or cast away. Other episodes are lighter: skeleton dancers representing the lords of the cremation ground, the deer and stag dancers, and comic figures such as the old man (Hashang) and his children, who entertain the crowd between the solemn dances. The Black Hat dance (zhwa nag), in which dancers in broad-brimmed hats perform a slow, powerful sequence of steps and turns, is associated by tradition with the monk Lhalung Palgyi Dorje, said to have killed the anti-Buddhist king Langdarma in the ninth century while disguised as a dancer (Kohn 2001; Pearlman 2002).

Each monastery has its own calendar. At Hemis in Ladakh (Figure 22.1), the largest festival, held on the tenth day of the fifth Tibetan month, honours Padmasambhava, the Indian master credited with establishing Buddhism in Tibet, whose eight manifestations appear in the dances; at Tawang the Torgya is held in winter; and in Sikkim the Pang Lhabsol and the dances held at the end of the year mark the ritual year of the former kingdom. Richard Kohn’s study of the Mani Rimdu festival of the Sherpa monasteries of Nepal, the most detailed account of a cham festival in its ritual context, shows that the public dances are only the visible part of a much longer cycle of rites performed by the monks over many days (Kohn 2001). Today the festivals draw large numbers of tourists, and state governments promote them as cultural heritage; the monks, for their part, continue to perform them as rites whose efficacy does not depend on the audience.

Figure 22.1. Masked monk dancers at the Hemis festival, Ladakh, 2014; the dancer in front holds a handbell and a small drum. Photo: Sarang Deshpande (Sdesh), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 22.7.1 The lay musicians of Ladakh
docs.text: Outside the monasteries, the music of Ladakh was long the work of hereditary musicians, the Mon and the Beda, who played the shawm (surna) and a pair of kettledrums (daman) at weddings, festivals, archery contests, polo matches and the courts of the kings and nobles. Like the drummers of the central Himalaya (below), they were indispensable and socially subordinated: the farming majority would not intermarry or eat with them. The court repertoire included songs and slow, stately dances such as the shondol, performed at the royal court of Leh, and Ladakhi villages have a large repertoire of songs for weddings, work, the seasons and the praise of lamas and kings, sung in groups and often accompanied by line dances. The Muslim communities of Leh and of Kargil, the latter largely Shia, add their own devotional songs and the elegies of Muḥarram (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 22.7.2 The Tibetan community in India
docs.text: Since 1959, when the Dalai Lama and many thousands of Tibetans took refuge in India, Dharamsala in Himachal Pradesh and the Tibetan settlements of Karnataka, Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim and elsewhere have been the main centres of Tibetan culture outside Tibet. The Tibetan Institute of Performing Arts, founded at Kalimpong in 1959 and soon moved to McLeod Ganj above Dharamsala, has trained performers of Tibetan folk song and dance, court music and the opera (a lce lha mo), whose annual festival it hosts; the great monasteries, re-established in south India, continue the ritual traditions described above. Keila Diehl’s study of music among the refugees of Dharamsala shows how the community balanced the preservation of a “pure” Tibetan culture against the pleasures of Hindi film song, Western rock and new forms of Tibetan popular music, and how young musicians used song to define what it meant to be Tibetan in exile (Diehl 2002).

docs.title: 22.8.1 Kashmir
docs.text:
The art music of the Kashmir valley is the sūfiyāna kalām or sūfiyāna mūsīqī, sung by a group of male singers who accompany themselves on the hammered dulcimer santūr, the long-necked lute sehtār, the sāz-e Kashmīr (a bowed lute) and the small drum dokra; its modal system of maqāms, distinct from both the Hindustani rāga and the Persian dastgāh, and its Sufi poetry in Persian and Kashmiri place it, as Józef Pacholczyk has shown, between the musics of Central Asia and of north India (Pacholczyk 1996). Its devotional setting is described in Chapter 9. The santūr entered Hindustani concert music in the second half of the twentieth century, above all through the Jammu-born musician Shivkumar Sharma, who adapted it for the performance of rāgas.

Popular music in the valley includes the chakkrī, a lively song in Kashmiri performed at weddings and gatherings with harmonium, rabāb, sāraṅgī, the clay pot nout and the drum; the lādī shāh, satirical ballads on current affairs sung by itinerant performers with an iron rattle; and the women’s wedding songs (wanvun), sung in alternation by two groups. The women’s dance rouf and the satirical theatre Bhāṇḍ Pāthar are described in Chapters 21 and 20. Jammu and the hills to its south and east belong to the Pahāṛī world of Himachal, and Ladakh to the Tibetan world described above.

docs.title: 22.8.2 Himachal Pradesh: the deities in procession
docs.text: In the valleys of Himachal Pradesh, above all in Kullu, Mandi, Shimla and Kinnaur, religious life centres on village deities (devtā) who are carried in palanquins to festivals, consulted through oracles and honoured with music. The music of the deity is played by hereditary musicians of low-caste communities on large drums (ḍhol, nagārā), the shawm (śahnāī), and long brass trumpets: the straight karnāl and the curved narsiṅgā or raṇsiṅgā, whose blasts announce the god’s arrival. At the Dussehra of Kullu, held in October, hundreds of village deities gather with their musicians to attend the god Raghunāth, and the valley resounds with their bands. The circle dance nāṭī, danced in long chains at fairs (Chapter 21), the songs of seasons and of love (jhūrī, lāmaṇ) and the narrative songs of local heroes complete a regional repertoire that has also been carried, since the 1980s, by a thriving cassette and video industry in the Pahāṛī languages.

docs.title: 22.8.3 Uttarakhand: drum, possession and dance
docs.text:
In Garhwal and Kumaon, the two regions of Uttarakhand, Andrew Alter’s study of Garhwali music shows how drumming lies at the centre of ritual and social life (Alter 2008). The hereditary drummers (Bājgī, Auji or Dās), Dalits whose low status coexists with their indispensable ritual knowledge, play the large double-headed ḍhol and the small kettledrum damaũ at weddings, festivals and above all at the rites of possession. Their rhythmic repertoire is vast and named: there are rhythms to call each deity, to accompany each phase of a rite, to announce events, and to accompany dances, and a body of drummers’ lore, the ḍhol sāgar, describes the drum, its parts and its sacred syllables. In the jāgar (Chapter 21) the singer-drummer (jagariyā) sings the deity’s story until the god “dances” in the body of a medium; in the Pāṇḍav līlā the drums call the heroes of the Mahābhārata into the bodies of village dancers, a performance William Sax has studied as a means by which Garhwalis enact their own personhood and community (Sax 2002).

Kumaon has its own forms. The choliyā, a dance of men with swords and shields performed in wedding processions to the music of ḍhol, damaũ, raṇsiṅgā and the bagpipe maśakbīn — introduced to the hills in the colonial period through military bands — re-enacts, in its leaps and mock combats, the martial culture of the region. The hurkiyās, bards who accompany themselves on the small hourglass drum huṛkā, sing ballads of local heroes and accompany agricultural work. Modern Garhwali and Kumaoni song, carried by cassettes from the 1980s, has its own stars, among whom the Garhwali singer and poet Narendra Singh Negi became one of the voices of the movement for a separate hill state, achieved in 2000. Peter Manuel’s study of the cassette industry noted the importance of such regional markets, which brought the songs of the hills to migrants in the cities of the plains (Manuel 1993).

docs.title: 22.9 Change and Continuity
docs.text:
Table 22.1 summarises some of the forms described in this chapter.

Table 22.1. Some performance traditions of the North-East and the Himalaya Form People or region Occasion and character Bihu Assamese, Brahmaputra valley Spring festival song and dance; ḍhol, pepā, gogonā Ojāpāli Assam (Darrang) Narrative singing with chorus and cymbals; Manasā and epic stories Zikir Assamese Muslims Sufi devotional songs ascribed to Azan Fakir Bāgurumbā, kherāi Bodo New year dance; ritual dance of the doudinī Khongjom parbā Meitei, Manipur Ballad of the battle of 1891 Shad Suk Mynsiem Khasi, Meghalaya Thanksgiving dance in two circles Wangala Garo, Meghalaya Harvest festival with dama drums Cheraw Mizo Bamboo-pole dance Lengkhawm Mizo Christians Hymns in Mizo style, sung with the drum Hojāgiri Reang (Bru), Tripura Women’s balancing dance Ponung Adi, Arunachal Pradesh Women’s circle dance at the harvest festival ’Cham Buddhist monasteries Masked ritual dance of monks Sūfiyāna kalām Kashmir Sufi art music in maqāms with santūr Jāgar Garhwal and Kumaon Ritual singing and drumming for possession Choliyā Kumaon Sword dance in wedding processions

Three forces have shaped these traditions in the last century and a half. The first is religious change. Conversion to Christianity transformed the music of the Naga, Khasi and Mizo peoples, first by displacing songs associated with the old religions and later by creating new forms — the Khasi choir, the Mizo lengkhawm — that are among the most vital music of the region; the spread of Vaiṣṇavism had done something similar in Manipur and Assam in earlier centuries, and the exile of Tibetan Buddhism has carried its ritual music to new homes in India. The second is the state. Since Independence, state governments, the Sangeet Natak Akademi, the Zonal Cultural Centres and the tourist industry have staged the dances of the region as emblems of its peoples, at Republic Day parades and at festivals such as Hornbill and the Hundred Drums Wangala; staging has preserved and revived many forms and has also turned rites into spectacles detached from their seasons. The third is the media: the radio stations of Guwahati, Shillong, Imphal, Aizawl, Kohima and Leh, the cassette and video industries and, now, the internet have created regional popular musics in dozens of languages that are scarcely known in the rest of India.

The region’s performers also face the pressures that mark its politics: insurgency and its suppression, migration, the tension between the claims of different communities to land and identity, and the long neglect of the north-east in national cultural institutions. In this setting music and dance are not only heritage. They are a means by which communities assert who they are, and the songs of a Khasi choir, a Bodo bāgurumbā or a Garhwali jāgar carry, in their different ways, claims to recognition as much as the pleasures of performance.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On the music of Tibetan Buddhism see Helffer (1994); on the masked dance Kohn (2001), a study of a single festival in its full ritual context, and Pearlman (2002), a general introduction; on the Tibetan exile community Diehl (2002). Alter (2008) and Sax (2002) study the music and ritual performance of Garhwal, and Pacholczyk (1996) the art music of Kashmir. For Assam see Goswami (1957) on the Bihu songs and Neog (1980) on the Vaiṣṇava background; for Manipur Doshi (1989); for the folk dances of the region Vatsyayan (1976). Volume 23, Jana–Jāti, treats the wider knowledge systems of the region’s Ādivāsī peoples.

docs.title: Chapter 23: Performing Arts in Modern and Contemporary India
docs.text: The preceding chapters have repeatedly reached the twentieth century, when every one of India’s performing arts was transformed, and each has told part of the story. Taken together, those transformations raise questions that no single art can answer: who pays for the arts when courts and temples no longer do, what recording and broadcasting did to them, and what becomes of an art when it travels. The sections that follow take up the institutions created by the independent Indian state and by civil society to support music, dance and theatre; the effect of radio, recording, film, television and the internet; the travels of Indian performers and their arts across the world and the growth of diaspora communities of practice; contemporary choreography and music that work with and against tradition; claims about the therapeutic uses of the arts; and the questions of caste, gender, livelihood and education that shape the arts today. It ends with some reflections on what the history told in this volume means for the future.

docs.title: 23.1.1 From court and temple to state and market
docs.text: Until the nineteenth century the performing arts were supported mainly by courts, temples, religious institutions, wealthy households and the communities that sponsored festivals and rituals. The colonial period and the abolition of the princely states after 1947 ended most court patronage; the decline of hereditary obligations, the reform movements against dedicated temple women and courtesans, and the growth of cities shifted support to new patrons: urban audiences buying tickets, the music societies (sabhās) of Madras and the music circles of the north, the recording and film industries, and the state (Chapters 7, 8 and 15).

docs.title: 23.1.2 National institutions
docs.text: After Independence the government of India created a set of national institutions for the arts. The Sangeet Natak Akademi, the national academy of music, dance and drama, was established in 1952 and inaugurated in 1953. It gives annual awards and fellowships, supports festivals, documentation and publication, and has played a decisive part in defining which dance forms are “classical” (Chapter 1). The National School of Drama (1959) trains theatre artists; the Kathak Kendra (1964) and the Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy (1954) are among its specialised institutes. The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (1987), the regional Zonal Cultural Centres (from 1985) and state academies support documentation and the performance of folk and tribal arts. Earlier private institutions, such as Kalakshetra (1936), the Kerala Kalamandalam (1930), the music schools founded by Bhatkhande and Paluskar and Tagore’s Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan, were joined by university departments: the Indira Kala Sangit Vishwavidyalaya at Khairagarh, founded in 1956, was the first university devoted to music and the performing arts (Dharwadker 2005; Subramanian 2006).

docs.title: 23.1.3 Honours and festivals
docs.text: The state honours performers with the Padma awards and, in a few cases, the Bharat Ratna, India’s highest civilian award, which has been given to the singer M. S. Subbulakshmi (1998), the sitārist Ravi Shankar (1999), the śahnāī player Bismillah Khan and the film singer Lata Mangeshkar (both 2001), and the singer Bhimsen Joshi (2009), among performing artists. Festivals — the December music season of Chennai, the Sawai Gandharva festival in Pune, the Dover Lane conference in Kolkata, dance festivals held at the temples of Khajuraho and Konark, the National School of Drama’s Bharat Rang Mahotsav — are central to the life of the arts. The Society for the Promotion of Indian Classical Music and Culture Amongst Youth (SPIC MACAY), founded in 1977, has brought performers to schools and colleges throughout India.

docs.title: 23.1.4 The state and “classical” culture
docs.text: State support has been indispensable, and also shaping. By defining certain forms as “classical” and others as “folk”, by choosing whom to honour and whom to send abroad, and by presenting the arts as the expression of a unified national heritage, the institutions of the state and of the urban cultural elite have influenced which traditions flourish and how they are understood. The histories in Chapters 15 to 18 show how the “classical” dance forms were constructed through this process, and Chapter 21 how folk and tribal arts were presented as national heritage. These processes are not unique to India — every modern state has made a national culture — but they need to be understood if the arts are to be studied and supported intelligently.

docs.title: 23.2.1 Recording
docs.text:
The first commercial recordings of Indian performers were made in Calcutta in November 1902 by the recording engineer Frederick Gaisberg of the British Gramophone Company, and within a decade the company and its competitors had recorded thousands of performers in the major cities of the subcontinent. Michael Kinnear’s discography of these early recordings shows how wide the net was cast: courtesan singers of ṭhumrī, ghazal and dādrā, actors and actresses of the Bengali, Parsi and Marathi stage, khayāl singers, instrumentalists, reciters of religious texts and singers of regional and devotional songs (Kinnear 1994). Gauhar Jan, one of the first artists recorded, became the first star of the Indian gramophone (below); in the following decades singers such as Janki Bai of Allahabad, Abdul Karim Khan and, in the south, Bangalore Nagarathnamma reached audiences far beyond their patrons. The Gramophone Company opened a record-pressing factory near Calcutta in 1908, and its “His Master’s Voice” label dominated the Indian market for most of the century.

The technology shaped the music. The 78 rpm record, limited to about three minutes a side, encouraged short forms — ṭhumrī, ghazal, devotional and film songs — and condensed versions of classical performances in which a rāga had to be presented in miniature; the long-playing record from the 1950s, and later the cassette and the compact disc, allowed full-length performances to circulate. The microphone, which reached the concert hall in the 1930s, changed the ideal of the voice, allowing a softer, more intimate style of singing and new balances between voice and instruments; Amanda Weidman has traced its effects on Karnatak singing (Weidman 2006). Recordings also preserved the art of performers who had no other record, among them many of the courtesan singers whose names survive only on the labels of early discs. In the 1980s cheap cassettes, as Peter Manuel has shown, broke the monopoly of the large record companies and created markets for regional, devotional and folk music that had never been recorded commercially (Manuel 1993).

docs.title: 23.2.2 The record business and its artists
docs.text:
The early record trade was fiercely competitive. Besides the Gramophone Company, European firms such as Nicole, Beka, Odeon and Pathé sent recording engineers on tours of the subcontinent in the decade before the First World War, and Indian dealers organised local sessions. The engineers recorded in hotel rooms and offices, on wax masters that were shipped to Europe for pressing; the earliest Indian discs were pressed in Hanover until the company’s Indian factory opened. To identify the singer to the distant engineers, many artists announced themselves at the end of a recording, and the cry “My name is Gauhar Jan” at the close of her discs became famous. Vikram Sampath’s biography of Gauhar Jan (1873–1930), a courtesan singer of Calcutta, of Armenian descent, who recorded several hundred sides in more than ten languages (Figure 23.1) and commanded fees that astonished contemporaries, shows how the first recording stars came from the world of the salon that the reformers were trying to close (Sampath 2010). Gerry Farrell has described how the companies chose what to record and how to sell it to an audience divided by language, region and religion, so that the record market mapped and in some ways created the categories through which Indian music was sold (Farrell 1993).

Figure 23.1. Gauhar Jan (1873–1930) on a coloured picture postcard of about 1910, from a photograph by D. A. Ahuja of Rangoon. Photo: D. A. Ahuja, Rangoon (photograph, c. 1910); postcard scan by Paper Jewels, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The records also changed what was performed. Singers compressed an ālāp and a composition into three minutes, chose short and popular genres, and adapted their art to the limits of the horn and, later, the microphone. In the south, Stephen Hughes has shown, the record companies of Madras turned the songs of the Tamil company drama into a mass commodity in the 1910s and 1920s, recording star singer-actors such as S. G. Kittappa and K. B. Sundarambal; when sound cinema arrived, these recordings had already made the theatre song a popular genre with its own stars, and early Tamil cinema was built on them (Hughes 2007). The modern song of the regional languages, whose history is told in Chapter 11, grew up in the same studios.

docs.title: 23.2.3 Radio
docs.text:
Broadcasting began in India in the 1920s with amateur radio clubs and a private Indian Broadcasting Company, which opened stations in Bombay and Calcutta in 1927. The government took over the service in 1930 and in 1936 renamed it All India Radio; after Independence it adopted the Hindi name Ākāśvāṇī. From the beginning music filled most of its hours, and All India Radio became the largest employer of musicians in India and an instrument of cultural policy. Its system of auditioning artists and grading them for fees and broadcasts, its staff musicians at every station, its National Programme of Music (from 1952) and its annual music festival made it the most important single patron of classical music after the princely courts, and a musician’s radio grade became a public measure of standing.

David Lelyveld has described how the radio’s administrators, from the colonial period onwards, saw themselves as guardians of a national musical standard and used broadcasting to shape taste (Lelyveld 1994). Under B. V. Keskar, Minister of Information and Broadcasting from 1952 to 1962, All India Radio emphasised classical music and restricted the broadcasting of film songs; listeners turned to Radio Ceylon, whose Hindi film-song programmes drew huge audiences, until All India Radio created its own popular channel, Vividh Bharati, in 1957.

The policies had a history. The first Controller of Broadcasting, Lionel Fielden, lent by the BBC in 1935, and the British composer John Foulds, who became director of European music at Delhi in 1937 and formed an orchestra of Indian and European instruments, shared with many Indian intellectuals the view that broadcasting should raise public taste. Matthew Rahaim has shown that the harmonium ban grew out of arguments, advanced by scholars, administrators and critics such as Rabindranath Tagore rather than by performers, that the tempered keyboard was alien to Indian intonation; the instrument, ubiquitous in devotional, theatrical and light classical music, was nevertheless kept off the air until 1971 and readmitted only gradually (Rahaim 2011). After Independence Keskar tightened the auditioning and grading of artists by panels of experts, encouraged the composition of “light music” on the model of the regional modern song as an alternative to film music, and limited the film songs that the radio played. On Radio Ceylon the weekly countdown of film songs Binaca Geetmala, presented from 1952 by Ameen Sayani, became one of the most popular radio programmes in South Asia. Isabel Huacuja Alonso has argued that listeners’ letters, request programmes and the reception of Indian, Pakistani and Ceylonese stations across the new borders made Hindi-Urdu radio a shared public space that escaped the control of the states that owned the transmitters (Huacuja Alonso 2023). Regional stations broadcast folk, devotional and light music in the regional languages and employed many performers of these traditions. Whatever its paternalism, the radio gave musicians a regular income at a time when court patronage had disappeared, and its archives preserve recordings of almost every important musician of the twentieth century.

docs.title: 23.2.4 Film
docs.text:
From the coming of sound in 1931, Indian cinema was a cinema of song and dance, and film music became the most widely heard music in India. The first Indian sound feature, Alam Ara (1931), already contained several songs, and the early sound films, many of them adapted from the plays of the Parsi and other company theatres (Chapter 19), were full of them. At first actors sang their own songs, and singer-actors such as K. L. Saigal were the stars of the 1930s; from the mid-1930s the practice of “playback”, in which songs were recorded in advance by professional singers and mimed by the actors, spread rapidly, and the playback singer became a figure of national fame. The studios of the 1930s — New Theatres in Calcutta, Prabhat in Pune, Bombay Talkies — employed music directors, singers and orchestras, and later the independent producers of Bombay and Madras hired them film by film.

Playback is usually said to have been first used in the New Theatres production Bhāgya Cakra (1935) and its Hindi version Dhoop Chhaon, whose music director was R. C. Boral; the idea is credited to the director Nitin Bose and the sound recordist Mukul Bose. Separating the singing voice from the acting body had large consequences. It allowed actors who could not sing to become stars and singers who did not act to become famous, and it concentrated the singing of an entire industry in a handful of voices. In the 1930s and 1940s several women composed for the screen — Jaddanbai, a courtesan singer who became a producer and music director, and Saraswati Devi (Khorshed Minocher-Homji), a Parsi musician who composed for Bombay Talkies — and the composer Ghulam Haider brought the rhythms of Punjabi folk music to the film song of Lahore and Bombay and launched the careers of Noor Jehan, who moved to Pakistan in 1947, and of the young Lata Mangeshkar. Lata Mangeshkar’s high, light and precise voice became, from about 1949, the dominant sound of the Hindi film heroine. Neepa Majumdar has shown how the separation of voice and body in playback allowed the film industry to attach to its heroines a voice of purity and respectability, distinct from the heavier, “professional” voices of the courtesan-trained singers of the previous generation (Majumdar 2009). Ashok Ranade’s study of the Hindi film song treats it as a genre in its own right, eclectic by design, which absorbed rāga, folk, devotional, theatrical and foreign music into a form that every Indian could recognise (Ranade 2006).

The music director composed the songs, often from a mixture of rāga, folk and devotional melody and Western popular music, while arrangers, many of them Goan musicians trained in Western music, wrote the orchestral parts for large studio ensembles of violins, mandolins, accordions, Indian instruments and later electronic keyboards. Gregory Booth’s study of the Bombay studio musicians describes this world of composers, arrangers and players and the division of labour that produced the Hindi film song (Booth 2008). Among the most celebrated composers of the Hindi cinema were Naushad, S. D. Burman, Shankar–Jaikishan, C. Ramchandra, Madan Mohan, Salil Chowdhury and R. D. Burman; among its singers Lata Mangeshkar (1929–2022), Mohammed Rafi (1924–1980), Kishore Kumar, Mukesh and Asha Bhosle. Classical musicians also worked for the cinema: in Baiju Bawra (1952), a film about a legendary rival of Tānsen, Naushad set songs in classical rāgas and used the voices of D. V. Paluskar and Amir Khan; Bade Ghulam Ali Khan sang for Mughal-e-Azam (1960); and Ravi Shankar wrote the music for Satyajit Ray’s first films. In the south, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam cinema developed their own traditions, from the singer-actor M. K. Thyagaraja Bhagavathar and the composers G. Ramanathan and K. V. Mahadevan to the partnership of M. S. Viswanathan and T. K. Ramamoorthy, Ilaiyaraaja, who from 1976 combined Tamil folk music with Western orchestral writing, and A. R. Rahman, whose work from the 1990s reached audiences throughout India and abroad.

Film dance drew on Kathak, Bharatanāṭyam, folk dance and, increasingly, global popular dance, and its choreographers created a hybrid idiom of their own. Anna Morcom’s study shows how film songs function within their films — as expressions of feeling, as dreams, as performances within the story — and how they circulate beyond them in radio, recordings and live performance (Morcom 2007). Film gave employment to many musicians and dancers trained in classical and hereditary traditions, and dancer-actresses such as Vyjayanthimala and Hema Malini were trained classical dancers. It also carried forward, often in stereotyped form, the figure of the courtesan dancer that the classical revival had tried to leave behind, and it offered work to professional women performers excluded from the respectable classical world, a history explored in Morcom’s study of “illicit” dance (Morcom 2013).

docs.title: 23.2.5 Television and the internet
docs.text: National television (Doordarshan, from 1959, expanding greatly from the 1980s) broadcast classical music and dance programmes as part of its public service; private television from the 1990s turned instead to film-based entertainment and talent contests. The internet and social media have made vast archives of recordings available, allowed teachers to teach students on other continents, and created new audiences and new forms of self-presentation for performers; they have also intensified competition for attention and reduced income from recordings. During the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020–21, when live performance stopped, online concerts and classes became a lifeline for many artists, and the crisis exposed the economic precariousness of most performers.

docs.title: 23.2.6 Archives
docs.text: Archives of recorded sound and film, among them the archives of All India Radio and the Sangeet Natak Akademi, the Archives and Research Centre for Ethnomusicology of the American Institute of Indian Studies, and many private collections, preserve a large part of the twentieth century’s music and dance. For the reader who wants to listen, they are the best starting point: the archive of All India Radio holds broadcasts of almost every important musician of the century, the Archives and Research Centre for Ethnomusicology holds field recordings of folk, tribal and ritual music from across the subcontinent, and Kinnear’s discography identifies the earliest commercial records, from Gauhar Jan onwards, some of which have since been reissued (Kinnear 1994). Digital recording cannot replace the embodied transmission from teacher to student on which the arts depend — a point every performer makes — but it has changed how students learn, how artists measure themselves against the past, and how scholars study the history of performance.

docs.title: 23.3.1 Dancers and musicians on the world stage
docs.text:
Indian performers have travelled abroad since the nineteenth century, but the international career of Indian dance began in earnest in the 1920s and 1930s. Uday Shankar (1900–1977), who partnered the ballerina Anna Pavlova and then founded his own company in Paris in 1931, created a theatrical dance that drew freely on classical and folk forms; his school at Almora (1938–1944) and his film Kalpana (1948) influenced a generation of Indian dancers, and Prarthana Purkayastha has placed his work in the history of Indian modern dance (Purkayastha 2014). Ram Gopal, Menaka and others toured Europe and America in the same period.

In music, the decisive figure was Ravi Shankar, whose tours from the 1950s, his collaborations with the violinist Yehudi Menuhin and his teaching of George Harrison of the Beatles made the sitār and Hindustani music known to audiences worldwide in the 1960s; he performed at the Monterey and Woodstock festivals and organised the Concert for Bangladesh (1971). Ali Akbar Khan founded a college of music in California in 1967. Gerry Farrell and Peter Lavezzoli have described the encounter of Indian music with Western classical, jazz and popular music, from the “raga rock” of the 1960s to the collaboration of the guitarist John McLaughlin with Zakir Hussain, L. Shankar and T. H. Vinayakram in the group Shakti (from 1975) (Farrell 1997; Lavezzoli 2006). These encounters were often unequal — Western musicians borrowed Indian sounds as exotic colour — but they also created lasting exchanges.

docs.title: 23.3.2 Diaspora communities
docs.text: The South Asian diaspora in Britain, North America, the Gulf, South-east Asia, Africa, the Caribbean and Australia has created its own institutions of music and dance: schools, temples and community halls where classical music and dance are taught, festivals such as the Tyāgarāja Ārādhana of Cleveland (Chapter 8), and a large professional class of teachers. For many families, learning Bharatanāṭyam or Karnatak music is a way of transmitting identity across generations; the araṅgēṯṯam has become a major rite of passage (Chapter 15). Janet O’Shea’s study of Bharatanāṭyam on the global stage shows how diaspora dancers have shaped the form, and how its meanings shift between Chennai, Toronto and London (O’Shea 2007). In Britain, choreographers such as Shobana Jeyasingh and Akram Khan have used Indian classical training to create contemporary dance recognised in the mainstream of British culture.

docs.title: 23.4.1 Dance
docs.text: Indian contemporary dance has grown from two roots: the modern dance of Uday Shankar and his successors, and the work of classically trained dancers who sought new forms. The most influential figure of the second group was Chandralekha (1928–2006), whose critique of the classical forms is described in Chapter 13 (Bharucha 1995). Kumudini Lakhia in Ahmedabad broke Kathak away from the solo format and the conventional themes of love and devotion; Astad Deboo (1947–2020) developed a contemporary solo style drawing on Kathak and Kathakaḷi; Daksha Sheth, Mallika Sarabhai, Aditi Mangaldas and many others have created new work, and institutions such as Attakkalari in Bengaluru have trained contemporary dancers. Ketu Katrak’s survey of contemporary Indian dance in India and the diaspora describes how choreographers address gender, caste, sexuality, the environment and the nation (Katrak 2011). Within the classical forms, dancers such as Alarmel Valli, Malavika Sarukkai, Madhavi Mudgal and Leela Samson have explored new interpretations and new poetry while working within the classical vocabulary.

docs.title: 23.4.2 Music
docs.text: Classical musicians have also experimented: with orchestral settings (Ravi Shankar’s sitār concertos), with collaborations between Hindustani and Karnatak musicians (jugalbandī), with Western classical, jazz and electronic musicians, and with new instruments adapted to Indian music, such as the slide guitar of Vishwa Mohan Bhatt and the mandolin of U. Srinivas. The boundary between “classical” and “fusion” is contested, and the market for fusion has grown much faster than that for classical concerts. At the same time, there has been a revival of interest in older and rarer forms — dhrupad, the rudra vīṇā, the padam and jāvaḷi of the hereditary dancers — and in the history of the communities who created them.

docs.title: 23.4.3 Popular music beyond film
docs.text: Film song dominated Indian popular music for most of the twentieth century, but it was never the only popular music, and its dominance has weakened since the 1980s. The cassette boom created large markets for devotional music, regional popular songs — Bhojpuri, Punjabi, Garhwali, Rajasthani and many more — and ghazal, often sung by performers who had no connection with cinema (Manuel 1993). Punjabi bhāṅgṛā, transformed in the British Punjabi diaspora of the 1980s into a dance music that combined the ḍhol with electronic beats, travelled back to India and became one of the most popular musics of the subcontinent. Independent rock, pop, electronic and hip-hop scenes have grown in Indian cities since the 1990s, and in the twenty-first century hip-hop in particular has given young people from working-class, Dalit, Ādivāsī and minority communities a medium in which to speak about caste, religion, migration and urban life in their own languages. These musics are often ignored in surveys of “Indian” music, but for most young Indians they are the music of everyday life, and many of their performers draw consciously on folk, devotional and classical sources.

docs.title: 23.4.4 A shared subcontinental heritage
docs.text: The traditions described in this volume do not belong to the Republic of India alone. Hindustani music, Kathak, qawwālī and ghazal are equally the heritage of Pakistan; the Bāul songs, Rabīndrasaṅgīt and much of the music of Bengal belong also to Bangladesh; Karnatak music and Bharatanāṭyam are central to the culture of the Tamils of Sri Lanka; and Nepal has its own traditions of court, temple and folk music, closely linked with those of north India. After 1947 the arts in each country developed under different conditions: in Pakistan, official ambivalence towards dance and some forms of music in certain periods coexisted with the global success of qawwālī and of popular musicians; in Bangladesh, music and dance became central to a Bengali national identity forged in the language movement and the war of 1971. Musicians and dancers continue to cross borders, and a history of the performing arts of South Asia written from any one national point of view is necessarily incomplete (Farrell 1997; Qureshi 1986).

docs.title: 23.5 Music, Dance and Therapy
docs.text:
Practitioners in India and abroad have developed forms of music therapy and dance movement therapy that draw on Indian music and dance — working, for example, with children with disabilities, survivors of trauma and elderly people — and the subject is increasingly discussed in professional and academic settings. At the same time, popular literature makes much larger claims: that particular rāgas cure particular diseases, that hand gestures balance the body’s energies, that dance practice reverses illness (Chapters 4 and 14).

Health and Safety Note

Recognised music and dance movement therapies, practised by trained therapists, can support the care of patients, but the claims that particular rāgas, mudrās or dances cure specific diseases are not supported by good evidence (Sections 4.13 and 14.11); claims attributed to named research institutions are often impossible to trace.

docs.title: 23.6 Caste, Gender and Livelihood
docs.text:
The histories in this volume show that the modern classical arts were built, in large part, on the knowledge of hereditary communities — devadāsīs, courtesans, naṭṭuvaṉārs, nāgasvaram players, Muslim kalāwants and mirāsīs — many of whom were marginalised in the process, while middle-class and upper-caste performers became the public face of the arts. In recent years these histories have been widely discussed. Scholars such as Amrit Srinivasan, Davesh Soneji, Janaki Bakhle and Lakshmi Subramanian, and performers such as T. M. Krishna, have argued that the classical arts must acknowledge their debts and open themselves to those excluded; Dalit artists have reclaimed instruments and forms associated with stigma, such as the paṟai drum, as arts of pride; and descendants of hereditary performers have begun to tell their own stories (Soneji 2012; Bakhle 2005; Krishna 2013).

Gender remains a central issue. Women dominate the classical dance forms as performers but were long excluded from many instruments, from the roles of conductor and teacher in some traditions, and from the all-male theatres; in Kathakaḷi, Kūṭiyāṭṭam and Sattriya women’s participation is recent and still debated. Male dancers have had to justify their presence in arts now seen as feminine (Chapter 13). And for almost all performers, regardless of community or gender, livelihoods are precarious: the market rewards a few stars, while most musicians, dancers and actors depend on teaching, irregular engagements and modest state support.

docs.title: 23.7 Education
docs.text: How the performing arts are taught has changed as much as where they are performed. This section first describes learning in the teacher’s household, then outlines the institutional history of music and dance education, and then turns to the present.

docs.title: 23.7.1 Learning from a master
docs.text:
Before the schools, and alongside them still, the arts were learnt in the teacher’s household (Section 1.5). Daniel Neuman’s study of Hindustani musicians in Delhi describes the older pattern as both a pedagogy and a social system (Neuman 1980). A disciple was formally accepted in a ceremony in which the teacher tied a thread on the pupil’s wrist (gaṇḍā bandhan) before witnesses, and the pupil offered gifts and sweets; from that moment the disciple owed the teacher service and loyalty, and the teacher owed the disciple knowledge, though how much and how fast was for the teacher to decide. Teaching was oral and direct — “from breast to breast” (sīna-ba-sīna), in the Persian phrase musicians use — and proceeded by the endless repetition of exercises, of a few rāgas and of compositions memorised phrase by phrase, with little explanation. Hereditary teachers often withheld their most valued compositions and techniques from pupils outside the family, and the stories musicians tell of their training are full of years of service, sudden revelations and knowledge gained by listening at the door.

The pupil’s own practice (riyāz) was expected to occupy many hours a day, and some musicians undertook a chillā, a period of forty days of solitary, intensive practice adapted from Sufi discipline. The regimen of Allauddin Khan at Maihar, whose pupils describe practice from before dawn and a teacher of great severity, became the emblem of this ideal (Chapter 7). In the south the corresponding ideal was gurukulavāsa, residence in the teacher’s house, in which the pupil learnt by accompanying the teacher to concerts and absorbing the repertoire over years (Section 8.8); dance was taught in the same way by the naṭṭuvaṉārs and Kathak masters, in the households of the hereditary families (Chapters 15 and 16).

The older pattern combined great strengths and real costs. It produced musicians who carried a repertoire and a style in their bodies, with a depth that the classroom rarely matches, and it bound teachers and pupils in relationships that often lasted a lifetime. It also excluded most people: outsiders, women of respectable families, and those who could not afford years of unpaid service. When middle-class pupils began to seek out hereditary teachers in the late nineteenth century, the terms of the relationship were renegotiated — fees replaced service, notation supplemented memory — and the reformers’ schools, described next, offered an alternative that did not require entering a musician’s household at all (Neuman 1980; Bakhle 2005).

docs.title: 23.7.2 An institutional history
docs.text:
The idea that music and dance could be taught in schools, to anyone who enrolled, rather than within hereditary families and households, is little more than a century old in India. One of the first institutions was the music school (gāyanśālā) founded in 1886 at Baroda by Sayajirao Gaekwad III under the court musician Maula Bakhsh, which taught music to pupils from outside the hereditary families with the help of a notation and graded lessons; Janaki Bakhle has shown how the Baroda court anticipated many of the reforms of the following decades (Bakhle 2005). V. D. Paluskar’s Gandharva Mahavidyalaya, founded in Lahore in 1901 and moved to Bombay in 1908, trained teachers who spread his schools and his devotional repertoire across north and west India, and the examinations of the Akhil Bharatiya Gandharva Mahavidyalaya Mandal, founded in 1931, became a standard qualification. V. N. Bhatkhande helped to found the Madhav Music College at Gwalior (1918) and the Marris College of Music at Lucknow (1926), later renamed after him, whose syllabus and notated textbooks were adopted by schools throughout the north; the Prayag Sangit Samiti of Allahabad, founded in 1926, conducted graded examinations that became, with those of the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya Mandal, the commonest qualification of north Indian music students.

In the south, the Music Academy of Madras ran a teachers’ college, the University of Madras established a department of Indian music in which the musicologist P. Sambamoorthy taught from the late 1930s, and the government of Madras founded a college of Karnatak music in 1949. For dance, Kalakshetra (1936) and the Kerala Kalamandalam (1930) became the model institutions (Chapters 15 and 18), and Tagore’s Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan taught music and dance, including Manipuri and the Bengali song traditions, within a liberal education. After Independence music and dance entered the universities: the Banaras Hindu University opened a college of music and fine arts in 1950 under the singer Omkarnath Thakur; the Baroda school became part of the Maharaja Sayajirao University; the Indira Kala Sangit Vishwavidyalaya at Khairagarh (1956) and the Rabindra Bharati University at Calcutta (1962) were founded as universities of the arts; and departments of music, dance and theatre spread to universities across India and the diaspora (Bakhle 2005; Weidman 2006).

These institutions made the arts available to many thousands of students, especially girls and young women from middle-class families, and gave teachers salaried employment. They also standardised what was taught — a syllabus of rāgas, compositions and items, an examination system, a theory drawn largely from Bhatkhande and the textbooks — and they tended to produce knowledgeable teachers and listeners rather than performers. Most performers of the twentieth century continued to learn, at least at the advanced stage, from a single teacher in the older way, and some later institutions, such as the ITC Sangeet Research Academy in Kolkata (1977), tried to combine the residential discipleship of the guru–śiṣya relationship with institutional support. The tension between the two models of learning, which Neuman, Bakhle and Weidman have each described, remains unresolved (Neuman 1980; Bakhle 2005; Weidman 2006).

docs.title: 23.7.3 Education today
docs.text: The arts are taught today in many settings: in the homes of teachers, in private schools and academies, in government institutions, in schools and universities, and online. University programmes have created qualifications, research and secure employment for teachers, but have also raised questions about whether the long, intensive apprenticeship of the traditional teacher–student relationship can be reproduced within an academic timetable. The National Education Policy of 2020 recommends integrating the arts, including India’s own traditions, into the school curriculum at all stages and treating them as part of the core of education rather than as extracurricular activities; how far this can be realised depends on the training and employment of qualified teachers and on the resources given to schools. Any such teaching will be most valuable if it presents the arts with their full and complex histories, as this volume has tried to do, rather than as an unchanging heritage.

docs.title: 23.8 UNESCO and Intangible Heritage
docs.text:
UNESCO’s programme for the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, launched with the proclamation of “Masterpieces” in 2001 and formalised by the Convention of 2003, has recognised several Indian performing traditions (Table 23.1). Inscription brings international attention and sometimes resources; it can also freeze traditions into “heritage” and shift authority from communities to experts and governments.

Table 23.1. Indian performing traditions on UNESCO’s lists of the Intangible Cultural Heritage (year of proclamation or inscription) Tradition Year Chapter Kūṭiyāṭṭam, Sanskrit theatre of Kerala 2001 19 Tradition of Vedic chanting 2003 4 Rāmlīlā, the traditional performance of the Rāmāyaṇa 2005 20 Rammaṇ, religious festival and ritual theatre of Garhwal 2009 21 Chhau dance 2010 21 Kālbeliyā folk songs and dances of Rajasthan 2010 21 Muḍiyēṯṯu, ritual theatre and dance drama of Kerala 2010 21 Buddhist chanting of Ladakh 2012 21 Saṅkīrtana, ritual singing, drumming and dancing of Manipur 2013 18 Garbā of Gujarat 2023 21

docs.title: 23.9 Concluding Reflections
docs.text:
This volume began with the Nāṭyaśāstra’s claim that drama contains every kind of knowledge, art and discipline. Its chapters have shown how wide the performing arts of India are — from the theory of rasa and the mathematics of tāla to the drum dances of Manipur and the possession rituals of Kerala — and how much their histories have been shaped by the people who practised them, the patrons who supported them and the societies in which they lived. They have also shown that much of what is now called “tradition” was made, or remade, in the last two centuries, often at the expense of the communities whose art it was.

Recognising this is not a reason to value the arts less. The rāgas, tālas, dances and plays described here are among the great achievements of human culture, and their survival through so many changes is evidence of their power. But it is a reason to study them honestly: to give credit to all who made them, Hindu and Muslim, Brahmin and Dalit, men and women, court and village; to distinguish history from legend; and to see the arts not as a fixed inheritance to be preserved unchanged but as living practices that each generation receives, questions and renews.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On the modern history of music see Bakhle (2005), Subramanian (2006) and Weidman (2006); on recording, radio and film, Kinnear (1994), Farrell (1993), Sampath (2010), Hughes (2007), Lelyveld (1994), Rahaim (2011), Huacuja Alonso (2023), Manuel (1993), Morcom (2007), Booth (2008), Majumdar (2009) and Ranade (2006); on Indian music abroad, Farrell (1997) and Lavezzoli (2006). For modern and contemporary dance see Purkayastha (2014), Katrak (2011), Bharucha (1995) and O’Shea (2007), and for modern theatre Dharwadker (2005). Morcom (2013) and Soneji (2012) discuss the performers excluded from the classical arts.

In Kūṭiyāṭṭam, the retrospective narration in gesture of the events leading up to an act nṛtta Pure dance, without representational meaning nṛtya Expressive dance, interpreting words and emotions ojāpāli (As.) Assamese narrative performance by a leader (ojā) and a chorus with cymbals (pāli) (Ch. 22) padam (Ta., Te.) Slow love song interpreted through abhinaya pakhāvaj (Hi.) The double-headed barrel drum of dhrupad, havelī saṅgīt and Kathak (Ch. 10) pallavi (Te., Ta.) The refrain and first section of a kṛti; also the single composed line of a rāgam–tānam–pallavi (Ch. 8) paṇ (Ta.) Melodic mode of early Tamil music and of the Tēvāram hymns pena (Mn.) Meitei fiddle with a coconut-shell body and a bow hung with bells, played in the Lai Haraoba prabandha Composed song with text and tāla, as described in the medieval treatises prasaṅga (Ka.) The sung text of a Yakṣagāna play pūrvaraṅga The ritual preliminaries before a Sanskrit play qawwālī (Ur.) Devotional song of the Sufi assemblies of South Asia, especially the Chishtī order Rabīndrasaṅgīt (Be.) The songs of Rabindranath Tagore, words and music (Ch. 11) rāga Melodic framework defined by notes, characteristic phrases, ornaments and mood rāgamālā “Garland of rāgas”: series of paintings or verses personifying rāgas raṅgapīṭha, raṅgaśīrṣa The front and rear parts of the stage in the playhouse of the Nāṭyaśāstra (Ch. 2) rasa Aesthetic experience, the “taste” of an emotion as savoured by the spectator rūpaka Drama; the ten major types (daśarūpaka) of Sanskrit theory sahṛdaya “Of like heart”: the sensitive, cultivated spectator sam (Hi.) First and principal beat of a tāla cycle samāʿ (Ar.) “Listening”: Sufi assembly for music and devotion saṃvādī (Hi.) See vādī saṃyuta hasta Combined (two-hand) gesture sañcāribhāva Transitory emotional state; also vyabhicāribhāva; thirty-three in the Nāṭyaśāstra saṅgīta Music; in the treatises, song, instrumental music and dance together sattra (As.) Vaiṣṇava monastery of Assam, home of Sattriya dance sopāna saṅgītam (Mal.) Kerala temple singing beside the steps of the sanctum, chiefly of the Gītagovinda, with the iṭakka drum soz (Ur.) Lament sung without instruments to a rāga-based melody in the Shia majlis śruti Microtonal interval; the ancient system divides the octave into twenty-two unequal śrutis sthāyī, antarā (Hi.) The first and second parts of a Hindustani composition, the second rising to the upper tonic (Ch. 7) sthāyibhāva Durable or dominant emotion; eight in the Nāṭyaśāstra sūfiyāna kalām (Ks.) The Sufi art music of Kashmir, sung in maqāms with santūr, sehtār and sāz (Ch. 22) sugam saṅgīt (Hi.), sugama saṅgīta (Ka.) “Light music”: the modern lyric song as a radio and concert genre (Ch. 11) svara Note; the seven are ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama, dhaivata, niṣāda (sa ri ga ma pa dha ni) svarūp (Hi.) “Own form”: a boy actor of the Rāmlīlā or Rāslīlā regarded, while in costume, as an embodiment of the deity tablā (Hi.) The pair of hand drums of Hindustani music, the wooden dāyāṃ and the metal or clay bāyāṃ (Ch. 10) tāla Rhythmic cycle; the theory of musical time tālī (Hi.) A clap marking a section of a Hindustani tāla; cf. khālī tān (Hi.) A rapid melodic run in khayāl and instrumental music (Ch. 7) tāṇḍava The vigorous style of dance, associated with Śiva tani āvartanam (Ta.) The percussion solo of a Karnatak concert (Ch. 5) tatkār (Hi.) Rhythmic footwork of Kathak ṭawāʾif (Ur.) Courtesan; professional woman singer and dancer of north India Terukkūttu (Ta.) The all-night street theatre of northern Tamil Nadu, associated with the cult of Draupadī (Ch. 20) teyyam (Mal.) Ritual performance of northern Kerala in which the performer becomes the deity (Ch. 21) thāṭ (Hi.) Parent scale; Bhatkhande classified Hindustani rāgas under ten ṭhekā (Hi.) The basic drum pattern that identifies a Hindustani tāla ṭhumrī (Hi.) Light-classical song genre of 19th-century Lucknow, interpreted in Kathak tihāī (Hi.) Phrase repeated three times to end on the sam tillāna (Te., Ta.) A brilliant composition of rhythmic syllables, the closing item of pure dance in the southern recital (Ch. 15) tīrmāṉam (Ta.) A cadence, usually stated three times, that closes a passage of pure dance (Ch. 13) tribhaṅga “Three bends”: posture bending at neck, waist and knee, characteristic of Odissi uparūpaka “Minor” dramatic type; many were forms of dance and song (Ch. 19) vādī, saṃvādī (Hi.) The predominant note of a Hindustani rāga and the second, consonant note, usually a fourth or fifth from it (Ch. 4) vāggeyakāra Composer of both words and music, as described in the Saṅgītaratnākara vārī (Mr.) The Vārkarī pilgrimage on foot to Pandharpur, made with singing varṇam (Ta., Te.) Central, longest item of a Bharatanāṭyam recital; also a Karnatak study piece vibhāva “Determinant”: the cause or stimulus of an emotion vidūṣaka The Brahmin jester of Sanskrit drama, most fully developed in Kūṭiyāṭṭam (Ch. 19) vīṇā (1) Ancient name for stringed instruments, including harps; (2) the stick zither (bīn) of north India; (3) the long-necked lute (Sarasvatī vīṇā) of south India vṛtti Dramatic style: verbal, grand, graceful and energetic Yakṣagāna (Ka.) The night-long dance-drama of coastal and southern Karnataka (Ch. 20) zikir (As., from Ar.) Assamese Muslim devotional songs ascribed by tradition to Azan Fakir (Ch. 22)
